Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: What does the term 'potable' water mean?
o: Water that has been abstracted but not yet treated at all
Water that is only suitable for industrial cooling processes
Water that has been stored in a service reservoir overnight
Water that is safe and wholesome for people to drink
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Potable water is defined as water that is fit and safe for human consumption.

n.0: Raw untreated water is not potable until it has been treated.
n.1: Water for cooling need not meet drinking-water standards.
n.2: Simply being stored does not by itself make water potable.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: The word 'wholesome' when applied to drinking water most closely means water that is:
o: Clear in appearance but not tested for any contamination
Safe to drink and meets the required quality standards
Warm enough to be comfortable for a person to drink
Taken directly from a natural spring without treatment
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Wholesome water meets legal quality standards and is safe to drink.

n.0: Appearance alone does not confirm the water is wholesome.
n.2: Temperature comfort is unrelated to wholesomeness.
n.3: Untreated spring water is not automatically wholesome.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of the following best describes drinking (potable) water?
o: It is free from harmful organisms and dangerous substances
It has a strong chlorine taste that most consumers would clearly notice
It is any water that comes out of a customer's tap
It is water that has simply been filtered through gravel
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Potable water must be free of harmful microbes and chemicals.

n.1: A strong taste is not a definition of potable water.
n.2: Water at a tap can be contaminated and so not potable.
n.3: Basic filtration alone does not guarantee potability.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: For water to be considered potable, it must be free from:
o: Harmful micro-organisms and hazardous chemical substances
Any dissolved minerals of any kind whatsoever
The removal of all colour, even where that colour is entirely natural
Every trace of chlorine used during the treatment
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Potable water must contain no harmful microbes or dangerous chemicals.

n.1: Safe drinking water can and does contain harmless minerals.
n.2: Natural harmless colour does not make water non-potable.
n.3: A safe chlorine residual is expected in potable water.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A member of the public asks you what 'drinking water quality' means. The most accurate answer is that the water is:
o: Cheap to produce because little treatment has been applied
Bottled at source and sold rather than piped to homes
Wholesome and safe, meeting the standards set for human consumption
Coloured slightly so that people can see it is treated
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Drinking-water quality means water is wholesome and meets the standards.

n.0: Cost of treatment is not what quality means.
n.1: Being bottled has nothing to do with the meaning of quality.
n.3: Water is not deliberately coloured to show treatment.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Potable water is intended primarily for:
o: Flushing out sewers and clearing blocked public drains
Filling ornamental lakes and large public boating ponds
Cooling machinery inside factories and power stations
Drinking, cooking and other domestic uses by the public
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Potable water is supplied for drinking, cooking and domestic use.

n.0: Sewer flushing does not require potable-quality water.
n.1: Ornamental water bodies do not need potable water.
n.2: Industrial cooling does not need drinking-quality water.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which statement about wholesome drinking water is correct?
o: It must be completely free of every kind of naturally dissolved salt
It has to be chilled before it can be given to the public
It only has to look clean when poured into a clear glass
It should not put the health of the person drinking it at risk
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Wholesome water must not endanger the health of the consumer.

n.0: Harmless dissolved salts are acceptable in wholesome water.
n.1: Chilling is not a requirement for wholesome water.
n.2: Clean appearance does not prove the water is wholesome.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: On a job you hear a colleague call the mains supply 'potable'. This tells you the water is:
o: Only safe once it has been boiled first
Suitable purely for washing down vehicles
Fit and safe for the public to drink
Fine for gardens but not for the kitchen
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Calling water potable means it is fit and safe for the public to drink.

n.0: Potable water is safe to drink without boiling.
n.1: Potable water exceeds what is needed to wash vehicles.
n.3: Potable water is suitable for kitchen use, not only gardens.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of these is NOT a requirement for water to be classed as potable?
o: That it is free from harmful bacteria as well as any other pathogens
That it does not contain dangerous levels of chemicals
That it has been kept cold throughout its journey to the tap
That it is wholesome and safe for people to consume
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Being kept cold is not a requirement for potable water.

n.0: Freedom from pathogens is a genuine requirement.
n.1: Safe chemical levels are a genuine requirement.
n.3: Being wholesome and safe is a genuine requirement.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: The public water supply that you work on is required by law to be:
o: Softened so that it never leaves any limescale
Wholesome and safe for consumers to drink
Perfectly still with no dissolved oxygen at all
Free of every mineral that gives water its taste
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Public supplies must legally be wholesome and safe to drink.

n.0: Softness is not a legal requirement for potability.
n.2: Dissolved oxygen does not stop water being potable.
n.3: Harmless taste-giving minerals are allowed in supplies.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: 'Wholesome' water is best summarised as water that is:
o: Clean, safe and does not harm the health of consumers
Rich in extra minerals added deliberately for flavour
Sourced only from deep boreholes rather than rivers
Guaranteed to stay fresh for years once it is bottled
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Wholesome water is clean, safe and harmless to health.

n.1: Wholesome water is not defined by added flavour minerals.
n.2: Wholesomeness does not depend on the type of source.
n.3: Long shelf life is not part of the meaning of wholesome.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which best explains why treated mains water is described as 'safe to drink'?
o: It has been passed once through a simple mesh screen
Harmful organisms and substances have been removed or controlled
It has been left standing so that dirt sinks to the base
It has been warmed to make any bad taste go away
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: It is safe because harmful organisms and substances are controlled.

n.0: A single mesh screen does not make water safe to drink.
n.2: Settling alone does not make water safe to drink.
n.3: Warming does not make contaminated water safe.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A householder asks if their tap water is 'drinkable'. Assuming it is a normal mains supply, the correct meaning of drinkable is that it is:
o: Merely clear enough to see through in a glass
Only usable for making hot drinks and not cold
Safe just for adults but never for children
Potable, meaning safe and wholesome to drink
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Drinkable mains water means potable: safe and wholesome to drink.

n.0: Clarity alone does not make water drinkable.
n.1: Potable water is fine cold as well as hot.
n.2: Potable water is safe for children as well as adults.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of the following waters would NOT normally be described as potable?
o: Treated water leaving a water treatment works
Wholesome water stored in a covered service reservoir
Safe drinking water delivered to a customer's tap
Raw river water that has not yet been treated
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Untreated raw river water is not potable.

n.0: Properly treated works water is potable.
n.1: Wholesome reservoir water is potable.
n.2: Safe water at the customer's tap is potable.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why is contamination of the public drinking water supply treated as a public-health emergency?
o: Because it always makes the water turn a bright colour
Because it can quickly make very large numbers of people ill
Because it slightly increases the cost shown on the water bill each year
Because it makes the pipes a little noisier than usual
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Contaminated mains water can rapidly cause illness in many people.

n.0: Contamination is often invisible, not brightly coloured.
n.2: Cost is not why contamination is an emergency.
n.3: Noisy pipes are unrelated to a public-health emergency.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A single contamination incident on a large water main is dangerous mainly because:
o: It usually only affects the operative who actually caused it
It merely changes the taste for a few minutes
Thousands of consumers could receive the unsafe water
It slows the flow of water for a short time
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: One incident can send unsafe water to thousands of consumers.

n.0: The risk is to the public, not just the operative.
n.1: The concern is illness, not a brief taste change.
n.3: Reduced flow is not the main danger of contamination.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: What is one of the most serious consequences of a drinking-water contamination event?
o: A short delay in reading customers' water meters
A small rise in the hardness of the water
A minor change to the colour of the pipework
A widespread outbreak of illness among consumers
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: A major consequence is a widespread outbreak of illness.

n.0: Meter reading delays are not a serious consequence.
n.1: Water hardness change is not a serious consequence.
n.2: Pipe colour is not a serious consequence of contamination.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Besides making people ill, a serious contamination incident can also:
o: Permanently improve the taste of the tap water
Destroy public confidence in the safety of the supply
Reduce the amount of chlorine needed in future
Make the water flow faster through the mains
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Contamination can badly damage public confidence in the supply.

n.0: Contamination does not improve taste; it is a hazard.
n.2: It does not reduce future chlorine requirements.
n.3: Contamination does not usefully speed up flow.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why must operatives take contamination risks so seriously on the clean-water network?
o: Even a small mistake can affect the health of many people
Because mistakes only ever affect one single house
Because the water company will always spot it first
Because any contamination will clear itself within a few short hours
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: A small error can put many people's health at risk.

n.1: Mistakes can affect far more than one house.
n.2: You cannot rely on the mistake being spotted first.
n.3: Contamination does not reliably clear on its own.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A burst main is repaired but debris is left inside the pipe. The main public-health concern is that:
o: The repair will probably need repainting again within the year
Consumers could be supplied with contaminated water
The water pressure gauge may read slightly high
The road surface above may crack over time
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Debris left in a main risks supplying contaminated water.

n.0: Repainting is not a public-health concern.
n.2: A gauge reading is not the main health concern.
n.3: Road cracking is not the drinking-water concern.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: What makes drinking-water contamination especially hard for the public to protect themselves against?
o: The water usually turns a very obvious, noticeable green colour
The water always froths up strongly in the glass
The water can look, smell and taste completely normal
The water becomes far too hot for anyone to drink safely
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Contaminated water can appear normal, so people cannot tell.

n.0: Contaminated water is usually not obviously coloured.
n.1: Frothing is not a reliable sign of contamination.
n.3: Temperature is not how people detect contamination.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Contamination of a public supply is regarded as more serious than contamination of a private well because:
o: Public water is always stored for much longer
Private wells are never used for drinking water
Far more people rely on the public mains supply
Public water is only used for washing clothes
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Public mains serve far more people, so the impact is larger.

n.0: Storage time is not the reason it is more serious.
n.1: Private wells are used for drinking water too.
n.3: Public water is used for drinking, not just washing.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: On site you realise unclean water may have entered the main you are working on. Why is this urgent?
o: Because the unsafe water could reach and harm many consumers
Because the job will now take somewhat longer for the team to finish off
Because your tools may need a quick rinse afterwards
Because the paperwork will need an extra signature
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: It is urgent because unsafe water could harm many consumers.

n.1: A longer job is not why the situation is urgent.
n.2: Rinsing tools is not the urgent public-health issue.
n.3: Extra paperwork is not the urgent concern.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why can a drinking-water contamination outbreak spread illness so rapidly?
o: Illness only ever passes very slowly from one person to another
Many households drink the same supply at the same time
The chlorine speeds up how quickly germs multiply
People rarely drink any of the water that is supplied
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Shared supply means many people are exposed at once.

n.0: Waterborne outbreaks can spread far faster than that.
n.2: Chlorine controls germs; it does not speed them up.
n.3: People do drink the supplied water, spreading exposure.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of these outcomes shows why contamination is treated as an emergency, not a minor fault?
o: A single customer noticing a slightly odd smell
A brief drop in pressure at one property
Large numbers of people needing medical treatment
A small stain appearing on one kitchen sink
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Many people needing treatment shows it is an emergency.

n.0: One odd smell is not evidence of an emergency.
n.1: A short pressure drop at one home is minor.
n.3: A single small stain is not an emergency.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: If a contamination event undermines trust in tap water, a likely knock-on effect is that:
o: People will automatically choose to drink far more tap water
Water bills will fall for everyone across the whole area
The mains will clean themselves out more quickly
People may turn to less safe alternative water sources
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Lost trust can push people towards less safe alternatives.

n.0: Lost trust reduces, not increases, tap-water use.
n.1: Contamination does not reduce bills.
n.2: Trust has no effect on how mains clean themselves.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why is prevention of contamination considered better than dealing with an outbreak afterwards?
o: Because outbreaks are cheap and simple to clear up
Because illness from water is never actually serious
Because the public never find out about outbreaks
Once people are ill the harm has already been done
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Prevention matters because an outbreak already causes harm.

n.0: Outbreaks are costly and difficult, not simple.
n.1: Waterborne illness can be very serious.
n.2: The public do learn of outbreaks; secrecy is not the point.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of the following is a recognised waterborne disease?
o: Chickenpox
Tetanus
Influenza
Cholera
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Cholera is a classic waterborne disease spread through contaminated water.

n.0: Chickenpox spreads person to person, not through water.
n.1: Tetanus comes from wounds, not from drinking water.
n.2: Influenza is a respiratory illness, not waterborne.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Cholera is caused by which type of organism?
o: A virus that also causes the common cold
A bacterium called Vibrio cholerae
A parasite carried only by biting insects
A fungus that grows on damp pipe surfaces
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.

n.0: Cholera is bacterial, not a cold virus.
n.2: Cholera is not spread by biting insects.
n.3: Cholera is not caused by a fungus.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Typhoid fever is caused by which organism?
o: Vibrio cholerae, the organism behind cholera
Cryptosporidium, a protozoan parasite
Salmonella typhi
Hepatitis A, which is a viral infection
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi.

n.0: Vibrio cholerae causes cholera, not typhoid.
n.1: Cryptosporidium causes cryptosporidiosis, not typhoid.
n.3: Hepatitis A is a separate viral disease.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Cryptosporidiosis in drinking water is caused by:
o: A bacterium that is easily killed by chlorine
A protozoan parasite called Cryptosporidium
A common airborne virus spread by coughing
A mould that grows inside old lead pipes
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Cryptosporidiosis is caused by the protozoan Cryptosporidium.

n.0: Cryptosporidium is a resistant parasite, not that bacterium.
n.2: Cryptosporidiosis is not an airborne coughing virus.
n.3: It is not caused by mould in pipes.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of these diseases can be spread through contaminated drinking water?
o: Measles
Malaria
Dysentery
Shingles
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Dysentery is a waterborne disease linked to sewage-contaminated water.

n.0: Measles is spread through the air, not water.
n.1: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, not drinking water.
n.3: Shingles is a reactivation of a virus, not waterborne.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Hepatitis A is best described as a waterborne disease that is:
o: A bacterial infection that is caught from the bites of insects
A viral infection spread by the faecal–oral route
A fungal infection picked up from damp soil
A parasite that lives only in warm sea water
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Hepatitis A is a virus spread by the faecal–oral route.

n.0: Hepatitis A is viral and not insect-borne.
n.2: Hepatitis A is not a fungal soil infection.
n.3: Hepatitis A is a virus, not a sea-water parasite.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Giardiasis is caused by:
o: A protozoan parasite found in contaminated water
A bacterium closely related to typhoid
A virus that is very similar to the one causing hepatitis
A chemical that leaches from copper pipes
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Giardiasis is caused by the protozoan parasite Giardia.

n.1: Giardiasis is protozoan, not a typhoid bacterium.
n.2: Giardiasis is not caused by a virus.
n.3: Giardiasis is a parasite, not a chemical.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Campylobacter is an example of an organism that can cause:
o: A skin rash that appears only on the hands
A long-term loss of hearing in adults
Gastrointestinal illness such as diarrhoea
A weakening of the bones over many years
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Campylobacter causes gastrointestinal illness like diarrhoea.

n.0: Campylobacter causes gut illness, not a hand rash.
n.1: Campylobacter does not cause hearing loss.
n.3: Campylobacter does not cause bone weakening.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which statement about waterborne diseases is correct?
o: They are all caused by the water being too hard
Many are spread when sewage contaminates drinking water
They are only ever caught from swimming pools
They come mainly from breathing in water vapour
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Waterborne diseases largely spread via sewage in drinking water.

n.0: Hard water does not cause waterborne disease.
n.2: They are not limited to swimming pools.
n.3: Most are ingested, not breathed in as vapour.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Gastroenteritis linked to drinking water is typically caused by:
o: Bacteria, viruses or parasites from faecal contamination
A build-up of harmless minerals in the water
Drinking water that has simply been left standing for far too long
A slightly raised temperature in the supply pipe
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Waterborne gastroenteritis comes from faecal microbes.

n.1: Harmless minerals do not cause gastroenteritis.
n.2: Standing alone is not the direct cause of the illness.
n.3: A warm pipe alone does not cause the disease.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which group of illnesses are all recognised waterborne diseases?
o: Asthma, eczema and hay fever
Arthritis, diabetes and anaemia
Sunburn, frostbite and cramp
Cholera, typhoid and dysentery
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Cholera, typhoid and dysentery are all waterborne diseases.

n.0: These are allergic conditions, not waterborne diseases.
n.1: These are not waterborne infections.
n.2: These are physical conditions, not waterborne diseases.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A community suffers an outbreak of diarrhoea and vomiting traced to the water supply. The likely cause is:
o: The water having a slightly higher mineral content
Micro-organisms that entered the water from sewage
A minor change in the colour of the water
The water being supplied at a lower pressure
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Such outbreaks usually come from sewage micro-organisms.

n.0: Higher minerals do not cause such outbreaks.
n.2: A colour change does not cause diarrhoea and vomiting.
n.3: Low pressure alone does not cause the illness.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why are waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid so dangerous?
o: They only cause a very mild and brief headache
They can be cured simply by drinking more water
They can spread rapidly and make many people seriously ill
They affect just one household in any outbreak
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: They spread fast and can cause serious illness in many people.

n.0: These diseases are serious, not merely a mild headache.
n.1: Drinking more water does not cure these diseases.
n.3: Outbreaks can affect far more than one household.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of the following correctly pairs a disease with its cause?
o: Cholera is caused by Cryptosporidium
Giardiasis is caused by Vibrio cholerae
Hepatitis A is caused by Salmonella typhi
Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Typhoid is correctly caused by Salmonella typhi.

n.0: Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae, not Cryptosporidium.
n.1: Giardiasis is caused by Giardia, not Vibrio cholerae.
n.2: Hepatitis A is a virus, not caused by Salmonella typhi.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Waterborne diseases are mainly passed on when:
o: Water is stored inside a metal container for a whole day
Water travels a long way through the mains
Water is left a little warmer than is usual
Human or animal waste gets into the drinking water
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: They spread when faecal waste contaminates drinking water.

n.0: Storing in metal does not spread these diseases.
n.1: Distance travelled does not itself spread disease.
n.2: A little extra warmth alone does not spread them.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: What is the main source of the microbiological (germ) risk to drinking water?
o: Small amounts of completely harmless limescale sitting in the pipe
A very slight metallic taste from old fittings
Contamination of the water by sewage or faecal matter
Air bubbles that get trapped inside the mains
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Faecal or sewage contamination is the main microbiological risk.

n.0: Limescale is not a microbiological health risk.
n.1: A metallic taste is not the main germ risk.
n.3: Air bubbles are not a microbiological risk.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why is human sewage so dangerous if it enters a drinking-water main?
o: It makes the water slightly harder to pump along the main
It carries disease-causing organisms from the gut
It gives the water a faint blue tint over time
It cools the water down by a few degrees or so
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Sewage carries gut pathogens that cause disease.

n.0: Difficulty pumping is not the danger from sewage.
n.2: A tint is not why sewage is dangerous.
n.3: Cooling is not the hazard posed by sewage.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: The faecal–oral route means that disease is passed when:
o: Faecal matter from one person is swallowed by another
Two people simply shake hands in passing
A person breathes in air near a flowing river
Someone touches a clean and dry work surface
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: The faecal–oral route means swallowing another's faecal matter.

n.1: A handshake alone is not the faecal–oral route.
n.2: Breathing near a river is not the faecal–oral route.
n.3: Touching a clean dry surface is not the route.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: On a job you notice a foul smell and signs that a nearby sewer may be leaking close to your open trench. Your main concern for the water main should be:
o: The strong smell simply making the job unpleasant to work in for you
The extra time needed to backfill the trench
Sewage getting into the main and contaminating the supply
The trench walls possibly collapsing inwards
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: The concern is sewage entering and contaminating the main.

n.0: An unpleasant smell is not the main hygiene concern.
n.1: Backfill time is not the contamination concern.
n.3: Trench collapse is a safety issue, not the hygiene risk.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which of these poses the greatest microbiological threat to a clean-water supply?
o: A short section of pipe that is only slightly discoloured
Contact between the drinking water and sewage
A small amount of harmless grit in the water
A minor rise in the temperature of the water
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Contact with sewage is the greatest microbiological threat.

n.0: Discoloured pipe is not the greatest germ threat.
n.2: Harmless grit is not a major germ threat.
n.3: A small temperature rise is not the main germ threat.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why must drinking-water pipes and sewage pipes never be allowed to connect or leak into each other?
o: Sewage would contaminate the drinking water with pathogens
The two pipes are always made from the very same metal
Sewage pipes carry water at a much higher pressure
The drinking-water pipe would end up slightly colder than before
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: A connection would let sewage pathogens contaminate the water.

n.1: Pipe material is not why they must be kept apart.
n.2: Pressure is not the reason they must not connect.
n.3: Temperature is not the reason to keep them apart.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Faecal contamination of drinking water is dangerous chiefly because human waste contains:
o: A high level of completely harmless dissolved oxygen
Large numbers of harmful bacteria and other pathogens
Only small amounts of clean and perfectly safe rainwater
A useful mix of harmless, healthy drinking minerals
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Human waste contains many harmful bacteria and pathogens.

n.0: Dissolved oxygen is not why sewage is dangerous.
n.2: Sewage is not clean rainwater.
n.3: Sewage does not usefully add drinking minerals.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which situation is most likely to introduce faecal contamination into a water main?
o: Floodwater mixed with sewage entering an open pipe
A short spell of dry, warm summer weather
The water simply being pumped slightly faster than is normal
A new length of clean, capped pipe on the bank
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Sewage-laden floodwater entering an open pipe is a key route.

n.1: Dry warm weather does not add sewage to a main.
n.2: Faster pumping does not introduce faecal matter.
n.3: Clean capped pipe is not a contamination source.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: The presence of faecal contamination in a water sample indicates that:
o: The water has simply been standing for too long
Sewage or waste has got into the water supply
The pipes have a slightly rough inner surface
The water contains a little more chlorine than usual
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Faecal contamination shows sewage has entered the supply.

n.0: Standing alone does not mean faecal contamination.
n.2: Rough pipe surfaces are not faecal contamination.
n.3: Extra chlorine is not a sign of faecal contamination.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Why does keeping sewage away from the clean-water network protect public health?
o: It simply keeps the water at a more constant temperature throughout
It makes the water flow more quietly in the pipe
It stops the main source of disease-causing germs getting in
It reduces the amount of limescale in the pipe
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Excluding sewage blocks the main source of waterborne germs.

n.0: Temperature control is not the public-health reason.
n.1: Quieter flow is not why sewage is excluded.
n.3: Limescale is not the reason to exclude sewage.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: A trench for a water pipe has filled with dirty, foul-smelling water. Before laying pipe you should be most concerned that:
o: The dirty water will simply make your boots muddy
The dirty water will only slow down the digging work
The dirty water could contaminate the new pipe with sewage
The dirty water might badly stain the outer coating of the pipe
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: The dirty water could carry sewage into the new pipe.

n.0: Muddy boots are not the contamination concern.
n.1: Slower digging is not a hygiene concern.
n.3: A stained coating is not the contamination risk.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which best explains why faecal matter is called the 'main' microbiological risk to drinking water?
o: It is the source of most disease-causing organisms in water
It is the only substance that ever discolours water
It is the heaviest material that can enter a pipe
It is the easiest contaminant for people to taste
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: Faecal matter supplies most of the pathogens found in water.

n.1: Faecal matter is not the only cause of discolouration.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant to why it is the main germ risk.
n.3: Faecal contamination is often undetectable by taste.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: If untreated sewage entered the mains, the most immediate danger to consumers would be:
o: Finding the water is a little cloudier than usual
Catching a waterborne disease from the pathogens present
Simply noticing that the water tastes slightly different today
Seeing the water pressure vary during the day
Why Water Hygiene Matters.w: The immediate danger is catching a waterborne disease.

n.0: Cloudiness is a symptom, not the main danger.
n.2: A taste change is not the main danger.
n.3: Varying pressure is not the disease danger.

Why Water Hygiene Matters.q: Which organism is commonly used as an indicator of faecal contamination in water?
o: Escherichia coli (E. coli)

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Weil's disease is carried in the urine of which animals?
o: Rats and other rodents that visit water and sewers
Foxes, badgers and other roaming wild mammals
Pigeons, gulls and other common town birds
Cattle, sheep and other grazing farm livestock
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Weil's disease (leptospirosis) is spread through the urine of rats and other rodents.

n.1: Weil's disease comes from rats' and rodents' urine, not foxes or badgers.
n.2: Birds are not the source; the bacteria are carried in rodent urine.
n.3: Farm livestock are not the recognised source; rats and rodents are.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: On a network job, where would you be most at risk of picking up Weil's disease?
o: On a dry, clean roadway well away from any water
Inside a locked, well-ventilated indoor plant room
On the flat roof of the treatment works building
In wet ground, standing water and sewers used by rats
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The risk is highest in water, wet ground and sewers where rats may have been.

n.0: Dry clean ground carries little risk; the danger is damp rat-contaminated places.
n.1: A clean indoor plant room is not the typical source of the infection.
n.2: Working at height on a roof is not where leptospira are found.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: The bacteria that cause Weil's disease usually get into water through what?
o: Rainwater running off from a clean building roof
Chlorine dosed into the main to disinfect it
Contamination by the urine of rats and other rodents
Rust flaking away from old cast-iron pipework
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Water becomes a risk when rats' or rodents' urine contaminates it.

n.0: Clean rainwater is not the source; rodent urine is.
n.1: Chlorine is a disinfectant, not a source of the disease.
n.3: Rust does not carry leptospira; contaminated urine does.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of the following is a recognised source of Weil's disease?
o: A clean, dry and well-heated site welfare cabin
Freshly chlorinated and flushed storage tanks
Sewers and other wet places frequented by rats
Sealed bottled drinking water from the shop
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Sewers and rat-frequented wet places are a recognised source of the disease.

n.0: A clean site cabin is not a source of leptospirosis.
n.1: Chlorinated water is disinfected and not a source.
n.3: Sealed bottled water is not contaminated with rodent urine.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why does standing water left in a trench pose a Weil's disease risk?
o: Rats may have urinated in or near it, contaminating the water
Standing water always gives off harmful chlorine gas
The water quickly lowers the oxygen in the trench
The cold of the water is itself what causes it
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Standing trench water may be contaminated by rodent urine and carry leptospira.

n.1: Standing water is not a chlorine hazard; it is a possible contamination hazard.
n.2: Low oxygen is a confined-space issue, not the cause of Weil's disease.
n.3: Cold water does not cause the infection; contamination by rodent urine does.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Weil's disease is another name for which infection?
o: Cryptosporidiosis, a parasite gut illness
Leptospirosis, spread by rodent urine
Legionellosis, linked to Legionella bacteria
Giardiasis, another waterborne gut bug
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Weil's disease is the common name for leptospirosis.

n.0: Cryptosporidiosis is a different, parasite-borne illness, not Weil's disease.
n.2: Legionellosis relates to Legionella, not to Weil's disease.
n.3: Giardiasis is a separate gut infection, not leptospirosis.

They only matter on the days you can actually see them
They present a real problem only in the summer months
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Rats matter because their urine can contaminate the water with leptospira.

n.2: Contamination is a risk whether or not the rats are visible.
n.3: The risk is present year-round wherever rodents contaminate water.

A tidy office used only for the site paperwork

n.3: An indoor office is not where rodent-contaminated water is found.

Only through being bitten directly by an infected rat

Only through the soles of a pair of intact rubber boots when out working on the water network

n.1: A bite is not the usual route; entry is through cuts and mucous membranes.
n.3: Intact boots protect you; the organism enters via broken skin and the face.

Because the risk exists only if that water happens to be warm
Because the organism can enter the body through the eyes

n.1: Swallowing is one route, but entry through the eyes is also a real risk.
n.2: Water temperature is not what makes the eye splash a risk.

n.1: A dry clean surface is not a route of entry into the body.
n.3: A hard hat protects the head and is not an entry point.

The nails on the ends of the fingers and toes
The hair growing on the head, arms and hands
The dry outer layer of clean, intact skin

n.2: Hair is not an entry point for the organism.
n.3: Dry intact skin acts as a barrier, not an entry point.

It could accidentally set off the site's confined-space alarm as part of the day's work out on site
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Dirty hands can carry leptospira into the body through the eyes and mouth.

n.3: Touching your face does not trigger gas or space alarms.

Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Covering the cut blocks a direct route for infection into the body.

n.3: Appearance is not the reason; protecting against infection is.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What are the typical early symptoms of Weil's disease?

Blurred vision that is quickly followed by dizziness
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Early Weil's disease is flu-like, with headache, fever and muscle pain.

n.1: A spreading chest rash is not the recognised early sign; flu-like symptoms are.
n.2: Hearing loss is not a listed symptom of Weil's disease.
n.3: Blurred vision alone is not the described early presentation.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: If left untreated, Weil's disease can progress to which serious conditions?
o: Broken bones together with dislocated joints
A permanent loss of the person's sense of smell
A slow but total loss of the person's eyesight
Jaundice and kidney or liver failure
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Untreated, it can progress to jaundice and kidney or liver failure.

n.0: It does not cause broken bones; it can cause organ failure.
n.1: Loss of smell is not a recognised progression of the disease.
n.2: Blindness is not the described serious outcome; organ failure is.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Weil's disease is taken very seriously because, in the worst cases, it can:
o: Cause a short, mild cold
Heal without any treatment
Cause only a mild headache
Prove fatal to the worker
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: In its most severe form Weil's disease can be fatal to the worker.

n.0: In severe cases it can be fatal, not merely a mild cold.
n.1: Severe cases need treatment and can be fatal if ignored.
n.2: At its worst it is far more serious than a headache; it can kill.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of the following best describes how Weil's disease usually first shows itself?
o: With immediate jaundice and a yellowing of the skin
With a painful and visibly swollen ankle and knee joint
With a persistent, dry and tickly cough and nothing else
Like a bout of flu, with headache, fever and aching muscles
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: It usually starts like flu, with headache, fever and aching muscles.

n.0: Jaundice is a later, more serious sign, not the usual first symptom.
n.1: Swollen joints are not the described early presentation.
n.2: A cough alone is not the recognised flu-like early presentation.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker gets a headache, fever and muscle pain a week after a wet chamber. What should they consider?
o: That it is simply ordinary tiredness and can be ignored
That they merely need to drink a lot more water than usual
That it could be early Weil's disease and needs a doctor
That it is certain to be an allergic reaction to their gloves
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Flu-like symptoms after wet work could be early Weil's disease and need a doctor.

n.0: Flu-like symptoms after wet work should not be brushed off as tiredness.
n.1: Rehydration alone is not the answer to possible Weil's disease.
n.3: A glove allergy would not explain fever and muscle pain after wet work.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) in someone who has done wet network work may signal:
o: Weil's disease that has become more serious
A harmless reaction of the skin to strong sunlight
Nothing more than simple dehydration in hot weather
A minor bout of eye strain from close-up work
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Jaundice can mean Weil's disease has progressed to a serious stage.

n.1: Jaundice is not a harmless suntan effect; it can signal serious illness.
n.2: Dehydration does not turn the skin and eyes yellow like jaundice.
n.3: Eye strain does not cause yellowing of the skin and eyes.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which statement about the symptoms of Weil's disease is correct?
o: Early symptoms are flu-like and easily mistaken for a minor illness
The symptoms only ever appear within the first hour
It causes no symptoms whatsoever right up until death
The very first sign of it is always a broken bone
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Its early symptoms are flu-like and can be mistaken for a minor illness.

n.1: Symptoms are not immediate; they develop over days and are flu-like at first.
n.2: It does cause symptoms, typically flu-like ones, before becoming severe.
n.3: Broken bones are not a symptom of the disease.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why can Weil's disease be dangerous to spot early?
o: Its early flu-like symptoms resemble an ordinary everyday illness
Because it produces no symptoms of any kind at all
Because it can only affect people over sixty years old
Because its symptoms only ever appear in the winter
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The early flu-like symptoms are easily mistaken for an ordinary illness.

n.1: It does have symptoms; the difficulty is they resemble ordinary flu.
n.2: Age is not the issue; the vague early symptoms are.
n.3: Symptoms are not season-limited; they mimic everyday illness.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why should a water or sewage worker carry a Weil's disease warning card?
o: So they are able to claim extra money for doing wet work
So a doctor knows they work with water and may have Weil's disease
So that they are permitted onto the worksite each morning
So they can jump ahead of others in the doctor's queue
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The card alerts a doctor to the water-work exposure so Weil's disease is considered.

n.0: The card is a medical warning, not a pay document.
n.2: The card is not a site access pass.
n.3: The card is to inform diagnosis, not to jump queues.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What should you tell any doctor treating you if you work with water or sewage?
o: That you would honestly rather not have any tests done
That your work exposes you to water and sewage, so Weil's disease is possible
That you have never once felt unwell before this moment
That you only ever work indoors in a clean, dry office
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Telling the doctor about water and sewage exposure helps them diagnose Weil's disease.

n.0: Withholding tests is unhelpful; you should flag the exposure risk.
n.2: Your past health is less important than flagging the exposure.
n.3: This would be untrue and would hide the real risk from the doctor.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A water worker feels feverish and shows the doctor their warning card. What is its purpose?
o: To alert the doctor to test for Weil's disease given the exposure
To prove that the worker holds a full and valid driving licence when working on the public water mains
To confirm the worker's correct National Insurance number
To show exactly which depot or site the worker is based at
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The card prompts the doctor to consider and test for Weil's disease.

n.1: The card concerns disease risk, not driving entitlement.
n.2: The card is a health warning, not an identity document.
n.3: The card is about medical risk, not site location.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: When should a water worker carry their Weil's disease warning card?
o: Only on the single day that they start a brand-new job
Only once they have already been diagnosed with the illness
At all times, so it is to hand if they fall ill
Only when they are working more than a mile from the depot
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: It should be carried at all times so it is available if illness strikes.

n.0: The card should be carried at all times, not just the first day.
n.1: The card is carried before any diagnosis so a doctor is alerted early.
n.3: Distance from base has nothing to do with carrying the card.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What key information does a Weil's disease warning card give to medical staff?
o: The holder's full blood group and any known drug allergies
The holder's next of kin and their emergency contact details
That the holder works with water or sewage and could have leptospirosis
The holder's height, weight, eye colour and other features
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: It tells staff the holder works with water or sewage and could have leptospirosis.

n.0: The card's purpose is to flag occupational exposure, not blood group.
n.1: It is a disease-risk warning, not a next-of-kin record.
n.3: Physical description is not what the card provides.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker off sick with flu-like symptoms sees their GP but does not mention their job. Why is that a problem?
o: The doctor will then refuse to see the worker at all
The worker will automatically lose their job on the network
The GP will immediately send the worker straight back to work
The doctor may not think to test for Weil's disease
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Without knowing the job, the doctor may not test for Weil's disease.

n.0: The doctor will still see them; the risk is a missed diagnosis.
n.1: Not mentioning the job does not cost them their job; it risks their health.
n.2: The concern is a missed diagnosis, not being sent back to work.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: You have diarrhoea and vomiting. What must you do before restricted work on potable water?
o: Carry on with the work but wash your hands far more often
Only tell your supervisor once the whole job has finished
Take a painkiller and simply carry on with the job as normal
Not do the work and report your illness to your supervisor
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You must not do potable water work while ill and must report it to your supervisor.

n.0: Extra hand washing does not make it safe to work on potable water while ill.
n.1: You must report before working, not afterwards.
n.2: Medication does not remove the risk of contaminating the water.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why must you not work on potable water supplies while you have a stomach upset?
o: Your work gloves would not fit you nearly as well when unwell
You would end up working more slowly and miss the day's target
You could pass organisms such as typhoid or E. coli into the water
The cold water in the main would only make your symptoms worse as part of the day's work out on site
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: An ill worker can shed organisms like typhoid or E. coli into the water.

n.0: Glove fit is irrelevant; the risk is contaminating the drinking water.
n.1: The concern is public health, not your work rate.
n.3: The rule protects the water supply, not primarily your comfort.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Who should you tell if you have sickness or diarrhoea before a potable network shift?
o: Your supervisor
A workmate on your gang
Nobody, if you feel able
The customer at the site
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Sickness and diarrhoea must be reported to your supervisor before potable work.

n.1: A workmate is not the right person; your supervisor must be told.
n.2: You must report it; feeling able is not the test for potable work.
n.3: The customer is not who you report your illness to; your supervisor is.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker recovering from food poisoning is unsure when they can return to potable work. What is safe?
o: Return the very moment they begin to feel slightly better
Return only once a workmate agrees that they look quite well
Report it and follow the employer's rules before going back
Never mention it to anyone so as not to worry the supervisor
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They should report it and follow the employer's clearance rules before returning.

n.0: Feeling a bit better is not enough; employer clearance rules apply.
n.1: A workmate's opinion is not the proper clearance route.
n.3: Hiding illness risks the water supply and is not acceptable.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why is a healthy-seeming worker with a recent stomach bug still a risk to potable water?
o: They will by now have completely forgotten their hygiene training
They can still carry and spread organisms while recovering
All of their hand tools will have rusted while they were off sick
They are certain to work far too quickly and make mistakes
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: A recovering worker may still carry and shed organisms into the water.

n.0: Recovery does not erase training; the risk is carrying organisms.
n.2: Rusty tools are not the concern; carriage of pathogens is.
n.3: Work speed is not the issue; possible carriage of organisms is.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which illness means you should not work on potable water and must report to your supervisor?
o: A slightly stiff neck after a poor night's sleep
A small bruise coming up on the forearm or shin
A mild bout of hay fever during the summer months
Diarrhoea, vomiting or a stomach upset
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Diarrhoea, vomiting or a stomach upset means no potable work and a report to your supervisor.

n.0: A stiff neck is not the reportable gut illness the rule refers to.
n.1: A bruise is not a gastrointestinal illness that would contaminate water.
n.2: Hay fever is not the diarrhoea or vomiting the rule targets.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: You suddenly feel sick with stomach cramps while working on a live main. What is right?
o: Finish the connection as quickly as possible and then go home
Swap over to a different fitting but otherwise keep working
Say nothing to anyone and just take a few extra short breaks
Stop, tell your supervisor and stay off the potable system
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You must stop, report to your supervisor and not continue on the potable system.

n.0: You should stop straight away, not push on with the potable work.
n.1: Changing fittings does not remove the contamination risk.
n.2: Staying silent risks the water supply; you must report it.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: People with diarrhoea or vomiting are kept off potable water work because they may carry:
o: Typhoid or E. coli
Only the common cold
Nothing at all harmful
Only harmless rust dust
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Such workers can carry organisms like typhoid or E. coli that endanger the water.

n.1: A cold is not the gut pathogen of concern here.
n.2: They can in fact carry organisms that endanger drinking water.
n.3: The concern is disease organisms, not rust particles.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Many employers require a worker to complete which of these before restricted network work?
o: A full written driving theory examination
A manual handling and weightlifting contest
A health questionnaire or screening
A weekly renewal of their first aid certificate
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Employers commonly require a health questionnaire or screening before restricted work.

n.0: A driving theory test is unrelated to health screening for water work.
n.1: Screening is a health check, not a lifting competition.
n.3: Weekly first aid renewal is not what pre-work screening involves.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Besides after an illness, when might an employer ask a worker to complete a health questionnaire?
o: After buying themselves a new pair of work boots
After successfully passing their annual work appraisal
After certain kinds of foreign travel
After moving house to a completely new home address
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Screening may be required after certain foreign travel as well as after illness.

n.0: New boots have nothing to do with health screening.
n.1: An appraisal is not the trigger for a health questionnaire.
n.3: A change of address does not trigger health screening.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why do employers screen workers' health before restricted operations on the network?
o: To help make sure a worker will not contaminate the potable water
To work out how much annual leave each worker should be given when working on the public water mains
To check that the worker can lift the very heaviest of tools
To set the worker's rate of pay for the coming twelve months
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Screening helps ensure a worker will not carry contamination into the potable water.

n.1: Health screening is about water safety, not leave allocation.
n.2: Screening protects the water supply, not to test strength.
n.3: Screening is a public-health check, not a pay review.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker returns from a holiday abroad after a stomach illness there. What is a likely requirement?
o: Simply signing in at the site reception desk as normal
Bringing back a small souvenir for the rest of the depot
Completing a health questionnaire before returning to the network
Working a full week of night shifts in order to readjust
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Illness abroad often means completing a health questionnaire before restricted work.

n.0: Signing in is not the same as the health screening this situation needs.
n.1: A souvenir has nothing to do with returning safely to water work.
n.3: Night shifts are not the health-clearance step required here.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Health screening questionnaires for water workers are mainly used to identify:
o: Those workers who would prefer either early or late shifts
Anyone who might pass an infection into the water supply
Which of the workers own and run their own private transport
Which worker happens to have the longest service at the depot
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Screening is mainly to identify anyone who might pass an infection into the water.

n.0: Shift preference is not what health screening is for.
n.2: Transport is irrelevant to a health questionnaire.
n.3: Length of service is not the purpose of the screening.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: After recovering from diarrhoea and vomiting, what may an employer require before you resume work?
o: A full retake of your manual handling lifting test
That you buy your own replacement set of work gloves
Attendance at a toolbox talk all about ladder safety
Health screening to confirm you are fit to return
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Employers may require health screening to confirm fitness before you resume potable work.

n.0: Manual handling is not the clearance needed after a gut illness.
n.1: Buying gloves is not the health-clearance step required.
n.2: A ladder talk is unrelated to clearing you after illness.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of these situations would most likely trigger a fresh health questionnaire?
o: Being issued with a brand-new company mobile phone
Changing over to a different work van to drive to site during everyday work on the distribution network
Returning to work after illness or certain foreign travel
Filling in and handing in a routine daily timesheet
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: A fresh questionnaire is typically triggered by illness or certain foreign travel.

n.0: A new phone does not trigger health screening.
n.1: Swapping vans is unrelated to health screening.
n.3: A timesheet is not a health-screening trigger.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: When should you always wash your hands on a network job?
o: Only once, right at the very end of the working shift
Only on the occasions when your hands look visibly dirty
Only when a supervisor or inspector happens to be watching when out working on the water network
Before eating, drinking or smoking and after using the toilet
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Always wash before eating, drinking or smoking and after using the toilet.

n.0: Once a shift is not enough; wash before eating and after the toilet.
n.1: Hands can carry organisms even when they look clean.
n.2: Hand washing is required regardless of who is watching.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why is hand washing before eating so important for a water worker?
o: It gently warms your cold hands up ready for your meal
It stops organisms on your hands being swallowed with your food
It takes away the lingering rubbery taste of your gloves
It helps make your rest break last a good deal longer
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Washing removes organisms so they are not swallowed with food.

n.0: The purpose is hygiene, not warming your hands.
n.2: Washing is about removing organisms, not taste.
n.3: Hand washing is a health measure, not a way to extend breaks.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker wants a quick sandwich but has handled pipework in a wet chamber. What should they do first?
o: Simply wipe their hands down the front of their overalls
Eat it as quickly as they can so the food is exposed less
Only bother washing if the sandwich is completely unwrapped
Wash their hands thoroughly before touching the food
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They must wash their hands thoroughly before handling any food.

n.0: Wiping on dirty overalls does not remove the organisms.
n.1: Eating fast does not protect against contaminated hands.
n.2: Handling food with dirty hands is a risk whether wrapped or not.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: After using the toilet on site, when should a water worker wash their hands?
o: Only on the occasions when they did not wear any gloves
Only at the very start and the very end of the working day
Only when the soap dispenser has just been freshly stocked
Every single time, before returning to any work or food
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Hands must be washed every time after using the toilet.

n.0: Hand washing after the toilet is required regardless of gloves.
n.1: It is required every time, not just twice a day.
n.2: You should wash every time; lack of soap must be reported, not skipped.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of these best protects both the worker and the water supply during breaks?
o: Washing hands before every break and after using the toilet
Keeping the work gloves on while eating your lunch
Giving the hands only a brief rinse under cold water
Using hand gel just the once at the end of the day
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Washing before every break and after the toilet protects worker and supply alike.

n.1: Dirty gloves at lunch can still transfer organisms to food.
n.2: A brief cold rinse is not thorough hand washing.
n.3: One squirt of gel at day's end is not adequate hand hygiene.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Proper hand washing on the network means:
o: Giving the hands a quick shake to get rid of the drips
Using clean water and soap, especially before eating and after the toilet
Wiping both of the palms clean on a dusty old rag
Dipping just the fingertips into the trench water
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Proper washing uses clean water and soap, especially before eating and after the toilet.

n.0: Shaking off drips does not clean the hands of organisms.
n.2: A dusty rag will not clean hands and may add contamination.
n.3: Trench water may itself be contaminated and must not be used.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why should you not rely on gloves alone instead of washing your hands?
o: Organisms can still reach your hands, so washing is still needed
Because gloves are far too expensive to keep on replacing
Because wearing gloves makes your hands too clean to eat with
Because washing your hands is really only for the office staff while out on a potable water network job
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Organisms can still reach the hands, so washing remains necessary even with gloves.

n.1: Cost is not the reason; hands still need washing for hygiene.
n.2: Gloves do not over-clean hands; washing is still required.
n.3: Hand washing applies to all water workers, not just office staff.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: How should a cut or graze be treated before working on the water network?
o: Covered over with a clean, waterproof dressing
Left fully open so that the fresh air can get to it
Simply wrapped up in a small piece of dry tissue paper
Smeared over with a little grease taken from the toolbox
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: A cut must be covered with a clean, waterproof dressing before work.

n.1: An open cut is an entry point for infection and must be covered.
n.2: Tissue is not a waterproof dressing and offers little protection.
n.3: Grease is not a suitable or hygienic wound covering.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why must cuts and grazes be covered on a network job?
o: To keep the plaster itself from getting wet, dirty and cold while out on a potable water network job
To make sure the injury will heal fully in under one day
To stop leptospira and other organisms entering the broken skin
To hide the cut away from the eyes of the site inspector
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Covering keeps leptospira and other organisms out of the broken skin.

n.0: The reason is preventing infection, not keeping the plaster dry.
n.1: Covering does not heal a wound in a day; it blocks infection.
n.3: Covering is for protection against infection, not concealment.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker notices a graze on their forearm before entering a wet chamber. What is correct?
o: Cover it with a waterproof dressing before starting work
Ignore it, since forearms rarely come into contact with water
Rinse the graze clean using the water inside the chamber
Wait a while to see whether or not it starts to bleed first
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The graze must be covered with a waterproof dressing before work begins.

n.1: Any break in the skin is a risk and should be covered.
n.2: Chamber water may be contaminated and must not be used on a wound.
n.3: A graze is already a risk; it should be covered without delay.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What type of dressing is required to cover a cut for water network work?
o: A waterproof dressing
A loose, unsecured cotton bandage on its own
A dry paper towel simply held in place by hand
A single strip of ordinary insulating tape only
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: A waterproof dressing is required to keep contaminated water out of the wound.

n.1: A loose bandage is not waterproof and lets water through.
n.2: A held paper towel is neither secure nor waterproof.
n.3: Insulating tape is not a suitable wound dressing.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A plaster comes loose and the cut is exposed while you work in wet ground. What should you do?
o: Keep going and replace the plaster during your next rest break
Stop and re-cover the cut with a fresh waterproof dressing
Press the loose old plaster back down using your muddy fingers
Pull your sleeve down over it to keep the cut out of sight
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Stop and re-cover the exposed cut with a fresh waterproof dressing.

n.0: An exposed cut in wet ground is an immediate risk to address now.
n.2: Muddy fingers add contamination; a fresh clean dressing is needed.
n.3: A sleeve is not a waterproof dressing and does not protect the wound.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Covering a cut before wet work mainly protects the worker by:
o: Keeping the worker's hands warm in the cold water
Blocking a route for infection to enter the body
Improving the worker's grip on the wet hand tools
Making the worker's gloves last a good deal longer
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Covering the cut blocks a route for infection into the body.

n.0: A dressing is for infection control, not warmth.
n.2: A plaster is not there to improve grip.
n.3: Covering a cut does not extend glove life; it prevents infection.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of these must you NOT do inside an excavation or trench?
o: Eat, drink or smoke
Wear your safety helmet
Keep your gloves on
Follow the dig plan
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You must never eat, drink or smoke inside an excavation or trench.

n.1: Wearing your helmet is required, not forbidden.
n.2: Keeping gloves on is good practice, not something banned.
n.3: Following the plan is expected, not prohibited.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why is eating, drinking and smoking not allowed in a trench?
o: It can carry contamination from the trench into your mouth
It noticeably slows down the digging out of the trench
It uses up the limited oxygen supply within the trench
It makes the trench walls collapse a great deal faster during everyday work on the distribution network
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Hand-to-mouth contact in a trench can carry contamination into the mouth.

n.1: The rule is about hygiene, not digging speed.
n.2: The rule targets contamination, not oxygen use.
n.3: Eating does not affect the stability of the trench walls.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Where should you go to eat or drink when working on an excavation?
o: To the very edge of the trench while still leaning into it
Out of the excavation to a clean welfare area
Anywhere that is convenient, as long as you are fairly quick
Down in the bottom of the trench if it is a dry day
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You should leave the excavation and use a clean welfare area to eat or drink.

n.0: Eating at the trench edge still risks transferring contamination.
n.2: Speed does not make eating in a dirty trench safe.
n.3: Even on a dry day, eating in the trench is not allowed.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker lights a cigarette while standing in a trench. Why is this poor hygiene practice?
o: Contaminants on the hands can pass to the mouth via the cigarette
The cigarette smoke will discolour the brand-new pipework
Cigarettes of any kind are banned on every outdoor worksite
It will make the trench far too warm and stuffy to work in
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Handling a cigarette can carry contaminants from the hands into the mouth.

n.1: The rule is about the worker's health, not staining pipe.
n.2: The specific issue is hand-to-mouth contamination in the trench.
n.3: A cigarette does not overheat a trench; the risk is contamination.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: The rule against eating, drinking and smoking in an excavation is mainly there to:
o: Keep loose litter and wrappers out of the finished trench
Save valuable time so that the job is finished much sooner
Protect the worker from swallowing harmful organisms
Cut down the amount of noise being made on the worksite
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The rule protects the worker from swallowing harmful organisms.

n.0: While litter is unwanted, the main aim is protecting the worker's health.
n.1: The rule is about hygiene, not saving time.
n.3: Eating and smoking are not noise issues.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: You are thirsty while working down a trench on a hot day. What is the correct thing to do?
o: Take one quick sip without letting the bottle touch your face
Climb out and have your drink in the clean welfare area
Ask a colleague to carefully pour some water into your mouth
Wait until the whole of the job is finished several hours later
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You should leave the trench and drink in the clean welfare area.

n.0: Even a quick sip in the trench risks hand-to-mouth contamination.
n.2: Drinking in the trench remains a contamination risk however it is done.
n.3: You should not go without fluids; leave the trench to drink safely.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What is the main purpose of the welfare facilities provided on a network job?
o: To store the heavy plant and hand tools safely overnight
To hold the spare pipe fittings, valves and other materials
To give workers a clean place to wash, eat and use the toilet
To provide somewhere sheltered to park the site van
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Welfare facilities give workers a clean place to wash, eat and use the toilet.

n.0: Welfare facilities are for the workers' hygiene, not tool storage.
n.1: Welfare units are not a materials store.
n.3: Welfare facilities are not a parking area.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why use the welfare facilities rather than the excavation for eating and washing?
o: They are a good deal warmer than standing in the open trench
They are usually much closer to where the site van is parked while carrying out restricted network work
They provide clean conditions that reduce the risk of infection
They keep the worker safely out of the supervisor's sight
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Welfare facilities give clean conditions that reduce the risk of infection.

n.0: Comfort is a minor point; the key reason is reducing infection risk.
n.1: Convenience is not the reason; hygiene and clean conditions are.
n.3: Welfare use is about hygiene, not avoiding the supervisor.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Good welfare facilities for water network operatives should include:
o: A generous supply of chilled and fizzy soft drinks only
A television set and a few comfortable padded armchairs
Clean water, soap and somewhere hygienic to eat
A securely locked cabinet for storing personal valuables
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Welfare should include clean water, soap and a hygienic place to eat.

n.0: Welfare is about hand washing and clean eating, not just soft drinks.
n.1: Entertainment is not the purpose of welfare facilities.
n.3: Valuables storage is not the core purpose of welfare provision.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A gang has no clean hand-washing facilities on site. What is the correct response?
o: Simply make use of the trench water to rinse your hands
Skip washing entirely until you eventually get home at night
Report it, as proper welfare facilities must be provided
Wipe your hands on your overalls and carry on eating anyway
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Missing hand-washing facilities must be reported, as welfare must be provided.

n.0: Trench water may be contaminated and must never be used to wash.
n.1: Going all day without washing is unsafe; welfare must be provided.
n.3: Wiping on overalls does not clean hands; the issue must be reported.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Using the welfare toilet and washing afterwards mainly helps to:
o: Keep the whole worksite tidy for the next site inspection
Give the worker a somewhat longer and more relaxing break during ordinary operations on the network
Prevent organisms being spread to food, others and the water
Reduce the total amount of water that the whole job uses
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Washing after the toilet stops organisms spreading to food, others and the water.

n.0: Tidiness is minor; the key aim is preventing the spread of organisms.
n.1: Welfare use is a hygiene measure, not a way to lengthen breaks.
n.3: Welfare hygiene is not about saving water on the job.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Welfare facilities are provided on network jobs primarily to support:
o: A faster overall completion of the excavation work
Good personal hygiene that protects health and the water supply
Some extra storage space for the site paperwork and files
A dry, sheltered place in which to charge the power tools
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Welfare supports good personal hygiene, protecting health and the water supply.

n.0: Welfare is about hygiene, not speeding up the dig.
n.2: Paperwork storage is not the purpose of welfare units.
n.3: Charging tools is not the reason welfare is provided.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Good personal hygiene on a network job protects:
o: Only the neat appearance of the finished piece of work
Only the total cost of the materials used on the job
Both the drinking water and the worker's own health
Only the speed at which the whole job gets done
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Good hygiene protects both the drinking water and the worker's own health.

n.0: Hygiene is about health and water quality, not appearance.
n.1: Hygiene does not exist to control material costs.
n.3: Hygiene protects health and water, not the pace of work.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: How does washing your hands protect the public who drink the water?
o: It makes the water coming out of the tap taste much sweeter during ordinary operations on the network
It noticeably increases the pressure inside the water main
It speeds up the flow of the water through the pipe
It stops organisms on your hands reaching the potable supply
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Clean hands stop organisms reaching the potable supply the public drinks.

n.0: Hand washing has no effect on the taste of the water.
n.1: Hand hygiene does not change water pressure.
n.2: Hand washing does not affect flow rate in the pipe.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker who follows good hygiene rules is helping to prevent:
o: General wear and tear on their own set of hand tools
Contamination of the potable water and illness in themselves
Delays to the work that are caused by bad weather on site when doing this kind of job on site
The site van from running out of fuel on the way home
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Good hygiene helps prevent water contamination and illness in the worker.

n.0: Hygiene is about health and water safety, not tool wear.
n.2: Personal hygiene has no bearing on weather delays.
n.3: Fuel use is unrelated to personal hygiene practices.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why is personal hygiene treated so seriously on the potable water network?
o: Because it affects how quickly the overalls start to wear out when doing this kind of job on site
Because poor hygiene could make the public's drinking water unsafe
Because it changes the colour of the finished run of pipe
Because it decides which worker will get the next job first
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Poor hygiene could make the public's drinking water unsafe, so it is taken seriously.

n.0: Hygiene rules exist to protect drinking water, not clothing wear.
n.2: Hygiene has nothing to do with pipe colour.
n.3: Hygiene is a public-health duty, not a job-allocation tool.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which action best sums up protecting both yourself and the water supply?
o: Working much faster to cut the time spent in the trench
Keeping all of the hand tools sharp and well oiled
Wearing brightly coloured high-visibility clothing on site
Washing hands, covering cuts and reporting any illness
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Washing hands, covering cuts and reporting illness protect worker and supply.

n.0: Speed does not equal hygiene; the listed hygiene steps do.
n.1: Tool care is good practice but is not the hygiene point here.
n.2: High-visibility clothing is about being seen, not hygiene.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A new operative asks how their own habits affect the public. What is the best explanation?
o: Their habits only ever affect the size of their own pay packet
Their habits make no difference at all once the pipes are laid
Their habits only really matter while they are in the office
Their hygiene can keep organisms out of the water people drink
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Their personal hygiene helps keep organisms out of the water the public drinks.

n.0: Their hygiene directly affects public drinking water, not just pay.
n.1: Hygiene matters throughout the work, not only before pipes are laid.
n.2: Hygiene matters most out on the network, not just in the office.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A rat is seen near an open valve chamber holding potable water. What is the hygiene concern?
o: It might well chew straight through the plastic pipework
Its urine could contaminate the water and spread Weil's disease
It could trip a worker who is climbing into the chamber
It will frighten away the rest of the working gang
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The concern is that rat urine could contaminate the water and spread Weil's disease.

n.0: The immediate hygiene concern is contamination, not pipe damage.
n.2: A trip hazard is not the Weil's disease concern being asked about.
n.3: The concern is contamination of the water, not fright.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which combination correctly lists ways leptospira can enter the body?
o: Through cuts, and through the eyes, nose and mouth
Through the ears and through the finger and toe nails
Through the hair and through unbroken, intact skin only
Only by eating food that has been dropped in the trench
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Leptospira enter through cuts and through the eyes, nose and mouth.

n.1: Ears and nails are not the recognised routes; cuts and mucous membranes are.
n.2: Hair and intact skin are not entry points for the organism.
n.3: Dropped food is one risk, but entry is chiefly via cuts and the face.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What is the safest response to feeling sick with vomiting on the morning of a potable job?
o: Report it and stay off potable work until you are cleared
Go in as planned but simply avoid touching the actual pipe
Take the job on but wear a face covering for the whole shift
Wait to see whether you feel any better by about lunchtime
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Report the sickness and stay off potable work until you are cleared to return.

n.1: Simply avoiding the pipe does not remove the contamination risk.
n.2: A face covering does not stop you carrying gut organisms into the work.
n.3: You should report it before work, not gamble on feeling better later.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A warning card is carried by water workers so that, if they fall ill:
o: A doctor is prompted to consider Weil's disease
They can readily prove exactly how long they have worked
They can claim free prescriptions from the chemist for life
They can be moved up the list for priority council housing
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The card prompts a doctor to consider Weil's disease if the worker falls ill.

n.1: The card is a medical alert, not a record of service length.
n.2: The card does not grant free prescriptions.
n.3: The card has nothing to do with housing.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Before entering a trench, a worker with a small cut on their hand should:
o: Give the cut a rinse in the nearest available puddle
Cover the cut with a waterproof dressing
Leave it be and simply keep that hand held up high
Rub a little barrier cream in and then do nothing else
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The cut should be covered with a waterproof dressing before work.

n.0: A puddle may be contaminated and must not be used on a cut.
n.2: Keeping a hand raised does not protect an open cut from infection.
n.3: Barrier cream alone is not a waterproof dressing over a cut.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker returns from abroad after a bad stomach upset there. Before restricted work they should expect to:
o: Complete a health questionnaire or screening first
Simply turn up and start work as though nothing had happened
Automatically take a full week of unpaid leave from work
Change over to an entirely different trade for a while
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Illness abroad usually means completing health screening before restricted work.

n.1: Recent illness abroad means screening may be needed before returning.
n.2: Unpaid leave is not the health-clearance step being described.
n.3: Changing trade is not what is required; health screening is.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: You have no soap or clean water at your work location. Before eating you should:
o: Report the missing facilities rather than eat with dirty hands
Make use of the water in the trench to rinse your hands
Eat quite carefully without letting your hands touch the food when doing this kind of job on site
Give your hands a wipe on a rag and then eat anyway
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Missing hand-washing facilities must be reported rather than eating with dirty hands.

n.1: Trench water may be contaminated and must never be used to wash.
n.2: You cannot make dirty hands safe by eating carefully; report it.
n.3: A rag does not clean your hands; the lack of welfare must be reported.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: The reason smoking is banned in a trench on the network is that:
o: Tobacco smoke reacts very badly with the chlorine in the main
The smoke gets in the way of seeing the pipe clearly
Loose cigarette ash can block up the new water main
Handling a cigarette can carry contamination to your mouth
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Handling a cigarette can carry contamination from the hands to the mouth.

n.0: The rule is about hand-to-mouth contamination, not chemical reactions.
n.1: Visibility is not the reason smoking is banned in the trench.
