n.2: Ash blocking the main is not the hygiene reason for the ban.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A colleague eats a sandwich in the trench 'to save time'. What should you tell them?
o: It is perfectly fine as long as they finish the sandwich quickly
They must eat out of the trench in the welfare area
It is allowed provided that they only use their left hand
It is quite safe because the sandwich itself is wrapped up
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They must leave the trench and eat in the clean welfare area.

n.0: Finishing quickly does not remove the contamination risk in the trench.
n.2: Which hand they use makes no difference to the contamination risk.
n.3: A wrapper does not protect against contaminated hands and surroundings.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: The main reason for good personal hygiene when working on potable water is to:
o: Make sure that the job comfortably passes its cost review
Keep the public's drinking water safe and protect your own health
Reduce the total amount of pipe that has to be used
Help the gang to finish the whole job ahead of schedule
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Good hygiene keeps the public's drinking water safe and protects the worker's health.

n.0: Hygiene is about safety and health, not cost reviews.
n.2: Hygiene does not affect how much pipe is needed.
n.3: Hygiene is not about beating the schedule.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Weil's disease enters the body most readily when a worker:
o: Is wearing a pair of fully intact and undamaged gloves
Keeps their safety glasses on properly throughout the job
Washes their hands with soap and water after every task
Has an uncovered cut exposed to contaminated water
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: An uncovered cut exposed to contaminated water is the readiest route in.

n.0: Intact gloves protect the hands rather than let the organism in.
n.1: Wearing eye protection reduces risk rather than increasing it.
n.2: Regular hand washing reduces the risk, it does not create it.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of these is a genuine early warning sign of Weil's disease?
o: A sudden and strong craving for very salty food
A gradual and welcome improvement in the eyesight
An itchy red rash only on the soles of the feet
A fever with headache and aching muscles
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Fever with headache and aching muscles is a genuine early sign.

n.0: A salt craving is not a symptom of Weil's disease.
n.1: Improved eyesight is not a symptom of the disease.
n.2: An itchy foot rash is not the described early warning sign.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: You cut your hand mid-task in a wet chamber and it is bleeding. What should you do?
o: Carry on working, as a little blood keeps the germs out
Dip the hand into the chamber water in order to rinse it
Clean and cover it and consider the Weil's disease risk
Wrap it up in your dirty work glove and simply continue
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Clean and cover the cut and bear the Weil's disease risk in mind.

n.0: Bleeding does not keep leptospira out; the cut must be cleaned and covered.
n.1: Chamber water may be contaminated and must not be used on the wound.
n.3: A dirty glove adds contamination; a clean waterproof dressing is needed.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Reporting sickness and diarrhoea to your supervisor before potable work matters because:
o: It guarantees the worker a fully paid day off from work
It means that somebody else will have to do your paperwork as part of the day's work out on site
It excuses the worker from having to wear their PPE
It lets the employer keep possible carriers away from the water
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Reporting lets the employer keep possible carriers away from the potable water.

n.0: Reporting is a safety duty, not a way to secure paid leave.
n.1: Reporting is about protecting the water, not shifting paperwork.
n.2: Reporting illness does not excuse you from wearing PPE.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which practice would put the potable water supply at risk?
o: Covering over a small graze with a waterproof plaster
Washing your hands with soap and water before the task
Working on a live main while suffering from diarrhoea
Completing the health questionnaire after being unwell
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Working on a live main while suffering diarrhoea risks contaminating the supply.

n.0: Covering a graze protects the supply rather than risking it.
n.1: Washing hands before work protects the supply.
n.3: Completing screening protects the supply; it does not put it at risk.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker asks why the eyes, nose and mouth matter for Weil's disease. The best answer is:
o: They are moist linings the organism can pass through into the body
They are the only places on the body a rat can bite you
They are well protected and simply cannot let anything in
They only really matter once you already feel quite ill
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The eyes, nose and mouth are moist linings the organism can pass through.

n.1: The point is entry through mucous membranes, not rat bites.
n.2: In fact these linings are recognised entry points, not sealed barriers.
n.3: They are entry routes at all times, not only once you feel unwell.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: When is it acceptable to eat your lunch sitting in the bottom of a trench?
o: When the weather outside is warm, dry and pleasant
When you happen to be working alone with no gang about
Never; you should eat in the clean welfare area
When the trench is more than a metre in overall depth
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: It is never acceptable; you should always eat in the clean welfare area.

n.0: Weather does not make eating in a trench acceptable.
n.1: Working alone does not make eating in the trench safe.
n.3: Trench depth does not make eating in it acceptable.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker has just used the site toilet and is about to handle a potable fitting. What must they do first?
o: Put a second pair of gloves on over the first and carry on
Give the fitting a rinse instead of washing their own hands
Wash their hands thoroughly at the welfare facilities
Get straight on with the job in order to save a little time
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They must wash their hands thoroughly at the welfare facilities first.

n.0: A second glove over unwashed hands does not replace hand washing.
n.1: Rinsing the fitting does not address the organisms on their hands.
n.3: Skipping hand washing after the toilet risks the water supply.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: The Weil's disease warning card is most useful at which moment?
o: When you become ill and need to see a doctor
When you very first apply for a job on the network
When you go to collect your weekly wages from the office
When you next go to renew your ordinary driving licence
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: It is most useful when you fall ill and need to see a doctor.

n.1: The card's value is at the point of illness, not at job application.
n.2: The card is a health alert, not a payslip.
n.3: The card has nothing to do with a driving licence.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What does covering a cut with a waterproof dressing achieve on a wet job?
o: It keeps contaminated water out of the wound
It makes the cut all but invisible to the naked eye
It stops the worker from feeling any pain at all
It allows the worker to skip washing their hands
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: A waterproof dressing keeps contaminated water out of the wound.

n.1: Concealment is not the purpose; keeping infection out is.
n.2: A dressing is for protection against infection, not pain relief.
n.3: A covered cut does not remove the need to wash hands.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why must welfare facilities include clean running water?
o: So that the gang is able to top up the water main from it
So that the workers can cool their bottled drinks down in it
So workers can wash off organisms before eating and after the toilet
So the whole site looks well equipped to any visitors
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Clean running water lets workers wash off organisms before eating and after the toilet.

n.0: Welfare water is for washing, not for filling the main.
n.1: Chilling drinks is not the purpose of welfare water.
n.3: Appearance to visitors is not why clean water is provided.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Personal hygiene is said to protect 'both the water and the worker'. The worker part refers to:
o: Not catching diseases such as Weil's disease from the work
Earning a small bonus for keeping a tidy and clean worksite
Avoiding too much general wear and tear on their work boots
Being the first person in the queue at the site canteen
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The worker part means not catching diseases such as Weil's disease from the work.

n.1: Protecting the worker means their health, not a tidiness bonus.
n.2: It refers to the worker's health, not their footwear.
n.3: It is about avoiding illness, not canteen queues.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker feels fine but had severe vomiting yesterday. About today's potable job, they should:
o: Report it and stay off until the employer's rules allow return
Assume they are fine now because the symptoms have all stopped
Only mention it if and when a supervisor happens to ask them
Work the job as normal but keep away from the welfare area
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They should report it and stay off until the employer's rules allow a return.

n.1: Symptoms stopping does not mean they cannot still carry organisms.
n.2: They should report it proactively, not wait to be asked.
n.3: Avoiding the welfare area does not make the potable work safe.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which is the correct order of good hygiene when taking a break on a trench job?
o: Eat down in the trench first and then wash your hands after
Wipe your hands on your overalls and then eat in the trench when out working on the water network
Leave the trench, wash your hands, then eat in the welfare area
Eat quickly first and then wash only if there is time
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Leave the trench, wash your hands, then eat in the welfare area.

n.0: You should wash and leave the trench before eating, not after.
n.1: Overalls do not clean hands and the trench is not for eating.
n.3: Washing before eating is essential, not optional.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why might an employer ask health questions after certain foreign travel?
o: Because the worker may have picked up an infection that could reach the water
Because foreign travel always makes people work more slowly
Because the worker's tools may have travelled abroad as well
Because every holiday taken must be reported for pay reasons
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Foreign travel may bring back an infection that could reach the water, hence the questions.

n.1: The concern is infection risk, not work speed.
n.2: It is about the worker's health, not their tools.
n.3: It is a health measure, not a pay-reporting rule.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker keeps a graze uncovered because 'it will dry out and heal'. What is wrong on a wet job?
o: Grazes should really be soaked in water so they heal faster
An uncovered graze is well known for attracting rats to a site while carrying out restricted network work
The open graze lets contaminated water and organisms into the body
Leaving the graze open slows the whole of the gang right down
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: An uncovered graze lets contaminated water and organisms into the body.

n.0: Soaking a graze in dirty water increases risk; it must be covered.
n.1: A graze does not attract rats; the concern is infection entry.
n.3: The issue is infection risk, not the gang's pace.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: What is the correct action if you cut yourself and there is no clean dressing to hand?
o: Carry on and simply let the cut air-dry as you keep working
Cover the cut over with a piece of dirty old rag for now
Stop work and get a proper waterproof dressing before continuing
Seal the cut up with a little mud to stop it bleeding
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Stop work and get a proper waterproof dressing before continuing.

n.0: An open cut on a wet job must be covered before continuing.
n.1: A dirty rag adds contamination and is not a suitable dressing.
n.3: Mud is contaminated and must never be used on a wound.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which statement about working while suffering diarrhoea is correct?
o: You may work provided that you use hand gel quite often
You may work if you still feel well enough to stand up
You should not work on potable water and must report it
You may work as long as you keep out of the deepest trenches
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: You must not work on potable water while suffering diarrhoea and must report it.

n.0: Hand gel does not make it safe to work on potable water while ill.
n.1: Feeling able to stand is not the test; you must stay off and report it.
n.3: Trench depth is irrelevant; you must not work on potable water while ill.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Good welfare provision on a network job would be shown by:
o: A large screen showing the latest football and sports scores
Clean toilets and hand-washing water being available
Plenty of extra spaces for parking private cars close by
A far bigger stock of spare pipe fittings kept in the van
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Clean toilets and hand-washing water show good welfare provision.

n.0: Entertainment screens are not what welfare provision means.
n.2: Parking is not the measure of good welfare provision.
n.3: Fittings stock is not a welfare facility.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: How do covering cuts and washing hands protect the public?
o: They make the water flow a good deal faster to people's homes
They bring down the price that people pay on their water bill
They noticeably improve the water pressure at the kitchen tap during ordinary operations on the network
They help stop organisms from workers reaching the drinking water
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: They help stop organisms from workers reaching the water the public drinks.

n.0: Hygiene does not change how fast water flows to homes.
n.1: Hygiene practices do not set water bills.
n.2: Hand hygiene and covering cuts do not affect tap pressure.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A supervisor is told a worker has sickness and diarrhoea. What should they do about potable work?
o: Send the worker straight down into the trench to get on
Ignore it entirely so long as the worker is wearing gloves
Move the worker onto a busier part of the water network
Keep the worker off potable water work until it is safe
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The supervisor should keep the ill worker off potable water work until it is safe.

n.0: An ill worker should be kept off, not sent into the potable work.
n.1: Gloves do not make it safe; the worker must be kept off the work.
n.2: Moving them around does not remove the contamination risk.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why tell a doctor you work with water and sewage, even for a minor illness?
o: So that they will always sign you off work for a full month
So that they can then charge your employer for the whole visit
So they can consider infections like Weil's disease in the diagnosis
So that you are able to avoid having any blood tests taken
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Telling the doctor lets them consider infections like Weil's disease in the diagnosis.

n.0: The point is accurate diagnosis, not automatic long sick leave.
n.1: It is about diagnosis, not billing your employer.
n.3: Flagging your work supports, rather than avoids, the right tests.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Which of these shows good personal hygiene on the potable network?
o: Eating your lunch quickly down in the open trench
Washing hands before eating and covering any cuts
Rinsing your muddy hands in the water in the pipe trench
Leaving any grazes open to the air while you are working
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Washing hands before eating and covering cuts shows good personal hygiene.

n.0: Eating in the trench is poor hygiene, not good practice.
n.2: Using trench water to wash is unsafe and poor hygiene.
n.3: Leaving grazes uncovered is poor hygiene on a wet job.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker asks whether Weil's disease can be caught from touching clean, treated tap water. The answer is:
o: Yes, because all water carries exactly the same high risk
Yes, but only when the treated tap water is very cold
Only if that treated tap water has first been boiled up
No; the risk comes from water contaminated by rats' urine
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: The risk comes from water contaminated by rats' urine, not clean treated tap water.

n.0: Not all water carries the risk; it is contaminated water that does.
n.1: Cold clean tap water is not the source of the disease.
n.2: Boiling does not create the risk; contamination by rodent urine does.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: Why is it important to wash your hands even if you have worn gloves all shift?
o: Gloves make the hands smell far too strongly of rubber
Washing hands is only ever needed by the site office staff
Organisms can still reach the skin, so washing is essential
Gloves are far too costly to keep taking off and putting on
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Organisms can still reach the skin under or around gloves, so washing is essential.

n.0: The reason is hygiene against organisms, not any rubber smell.
n.1: Hand washing applies to everyone doing the work, not just office staff.
n.3: Cost is not the reason; the hands still need washing for hygiene.

Personal Health & Hygiene.q: A worker is unsure whether a mild stomach upset counts as a reason to report. What is correct?
o: No, a stomach upset is far too minor to be worth reporting
Only if the upset has lasted for a good three days or more
Yes; a stomach upset should be reported before potable work
Only when the worker has actually been physically sick as well
Personal Health & Hygiene.w: Even a mild stomach upset should be reported before doing potable water work.

n.0: A stomach upset can still mean carrying organisms and must be reported.
n.1: There is no such waiting rule; report it before potable work.
n.3: Vomiting is not required; a stomach upset alone should be reported.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is an example of microbiological contamination of drinking water?
o: Diesel fuel and solvents that have leaked into the open trench
Loose soil, grit, small stones and sand inside the pipe bore
Bacteria, viruses and protozoa carried in from foul water and soil
Metal swarf and filings left behind after cutting the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Microbiological contamination means living organisms such as bacteria, viruses and protozoa, usually from sewage.

n.0: Fuel and solvents are chemical contamination.
n.1: Soil, grit and stones are physical contamination.
n.3: Swarf is physical debris, not a living organism.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A fitter spills two-stroke oil right next to an open pipe end. This is an example of which type of contamination?
o: Microbiological contamination from living organisms
Chemical contamination from the oil entering the works
Physical contamination from solid foreign matter and debris
Thermal contamination from the temperature change
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Oils, fuels and solvents are chemicals, so this is chemical contamination.

n.0: That involves bacteria or viruses, not oil.
n.2: That means solids such as soil or debris.
n.3: Temperature is not one of the three types.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Soil, stones, grit and metal swarf getting into a main are examples of which type of contamination?
o: Chemical contamination from fuels and solvents
Microbiological contamination from organisms
Thermal contamination from a sudden change in heat
Physical contamination from solid foreign matter
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Solid foreign matter such as soil, stones and swarf is classed as physical contamination.

n.0: That means substances such as fuel or solvents.
n.1: That means living organisms such as bacteria.
n.2: Temperature is not a recognised type.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: What are the three recognised types of contamination on a clean water network?
o: Bacterial, viral and fungal forms of contamination
Microbiological, chemical and physical contamination
Solid, liquid and gaseous forms of contamination
Natural, man-made and purely accidental contamination
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: The scheme groups contamination into microbiological, chemical and physical types.

n.0: These are sub-types of the microbiological group only.
n.2: These are states of matter, not the named types.
n.3: These describe origins, not the three types.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of the following would be classed as microbiological contamination?
o: Weedkiller and pesticide sprayed alongside the open trench
Cryptosporidium protozoa washed in from the soil and ground
A loose screw with small stones sitting in the pipe bore
Petrol and diesel vapour drifting right across the excavation
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Cryptosporidium is a protozoan, a living organism, so it is microbiological contamination.

n.0: Weedkiller is a chemical contaminant.
n.2: A screw and stones are physical contamination.
n.3: Petrol is a chemical, not a micro-organism.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A dead insect and some leaves are found inside a pipe fitting. This is best described as:
o: Physical contamination from solid debris
Chemical contamination from a substance
Microbiological contamination from germs
Not classed as contamination at all here
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Insects, leaves and other solid debris are physical contamination.

n.1: No chemical substance is involved here.
n.2: The concern is the solid matter, which is physical.
n.3: Any foreign matter in the pipe is contamination.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which type of contamination presents the greatest immediate risk of making the public ill?
o: Physical contamination from soil and debris
Chemical contamination from fuels and oils
Microbiological contamination from sewage organisms
All three types are considered equally harmless
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Micro-organisms from sewage can cause rapid, widespread illness, so this is the biggest danger.

n.0: Debris is undesirable but rarely causes disease.
n.1: Chemicals are serious but micro risk is worst.
n.3: None are harmless; organisms are the top danger.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Using the wrong jointing paste or lubricant on a drinking water main is an example of:
o: Physical contamination of the supply
Chemical contamination of the supply
Microbiological contamination of it
Acceptable practice if it seals well
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Non-approved compounds and lubricants add chemicals to the water, so this is chemical contamination.

n.0: No solid debris is being introduced.
n.2: No living organisms are involved.
n.3: Only approved products may be used on the main.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Bacteria and viruses that cause waterborne disease mainly come from which source?
o: Clean topsoil taken from a domestic garden
Approved, certified potable pipe lubricant and paste
Sewage and foul water in and around the works
New, unopened, bagged plastic pipe fittings
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: The main source of harmful bacteria and viruses is sewage and foul water.

n.0: Soil is a source but foul water carries the worst.
n.1: Approved products are not a source of organisms.
n.3: Clean stored fittings carry no sewage organisms.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which list contains only examples of chemical contamination?
o: Fuel, oil, solvents and weedkiller near the works
Soil, grit, metal swarf and small loose stones
Bacteria, viruses and protozoa from foul water
Insects, dead leaves and general loose site debris
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fuel, oil, solvents and weedkiller are all chemicals.

n.1: These are physical contaminants.
n.2: These are microbiological contaminants.
n.3: These are physical contaminants.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Standing water at the bottom of a trench is a particular concern because it can carry:
o: Only clean, harmless rainwater on every occasion
Harmful micro-organisms from the surrounding ground
Approved lubricant that will help with jointing
Nothing at all that could affect the open main in practice
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Trench water is dirty and can carry bacteria and other micro-organisms into an open main.

n.0: Trench water cannot be assumed clean.
n.2: Trench water is a hazard, not a jointing aid.
n.3: It can contaminate the main and must be kept out.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Swarf and filings are left in the bore after cutting a pipe. These are best described as:
o: Physical contamination to be flushed out
Chemical contamination to be neutralised
Microbiological contamination to be dosed
Harmless material that is safe to leave
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Metal filings are solid debris, a physical contaminant that must be removed before use.

n.1: Metal filings are not a chemical substance.
n.2: They are not living organisms.
n.3: Debris must never be left in a drinking main.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why are protozoa such as Cryptosporidium grouped with microbiological contamination?
o: They are living organisms that can cause illness
They are a type of dissolved chemical pollutant
They are small pieces of physical grit and sand
They are only ever found inside sealed clean pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Protozoa are micro-organisms, so they sit in the microbiological group with bacteria and viruses.

n.1: Protozoa are organisms, not chemicals.
n.2: They are microscopic organisms, not debris.
n.3: They come from soil and foul water.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A drum of solvent stored beside an open excavation is mainly a risk of:
o: Physical contamination from the empty metal drum
Microbiological contamination of the subsoil
No real risk provided the lid is only dented
Chemical contamination if the solvent spills in
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Solvents are chemicals, so a spill into the works would cause chemical contamination.

n.0: The concern is the solvent, which is chemical.
n.1: Solvents are not living organisms.
n.2: A dented lid does not remove the spill risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which statement about the three types of contamination is correct?
o: Chemical means bacteria and viruses from sewage
Physical means solid debris such as soil and swarf
Microbiological means fuels, oils and jointing solvents
Physical means dissolved weedkiller in the water
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Physical contamination is solid foreign matter like soil, stones and swarf.

n.0: Bacteria and viruses are microbiological.
n.2: Fuel and oil are chemical, not microbiological.
n.3: Dissolved weedkiller is a chemical.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Human sewage getting into the water supply is dangerous mainly because it carries:
o: Only harmless dissolved minerals and trace salts
Nothing worse than a slightly cloudy colour
Disease-causing bacteria, viruses and protozoa
Approved disinfectant chemicals for the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Sewage carries harmful micro-organisms that can cause serious waterborne disease.

n.0: Sewage carries harmful organisms, not just minerals.
n.1: The danger is the organisms, not appearance.
n.3: Sewage is a contaminant, not a disinfectant.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A mate uses garage oil instead of approved lubricant on a joint. The main problem is that:
o: The oil is a chemical contaminant of the water
The oil makes the joint far too slippery
The oil only adds harmless loose debris
There is no problem if the joint seals
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Garage oil is an unapproved chemical and contaminates the drinking water.

n.1: Slipperiness is not the health concern.
n.2: Oil is a chemical, not harmless debris.
n.3: A good seal does not make oil safe.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these best describes physical contamination?
o: Living micro-organisms carried in from foul water
Fuels, solvents and non-approved jointing chemicals
Solid foreign matter such as grit, stones or swarf
Dissolved gases taken in from the atmosphere above
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Physical contamination is solid material that should not be in the pipe.

n.0: These are microbiological contamination.
n.1: These are chemical contamination.
n.3: Dissolved gases are not physical debris.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Weedkiller and pesticide overspray reaching an open main would be classed as:
o: Physical contamination of the main
Chemical contamination of the supply
Microbiological contamination there
A form of contamination that need not be reported
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Weedkiller is a chemical, so this is chemical contamination.

n.0: No solid debris is involved.
n.2: No living organisms are involved.
n.3: Any contamination risk must be reported.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which pairing of contamination type and example is correct?
o: Chemical paired with loose, angular stones and grit in the bore
Physical paired with diesel spilt into the open trench
Microbiological paired with approved potable jointing paste
Microbiological paired with protozoa from soil and foul water
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Protozoa are living organisms, correctly paired with microbiological contamination.

n.0: Stones and grit are physical, not chemical.
n.1: Diesel is chemical, not physical.
n.2: Approved paste is not a micro-organism.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Insects and vermin are a contamination worry mainly because they:
o: Add a useful lubricant film to the joint
Carry micro-organisms into the pipe or fitting
Only ever slightly block the flow of water
Are purely a chemical hazard on the site
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Insects, rodents and other vermin carry micro-organisms and can introduce them into the supply.

n.0: They provide no benefit; they are a hazard.
n.2: Blockage is minor next to the micro risk.
n.3: The risk they bring is microbiological.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Rust flakes and pipe scale come loose inside an old main. These are:
o: Chemical contamination to be neutralised
Physical contamination that should be flushed
Microbiological contamination to be dosed
Safe to leave since they will soon settle
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Loose rust and scale are solid debris, a physical contaminant to be flushed out.

n.0: Rust flakes are solid debris, not a dosed chemical.
n.2: They are not living organisms.
n.3: Loose debris must be removed, not left.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which single word best sums up the source of most harmful microbiological contamination?
o: Sunlight
Sewage
Sandbags
Steelwork
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Most harmful micro-organisms come from sewage and foul water.

n.0: Sunlight is not a source of contamination.
n.2: Sandbags are not a source of organisms.
n.3: Steelwork is not a source of organisms.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Fuel, oil and solvents share which feature that makes them chemical contaminants?
o: They are living organisms that quickly multiply
They are lumps of solid physical site debris in most cases
They are refined substances that pollute the water
They are always completely safe and harmless
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fuels, oils and solvents are chemical substances that pollute drinking water.

n.0: They are chemicals, not living organisms.
n.1: They are liquids, not physical debris.
n.3: They are harmful and must be kept out.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Cloudy water carrying fine soil particles from the trench is an example of:
o: Physical contamination of the water
Chemical contamination of the water
Microbiological contamination there
A reliable sign the water is safe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fine soil particles are solid matter, so this is physical contamination.

n.1: No chemical substance is in the particles.
n.2: The visible cloudiness is soil, which is physical.
n.3: Cloudy water indicates contamination, not safety.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is a common source of contamination during work on the network?
o: Sealed, certified plastic pipe kept in its wrapping
Water tested and confirmed clean at the treatment works
Dirty tools and unclean fittings used on the pipe
A calibrated pressure gauge fitted to the test rig
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Dirty tools and fittings are a frequent source of contamination during work on the main.

n.0: Clean sealed pipe is not a source.
n.1: Treated water is not the source.
n.3: A gauge is equipment, not a source.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Foul water and sewage are dangerous sources of contamination because they contain:
o: Only clean, dissolved and harmless minerals
Large numbers of disease-causing micro-organisms
Approved network disinfectant in solution
Nothing at all that could ever cause harm
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Sewage carries high numbers of harmful micro-organisms, making it the most dangerous source.

n.0: It carries harmful organisms, not just minerals.
n.2: Sewage is a hazard, not a disinfectant.
n.3: It is one of the most harmful sources on site.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative who is unwell with sickness or diarrhoea is a contamination risk because they:
o: Will simply work a little more slowly
Can pass harmful micro-organisms to the water
Cannot lift the heavier pipe and fittings
Have no effect at all on the water supply
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A sick operative can transfer harmful micro-organisms to the water and should not work on the main.

n.0: Speed is not the contamination concern.
n.2: Lifting is not the health risk to the supply.
n.3: An unwell operative can contaminate the supply.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of the following is a recognised source of contamination in an excavation?
o: Freshly opened certified pipe straight from stock
A clean, capped stub end left ready for connection
Treated, disinfected water already inside the main
Dirty standing water pooled in the trench bottom
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Dirty standing water in the trench can enter open pipework and contaminate it.

n.0: Certified pipe is clean, not a source.
n.1: A capped end is protected, not a source.
n.2: Treated water is the product, not a source.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Surface run-off after heavy rain is a contamination source mainly because it can:
o: Cool the exposed pipe to a much safer level
Clean out the inside of the main free of charge
Improve the overall taste of the water supply
Wash dirt and foul matter into the open works
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Run-off carries soil, muck and possibly sewage into open excavations and pipework.

n.0: Cooling is irrelevant; run-off brings dirt.
n.1: Run-off dirties the works, it does not clean.
n.2: Run-off worsens quality, not taste.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: The operative themselves can be a source of contamination through:
o: Wearing the correct, clean disposable gloves
Washing their hands thoroughly before starting
Dirty, unwashed hands touching the inside of pipe
Keeping all fittings sealed until they are needed
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Unwashed, dirty hands can transfer micro-organisms into the pipe, making the operative a source.

n.0: Clean gloves reduce the risk.
n.1: Hand washing reduces the risk.
n.3: Keeping fittings sealed is good practice.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Vermin and animals around the works are a contamination source because they:
o: Provide a useful film of pipe lubricant
Help to keep the trench clear of water
Have no real bearing on water quality on this job
Carry and spread harmful micro-organisms
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Rats and other animals carry micro-organisms that can contaminate exposed pipework.

n.0: Animals give no benefit to the work.
n.1: They do not drain the trench.
n.2: They are a genuine contamination source.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which storage practice makes fittings a contamination source rather than a clean part?
o: Keeping them bagged and sealed until fitting
Storing them off the ground on a clean rack
Leaving them lying uncovered in the mud and dirt
Swabbing them clean just before installation
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fittings left uncovered in dirt pick up soil and organisms and become a source of contamination.

n.0: Bagged fittings stay clean.
n.1: Clean raised storage keeps them safe.
n.3: Swabbing keeps them clean.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A spade used to dig the trench is then used to tap a fitting into the bore. This spade is:
o: A source of physical and microbiological contamination
A safe tool to use simply because it is made of metal
Only ever a risk of chemical contamination on the job
Perfectly fine to use as long as it happens to look dry
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A dirty spade carries soil and organisms into the pipe, a physical and microbiological source.

n.1: Metal does not make a dirty tool safe.
n.2: The risk is soil and organisms, not chemicals.
n.3: Looking dry does not mean it is clean.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which ground condition increases the contamination risk to an open main?
o: Clean, dry and undisturbed natural subsoil
Ground polluted with fuel or with foul water
A properly shored and well-drained dry trench
Firm ground well away from any nearby drains
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Ground polluted with fuel or sewage is a direct source of contamination for an open main.

n.0: Clean dry ground is a lower risk.
n.2: A dry, managed trench reduces risk.
n.3: Being away from drains lowers the risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A leaking sewer running close to a water main under repair is a serious source because it:
o: Adds a helpful boost of pressure to it
Keeps the excavation conveniently warm
Has no real link to the water supply
Can let foul water reach the open pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A nearby leaking sewer can allow foul water to reach and contaminate the open water main.

n.0: A sewer leak endangers the main, it does not help.
n.1: Warmth is irrelevant to the risk.
n.2: It is a direct foul-water source.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which everyday item, if used on the main, can act as a chemical source of contamination?
o: A tin of unapproved grease or jointing paste
A certified potable-water lubricant compound
A clean swab used only for wiping the socket
An approved chlorine dosing tablet for the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Unapproved grease or paste introduces chemicals into the supply and is a chemical source.

n.1: Certified lubricant is approved for use.
n.2: A clean swab is a hygiene aid, not a source.
n.3: Approved dosing is a control, not a contaminant.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Food, drink and cigarette ends left in the excavation are a contamination source because they:
o: Attract vermin and carry micro-organisms
Usefully help to mark where the pipe is
Keep the operative in reasonable spirits
Have no effect at all on the open main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Litter such as food and cigarette ends attracts vermin and carries organisms into the works.

n.1: Litter is not a marker and should not be there.
n.2: Personal comfort is not relevant to the hazard.
n.3: They are a genuine contamination source.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is the most dangerous source of microbiological contamination on site?
o: Clean rainwater held in a properly sealed water butt
Human faecal matter and raw sewage in the ground
Certified pipe fittings still inside their bags
Treated, disinfected water flowing in the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Faecal matter and sewage carry the highest load of harmful organisms and are the biggest danger.

n.0: Sealed clean water is not the concern.
n.2: Bagged fittings are clean and protected.
n.3: Treated water is the product being protected.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A rag pulled from a mucky overall pocket is used to wipe a pipe end. That rag is:
o: A perfectly suitable clean wiping cloth to use
Only ever a chemical hazard to the pipe bore
Completely harmless simply because it is fabric
A likely source of harmful micro-organisms
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A dirty rag from an overall pocket carries organisms and contaminates the pipe end.

n.0: A dirty rag is not a suitable clean cloth.
n.1: The main risk is micro-organisms, not chemicals.
n.2: Being fabric does not make it safe.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Groundwater seeping into a trench from the surrounding soil is a source of contamination because it:
o: Is guaranteed to be of drinking quality
Sterilises the pipe as it flows past it
Brings soil bacteria to the open pipework
Cannot ever reach the open pipe at all from here
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Seeping groundwater carries soil organisms that can enter exposed pipework.

n.0: Groundwater cannot be assumed potable.
n.1: It contaminates rather than sterilises.
n.3: It can reach and contaminate open pipe.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why should tools that touch the inside of a pipe be kept separate from general dig tools?
o: General tools are simply heavier to carry around as a rule
Keeping them separate makes them last much longer
General tools carry soil and organisms into the pipe
It makes no real practical difference on the site
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Keeping clean and dirty tools separate stops soil and organisms being carried into the pipe.

n.0: Weight is not the reason for separation.
n.1: Tool life is not the hygiene reason.
n.3: It makes a real difference to hygiene.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these best describes why the ground itself is a source of contamination?
o: Soil is a fully certified, clean laid material
Soil disinfects any pipe that it happens to touch
Soil only ever contains completely harmless sand
Soil naturally holds bacteria and other organisms
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Soil naturally contains bacteria and other micro-organisms, making the ground a source.

n.0: Soil is not certified clean; it holds organisms.
n.1: Soil contaminates rather than disinfects.
n.2: Soil holds organisms, not just sand.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A bird has been getting into an unsealed hydrant chamber. This is a source of:
o: Chemical contamination from the bird's own feathers
Physical contamination only, with no risk
No contamination that is worth noting here
Microbiological contamination from droppings
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Bird droppings carry micro-organisms, so an accessible chamber is a microbiological source.

n.0: Feathers are not a chemical hazard.
n.1: The droppings carry organisms, a real risk.
n.2: Animal access is a genuine risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these on site would you treat as a likely source of chemical contamination?
o: A sealed, unopened bottle of clean drinking water
A leaking can of fuel sat near the excavation
A bag of clean, certified pipe fittings
A length of new, capped plastic water pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A leaking fuel can beside the dig can introduce chemicals into the works.

n.0: A sealed bottle is not a source of contamination.
n.2: Clean certified fittings are not a chemical source.
n.3: New capped pipe is clean and protected.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: What is the most common way contamination gets into a water main during work?
o: Through an open, unprotected pipe end
Straight through the solid pipe walls
By the water slowly evaporating away
Through a correctly fitted, sound valve
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Open, unprotected pipe ends are the main route by which contamination enters a main.

n.1: Sound pipe walls do not let contamination through.
n.2: Evaporation does not introduce contamination.
n.3: A correctly fitted valve is not an entry point.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Contamination can enter a main during jointing if the operative:
o: Lets the clean pipe end touch the dirty trench
Keeps the bore clean and capped throughout
Uses only the correct, approved lubricant
Wipes the socket over with a clean swab
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Allowing the clean bore to touch dirty ground lets contamination into the main during jointing.

n.1: Keeping it clean and capped prevents entry.
n.2: Approved lubricant is correct practice.
n.3: Swabbing clean helps prevent contamination.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Backflow can introduce contamination into a main when:
o: Dirty water is drawn or pushed back into it
Clean water flows out through a customer tap
The main is fully charged, sealed and sound
Pressure stays steady, positive and normal
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Backflow is dirty water being drawn or forced back into the main, carrying contamination with it.

n.1: Normal outward flow is not backflow.
n.2: A sealed, charged main resists backflow.
n.3: Positive pressure helps prevent backflow.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative leaves for lunch with a pipe end open in a wet trench. The risk is that:
o: Trench water and dirt enter the open main
The pipe end dries out and then cracks
The water pressure rises far too high
Nothing happens, as it is only lunch every time
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: An open end in a wet trench lets dirty water and debris flow straight into the main.

n.1: A wet trench does not dry the pipe out.
n.2: Pressure is not the concern with an open end.
n.3: Even a short time open allows contamination in.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: How does contamination most often get in when an unclean fitting is installed?
o: The fitting simply refuses to seal at all
The fitting changes the water colour itself
Dirt on the fitting is carried into the flow
The fitting cools the water down too far on the works
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A dirty fitting brings its soil and organisms straight into contact with the water.

n.0: A dirty fitting can still seal yet contaminate.
n.1: Colour change is a symptom, not the route.
n.3: Temperature is not the contamination route.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why does a sudden drop in main pressure raise the contamination risk?
o: It can allow dirty water to be sucked back in
It makes the pipe walls become much thicker
It sterilises the whole inside of the main
It has no effect at all on contamination in practice
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A pressure drop can cause backflow, sucking contaminated water into the main.

n.1: Pressure does not change wall thickness.
n.2: Low pressure does not sterilise anything.
n.3: Low pressure is a real backflow risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Contamination is most likely to enter the network at points where:
o: The main runs sealed underground
The water is under full pressure
Valves are shut and fully intact
The pipe is opened up or is cut into
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Opening or cutting into a main exposes the inside and is where contamination gets in.

n.0: Sealed intact pipe keeps contamination out.
n.1: Full pressure helps keep contamination out.
n.2: Intact valves are not an entry point.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Mud is knocked off a boot and drops into an open socket before jointing. This shows how:
o: Water can evaporate out of the open socket
The joint becomes much stronger with mud
Pressure is somehow added into the main in most cases
Loose debris can fall straight into the pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Loose mud dropping into an open socket is a direct example of debris entering the pipe.

n.0: Evaporation is not what is happening here.
n.1: Mud weakens hygiene, it does not strengthen.
n.2: Dropping mud does not add pressure.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which action allows contamination into a main rather than preventing it?
o: Fitting caps to both ends before laying pipe
Swabbing the socket clean before jointing up
Dragging pipe through the open trench uncapped
Keeping the fittings bagged until they are used
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Dragging uncapped pipe through the trench lets soil and water into the bore.

n.0: Capping prevents contamination.
n.1: Swabbing prevents contamination.
n.3: Bagging keeps fittings clean.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Contamination can be introduced through connections if:
o: A proper air gap is kept and maintained on this job
A cross-connection links foul and clean pipes
An approved backflow device is fitted well
The clean and foul systems stay separate
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A cross-connection between foul and clean pipework lets contamination pass into the supply.

n.0: An air gap prevents backflow.
n.2: A backflow device is a safeguard.
n.3: Keeping them separate prevents contamination.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A new pipe is stored with one end lying in a puddle. Before use the operative should:
o: Fit it quickly before the puddle spreads
Assume the puddle water is perfectly safe
Reject the pipe, or clean and swab that end
Cut off the pressure to the main and carry on
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A pipe end that sat in a puddle is contaminated and must be cleaned and swabbed or rejected.

n.0: Speed does not remove the contamination.
n.1: Puddle water cannot be assumed safe.
n.3: Pressure is not the issue; the dirty end is.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: How can contamination get into a main during a flushing or connection job?
o: By dirty hoses or fittings touching the water
By using clean, disinfected hoses throughout
By keeping every open pipe end properly capped
By working only with clean, freshly washed hands
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Dirty hoses and fittings put contamination straight into the flowing water.

n.1: Clean, disinfected hoses prevent this.
n.2: Capping ends prevents entry.
n.3: Clean hands reduce the risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why is jointing a particular moment of risk for getting contamination into a main?
o: The clean bore is briefly open to the surroundings
The water supply is always switched off first
The pipe stays fully sealed at that very point
No dirt is able to reach the joint area at all
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: During jointing the bore is open, so soil, water or dirty hands can introduce contamination.

n.1: The bore is still open even if water is off.
n.2: It is open, not sealed, during jointing.
n.3: Dirt can readily reach an open joint.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A hose used earlier to pump out foul water is grabbed to flush a clean main. The danger is:
o: The hose is simply too short to reach
The hose lowers the pressure in the main
There is no danger at all once it is wet
Foul residue in the hose enters the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A hose used on foul water carries residue that would contaminate the clean main.

n.0: Length is not the hygiene concern.
n.1: Pressure is not the issue here.
n.2: Wetness does not remove foul residue.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Contamination can enter through an open end even quickly because:
o: Pipe ends will seal themselves over enough time
Dirt, water and insects can get in within moments
Open pipe ends only ever draw in clean fresh air
Very short periods of exposure are always safe as a rule
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: It only takes moments for dirt, water or insects to enter an unprotected open end.

n.0: Open ends do not self-seal.
n.2: They can draw in dirt and water too.
n.3: Even brief exposure allows contamination.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these describes contamination entering a main by backflow?
o: Clean, treated water pushed out to a customer's tap
Water flowing normally down along the pipe
Trapped air venting from a high point valve
Non-potable water siphoned back into the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Backflow is non-potable water being drawn back into the main against the normal flow.

n.0: That is normal forward supply.
n.1: Normal flow is not backflow.
n.2: Venting air is not backflow of dirty water.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative sneezes over an open pipe end without covering up. This can introduce:
o: A useful amount of extra water pressure to it
A helpful dose of chlorine into the water
Nothing at all, since saliva is sterile
Micro-organisms directly into the open main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A sneeze over an open end can carry harmful micro-organisms straight into the main.

n.0: A sneeze adds no pressure.
n.1: It adds contamination, not disinfectant.
n.2: Saliva carries organisms and is not sterile.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Contamination gets into fittings before installation most often when they are:
o: Kept sealed inside their own packaging
Stored clean and up off the ground level
Left lying uncovered on the dirty ground
Swabbed over just before they are fitted
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fittings left uncovered on the ground pick up contamination before they are even installed.

n.0: Sealed fittings stay clean.
n.1: Clean raised storage protects them.
n.3: Swabbing keeps them clean.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why must a main be kept charged and under pressure where possible during work?
o: Positive pressure helps keep contamination out
High pressure makes the jointing much easier
The pressure helps keep the operative warm every time
It has no real bearing on contamination risk
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Keeping the main under positive pressure resists the ingress of contamination.

n.1: Pressure is not about ease of jointing.
n.2: Pressure is unrelated to warmth.
n.3: Positive pressure is a key defence.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Soil is allowed to wash into a valve chamber that connects to the main. This matters because:
o: The soil will support and steady the pipe better
The valve chamber will now drain far more quickly
It is really only a matter of general tidiness on the works
The soil can reach the pipework and contaminate it
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Soil washing into a connected chamber can reach the pipework and contaminate the supply.

n.0: Loose soil does not usefully support pipe.
n.1: Soil ingress does not aid drainage.
n.2: It is a genuine contamination route.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: What should be done with any open pipe end that is to be left unattended?
o: Leave it open to get some fresh air
Fit a clean cap or plug to seal it
Point it downwards into the open trench
Cover it over loosely with some soil
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Every open end must be capped or plugged to keep contamination out.

n.0: An open end lets contamination in.
n.2: Pointing down still lets in dirt and water.
n.3: Soil is a contaminant, not a proper seal.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why is capping open ends one of the most important hygiene habits on the network?
o: It makes the length of pipe much easier to lift
It saves the cost of buying end fittings later on
It stops dirt, water and insects entering the main
It keeps the pipe ends looking neat and tidy in practice
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Capping ends is a simple, vital step that keeps contamination out of the main.

n.0: Capping is about hygiene, not handling.
n.1: The purpose is contamination control.
n.3: Tidiness is not the reason; hygiene is.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative is called away mid-job with a pipe end open. They should first:
o: Leave it and just deal with it later in most cases
Lay the open end down in trench water
Cap or plug the open end before leaving
Throw a rag loosely over the open end
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Before leaving, the open end must be properly capped or plugged.

n.0: Leaving it open invites contamination.
n.1: That directly contaminates the pipe.
n.3: A loose rag is not a proper seal.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is a correct way to protect a stored length of pipe with open ends?
o: Keep both ends capped until the pipe is used
Remove the caps so it can breathe freely
Store it open end down into the trench mud
Leave just one end open for convenience on this job
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Stored pipe should have both ends capped until the moment it is installed.

n.1: Pipe needs sealing, not breathing.
n.2: An open end in mud gets contaminated.
n.3: Any open end is a contamination risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: If a proper end cap is not to hand, the safest action is to:
o: Open the pipe anyway and simply hope for the best
Get a suitable cap or plug before opening the pipe
Seal the open end using some loose trench backfill
Stuff the open end tightly with a dirty site cloth
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: You should have the correct cap or plug ready before exposing the pipe, keeping it protected.

n.0: Working without protection risks contamination.
n.2: Backfill is dirt, not a clean seal.
n.3: A dirty cloth introduces contamination.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Capping open ends is especially important when the trench is:
o: Perfectly dry and free of dust
Freshly shored and quite empty
Signed and fenced off correctly
Wet or holding standing water
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A wet trench makes an uncapped end far more likely to take in dirty water, so capping is vital.

n.0: Capping still matters, but a wet trench is worst.
n.1: Shoring does not remove the need to cap.
n.2: Signage does not stop water entering an end.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: At the end of the shift the connection is not finished. The open main should be:
o: Left open and ready to work on in the morning
Filled up with trench spoil for the overnight period
Securely capped and left under pressure if possible
Covered over with just a plastic bag and some tape
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: An unfinished open main should be securely capped and, where possible, kept under pressure overnight.

n.0: An open main overnight invites contamination.
n.1: Spoil is a contaminant, not a seal.
n.3: A taped bag is not a secure cap.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: What is the main purpose of a pipe plug or cap during works?
o: To make the pipe heavier and more stable to lay
To colour-code the different pipes around the site
To raise the water pressure inside the pipe bore
To keep the inside of the pipe clean and protected
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Caps and plugs exist to keep the pipe interior clean and free of contamination.

n.0: They are for hygiene, not weight.
n.1: They are not colour-coding devices.
n.2: They protect the bore, not raise pressure.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which statement about open ends is correct?
o: They should never be left open to the trench
They are fine left open if the weather is dry
They only need capping during the winter months
They can safely be left open for a few hours
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Open ends must never be left exposed to the trench; they must be capped or plugged.

n.1: Dry weather still allows dust and insects in.
n.2: Capping is required in all seasons.
n.3: Even a short time open is a real risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative caps a pipe end but the cap itself is caked in mud. The correct step is to:
o: Fit the muddy cap onto the end as it is as a rule
Skip the cap now that one has been found
Wipe the pipe end over with the muddy cap
Clean the cap before fitting it to the pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A cap must itself be clean, or it will contaminate the very end it is meant to protect.

n.0: A muddy cap carries contamination onto the pipe.
n.1: The end still needs a clean seal.
n.2: That spreads contamination onto the bore.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Keeping ends capped mainly protects against contamination entering through:
o: The solid outer wall of the pipe run
A properly closed and sealed valve
The exposed open opening of the pipe
The sound certified factory joint
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Caps protect the exposed opening, which is the route by which contamination would enter.

n.0: Sound walls are not an entry point.
n.1: A sealed valve is not the opening protected.
n.3: A sound factory joint is not the exposed end.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why should caps and plugs be kept clean and stored properly on the vehicle?
o: So that they take up rather less space inside the van every time
So that they can be sold on again at the end of the job
So that they are much lighter and easier to carry about
So they do not contaminate the pipe when they are fitted
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A dirty cap contaminates the pipe, so caps must be kept clean and stored properly.

n.0: Storage neatness is not the reason.
n.1: Caps are equipment, not stock to sell.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant to the purpose.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A fitting will only be open 'for a minute' while a tool is fetched. Best practice is to:
o: Leave it open, as it is only for a minute
Cap the open end even for that short time
Rest the open end down on the spoil heap
Blow into the open end to keep it clear
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Ends should be capped even for short periods, as contamination can enter in moments.

n.0: A minute is long enough for contamination.
n.2: Spoil directly contaminates the end.
n.3: Breath carries micro-organisms into the pipe.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these shows a failure to keep pipe ends protected?
o: Laying uncapped pipe overnight in an open trench
Fitting a clean plug to the end before a break
Capping both ends before the pipe is stored away
Keeping the plug on right up until connection
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Leaving uncapped pipe overnight in the trench is a clear failure to protect the ends.

n.1: That is correct protection.
n.2: That is good practice.
n.3: That is the correct approach.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: The habit of capping ends supports the wider aim of:
o: Keeping treated drinking water free of contamination
Speeding up the digging of the trench each day
Reducing the total amount of pipe that is used
Making the finished pipe run look a lot neater
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Capping ends helps keep the treated water clean, which is the whole point of hygiene rules.

n.1: Capping is unrelated to dig speed.
n.2: It does not affect pipe quantities.
n.3: Appearance is not the aim; clean water is.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative finds a stub main on site with no cap fitted. They should:
o: Ignore it, since it is not their own pipe
Push some loose spoil into the open end
Assume that someone else will deal with it
Report it and get the end properly capped
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: An uncapped stub is a contamination risk that should be reported and properly capped.

n.0: Contamination risks must not be ignored.
n.1: Spoil contaminates rather than protects.
n.2: You should act, not assume it is handled.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why is it not acceptable to plug an open end with rag or paper?
o: They are simply too expensive to use up on the works
They make the pipe far too heavy to lift
They happen to be the wrong colour code
They shed fibres and carry contamination in
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Rag and paper are not clean, sealed caps; they shed fibres and can carry contamination.

n.0: Cost is not the issue.
n.1: Weight is not the concern.
n.2: Colour coding is irrelevant here.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: On arriving at site, which of these should be treated as a contamination risk?
o: A clean, dry and properly capped pipe stub end
Pipe fittings still sealed in their bags
A tidy, well-drained and shored trench
A foul smell coming up from the excavation
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A foul smell can indicate sewage or foul water, a clear contamination risk to investigate.

n.0: A clean capped stub is protected, not a risk.
n.1: Sealed fittings are clean.
n.2: A dry, tidy trench is lower risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative notices an oily rainbow sheen on the water in the trench. This suggests:
o: The water here is especially clean and pure
The pipe has just been freshly disinfected
Possible chemical contamination in the ground
There is really nothing at all to worry about
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: An oily sheen points to fuel or oil in the ground, a chemical contamination risk.

n.0: A sheen indicates pollution, not cleanliness.
n.1: A sheen is not a sign of disinfection.
n.3: It is a genuine chemical risk to act on.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which finding should make an operative stop and seek advice before connecting?
o: A properly labelled clean water supply main
Correctly stored and capped lengths of pipe
Clear signs of sewage or foul water in the dig
A dry trench with firm, clean and well-shored sides
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Signs of sewage mean a serious contamination risk, so work should stop until advice is taken.

n.0: A labelled clean main is normal.
n.1: Capped stored pipe is good practice.
n.3: A clean dry trench is not a warning sign.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Discoloured or cloudy water appearing during work can be a sign of:
o: A perfectly healthy and entirely normal water supply
Water that is somehow safer than it was before
The correct chlorine levels being reached now
Contamination or disturbed material in the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Discoloured or cloudy water can signal contamination or disturbed debris and should be investigated.

n.0: Discolouration is not a sign of health.
n.1: It suggests a problem, not extra safety.
n.2: Cloudiness is not a chlorine indicator.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Rats are seen around an open chamber connected to the main. The operative should:
o: Carry on working, as animals do no harm in practice
Treat it as a contamination risk and act on it
Leave the chamber open to let them get out
Assume that the water will be perfectly fine
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Vermin near open pipework is a real contamination risk that must be acted upon.

n.0: Vermin carry organisms and are a real hazard.
n.2: Leaving it open increases the risk.
n.3: You must act rather than assume.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is a warning sign of possible contamination that should be reported?
o: Cool, clear water running at the correct pressure
Neatly bagged, clean and certified new fittings
A capped main sitting under steady, normal pressure
An unusual chemical or fuel smell in the trench
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: An unusual chemical or fuel smell suggests contamination and should be reported.

n.0: Normal clear water is not a warning sign.
n.1: Clean bagged fittings are not a hazard.
n.2: A capped main is well protected.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: The previous gang left a pipe end open overnight in a wet trench. The operative should:
o: Suspect contamination and not simply connect it
Connect it quickly in order to make up lost time
Assume the overnight water has cleaned it out
Ignore it, since it was not their own doing
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A pipe left open overnight in water should be treated as contaminated, not simply connected.

n.1: Speed must not override hygiene.
n.2: Standing water contaminates, not cleans.
n.3: The risk must be dealt with regardless.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Recognising contamination risks on site mainly relies on the operative:
o: Staying alert to smells, sights and conditions
Only checking the job paperwork back in the parked van
Waiting for a lab result before even looking
Trusting that all sites are always kept clean
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Operatives spot risks by staying alert to what they smell, see and find around the works.

n.1: Paperwork alone will not reveal hazards.
n.2: Alertness comes before any lab result.
n.3: Sites cannot be assumed clean.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these is NOT a contamination warning to look out for on site?
o: A strong smell of sewage in the nearby ground
An oily film sitting on the trench water
Clean water running clear at the normal pressure
Rodent droppings found inside an open valve chamber
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Clear water at normal pressure is a good sign, not a contamination warning.

n.0: Sewage smell is a serious warning.
n.1: An oily film indicates chemical contamination.
n.3: Droppings signal a microbiological risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative finds a cut main right next to a leaking drain. The safest response is to:
o: Connect it first and then mention it later
Seal up the leaking drain with the water pipe
Assume that the drain water is clean enough
Report the risk and not connect until advised
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A cut main beside a leaking drain is a foul-water risk; report it and hold off connecting.

n.0: Connecting first risks the supply.
n.1: That is not a valid or safe fix.
n.2: Drain water must be treated as foul.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Why should an operative be suspicious of any standing water in an excavation?
o: It always proves the pipe is fully watertight
It may carry contamination into open pipework
It usefully keeps the fittings cool and damp
It shows that the trench is very well drained
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Standing water in a dig is a likely contamination source for any open pipework nearby.

n.0: Standing water does not prove watertightness.
n.2: Cooling is irrelevant; it is a hazard.
n.3: Standing water shows poor drainage.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Fittings on site are lying uncovered in the dirt. The operative should recognise that they:
o: Are fine to fit as they are, since they are dry
Only need a quick shake to get them ready to use
Are contaminated and must be cleaned or replaced
Cannot possibly be contaminated out on the site
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Fittings left in the dirt are contaminated and must be cleaned, swabbed or replaced before use.

n.0: Being dry does not make them clean.
n.1: A shake does not remove contamination.
n.3: Uncovered fittings in dirt are contaminated.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these smells on site is the strongest signal of microbiological contamination risk?
o: A pleasant smell of fresh cut grass
A distinct sewage or foul drains smell
A smell of clean, ordinary rainwater
A faint smell of brand new plastic pipe
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A sewage or drains smell strongly suggests foul water and a microbiological risk.

n.0: Cut grass is not a contamination indicator.
n.2: Clean rain smell is not a warning sign.
n.3: New pipe smell is not a contamination signal.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: An operative is unsure whether a main has been contaminated. The correct action is to:
o: Carry on regardless and just connect it up anyway
Stop, report it and get guidance before proceeding
Take a guess and hope that it is probably fine in most cases
Say nothing about it to keep the job moving on
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: If in doubt about contamination, stop, report and seek guidance before going further.

n.0: Proceeding when unsure risks the supply.
n.2: Guessing is not acceptable with drinking water.
n.3: Concerns must be raised, not hidden.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Recognising a contamination risk early is important because it lets the operative:
o: Finish the whole job a good deal more cheaply
Get away with not wearing protective gloves
Skip having to cap the open pipe ends at all
Act to protect the supply before harm is done
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Spotting risks early allows action to protect the supply before contamination reaches the public.

n.0: Cost saving is not the purpose.
n.1: It does not remove the need for gloves.
n.2: Ends must still be capped regardless.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Dust and debris are blowing across an open pipe end on a windy day. The operative should:
o: Let the wind blow the pipe clean by itself
Cap the end to keep debris out of the bore
Wait for the wind to drop away naturally
Assume the wind cannot cause any real harm
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Wind-blown debris is a contamination risk, so the end should be capped to keep the bore clean.

n.0: Wind carries debris in; it does not clean.
n.2: Waiting leaves the pipe exposed.
n.3: Wind-blown debris is a real risk.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: Which of these best shows good awareness of contamination risk on site?
o: Opening up the main first and then looking around later
Ignoring any bad smells in order to keep to schedule on this job
Assuming the ground on every site is always kept clean
Checking the trench for foul water before opening the main
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: Checking the trench for foul water before opening the main shows proper risk awareness.

n.0: Checks come before opening.
n.1: Smells are warnings not to ignore.
n.2: Ground must be assessed, not assumed.

Contamination: Types & Sources.q: A strong smell of fuel rises from the ground as a trench is dug near the main. The operative should:
o: Carry on digging, as a fuel smell is quite normal
Open the main up to let the smell clear away faster
Stop, treat it as chemical contamination and report it
Ignore the smell as long as the water still looks clear
Contamination: Types & Sources.w: A fuel smell from the ground signals chemical contamination and must be reported before work continues.

n.0: A fuel smell is a warning, not normal.
n.1: Opening the main risks drawing in the contaminant.
n.3: Clear water does not rule out chemical contamination.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: In simple terms, what does 'backflow' mean on a clean water supply?
o: Water flowing the wrong way back into the clean supply, carrying contamination with it
Water flowing faster than normal through a section of main under high pressure
Water being drawn off a hydrant to fill a tanker for site use
Water sitting still in a dead-leg until it is flushed away to waste
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Backflow is water travelling the wrong way, back towards the clean main, and it can drag pollution in with it.

n.1: High flow in the normal direction is not backflow; direction is what matters.
n.2: Drawing water off in the normal direction is ordinary use, not backflow.
n.3: Stagnant water in a dead-leg is a separate issue and is not reverse flow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is backflow treated as a serious hazard to the public supply?
o: It can pull contaminants into treated water that people then drink
It slows the delivery of water to properties at the end of the main
It makes the water look cloudy but leaves it perfectly safe to drink
It only wastes a small amount of water at the point of the fitting
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Reverse flow can carry dirty or chemical-laden water into the drinking supply, so it is a public health risk.

n.1: Backflow is a contamination risk, not merely a delivery-speed problem.
n.2: The danger is unsafe water, not just appearance; it can be genuinely harmful.
n.3: The harm is contamination of many users, not a little wasted water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which statement best captures the direction of flow that defines backflow?
o: Water moves from the mains outward to the customer as normal
Water moves downhill through the pipe under the force of gravity
Water moves round a ring main to balance pressure between zones
Water moves from a fitting or appliance back towards the mains
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Backflow is reverse movement, from the property side back towards the clean main.

n.0: Mains-to-customer is the correct, intended direction, not backflow.
n.1: Gravity flow in the normal direction is ordinary and not backflow.
n.2: Balancing flow around a ring main is normal network behaviour.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Backflow is dangerous mainly because the water that flows back may contain what?
o: Extra chlorine added deliberately at the treatment works
Harmless air that has been drawn into the pipework
Clean water that has simply been warmed by the sun
Germs or chemicals picked up on the customer side of the connection
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The returning water can carry bacteria or chemicals from the customer's own system into the main.

n.0: Chlorine dosing at the works is controlled and not the backflow hazard.
n.1: Air ingress is a nuisance but is not the contamination risk being described.
n.2: Warm clean water is not the pollution that makes backflow dangerous.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A customer's premises are connected to the public main. Why does backflow from those premises concern the water company?
o: The premises would be billed for water they did not actually use
The main would lose pressure permanently once flow reverses once
The premises would receive water that is slightly warmer than usual
Pollution from the premises could spread to other customers on the same main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Contamination that flows back does not stay local; it can travel to neighbouring properties on the shared main.

n.0: Billing is not the safety concern raised by backflow.
n.1: A single reverse-flow event does not cause a permanent pressure loss.
n.2: Water temperature is not the reason backflow is a health concern.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these is the clearest sign that you understand why backflow protection matters?
o: You make sure water always reaches the highest tap in a building
You keep any possible pollutant from being able to enter the drinking main
You ensure the main is kept at the lowest safe working pressure
You allow water to drain back to waste after every single job
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The whole point of backflow protection is to stop contaminants ever reaching the potable supply.

n.0: Reaching the top tap is about supply, not about protecting water quality.
n.2: Running the main at low pressure would make back-siphonage more likely, not safer.
n.3: Draining back to waste is unrelated to preventing contamination of the main.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Backflow can occur even when the mains supply is working normally. Which situation still allows it?
o: The pressure on the customer's side becomes higher than the mains pressure
The mains pressure stays well above the pressure at every appliance
The water in the main is flowing steadily towards the customer
The customer's stop tap has been fully closed for the day
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: If pressure on the customer side climbs above the main (back-pressure), water can be pushed back in even with a healthy main.

n.1: When the main stays higher, flow is held in the correct direction.
n.2: Steady flow towards the customer is normal delivery, not backflow.
n.3: A closed stop tap isolates the property and prevents flow either way.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which everyday description matches what a backflow event actually does?
o: It pushes clean water out of a burst pipe onto the road surface
It raises the temperature of the water inside the service pipe
It lets used or dirty water travel back up a pipe into the clean supply
It adds a small amount of extra pressure to the whole network
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: In a backflow event, contaminated water moves back up the pipe and can enter the clean supply.

n.0: Water escaping from a burst is a leak, not reverse contamination of the main.
n.1: Backflow is about direction and contamination, not temperature.
n.3: Backflow does not add useful pressure; it is an unwanted reverse movement.
