Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why can a single backflow incident affect a large number of people?
o: Water companies always shut down an entire town after any incident
Contaminated water can be carried along the shared main to many properties
Every property has its own separate main that cannot be reached
The contamination stays trapped inside one tap and goes no further
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Because properties share the main, pollution that flows back can reach numerous connected homes and businesses.

n.0: Automatic town-wide shutdowns are not what makes an incident wide-reaching.
n.2: Properties share mains; they are not each fed by an isolated pipe.
n.3: Contamination in the main is not confined to a single tap.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: The core reason we guard against backflow on potable networks is to protect what?
o: The quality and safety of the drinking water reaching the public
The flow rate available at the very end of a long main
The paint and coating on the inside of the water pipes
The record of how much water each customer has drawn
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Backflow protection exists to keep the drinking water safe and clean for everyone on the supply.

n.1: Flow rate at the main's end is a supply issue, not the safety reason.
n.2: Pipe coatings are a durability matter, not the reason for backflow control.
n.3: Metering records are unrelated to preventing contamination.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which pairing correctly separates normal flow from backflow?
o: Normal flow goes tap to main; backflow goes main to tap
Normal flow goes main to tap; backflow goes tap back to main
Normal flow and backflow both travel from the main to the tap
Normal flow and backflow both travel from the tap to the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Water should travel from the main out to the tap; backflow is the unwanted reverse of that.

n.0: This reverses the two directions and is incorrect.
n.2: Backflow by definition is the reverse of normal flow, not the same direction.
n.3: Normal flow is main-to-tap, so both cannot be tap-to-main.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A backflow risk is present wherever the clean supply could meet what?
o: Any source of water or liquid that is not fit to drink
Another length of brand-new potable pipe of the same size
A pressure gauge fitted to check the mains pressure
A meter recording the volume used by the property
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The hazard arises where drinking water could be joined to something unwholesome that might flow back.

n.1: Joining clean pipe to clean pipe is not itself a contamination hazard.
n.2: A pressure gauge does not introduce a pollutant to flow back.
n.3: A meter measures use and is not a source of contamination.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is it wrong to assume the mains pressure will always stop backflow on its own?
o: Mains pressure is measured only once when the pipe is first laid
Mains pressure is the same value in every pipe across the country
Mains pressure is set by the customer at their own stop tap
Mains pressure can drop or be exceeded, leaving the supply unprotected
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Pressure is not guaranteed; it can fall or be overcome, so physical protection is still needed.

n.0: Pressure is not a one-off reading; it changes constantly in use.
n.1: Pressure varies by location and demand, not a single national value.
n.2: Customers do not set mains pressure; the network does.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What is 'back-siphonage'?
o: Backflow caused by extra pressure building on the customer's side
Backflow caused by a drop or loss of pressure in the mains
Water hammer felt when a valve is shut too quickly on site
Air being deliberately pumped into a main to test for leaks
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Back-siphonage happens when mains pressure falls and the low pressure sucks water backwards into the main.

n.0: That describes back-pressure, the other cause of backflow, not back-siphonage.
n.2: Water hammer is a pressure surge, not the siphoning of water back.
n.3: Air testing is a planned procedure, not back-siphonage.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which event on the network is most likely to trigger back-siphonage?
o: A burst main that suddenly drops the pressure in the pipe
A quiet night period when almost no water is being used
A gentle steady demand across an ordinary working day
A newly opened valve that slowly refills an empty section
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A burst causes a sharp pressure loss, and that low pressure can siphon water backwards.

n.1: Low overnight demand tends to keep pressure high, not cause a loss.
n.2: Steady moderate demand does not usually collapse the pressure.
n.3: Slowly refilling a main is a controlled action, not a sudden pressure loss.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Heavy demand from firefighting draws huge volumes from a main. How can this cause back-siphonage nearby?
o: The extra flow raises pressure so much that pipes push water outward
The cold water freezes and blocks the pipe against any movement
The chlorine level rises and stops any water moving backwards
The sudden large draw lowers pressure and can pull water back into the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A large, rapid demand can collapse local pressure, and the resulting suction pulls water back from connected fittings.

n.0: A big draw lowers pressure locally; it does not raise it.
n.1: Freezing is unrelated to the pressure-driven siphon effect.
n.2: Chlorine level does not govern whether siphonage occurs.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Back-siphonage and back-pressure are the two types of backflow. What sets back-siphonage apart?
o: It is driven by high pressure downstream pushing water backwards
It only happens inside sealed tanks that hold no air at all
It is driven by low pressure in the supply pulling water backwards
It only happens when a pump is deliberately run in reverse
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Back-siphonage is the low-pressure (suction) type; back-pressure is the opposite, high-pressure type.

n.0: High downstream pressure pushing water back is back-pressure, not siphonage.
n.1: Siphonage is not limited to sealed airless tanks.
n.3: A reversed pump is not required for siphonage to occur.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: During a mains repair the pressure is dropped low. Why is this a back-siphonage risk?
o: Low pressure forces extra clean water out through every open tap
Low pressure automatically closes all the check valves on the system
Low pressure can siphon water from connected fittings back into the main
Low pressure makes the water too heavy to move in any direction
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: When pressure is deliberately lowered, any connected source can be sucked back, so protection matters most then.

n.0: Low pressure reduces, not increases, the water pushed out of taps.
n.1: Low pressure does not by itself guarantee every check valve seals.
n.3: Water does not become 'too heavy'; low pressure enables reverse flow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which phrase best completes the sentence: back-siphonage occurs when mains pressure ...?
o: rises above the safe maximum for the pipe material
falls below the pressure at a connected fitting or vessel
matches exactly the pressure at every property served
is measured and logged by the company each morning
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Siphonage needs the main to become the lower pressure, so water is drawn from the higher-pressure fitting backwards.

n.0: A pressure rise is not the trigger for the suction effect.
n.2: Equal pressures give no driving force for reverse flow.
n.3: Logging pressure is monitoring, not a cause of siphonage.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why does a hose left in a bucket become dangerous specifically during a pressure drop?
o: The bucket water freezes solid and cracks the connected hose
The falling pressure can siphon the bucket's dirty water into the pipe
The rising pressure blows the hose clean out of the bucket
The bucket water evaporates before it can reach the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A pressure drop turns the submerged hose into a siphon, pulling the bucket's contents back towards the main.

n.0: Freezing is not the mechanism; suction is.
n.2: The hazard here is a pressure fall, not a rise blowing the hose out.
n.3: Evaporation does not prevent the suction of liquid back up the hose.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A tanker is drawing hard from a hydrant and the local pressure sags. What backflow type is most in play?
o: Back-pressure, because the tanker has raised the system pressure
Water hammer, because a valve slammed shut somewhere on the main
Air-lock, because trapped air has stopped the water moving at all
Back-siphonage, because the heavy draw has lowered the pressure
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The heavy draw drops pressure, so any connected source can be siphoned back; this is back-siphonage.

n.0: The tanker lowers pressure by drawing hard, so it is not back-pressure.
n.1: Water hammer is a surge event, not the sustained suction described.
n.2: An air-lock stops flow but is not the reverse-suction hazard here.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these keeps back-siphonage from contaminating the main when pressure is lost?
o: A longer service pipe run to the property boundary
A larger diameter main carrying more water overall
A suitable air gap or backflow device fitted at the connection
A brighter warning label stuck onto the outside tap
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Physical protection such as an air gap or check device stops the siphon reaching the main during a pressure loss.

n.0: Pipe length does not stop reverse flow during a pressure drop.
n.1: A bigger main does not by itself provide backflow protection.
n.3: A label warns people but does not physically prevent siphonage.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is back-siphonage often described as the main 'sucking' water in?
o: The main heats up and expands, pulling water along with it
A pump inside the main actively vacuums water from the taps
Gravity always pulls water downhill towards the lowest point
Low pressure in the main draws water from higher-pressure connections
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The pressure difference acts like suction, drawing water from the connected side into the lower-pressure main.

n.0: Thermal expansion is not the cause of the suction effect.
n.1: There is no vacuum pump in the main creating this; it is pressure difference.
n.2: Gravity alone does not explain suction back into a pressurised main.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Back-siphonage is most likely at a moment when the main is doing what?
o: Holding a steady, healthy pressure throughout the day
Sitting empty and switched off for planned maintenance
Being flushed slowly to clear discoloured water away
Losing pressure quickly, for example after a burst or big draw
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Rapid pressure loss creates the suction that drives back-siphonage.

n.0: Steady healthy pressure resists reverse flow.
n.1: An empty, isolated main is not under the live suction that siphons water in.
n.2: Slow flushing is controlled forward flow, not a siphonage trigger.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which statement about back-siphonage is correct?
o: It only happens when a booster pump is switched on
It cannot happen unless the water is warmer than the pipe
It relies on a pressure difference, not on any pump
It only affects plastic pipes and never metal ones
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Back-siphonage is driven purely by the pressure difference between the main and the connected source.

n.0: No pump is required; the pressure drop alone drives it.
n.1: Temperature is not what governs siphonage.
n.3: Pipe material does not decide whether siphonage occurs.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What is a 'cross-connection' on a water system?
o: A planned junction where two clean mains are joined together
A meter fitted where the service pipe enters the property
A short branch installed to feed an extra drinking tap
An unintended link between potable water and a non-potable source
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A cross-connection is any accidental connection that lets non-potable water reach the clean supply.

n.0: Joining two clean mains on purpose is normal pipework, not a cross-connection hazard.
n.1: A meter is a measuring device, not a link to a non-potable source.
n.2: A branch feeding a clean tap is ordinary potable pipework.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these is a classic example of a cross-connection?
o: A hose left dangling in a tank of non-drinking water
A tap fitted with a swivel aerator on its outlet
A stop tap installed at the property boundary
A pressure-reducing valve set on the incoming main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A hose in a non-potable tank links the clean supply to dirty water and is a textbook cross-connection.

n.1: An aerator is a harmless outlet fitting, not a link to a pollutant.
n.2: A boundary stop tap is a normal isolation fitting.
n.3: A pressure-reducing valve controls pressure, not a contamination link.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: An operative runs a hose from a standpipe into a pond to fill a bowser. Why is this a cross-connection risk?
o: Pond water is always cleaner than the water in the main
Pond water could be drawn back through the hose into the clean supply
The hose would burst because the pond water is too cold
The bowser would overfill and spill onto the ground
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The submerged hose links potable water to pond water, so on a pressure drop the pond water could be siphoned back.

n.0: Pond water is non-potable and cannot be assumed cleaner than the main.
n.2: Temperature is not the reason this is a cross-connection risk.
n.3: Overfilling is a spillage nuisance, not the contamination hazard here.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of the following would count as a cross-connection to avoid?
o: A drinking-water pipe joined to another drinking-water pipe
A drinking-water pipe fitted with an approved double check valve on site
A drinking-water pipe protected by a proper air gap
A drinking-water pipe joined to a pipe carrying recycled grey water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Linking potable pipe to grey water allows contamination to cross over, which is exactly what must be avoided.

n.0: Joining two potable pipes is not a cross-connection hazard.
n.1: A double check valve is protection, not an unguarded cross-connection.
n.2: An air gap is protection against, not an example of, a cross-connection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why are cross-connections considered so risky even if they look harmless?
o: They always leak clean water onto the floor straight away
They make the water pressure rise above safe limits at once each time
They can quietly let contaminated water enter the drinking supply
They can only ever affect the property where they are made
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A cross-connection may sit unnoticed until a pressure change lets pollution flow across into the clean supply.

n.0: A cross-connection need not leak; the danger is hidden reverse flow.
n.1: They do not automatically raise pressure to unsafe levels.
n.3: Contamination can spread beyond the single property via the main.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A puddle has formed around the open end of a hose lying on the ground. Why is this a cross-connection concern?
o: The puddle keeps the hose end cool and prevents any risk
The puddle proves the main is already losing its pressure each time
The puddle water is filtered clean as it enters the hose
Dirty puddle water could be siphoned into the hose and the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: If the hose end sits in the puddle, a pressure drop could draw that contaminated water back into the supply.

n.0: Keeping the hose 'cool' is irrelevant; the risk is contamination.
n.1: A puddle is not evidence of mains pressure loss.
n.2: Puddle water is not filtered; entering the hose would pollute the supply.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which working practice most directly removes a cross-connection risk?
o: Painting all the non-potable pipes a brighter warning colour during the task
Keeping potable outlets physically separate from any non-potable water
Running the potable pipe at a slightly higher flow rate
Recording the location of every pipe in the site diary
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Physically separating clean outlets from non-potable water prevents any accidental link forming.

n.0: Colour coding helps identification but does not remove a physical link.
n.2: A higher flow rate does not stop a cross-connection existing.
n.3: Recording pipe locations is good practice but does not separate them.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A cross-connection is best defined by which key feature?
o: It is an approved path fitted with a tested backflow device
It is a deliberate path between two treated water supplies
It is an unintended path between clean and unclean water
It is a temporary path used only to flush a new main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The defining feature is that the link is unintended and joins potable to non-potable water.

n.0: An approved, protected path is not the hazard being defined.
n.1: Two treated supplies joined on purpose is not a cross-connection hazard.
n.3: A controlled flushing arrangement is not an accidental cross-connection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Filling a chemical sprayer directly from a drinking tap with the hose in the liquid is dangerous because it creates what?
o: A pressure boost that helps the sprayer work better during the task
A cross-connection between the chemicals and the clean supply
A harmless overflow that simply runs to the drain
A cooling effect that protects the tap from damage
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The submerged hose in the chemical creates a direct link, so the chemical could be drawn back into the supply.

n.0: Any 'boost' is irrelevant next to the contamination hazard created.
n.2: The concern is contamination flowing back, not a harmless overflow.
n.3: Cooling the tap is not the issue; the chemical link is.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these is NOT a cross-connection?
o: A hose end submerged in a tank of non-potable water
A drinking pipe joined straight to a rainwater harvesting pipe
A standpipe hose left lying in a muddy puddle
A tap discharging into a basin with a proper air gap below it
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A tap with a proper air gap above the basin has no physical link to the dirty water, so it is not a cross-connection.

n.0: A submerged hose in non-potable water is a cross-connection.
n.1: Joining a drinking pipe to rainwater pipe is a cross-connection.
n.2: A hose in a puddle forms a potential cross-connection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why can a temporary site connection become a cross-connection if not managed?
o: It always improves the taste of the water on site on site
It permanently increases the pressure across the whole main on a typical job
It can link the clean supply to dirty site water without anyone noticing
It can only carry water in the correct forward direction
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Temporary connections on messy sites can easily bridge clean water and contaminated water if left unprotected.

n.0: Taste is irrelevant to the contamination hazard.
n.1: It does not permanently raise pressure across the main.
n.3: Without protection it can carry water backwards, which is the risk.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: The safest general rule for avoiding cross-connections is to do what?
o: Always fit the longest possible hose to reach the source
Always draw water at the highest pressure the main allows on site
Never let a potable outlet touch or sit in non-potable water
Always leave the outlet running so water cannot flow back
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Keeping potable outlets clear of non-potable water is the simplest way to prevent a cross-connection.

n.0: Hose length does not determine whether a cross-connection forms.
n.1: High pressure does not remove a physical cross-connection.
n.3: Leaving a tap running is unreliable and does not physically prevent backflow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What is the main consequence of a backflow event on a potable main?
o: A small saving in the energy used to pump the water during the task
A faster flow of water to the furthest properties
A neater arrangement of the pipes below the ground
Contamination of the drinking water that many people rely on
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Backflow contaminates the clean supply, putting the health of everyone on that main at risk.

n.0: Backflow is a hazard, not an energy saving.
n.1: It does not usefully speed delivery; it pollutes the supply.
n.2: Backflow has nothing to do with tidier pipework.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Following a serious backflow contamination, what response is the water company likely to need?
o: Increase everyone's water bill to cover the extra flow
Lower the pressure across the town for the rest of the year
Fit larger meters on every property on the street
Warn customers and flush or disinfect the affected supply
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A contamination usually means issuing warnings (such as boil or do-not-drink notices) and cleaning the affected pipes.

n.0: Billing changes are not the safety response to contamination.
n.1: A year-long pressure reduction is not the standard remedy.
n.2: Fitting larger meters does nothing to address contamination.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why can the consequences of one backflow incident be so wide-ranging?
o: The pollution turns instantly harmless once it leaves the tap
Polluted water can travel along the main to homes and businesses
The pollution is trapped in the fitting and never moves at all
The pollution only affects the pressure, never the water quality
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Because the main is shared, contaminated water can reach many connected premises before it is caught.

n.0: Contamination does not become harmless simply by moving through pipes.
n.2: The pollutant is not trapped; it can spread through the main.
n.3: The harm is to water quality, not merely pressure.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A backflow of garden chemicals reaches the main. What is the realistic public health outcome?
o: People would notice only a slightly higher water bill
People would enjoy water that tastes fresher than before on site
People would see the pressure improve at their taps
People could be made ill by drinking the contaminated water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Chemical contamination in the supply can cause genuine illness to those who drink it, which is why prevention matters.

n.0: A billing change is trivial next to the health risk.
n.1: Contaminated water does not taste fresher; it is a hazard.
n.2: Pressure improvement is irrelevant to a poisoning risk.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which outcome shows why backflow prevention is a legal and safety priority?
o: Keeping the pipe network looking tidy and well organised
Making sure water arrives a few seconds faster at the tap during the task
Reducing the paperwork the water company has to file
Preventing illness and outbreaks linked to polluted drinking water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The priority is protecting public health, because backflow can cause sickness and even disease outbreaks.

n.0: Tidy pipework is not the reason for the legal priority.
n.1: Delivery speed is not the safety driver here.
n.2: Reducing paperwork is not why backflow prevention is required.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: If backflow introduces bacteria into the main, what may customers experience?
o: Sickness such as stomach upsets from drinking the water
A pleasant improvement in how the water tastes
A permanent increase in their available water pressure on site
A reduction in the hardness of the water supplied
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Bacterial contamination can cause gastrointestinal illness among those who drink the affected water.

n.1: Contamination worsens, not improves, water quality.
n.2: There is no pressure benefit from contamination.
n.3: Backflow does not soften the water; it pollutes it.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Beyond illness, what other consequence often follows a confirmed backflow contamination?
o: A do-not-drink or boil notice while the supply is made safe
An automatic discount applied to every customer bill
A permanent boost to the pressure across the district each time
A change of the water source to a completely new one
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Customers may be told not to drink the water, or to boil it, until the supply has been flushed and confirmed safe.

n.1: Bill discounts are not the standard consequence of contamination.
n.2: There is no automatic pressure boost from an incident.
n.3: The source is not routinely swapped after a backflow event.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is it fair to say the consequences of backflow fall on the whole community, not just one site?
o: The contaminated water can be delivered to every connected property
Only the operative who caused it ever drinks the bad water
The water company keeps the incident secret from all customers each time
The pollution is billed evenly across the district accounts
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Because the network is shared, the results of a backflow event can reach all the properties fed by that main.

n.1: The person at fault is not the only one exposed to the risk.
n.2: Companies must warn affected customers, not hide the incident.
n.3: Consequences are about health, not how costs are billed.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A contractor causes backflow that pollutes the supply. Which best describes the seriousness of this?
o: It is a minor issue affecting only the contractor's own tap
It is a routine event that needs no action or reporting
It is purely a paperwork matter with no real-world effect
It is a public health incident that can affect many people
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Polluting the shared supply is a serious public health incident, not a private or trivial matter.

n.0: The impact reaches the shared main, not just one tap.
n.1: Contamination is not routine and does require action.
n.2: It has real health effects, not just paperwork.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What long-term consequence can follow repeated poor backflow control on a site?
o: A steady fall in the water pressure across the county in everyday operation
Loss of trust and possible enforcement action against those responsible
A gradual improvement in the taste of the local water
A reduction in the number of pipes needed on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Persistent failures can lead to enforcement and damage the reputation and standing of those responsible.

n.0: County-wide pressure decline is not a consequence of site failures.
n.2: Poor control worsens, not improves, water quality.
n.3: It does not reduce the pipework a site requires.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which method gives the most reliable protection against backflow?
o: A single check valve fitted to a low-risk cold tap
A longer pipe run before the water reaches the outlet during the task
A warning notice fixed to the wall beside the outlet
A physical air gap between the water outlet and any liquid below
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: An air gap physically breaks the connection, so it is the most reliable form of backflow protection.

n.0: A single check valve suits low risk but is less reliable than an air gap.
n.1: A longer pipe does not stop reverse flow.
n.2: A notice informs people but provides no physical protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: How is the level of backflow protection chosen for a particular connection?
o: It is set by the length of the pipe run to the outlet under normal working conditions
It is decided by the colour of the pipe being used on site
It is matched to the fluid category, so higher risks get greater protection
It is fixed at the same low level for every situation on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Protection is selected according to the fluid risk category; the more hazardous the fluid, the stronger the protection required.

n.0: Pipe length does not determine the required protection level.
n.1: Pipe colour aids identification but does not set protection.
n.3: One fixed low level would not cover higher-risk situations.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What does an air gap actually do to prevent backflow?
o: It seals the pipe tightly so no water can ever pass each time
It filters the water to remove any harmful bacteria
It boosts the pressure so water only flows forward
It leaves an open space so water cannot be drawn back up
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: An air gap is an unbridged open space; with no continuous water path, backflow cannot occur across it.

n.0: An air gap is deliberately open, not a tight seal.
n.1: An air gap does not filter; it breaks the connection.
n.2: It does not boost pressure; it physically separates the water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: When is a single check valve an appropriate choice?
o: For the very highest-risk fluids such as strong chemicals during the task
For every connection regardless of the fluid category
Only for pipes that carry no water at all on site
For lower-risk backflow situations where the fluid is less hazardous
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A single check valve suits lower-risk categories; higher risks need double check valves or an air gap.

n.0: High-risk fluids need stronger protection than a single check valve.
n.1: Protection must match the risk, so one type does not fit all.
n.2: Check valves are for water-carrying pipes, so this makes no sense.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why might a double check valve be fitted instead of a single one?
o: To give greater protection where the backflow risk is higher
To make the water flow more quickly through the fitting each time
To reduce the cost of the installation on site
To allow water to flow freely in both directions
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Two check valves in series give more assurance against reverse flow, suiting a higher fluid risk category.

n.1: Check valves are about direction control, not speeding up flow.
n.2: A double valve is not chosen simply to cut cost.
n.3: Check valves prevent reverse flow, not allow it.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A connection carries a raised backflow risk. What is the correct approach to protection?
o: Fit whatever device happens to be closest in the van in everyday operation
Fit protection rated for that higher risk, not a lower-grade device
Fit the cheapest device available to save money on site
Fit no device because the mains pressure will cope
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The device must be matched to the fluid category, so a higher risk demands a higher-rated form of protection.

n.0: Convenience does not justify an under-rated device.
n.2: Cost must not override matching protection to the risk.
n.3: Relying on mains pressure alone is not acceptable protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which statement about check valves is correct?
o: They let water pass equally in both directions at all times each time
They filter out any dirt carried in the flowing water
They add chlorine to the water as it passes through
They are designed to let water pass one way and stop it returning
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A check valve allows forward flow but closes to prevent water travelling back, guarding against backflow.

n.0: A check valve is directional; it does not pass water both ways freely.
n.1: A check valve is not a filter.
n.2: A check valve does not dose chlorine.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is an air gap often preferred for higher-risk situations over a mechanical valve?
o: It has no moving parts to fail and cannot be bridged by water
It is always cheaper to install than any valve in everyday operation
It increases the water pressure at the outlet
It removes the need to keep the outlet clean
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: An air gap has nothing to wear out or jam and physically breaks the water path, making it very dependable.

n.1: Cost is not the reason an air gap is favoured for high risk.
n.2: An air gap does not raise outlet pressure.
n.3: An air gap does not remove the need for basic hygiene.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A fitting protects against a low-risk backflow only. Why must it not be used on a high-risk connection?
o: It would make the water flow too fast for the pipe during the task
It would add too much pressure to the whole system
It would filter the water more than is necessary
It would not be strong enough to stop the more hazardous fluid
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Protection must match the risk; a low-risk device would leave a high-risk connection inadequately protected.

n.0: The concern is protection level, not flow speed.
n.1: Under-rated protection is a safety issue, not a pressure one.
n.2: A backflow device is not primarily a filter.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which combination correctly links risk to protection?
o: Higher fluid risk needs a weaker form of backflow protection
All fluid risks are covered by exactly the same single device on site
Fluid risk has no bearing on the protection that is chosen
Higher fluid risk needs a stronger form of backflow protection
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The greater the hazard of the fluid, the greater the protection required against it flowing back.

n.0: Higher risk demands stronger, not weaker, protection.
n.1: One device cannot cover every risk category.
n.2: Fluid risk is precisely what determines the protection level.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What is the practical purpose of matching a backflow device to the fluid category?
o: To make sure the pipe is the correct length for the job
To make sure the protection is adequate for the hazard present
To make sure the water is delivered at a warmer temperature
To make sure the fitting is the most colourful option available
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Matching the device to the fluid category ensures the level of protection genuinely suits the hazard.

n.0: Device selection is about risk, not pipe length.
n.2: It is unrelated to water temperature.
n.3: Appearance is irrelevant to protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is a warning label alone never accepted as backflow protection?
o: It cannot physically stop contaminated water flowing back
It fades too quickly in the sunlight to be read during the task
It makes the pipe harder to identify on site
It slows the water down more than is allowed
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A label may inform people but provides no physical barrier, so it cannot prevent backflow on its own.

n.1: Fading is not the core reason; it simply provides no barrier.
n.2: A label aids, not hinders, identification.
n.3: A label does not affect flow speed.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A standpipe drawing from a hydrant must be fitted with what backflow protection?
o: A double check valve to prevent contamination of the main
A single check valve, since a hydrant is always low risk
No protection at all, because hydrants are already sealed
A simple filter to catch any dirt in the water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Standpipes on hydrants require a double check valve because of the higher risk of drawing water into an unknown environment.

n.1: A single check valve is not sufficient protection for a standpipe.
n.2: A standpipe is not exempt; it needs a double check valve.
n.3: A filter catches dirt but does not prevent backflow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why do standpipes need particularly careful backflow protection?
o: They are always connected to sealed indoor plumbing only during the task
They are used in uncontrolled places where contamination is likely
They draw water far more slowly than any indoor tap
They are only ever used to fill sealed drinking bottles
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Standpipes are used on sites and in the field where hoses may reach dirty water, so strong protection is essential.

n.0: Standpipes are used outdoors in uncontrolled settings, not just indoors.
n.2: Draw rate is not the reason they need protection.
n.3: Standpipes are used for many purposes, not only clean bottles.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: An operative fits a standpipe with only a single check valve. Why is this wrong?
o: A standpipe needs no valve of any kind to be safe
A standpipe should have a pressure gauge instead of a valve
A standpipe on a hydrant requires a double check valve
A standpipe should be fitted with a filter rather than a valve
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The correct protection for a hydrant standpipe is a double check valve, not a single one.

n.0: A standpipe does need protection, so 'no valve' is wrong.
n.1: A gauge measures pressure but does not prevent backflow.
n.3: A filter does not prevent backflow into the main.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: The double check valve on a standpipe is there to protect what?
o: The standpipe body from rusting in wet conditions under normal working conditions
The hose from splitting under too much pressure on site
The public main from contamination flowing back through the standpipe
The operative from getting splashed while working on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The valve stops any contamination on the standpipe side from being drawn back into the public main.

n.0: The valve is not there to prevent the standpipe rusting.
n.1: It is not fitted to stop the hose splitting.
n.3: It protects the water, not the operative from splashes.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Before using a standpipe on a hydrant, which check is most important for backflow safety?
o: That the standpipe has been painted a bright colour
That an approved double check valve is fitted and working
That the hose attached is the longest one available
That the water is drawn at the maximum possible speed on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Confirming a working double check valve is in place is the key backflow-safety check before drawing water.

n.0: Paint colour does not affect backflow safety.
n.2: Hose length is not the safety point here.
n.3: Drawing at maximum speed does not improve backflow protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is it not acceptable to draw from a hydrant with a bare standpipe and no valve?
o: The water would come out too clean to be measured in everyday operation
The standpipe would be too heavy to lift safely
The hydrant would refuse to open without a valve
Contaminated water could be siphoned straight back into the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Without a double check valve, a pressure drop could siphon dirty water back into the public supply.

n.0: Water being 'too clean' is not a real hazard.
n.1: Weight is not the reason a valve is required.
n.2: The hydrant can physically open regardless; the risk is contamination.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which best describes correct standpipe practice on a hydrant?
o: Use an approved standpipe with a double check valve every time
Use any spare standpipe as long as it fits the hydrant
Use a standpipe only when the main pressure is very low in practice
Use a standpipe without a valve for short jobs only
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Correct practice is always to use an approved standpipe fitted with a double check valve.

n.1: Merely fitting the hydrant does not make a standpipe compliant.
n.2: Standpipes are not restricted to low-pressure conditions.
n.3: Even short jobs require the double check valve; there is no exemption.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: The double check valve on a standpipe works by doing what?
o: Allowing water to flow freely in either direction in practice
Storing water inside the valve for later use
Allowing water out but closing to stop it flowing back in
Heating the water slightly as it passes through
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The valve permits forward flow to the hose but shuts against any reverse flow towards the main.

n.0: It does not allow free two-way flow; that would defeat its purpose.
n.1: It does not store water.
n.3: It does not heat the water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: If a standpipe's check valve is found to be faulty, what should happen?
o: It should be taken out of use until the valve is put right
It should be used carefully at a lower flow for now
It should be used only in the mornings until repaired each time
It should be used as normal because faults are rare
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A faulty check valve means the standpipe cannot protect the main, so it must not be used until fixed.

n.1: A faulty valve is unsafe at any flow rate.
n.2: Time of day does not make a faulty valve safe.
n.3: Rarity of faults does not justify using a known-faulty valve.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why should you never leave a hose end submerged in water when connected to the supply?
o: A pressure drop could siphon that water back into the main
The hose would float to the surface and disconnect itself on site
The water would slowly warm up inside the hose
The hose would become too heavy to lift out
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A submerged hose becomes a siphon; if pressure falls, the surrounding water can be pulled back into the supply.

n.1: Floating is not the hazard; contamination by siphonage is.
n.2: Warming is irrelevant to the backflow risk.
n.3: Weight is not the reason submersion is dangerous.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: An operative leaves a running hose lying in a full trough and walks away. What is the danger?
o: The trough would overflow and flood the whole yard in everyday operation
The hose would kink and stop the water completely
Trough water could be drawn back through the hose if pressure drops
The water in the trough would evaporate too fast
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: If the mains pressure drops, the submerged hose can siphon the trough water back towards the clean supply.

n.0: Overflow is a spillage issue, not the contamination hazard.
n.1: A kink stops flow but is not the backflow danger described.
n.3: Evaporation is irrelevant to the siphon risk.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What is the correct way to fill a tank so the hose cannot cause backflow?
o: Push the hose end right to the bottom of the tank
Coil the hose neatly inside the tank while filling on site
Tie the hose end just below the water surface
Keep the hose end above the water with a clear air gap
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Holding the hose end above the water leaves an air gap, so nothing can be siphoned back.

n.0: Pushing the hose to the bottom submerges it and creates the risk.
n.1: Coiling it inside still leaves the end submerged.
n.2: Tying it below the surface keeps it submerged and unsafe.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A hose is left in a bucket of dirty water overnight while still attached to a tap. Why is this poor practice?
o: The dirty water could be siphoned into the supply on a pressure loss
The bucket would be stolen before the morning shift in everyday operation
The hose rubber would dissolve in the dirty water
The tap washer would wear out much more quickly on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The submerged hose bridges the dirty water and the clean supply, so a pressure drop could pull contamination in.

n.1: Theft is not the water-safety concern here.
n.2: The hose is not expected to dissolve; the risk is siphonage.
n.3: Washer wear is not the backflow hazard.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which simple habit best prevents a hose from causing backflow?
o: Always keep the hose outlet clear of any standing water
Always use the widest hose you can find on site in practice
Always fill containers as quickly as possible
Always leave the tap slightly open between jobs
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Keeping the outlet out of standing water removes the siphon path and prevents backflow.

n.1: Hose width does not prevent backflow.
n.2: Filling speed is unrelated to the siphon risk.
n.3: Leaving the tap open does not stop reverse flow and wastes water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A hose end is resting in a puddle while the supply is connected. What should you do?
o: Leave it as the puddle is only rainwater and harmless during the task
Push it deeper so the puddle cannot splash the hose
Lift the hose clear of the puddle so no water can be drawn back
Turn the pressure up so water cannot flow backwards
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Lifting the hose out of the puddle removes the siphon path and protects the supply.

n.0: Puddle water is not safe to assume harmless; it can be drawn back.
n.1: Pushing it deeper makes the submersion worse.
n.3: Higher pressure does not reliably stop a siphon if pressure later drops.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why is a submerged hose sometimes described as a 'ready-made siphon'?
o: It is already curved into the shape of a siphon tube
It always contains trapped air that starts the siphon during the task
A pressure drop can immediately pull the surrounding water up it
It has a special valve built in to start siphoning
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Because the hose links the main to the surrounding water, a pressure drop can instantly siphon that water back.

n.0: The shape of the hose is not what creates the siphon risk.
n.1: Trapped air is not what makes it a siphon hazard.
n.3: An ordinary hose has no built-in siphon valve.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: When filling a cattle trough from the mains, the safest arrangement is which?
o: The hose inlet sits permanently below the water line in practice
The hose is weighted down to the base of the trough
The hose end is wedged just under the water surface
The hose or inlet discharges above the water with an air gap
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Discharging above the water with an air gap means trough water can never be siphoned into the supply.

n.0: An inlet below the water line is submerged and unsafe.
n.1: Weighting the hose down keeps it submerged.
n.2: Wedging it just under the surface still leaves it submerged.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What does leaving a hose submerged fail to provide that keeping it clear does provide?
o: A faster flow of water into the container being filled each time
A neater appearance for the working area on site
A warmer temperature for the water being delivered
An air gap that physically breaks the path back to the main
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Keeping the hose clear maintains an air gap, which submersion removes, so submersion loses that protection.

n.0: Flow speed is not the protective feature being lost.
n.1: Tidiness is not the safety point.
n.2: Temperature is unrelated to the air-gap protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: The golden rule for hoses on the potable supply is best stated as which?
o: Always leave the hose end resting in the water you are filling
Never let the hose end sit in the water you are filling
Only submerge the hose end when the pressure is high
Submerge the hose end but keep the tap almost closed
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The rule is simple: keep the hose end out of the water, so it can never siphon back.

n.0: Leaving it in the water is exactly what causes the risk.
n.2: High pressure does not make submersion safe.
n.3: A nearly closed tap does not remove the submersion hazard.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these best sums up the aim of all backflow prevention methods?
o: To keep the water pressure as high as it can go
To make the pipework easier to install quickly
To stop any pollutant ever reaching the clean drinking supply
To reduce the amount of chlorine the water needs on a typical job
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Every method, from air gaps to check valves, exists to keep pollutants out of the potable supply.

n.0: High pressure is not the aim of backflow prevention.
n.1: Ease of installation is not the purpose.
n.3: Chlorine dosing is a separate matter from backflow prevention.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A jet-washer is connected to a drinking tap with its lance sitting in a bucket of detergent. What is the hazard?
o: The detergent would make the water taste much cleaner
The detergent could be drawn back into the supply as a cross-connection
The jet-washer would run out of pressure straight away in everyday operation
The bucket would freeze and crack in cold weather on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The lance in the detergent links the clean supply to a chemical, so it can be drawn back into the main.

n.0: Detergent in the supply is a hazard, not a cleaner taste.
n.2: Loss of pressure is not the contamination concern.
n.3: Freezing is unrelated to the cross-connection hazard.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: During a nearby burst, several outdoor taps briefly 'gurgle' and lose flow. Why is backflow protection vital right then?
o: The gurgling proves the water has become perfectly safe in practice
The taps are self-cleaning while the pressure is low
The burst raises the pressure and pushes water outward
The pressure loss can siphon water back from anything connected
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The burst has dropped the pressure, so any submerged hose or connected source can be siphoned back into the main.

n.0: Gurgling is a sign of pressure loss, not of safe water.
n.1: Low pressure does not make taps self-clean.
n.2: A burst lowers local pressure; it does not raise it.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these is the most serious possible consequence of backflow into a public main?
o: A slightly higher electricity cost at the pumping station
A short delay in filling a tank on one site
An outbreak of illness among people who drink the water
A small stain left on the inside of one pipe
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The gravest consequence is a public health outbreak from contaminated drinking water.

n.0: Pumping costs are trivial next to a health outbreak.
n.1: A filling delay is minor compared with illness.
n.3: A pipe stain is insignificant against a health risk.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Two operatives disagree about a hydrant standpipe. Who is correct on backflow protection?
o: The one who says a single check valve is enough
The one who says no valve is needed on a hydrant on site
The one who says only a filter is required
The one who says it must carry a double check valve
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A hydrant standpipe must have a double check valve, so that operative is correct.

n.0: A single check valve does not meet the requirement.
n.1: A hydrant standpipe is not exempt from needing a valve.
n.2: A filter does not provide backflow protection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: You return to a job and find the hose end has slipped under the surface of a water butt. What is the priority action?
o: Leave it, since water butts hold only clean rainwater each time
Push it further in so it cannot slip out again
Increase the flow so the butt fills more quickly
Lift the hose end clear to restore the air gap immediately
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Restoring the air gap by lifting the hose clear removes the siphon risk straight away.

n.0: Water-butt water is non-potable and must not be assumed clean.
n.1: Pushing it further in worsens the submersion.
n.2: Faster flow does not remove the backflow risk.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which short definition of backflow would you give a new operative?
o: Water going the wrong way and taking pollution into the clean supply
Water going the right way from the main to the customer on a typical job
Water standing still in a pipe until it is used
Water being measured as it passes through the meter
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Backflow is simply water flowing the wrong way and carrying contamination into the potable supply.

n.1: Main-to-customer is the correct direction, not backflow.
n.2: Standing water is stagnation, not backflow.
n.3: Metering measures flow; it is not backflow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these arrangements has NO cross-connection risk?
o: A hose from a tap left inside a tank of pond water on site
A tap filling a jug held below it with a clear air gap
A drinking pipe teed into a recycled water pipe
A hose outlet lying in a puddle beside the tank
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: A tap filling a jug with an air gap has no physical link to any non-potable water.

n.0: A hose inside a pond-water tank is a clear cross-connection.
n.2: Teeing a drinking pipe into recycled water is a cross-connection.
n.3: A hose lying in a puddle is a potential cross-connection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why does relying only on 'being careful' not count as proper backflow protection?
o: Being careful uses too much water on every job on a typical job
Being careful raises the pressure in the main
Physical safeguards are needed because human care can lapse
Being careful changes the taste of the water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Approved physical protection is required because care alone can fail, whereas an air gap or valve keeps working.

n.0: Care does not inherently waste water; that is not the point.
n.1: Care has no effect on mains pressure.
n.3: Care does not alter the taste of the water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which condition must exist for back-siphonage to draw water into the main?
o: The main must be at a higher pressure than the connected source
The main must be at a lower pressure than the connected source
The connected source must be sealed off from all air
The connected source must be warmer than the mains water
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Siphonage needs the main to be the lower pressure so the higher-pressure source is drawn backwards.

n.0: If the main is higher, flow is held forward and siphonage cannot occur.
n.2: Sealing off air is not the condition that drives siphonage.
n.3: Temperature difference is not what causes back-siphonage.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Why must every operative take backflow seriously even on a small job?
o: A single lapse can contaminate the supply for many people
A small job never involves any water at all
A small job is checked twice by a supervisor on a typical job
A small job uses only bottled water on site
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Even a minor task can create a backflow path that pollutes the shared supply, so the risk is always real.

n.1: Small water jobs still involve water and carry the risk.
n.2: Double-checking is not guaranteed and does not remove the hazard.
n.3: Small jobs still use mains water, not only bottled water.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: What makes a hose left in a tank of non-potable water a cross-connection?
o: It carries clean water at a higher than normal speed on site
It forms a physical link between clean and unclean water
It measures how much water enters the tank
It keeps the tank water at a steady temperature
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The hose bridges the potable supply and the non-potable tank, which is exactly what a cross-connection is.

n.0: Flow speed does not define a cross-connection.
n.2: Measuring volume is a meter's job, not a cross-connection.
n.3: Temperature control has nothing to do with a cross-connection.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which is the correct order of reliability, strongest first, for common backflow protection?
o: Single check valve, then double check valve, then air gap
Double check valve, then air gap, then single check valve
Air gap, then double check valve, then single check valve
Single check valve, then air gap, then double check valve
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: An air gap is the most reliable, a double check valve next, and a single check valve suits only the lowest risk.

n.0: This reverses the order; a single check valve is the weakest.
n.1: An air gap outranks a double check valve, not the other way round.
n.3: A single check valve is the weakest and should not come first.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: A standpipe is used to fill a bowser on a dusty site. Why is the double check valve so important here?
o: It makes the bowser fill up noticeably faster
It keeps the standpipe from rattling as water flows
It stops any dirty site water being drawn back into the main
It stops the bowser from being overfilled by mistake in practice
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: On a dusty, uncontrolled site the double check valve is what prevents contamination reaching the public main.

n.0: The valve is for protection, not faster filling.
n.1: Reducing rattle is not the purpose of the valve.
n.3: It does not control overfilling; that is down to the operator.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these correctly describes safe hose use when filling from the mains?
o: The outlet is pushed under the water to reduce splashing
The outlet is left in the water once filling has started
The outlet is held under the surface to stop it whipping
The outlet stays above the water leaving an air gap
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: Keeping the outlet above the water preserves an air gap, so nothing can be siphoned back.

n.0: Pushing it under the water creates the very risk to be avoided.
n.1: Leaving it submerged once started is still unsafe.
n.2: Holding it under the surface still submerges it.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: Which of these correctly names the two types of backflow?
o: Back-siphonage and back-pressure
Back-siphonage and water hammer on site
Back-pressure and air-locking
Water hammer and stagnation
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The two types of backflow are back-siphonage (low pressure) and back-pressure (high downstream pressure).

n.1: Water hammer is a surge, not a type of backflow.
n.2: Air-locking is a flow nuisance, not a type of backflow.
n.3: Neither water hammer nor stagnation is a type of backflow.

Backflow & Cross-Connection.q: An operative spots a garden hose from a house tap left inside a fish pond. What is the correct concern?
o: The fish would be harmed by the clean tap water during the task
The hose would sink and be hard to pull out
The pond would overflow and flood the garden
Pond water could be siphoned back into the drinking supply
Backflow & Cross-Connection.w: The submerged hose is a cross-connection; a pressure drop could siphon pond water into the potable supply.

n.0: The health concern is the drinking supply, not the fish.
n.1: Difficulty pulling the hose out is not the water-safety issue.
n.2: Overflow is a nuisance, not the contamination hazard.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why must pipes, fittings and tools be kept clean during clean-water work?
o: To make the pipe fittings easier to push together properly
To keep the tools from rusting in the trench
To stop dirt and germs getting into the drinking water
To help the pipe joints look neat when finished
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Anything on the pipe, fitting or tool can be washed into the main and contaminate the drinking water.

n.0: Ease of assembly is not the reason cleanliness is required.
n.1: Preventing rust is a maintenance point, not the hygiene reason.
n.3: A tidy appearance is not why cleanliness matters here.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A fitting has fallen in the mud on site. What should you do before using it?
o: Clean it thoroughly so no soil or dirt remains
Fit it quickly before the mud on it dries out hard
Wipe only the outside and fit it as normal
Leave the mud on as it will wash away later
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Soil carries germs, so a dropped fitting must be cleaned fully before it goes near the drinking water.

n.1: Fitting it dirty puts soil straight into the main.
n.2: The inside touching the water must be clean too, not just the outside.
n.3: Contamination will not simply wash itself away safely.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: How should tools used on the drinking-water main be kept?
o: Coated all over in grease to stop them corroding
Clean and free of dirt before touching the pipe
Stored loose in the bottom of the trench
Marked with paint so they are easy to find
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean tools stop dirt and germs being carried onto the pipe and into the water.

n.0: Grease is itself a contaminant on clean-water surfaces.
n.2: Leaving tools in the trench lets them pick up soil and water.
n.3: Marking tools does nothing to keep them clean.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which item is most likely to carry contamination onto a new water main?
o: A brand-new fitting still in its wrapper
A length of pipe kept capped and dry
A clean cloth kept for the job only
A dirty tool that has not been cleaned
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A dirty tool can transfer soil and germs directly onto the pipe and into the water.

n.0: A wrapped new fitting is protected and clean.
n.1: Capped, dry pipe has been kept clean inside.
n.2: A clean dedicated cloth is not a source of contamination.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: What is good practice for cloths or rags used on clean-water fittings?
o: Use any rag that happens to be in the van
Use the same rag left in the trench overnight
Use oily rags from the plant maintenance kit
Use clean ones kept only for this purpose
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean, dedicated cloths avoid spreading dirt, oil or germs onto surfaces that meet the water.

n.0: A random rag may already be soiled or oily.
n.1: A rag left in the trench picks up soil and moisture.
n.2: Oily maintenance rags contaminate clean-water surfaces.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Before making a joint on a new main, the mating surfaces should be:
o: smeared with wet mud to help the seal grip better
left as found to save time on the joint
rubbed with soil to roughen the surface
wiped clean so no grit or soil is present
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Grit or soil on the joint faces can be pushed into the main and spoil the seal, so they are wiped clean.

n.0: Mud is a contaminant and will not help the seal.
n.1: Leaving them dirty carries soil into the water.
n.2: Roughening with soil adds contamination, not grip.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Where should clean fittings be placed while you get ready to fit them?
o: On a clean surface, not on the bare soil
Straight down onto the wet trench floor
In the spoil heap beside the excavation
On the ground wherever is nearest to reach
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Keeping fittings off the bare soil stops them picking up dirt and germs before they go in the main.

n.1: The wet trench floor will soil the fitting.
n.2: The spoil heap is dirty excavated ground.
n.3: Bare ground of any kind can contaminate the fitting.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A jointing tool has been resting on the spoil heap. Before use on the main you should:
o: blow the loose bits off it and use it as it is
use it as it is to keep up with the gang
dip it in the trench water to rinse it
clean it so no soil is carried onto the pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Spoil is dirty soil, so the tool must be properly cleaned before it touches clean-water surfaces.

n.0: Blowing off loose bits leaves plenty of soil behind.
n.1: Working speed is no reason to carry soil into the main.
n.2: Trench water is itself dirty and would not clean it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping the work area and equipment clean on a water job is mainly about:
o: making the job finish more quickly
reducing the amount of tools needed
protecting the quality of the drinking water
keeping the site inspector happy on the day
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The whole point of site cleanliness is to keep contamination out of the public drinking-water supply.

n.0: Speed is not the purpose of cleanliness.
n.1: Cleanliness does not change how many tools are needed.
n.3: Pleasing an inspector is a side effect, not the reason.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which practice best keeps a new main free of contamination?
o: Dragging pipe through the mud to the trench
Handling pipe and fittings with clean hands and tools
Resting fittings on the ground between jobs
Using whatever tool is closest to hand
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean hands and tools stop germs and dirt being passed onto the pipe and into the water.

n.0: Dragging pipe through mud coats it in contamination.
n.2: Resting fittings on the ground soils them.
n.3: Grabbing any tool may bring dirt onto the pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: You notice soil inside a coupling you are about to fit. You should:
o: fit it and flush it through afterwards
remove the soil and clean it before fitting
tap it upside down and fit it anyway
push it on quickly before anyone sees
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Soil inside a fitting goes straight into the water, so it must be cleaned out before the coupling is used.

n.0: Flushing later does not guarantee the soil is removed.
n.2: Tapping it leaves soil behind in the coupling.
n.3: Hiding the problem still contaminates the main.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Good hygiene means tools used on foul or dirty work should be:
o: shared freely between both types of job
stored in the same bag as clean tools
kept separate from clean-water tools
used on the main to save carrying two sets
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Keeping dirty-job tools apart stops them contaminating the clean-water tools and the main.

n.0: Sharing tools spreads contamination onto clean work.
n.1: Mixing them in one bag transfers dirt to clean tools.
n.3: Using foul tools on the main contaminates the water.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: How should pipe and fittings be stored on site before use?
o: Off the ground on boards or racks, kept clean
Flat on the bare soil next to the trench
Half-buried in the spoil to stop them rolling
Wherever there is space on the muddy ground
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Storing pipe off the ground on boards or racks keeps it out of the mud and free from contamination.

n.1: Bare soil soils the pipe and fittings.
n.2: Burying pipe in spoil coats it in dirt.
n.3: Muddy ground contaminates anything laid on it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why are end caps left on new pipe and fittings until they are fitted?
o: To make the whole pipe stack look tidy on the site
To stop the pipe rolling around the store
To keep the inside clean until the moment of use
To protect the paint on the outside surface
Hygienic Site Practices.w: End caps stop dirt, insects and germs getting inside the pipe before it is jointed.

n.0: Tidiness is not the reason for keeping caps on.
n.1: Caps are about cleanliness inside, not stopping rolling.
n.3: The concern is the inside of the pipe, not outside paint.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: When should the end caps be removed from a length of new pipe?
o: As soon as the pipe is delivered to site
Only when you are ready to make the joint
The night before, to speed up the morning
When the pipe is first placed by the trench
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Leaving caps on until the last moment keeps the inside clean right up to jointing.

n.0: Removing caps at delivery leaves the pipe open for days.
n.2: Uncapping the night before lets dirt in overnight.
n.3: Placing pipe by the trench does not require caps off yet.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Pipe left lying directly on the ground overnight is a problem because:
o: it may fade in colour by the morning
dirt, water and vermin can get into it
it becomes too heavy to lift by hand
it will not fit the couplings any longer
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Ground contact and open ends let soil, standing water and vermin contaminate the pipe.

n.0: Colour fading is not a hygiene risk.
n.2: Lying on the ground does not change the pipe's weight.
n.3: Ground storage does not alter the coupling size.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A stack of fittings has lost its protective caps. Before use you should:
o: fit them straight away without checking
clean and check each one for contamination
rinse them once or twice in the trench water
cap them again and fit them unchecked
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Once caps are off, fittings may have picked up dirt, so each must be cleaned and checked before use.

n.0: Fitting uncapped items risks putting dirt in the main.
n.2: Trench water is dirty and would not clean them.
n.3: Re-capping without checking does not remove any dirt already in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The best surface to store pipe on before laying is:
o: the loose spoil dug from the trench
the wet clay at the edge of the dig
clean timber boards or a proper pipe rack
any old flat patch of bare mud on the site
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Boards or racks keep pipe clean, supported and clear of the dirty ground.

n.0: Spoil is dirty and will contaminate the pipe.
n.1: Wet clay soils the pipe and holds germs.
n.3: Bare mud contaminates anything stored on it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Storing pipe off the ground also helps by:
o: keeping the ends clear of standing water
making the pipe cure faster in the sun
letting the couplings shrink to size
removing the need to cap the open ends
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Raised storage keeps open ends out of puddles and mud that would contaminate the inside.

n.1: Pipe does not need to 'cure' in this way.
n.2: Storage does not shrink couplings.
n.3: Caps are still needed even when pipe is off the ground.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: a delivery arrives and the gang is busy. The pipe should be:
o: tipped onto the verge to deal with later
rolled into the open trench for now
left in the mud until someone is free
stacked off the ground with caps left on
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Even when busy, pipe must go onto clean supports with caps on so it stays clean.

n.0: The verge is dirty ground and soils the pipe.
n.1: The open trench may be wet and dirty.
n.2: Leaving it in the mud contaminates the pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why keep fittings in their packaging until needed?
o: The wrapping stops them being counted
The wrapping makes them heavier to handle
The wrapping keeps them clean until fitting
The wrapping keeps them warm in cold weather
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Original packaging protects fittings from dirt and germs right up to the point of use.

n.0: Packaging does not prevent stock being counted.
n.1: Weight is not the reason for keeping wrapping on.
n.3: Keeping fittings warm is not the hygiene purpose.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: End caps and plugs supplied with new pipe should be treated as:
o: protection to keep the pipe clean, not waste
packaging to throw away on delivery
spare parts for a completely different job
scrap that should be recycled away straight off
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The caps and plugs are there to keep the pipe clean, so they are kept and used, not discarded.

n.1: Throwing them away leaves the pipe unprotected.
n.2: They are not spares for another job.
n.3: Scrapping them removes the pipe's protection.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A pallet of fittings is standing in a puddle. The correct action is to:
o: move it onto a clean, dry, raised surface
leave it as the wrapping will keep water out
push it deeper so it stops floating away
open it and let the fittings drain in the sun
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Fittings must be kept clear of standing water, so the pallet is moved somewhere clean and dry.

n.1: Wrapping is not a guarantee against standing water.
n.2: Pushing it into the puddle makes the risk worse.
n.3: Draining wet fittings still leaves them contaminated.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping stored pipe capped and raised mainly protects against:
o: theft of the pipe from the site compound area
contamination getting inside before laying
the pipe warping in warm summer weather
extra delivery charges from the supplier
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The purpose is hygiene: caps and raised storage keep dirt and germs out of the pipe.

n.0: Security is a separate issue from hygiene.
n.2: Warping is not the reason for capping pipe.
n.3: Delivery charges are unrelated to storage hygiene.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: When work stops for a break, open pipe ends should be:
o: left open so the pipe can dry inside
covered loosely with a handful of soil
capped or plugged to keep the inside clean
pointed downwards and simply left uncapped there
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Capping or plugging every open end keeps dirt, water and vermin out while work is paused.

n.0: Leaving ends open lets contamination straight in.
n.1: Soil placed over the end is itself a contaminant.
n.3: Pointing down does not stop dirt or vermin entering.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: At the end of the working day, any open end of the new main must be:
o: left open ready for the next shift
stuffed with a rag to save fittings
wrapped in the empty cement bag nearby
sealed with a proper cap or plug
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A proper cap or plug keeps the main clean overnight; makeshift covers are not reliable.

n.0: An open end lets in dirt, water and vermin overnight.
n.1: A rag is not a clean, secure seal.
n.2: A cement bag is dirty and not a proper seal.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why plug an open end even for a short break?
o: It stops the pipe cooling down too fast
It keeps the pipe from rolling into the trench
It saves having to measure the pipe again
Contamination can enter in a very short time
Hygienic Site Practices.w: It only takes a moment for soil, water or vermin to get in, so ends are plugged even briefly.

n.0: Pipe temperature is not the concern here.
n.1: Plugging an end is not about stopping rolling.
n.2: Plugging has nothing to do with re-measuring.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A rat could enter a new main most easily through:
o: a properly made push-fit joint
a capped end left overnight
an open, uncapped pipe end
a plugged branch connection
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Vermin get in through open ends, which is exactly why ends are capped when work stops.

n.0: A sound joint does not give access.
n.1: A capped end keeps vermin out.
n.3: A plugged branch is sealed against vermin.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: rain is starting and the gang leaves for shelter. The open main should be:
o: left open as rain is only clean water
tilted up and abandoned until it clears
filled up with spoil to block off the opening
plugged first so rainwater cannot run in
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Rain runs dirt into an open main, so the end is plugged before the gang leaves.

n.0: Rain running off a site is not clean.
n.1: Tilting does not stop water and dirt entering.
n.2: Spoil placed in the pipe contaminates it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The correct item to close a temporarily open pipe end is:
o: a lump of clay pressed into the bore
a screwed-up feed sack from the site
a handful of the loose excavated material used
a clean cap or plug made for the pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A clean, purpose-made cap or plug seals the end without adding any contamination.

n.0: Clay pressed in the bore is dirty and crumbles inside.
n.1: A feed sack is dirty and not a proper seal.
n.2: Excavated material is contaminated soil.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: If a cap is not to hand when you must stop work, you should:
o: carry on and leave the end fully open
block it with the nearest dirty object
get a clean plug before leaving the end open
ignore it altogether because the break is short
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The end must be sealed with something clean, so you obtain a proper plug rather than leave it open.

n.0: Leaving it open invites contamination in.
n.1: A dirty object seals nothing and adds dirt.
n.3: Even short breaks allow contamination in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Capping open ends when work stops is important because the pipe is:
o: easier to store when the ends are shut
less likely to be stolen when capped
part of a supply people will drink from
protected from sunlight fading its colour
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The main carries drinking water, so keeping its inside clean protects public health.

n.0: Storage is not the reason for capping on a live job.
n.1: Security is separate from the hygiene purpose.
n.3: Sun fading is not a drinking-water hygiene issue.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: You return from lunch to find a cap has come off the main. You should:
o: carry straight on without a second look
check and clean the end before continuing
put the cap back and joint immediately
flush later and keep working for now
Hygienic Site Practices.w: With the end exposed, contamination may have entered, so it is checked and cleaned before work resumes.

n.0: Ignoring it risks jointing over contamination.
n.2: Re-capping without cleaning traps any dirt inside.
n.3: Delaying a flush leaves possible contamination in place.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which is the best reason to plug a pipe end left in the trench overnight?
o: It keeps soil, water and vermin out of the bore
It stops the trench sides drying out
It makes the whole pipe simpler to lift back out
It reduces the noise from passing traffic
Hygienic Site Practices.w: An overnight plug protects the inside of the pipe from all the things that could get in.

n.1: Plugging the pipe does not affect the trench sides.
n.2: A plug does not make the pipe easier to lift.
n.3: Noise reduction is not the purpose of plugging.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A partly built main is to be left over a long weekend. The open ends should be:
o: left open so air can move through freely
loosely covered with a sheet of ply
sealed only if bad weather is forecast
securely capped and checked before leaving
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Over a long shutdown the ends must be securely capped and checked to keep the main clean.

n.0: Open ends let contamination in over the shutdown.
n.1: A loose sheet is not a secure seal.
n.2: Ends are capped regardless of the forecast.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Plugs and caps used to close open ends should themselves be:
o: clean before they are put on the pipe
muddy so they grip the bore tightly
coated in oil to slide in easily
any old size that roughly fits
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A dirty or oily plug would contaminate the very end it is meant to protect, so it must be clean.

n.1: Mud on a plug puts dirt straight into the bore.
n.2: Oil on a plug contaminates the clean-water surface.
n.3: A poorly fitting plug leaves gaps for dirt to enter.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Leaving open ends unplugged during work stoppages mainly risks:
o: the pipe going out of round in the sun
dirt and germs entering the drinking-water main
the joint compound setting too quickly
extra wear on the capping equipment
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The real risk of an open end is contamination getting into the water people will drink.

n.0: Pipe shape is not the concern of an open end.
n.2: Joint compound setting is unrelated to open ends.
n.3: Wear on equipment is not the hygiene risk.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Before laying pipe, water standing in the trench should be:
o: bailed or pumped out so the bed is clear
left in place to cushion the new pipe
topped up so the pipe floats into line
stirred round so the silt settles out evenly
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The trench is de-watered first so pipe is not laid into standing water that could contaminate it.

n.1: Standing water is a contamination risk, not a cushion.
n.2: Floating pipe into place is not sound practice.
n.3: Stirring the water does not make it safe to lay in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why must pipe never be laid in standing or foul water?
o: The water can make the joints set far too slowly indeed
The water washes the markings off the pipe
The water makes the pipe too slippery to hold
The water can contaminate the inside of the main
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Standing or foul water can get into the pipe and contaminate the drinking supply.

n.0: Joint setting time is not the reason for de-watering.
n.1: Losing pipe markings is not the hygiene concern.
n.2: Grip on the pipe is not why water is removed.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: the trench has filled with muddy water after rain. You should:
o: lay the pipe and let the water drain past it
lay the pipe quickly while the water is shallow
add stone until the water is out of sight
pump it out before laying any pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Muddy water must be pumped out so pipe is laid on a clean, water-free bed.
