n.0: Laying in the water lets contamination reach the pipe.
n.1: Shallow water is still a contamination risk.
n.2: Burying water under stone leaves foul water in the trench.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Foul water has seeped into the trench from a nearby drain. The safe action is to:
o: stop, remove the water and deal with the source
carry on laying as the pipe is sealed anyway
bail a little out and lay between seepages
lay the pipe a little higher to keep it just clear
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Foul seepage is a serious risk, so work stops, the water is removed and the source is dealt with before laying.

n.1: An open end means the pipe is not sealed against foul water.
n.2: Bailing between seepages still leaves foul water present.
n.3: Raising the pipe does not remove the foul-water hazard.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The main reason to keep the trench de-watered while laying is to:
o: keep foul water out of the open pipe
make the trench easier to walk along
stop the bedding stone floating up
help the excavator reach the bottom
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A dry trench keeps standing and foul water from entering the open pipe during laying.

n.1: Ease of walking is not the hygiene purpose.
n.2: Bedding stone movement is not the main concern.
n.3: Machine access is not why the trench is de-watered.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which trench condition is acceptable for laying clean-water pipe?
o: A shallow layer of rainwater over the bed
A clean bed that has been de-watered
A trickle of foul water along the bottom
Soft mud with puddles between the stone
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Pipe is only laid on a clean, de-watered bed so nothing contaminates the main.

n.0: Even a shallow layer of water is a contamination risk.
n.2: Any foul water in the trench is unacceptable.
n.3: Mud and puddles can contaminate the open pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: If the trench keeps filling with water faster than you can bail, you should:
o: lay the pipe between the rising floods
set up pumping to keep the bed clear
give up de-watering and lay it wet
wait for the water to soak away on its own
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Continuous inflow calls for proper pumping so the bed stays clear enough to lay clean pipe.

n.0: Laying between floods still puts pipe near foul water.
n.2: Laying it wet risks contaminating the main.
n.3: Waiting is not reliable when water keeps flowing in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Standing water left in a trench is a hygiene risk because it may contain:
o: only clean and harmless rainwater really
only chlorine that protects the pipe
nothing of any real concern at all
soil, germs and other contamination
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Trench water typically carries soil and germs, which is why pipe is never laid in it.

n.0: Trench water is not simply clean rainwater.
n.1: It contains no protective chlorine.
n.2: Treating it as harmless ignores the real risk.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Pumping water out of a trench should be done:
o: so it discharges away from the open pipe
straight back down into the open pipe end again
into the next section still to be laid
over the fittings stored beside the dig
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The discharge is directed away so the removed water cannot run back into the pipe or over clean fittings.

n.1: Discharging into the pipe defeats the purpose entirely.
n.2: Sending it into the next section spreads the water.
n.3: Wetting stored fittings contaminates them too.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: the bed looks dry but one puddle remains where the pipe will sit. You should:
o: lay across it as one puddle is harmless
clear that puddle before laying over it
cover the puddle with a scoop of spoil
push the pipe through and mop up later
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Any water where the pipe will sit must be cleared, as even one puddle can contaminate the main.

n.0: A single puddle is still a contamination risk.
n.2: Spoil over the puddle adds dirt as well.
n.3: Laying first leaves the pipe sitting in water.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Laying pipe into foul water could result in:
o: a stronger joint once it dries out
a faster job with less pumping needed
cleaner pipe because of the extra rinse
contamination of the public drinking supply
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Foul water carries germs into the main and can contaminate the water people drink.

n.0: Foul water does not strengthen a joint.
n.1: Skipping de-watering trades safety for speed wrongly.
n.2: Foul water contaminates, it does not clean, the pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The bed of the trench should be prepared so that:
o: the pipe sits in a channel of running water
the pipe is bedded down into soft wet clay
the pipe floats until the backfill is added
the pipe rests on clean, water-free support
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A clean, de-watered, well-supported bed keeps the pipe out of contact with contaminating water.

n.0: Running water in the trench is a contamination source.
n.1: Wet clay soils the pipe and holds germs.
n.2: A floating pipe is sitting in standing water.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping the trench free of standing water protects mainly against:
o: germs and dirt entering the new main
the pipe sinking below the design level
the excavator getting bogged down
delays waiting for the ground to firm up
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The purpose of de-watering is hygiene: keeping germs and dirt out of the drinking-water main.

n.1: Pipe level is a separate setting-out issue.
n.2: Machine access is not the hygiene reason.
n.3: Programme delays are not the hygiene purpose.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A new clean-water main should be kept well away from:
o: any other clean-water mains sited nearby
sewers, drains and other foul services
the marker tape that is laid above it
the clean bedding stone around the pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Separation from sewers and drains reduces the risk of foul contamination reaching the drinking-water main.

n.0: Clean-water mains are not a foul-contamination risk.
n.2: Marker tape is part of the clean-water works.
n.3: Bedding stone is clean material around the pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why is a clean-water main not laid in the same trench as a sewer?
o: The sewer would just end up making the water main colder
The two pipes would be harder to colour-code
The sewer needs more bedding stone than water
A leak from the sewer could contaminate the water
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Keeping foul and clean apart means a sewer leak is far less likely to reach the drinking water.

n.0: Temperature is not the reason for separation.
n.1: Colour-coding is not the hygiene concern.
n.2: Bedding quantities are not why they are kept apart.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: your route crosses close to a foul drain. Good practice is to:
o: lay the main touching the drain to save space
rest the new main on top of the drain
keep the required separation from the drain
share one trench for both to speed the job
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Maintaining the required separation keeps the clean-water main away from the foul drain.

n.0: Touching the drain removes any protective separation.
n.1: Resting on the drain puts the main in a foul position.
n.3: Sharing a trench brings foul and clean together.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Storing a length of new main next to an open cesspit is wrong because:
o: the pit would make the pipe rust faster
the smell would put the gang off working
the pit takes up room needed for spoil
foul matter could contaminate the pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A foul environment can contaminate the pipe, so new main is kept well away from it.

n.0: Rusting is not the hygiene issue with a cesspit.
n.1: The smell is unpleasant but not the real risk.
n.2: Space for spoil is not the hygiene concern.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which situation puts a new water main most at risk of foul contamination?
o: Laying it in a clean, separated trench
Laying it on a clean, de-watered bed
Laying it right beside a leaking sewer
Laying it with proper marker tape above
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A leaking sewer alongside the main is a direct route for foul contamination.

n.0: A clean, separated trench is the safe way to lay it.
n.1: A clean, de-watered bed keeps the main protected.
n.3: Marker tape is part of good, safe practice.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: If a new main must pass near foul ground, the operative should:
o: follow the required separation and precautions
ignore it as the pipe is sealed anyway
shorten the route through the foul area
lay it much faster to spend less time down there
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Set separations and precautions are followed so the main stays protected from the foul ground.

n.1: An open, being-laid main is not fully sealed.
n.2: A shorter route still runs through foul ground.
n.3: Working faster does not remove the contamination risk.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping the new main clear of foul services is mainly to protect:
o: the paint finish on the outside of the pipe
the working life of the excavator
the tidy appearance of the finished trench
the quality of the water people will drink
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Separation from foul services guards the drinking-water quality inside the main.

n.0: Outside paint is not the reason for separation.
n.1: Machine life is unrelated to foul separation.
n.2: Trench appearance is not the hygiene purpose.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: An open pipe end lying beside a foul ditch should be:
o: moved away and kept capped and clean
left there as it will be jointed soon
rinsed in the ditch before it is used
rolled into the ditch to keep it out of the way
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The pipe is kept clean and away from the foul ditch, with its end capped until use.

n.1: Leaving it by the ditch risks foul contamination.
n.2: Rinsing in the ditch contaminates the pipe.
n.3: Putting it in the ditch is the worst possible place.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why should spoil from a foul excavation not be mixed with clean-water bedding?
o: It could carry contamination onto the new main
It would make the bedding a different colour
It would be much heavier to shovel into its place
It would set harder than the clean stone
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Foul spoil can bring germs and dirt to the pipe, so it is kept out of clean-water bedding.

n.1: Colour is not the hygiene concern with foul spoil.
n.2: Weight is not why foul spoil is kept separate.
n.3: Setting behaviour is not the hygiene issue.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: a foul manhole is right beside your excavation. You should:
o: rest tools on the manhole to save space
keep the new main and fittings clear of it
store the fittings on top of the manhole cover
wash pipe ends in the manhole chamber
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The manhole is a foul point, so the main, fittings and tools are kept away from it.

n.0: Resting tools there risks contaminating them.
n.2: Storing fittings on it puts them in a foul spot.
n.3: Washing pipe in it contaminates the main directly.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A clean-water main run alongside a foul sewer should have:
o: no gap at all to keep the trench narrow
the specified separation and protection
the foul pipe laid above the water main
both pipes sharing the same bedding
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The specified separation and protection keep the main safe from the foul sewer.

n.0: No gap removes the protection between them.
n.2: A foul pipe above the water main can leak onto it.
n.3: Shared bedding brings foul and clean together.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping fittings away from foul areas on site helps ensure:
o: they are much quicker to count at the very end
they weather to match the pipe colour
they stay clean until they join the main
they are easier to stack on the lorry
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Kept clear of foul areas, fittings stay clean right up to the point they are jointed.

n.0: Counting is not the hygiene reason.
n.1: Weathering to match colour is irrelevant to hygiene.
n.3: Stacking convenience is not the purpose here.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A tool has been used in foul water. Before using it on the clean main you must:
o: disinfect it so it is safe to use
dry it off and use it straight away
rinse it once under the tap and use it
leave it in the sun for an hour first
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A tool exposed to foul water must be disinfected before it touches clean-water surfaces.

n.1: Drying alone does not kill the germs on it.
n.2: A quick rinse does not disinfect the tool.
n.3: Sunlight is not a reliable way to disinfect a tool.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why disinfect tools that have been in dirty water?
o: To make all the tools shine up like new again
To stop the tools from going blunt
To kill germs before they reach the main
To make the tools lighter to carry
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Disinfection removes the germs picked up from dirty water so they cannot contaminate the main.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason for disinfecting.
n.1: Disinfection does not affect a tool's edge.
n.3: It has nothing to do with a tool's weight.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: you drop your cutter into the foul trench water. You should:
o: shake it dry and carry on cutting
clean and disinfect it before further use
wipe it on your overalls and continue
use it on the spare pipe offcuts only for now
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The cutter is now contaminated, so it is cleaned and disinfected before any further clean-water use.

n.0: Shaking it dry leaves the germs on it.
n.2: Wiping it on overalls does not disinfect it.
n.3: Even offcuts become part of the clean main.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A tool that has been in dirty water but is not disinfected should be:
o: used only on the most important joints
kept off clean-water work until treated
shared around the whole gang as per normal
stored with the clean tools for later
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Until it is disinfected the tool is a contamination risk and is kept away from clean-water work.

n.0: Important joints are exactly where contamination must not go.
n.2: Sharing it spreads the contamination around.
n.3: Storing it with clean tools contaminates them too.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Disinfecting a contaminated tool is important because dirty water can carry:
o: extra weight that tires the operative
rust that spreads to other tools
paint that marks the pipe surface
germs that could make people ill
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Dirty water carries germs, and disinfection stops them reaching the drinking-water main.

n.0: Weight is not the hazard from dirty water.
n.1: Rust is a durability issue, not the germ hazard.
n.2: Paint marks are not the contamination concern.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which is the correct order after a tool falls in foul water?
o: Use it, then disinfect it afterwards
Disinfect it, then roll it in the spoil
Dry it, then store it without cleaning
Clean off the dirt, then disinfect it
Hygienic Site Practices.w: You remove the visible dirt first and then disinfect, so the tool is safe before it is used again.

n.0: Using it first has already risked contamination.
n.1: Rolling a disinfected tool in spoil re-contaminates it.
n.2: Drying without cleaning leaves dirt and germs on it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A colleague wants to borrow your saw that has been in dirty water. You should:
o: tell them it needs disinfecting first
hand it over as it looks clean enough
lend it but say to rinse it after
lend it only for cutting the spoil boards
Hygienic Site Practices.w: The saw is contaminated, so it must be disinfected before anyone uses it on clean-water work.

n.1: Looking clean does not mean it is free of germs.
n.2: Rinsing afterwards does not undo contamination during use.
n.3: Any clean-water cutting risks carrying germs in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Tools kept for clean-water work should ideally be:
o: reserved for that work and kept disinfected
the same set used for the foul drainage
left lying in the open trench between the shifts
swapped freely with the muckaway gang
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Dedicated, disinfected tools avoid the risk of carrying foul contamination onto the clean main.

n.1: Sharing with foul drainage work spreads contamination.
n.2: Leaving tools in the trench lets them pick up dirt.
n.3: Swapping with other gangs risks bringing in germs.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: you finish a foul repair and move to a clean-water job. Your tools should be:
o: used as they are to keep momentum
disinfected before you start the clean job
just given a wipe over with a dry cloth first
left dirty as the next job is quick
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Moving from foul to clean work means the tools are disinfected first to protect the clean main.

n.0: Carrying on risks bringing foul germs to the main.
n.2: A dry wipe does not disinfect the tools.
n.3: A quick job still needs clean tools.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The best reason to disinfect and not just rinse a contaminated tool is that:
o: rinsing takes far longer to do
rinsing may leave germs behind
rinsing makes the tool rust faster
rinsing removes the tool markings
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Rinsing can leave germs on the tool, so proper disinfection is needed to make it safe.

n.0: Rinsing is not slower than disinfecting.
n.2: Rusting is not the reason to prefer disinfection.
n.3: Tool markings are not the concern here.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: If you are unsure whether a tool has been in foul water, the safe approach is to:
o: assume it is clean and use it
treat it as dirty and disinfect it
give it a quick shake and carry on
ask later and keep working now
Hygienic Site Practices.w: When in doubt, the tool is treated as contaminated and disinfected before use on the clean main.

n.0: Assuming it is clean risks contaminating the water.
n.2: A shake does nothing to make it safe.
n.3: Working on while unsure risks contamination.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Disinfecting tools is part of keeping which safe?
o: The site's fuel and oil store
The excavator's hydraulic system
The public drinking-water supply
The gang's tea-break area
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Tool disinfection is a hygiene measure that protects the drinking-water supply from contamination.

n.0: The fuel store is not what tool hygiene protects.
n.1: Hydraulics are unrelated to water hygiene.
n.3: The break area is not the point of disinfecting tools.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A bucket used to bail foul water from the trench should be:
o: kept away from clean pipe unless disinfected
used next to carry clean jointing water
stored away inside the open end of the new pipe
tipped out over the stored fittings
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A foul-water bucket is contaminated, so it is kept from clean pipe unless it has been disinfected.

n.1: Using it for clean water spreads contamination.
n.2: Storing it in the pipe contaminates the bore.
n.3: Tipping it over fittings soils them.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why should operatives wear clean overalls on clean-water work?
o: Clean overalls make the gang look faster
Clean overalls keep the operative warmer
Clean overalls last much longer than dirty ones
Dirty clothing can carry germs to the main
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean overalls reduce the chance of germs and dirt being carried onto the pipe and into the water.

n.0: Appearance of speed is not the hygiene reason.
n.1: Warmth is not why clean overalls are worn.
n.2: Garment life is not the hygiene point.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A tidy work area helps hygiene mainly by:
o: reducing the dirt that can reach the main
making the job look good to passers-by
leaving more room to park the vehicles
cutting the time spent tidying at the end
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A tidy site keeps dirt and rubbish away from the pipe, lowering the contamination risk.

n.1: Appearance to passers-by is not the hygiene aim.
n.2: Parking space is not the hygiene benefit.
n.3: Saving tidy-up time is not the point.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: your overalls are covered in foul mud from an earlier job. Before the clean-water work you should:
o: change into clean, dry overalls
brush the worst off and carry on
turn them inside out and continue
spray them with water and keep working
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Foul-mud-covered overalls are a contamination risk, so you change into clean ones before the clean-water job.

n.1: Brushing leaves plenty of dirt and germs on them.
n.2: Turning them inside out does not make them clean.
n.3: A quick spray does not remove the contamination.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Personal cleanliness on a water job matters because germs can be spread by:
o: dirty hands, clothing and equipment
the colour of the operative's overalls
the make of boots the operative wears
the number of people in the gang
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Germs travel on dirty hands, clothing and kit, so personal cleanliness helps keep the main clean.

n.1: Overall colour has no effect on hygiene.
n.2: Boot brand is irrelevant to contamination.
n.3: Gang size is not itself a contamination route.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Leaving rubbish and offcuts around the excavation is poor practice because it:
o: blocks the view of the marker tape
makes the spoil heap look untidy
can fall in and contaminate the main
uses up space needed for the pump
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Loose rubbish can drop into the trench or pipe and contaminate the drinking-water main.

n.0: Marker-tape visibility is not the hygiene reason.
n.1: Untidiness alone is not the contamination point.
n.3: Pump space is not why rubbish is cleared.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which best describes good hygiene housekeeping on a clean-water site?
o: Old overalls, muddy hands and some loose spoil
Any overalls as long as work gets done
Dirty kit kept close by to save on walking
Clean overalls, clean hands and a tidy area
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean overalls, clean hands and a tidy area together keep contamination away from the main.

n.0: Muddy hands and loose spoil spread contamination.
n.1: Ignoring hygiene to finish work risks the supply.
n.2: Keeping dirty kit close brings dirt to the pipe.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Washing your hands before handling clean-water fittings helps to:
o: warm your hands up first before the work
stop germs passing from your hands to the main
remove the grip so the fitting slides on easily
speed up the jointing of the new pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean hands prevent germs being transferred onto fittings that meet the drinking water.

n.0: Warming hands is not the hygiene reason.
n.2: You want grip, not less of it, when jointing.
n.3: Hand washing is about hygiene, not speed.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: you have just eaten lunch with mucky hands and return to jointing. You should:
o: wash your hands before touching the fittings
get straight back to the jointing work
wipe your hands on your trouser leg
put gloves on over the dirty hands and then start
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Dirty hands can carry germs to the fittings, so they are washed before jointing resumes.

n.1: Starting with dirty hands risks contaminating the main.
n.2: Wiping on trousers does not clean your hands.
n.3: Gloves over dirty hands still risk transfer.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A tidy site with materials stored neatly helps keep the main clean because:
o: neat stacks make the whole site photograph well
clean materials are less likely to be soiled
tidy sites always finish ahead of time
neat stacks reduce the delivery costs
Hygienic Site Practices.w: When materials are stored neatly and clean, there is less chance of them being contaminated before use.

n.0: Photographs are not the hygiene reason.
n.2: Finishing early is not guaranteed by tidiness.
n.3: Delivery costs are unrelated to hygiene.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Eating or drinking should be kept away from the open trench to avoid:
o: food or waste dropping into the pipe
the gang taking longer breaks
crumbs attracting the site inspector
the food getting cold too quickly
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Keeping food away from the trench stops scraps or waste contaminating the open main.

n.1: Break length is not the hygiene concern.
n.2: Attracting an inspector is not the real risk.
n.3: Food temperature is not the point.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Overalls used for foul work and clean-water work should be:
o: kept separate to avoid cross-contamination
worn for whichever job comes first
the exact same set to save on kit
swapped between operatives each day
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Separate overalls stop foul-work contamination being carried onto clean-water work.

n.1: Wearing the same set across both spreads contamination.
n.2: Sharing one set risks carrying germs across jobs.
n.3: Swapping overalls between people spreads dirt.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The overall aim of clean overalls and a tidy site is to:
o: impress the client on their visit
reduce the amount of PPE needed
make the vans easier to load up
prevent contamination reaching the water
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Personal and site cleanliness are about keeping contamination out of the public drinking-water supply.

n.0: Impressing the client is not the hygiene purpose.
n.1: Cleanliness does not reduce PPE needs.
n.2: Van loading is unrelated to water hygiene.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The inside (bore) of a new water pipe should be kept:
o: slightly damp to help the joint slide
coated in grease to stop it corroding
clean and dry until the pipe is jointed
open to the air to let it breathe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A clean, dry bore keeps dirt and germs out of the water the pipe will carry.

n.0: Damp inside the bore can hold contamination.
n.1: Grease in the bore is itself a contaminant.
n.3: Leaving the bore open lets dirt and vermin in.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Something has fallen inside a length of pipe before jointing. You should:
o: joint the pipe and flush it later
remove it and check the bore is clean
shake the pipe and hope it drops out
leave it as it will wash through in use
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Anything in the bore must be removed and the pipe checked, so nothing contaminates the water.

n.0: Flushing later is not a substitute for removing it now.
n.2: Shaking may not clear it and leaves it uncertain.
n.3: Objects do not reliably wash through and clear.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Why is the bore of the pipe the most important part to keep clean?
o: It is the part people can see the most
It is where all of the pipe markings are printed
It is the strongest part of the pipe wall
It is the surface the drinking water touches
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Water flows against the bore, so any contamination there goes straight into the supply.

n.0: Visibility is not why the bore matters most.
n.1: Markings are usually on the outside, not the bore.
n.2: Strength is not the hygiene reason.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: you spot a snail inside the open pipe end. You should:
o: joint over the top of it and carry on
push it further down inside with a rod
clean it out before making the joint
ignore it as it is only a small one
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Any living thing in the bore is contamination and must be cleaned out before jointing.

n.0: Jointing over it traps contamination in the main.
n.1: Pushing it along leaves it in the water pipe.
n.3: Size does not make contamination acceptable.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Which of these best protects the inside of a new main?
o: Leaving both ends open to dry the bore out
Storing pipe with its ends in the mud
Rinsing out the bore with dirty trench water
Capping ends and keeping the bore clean
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Capped ends and a clean bore keep contamination out of the inside of the main.

n.0: Open ends let dirt and vermin into the bore.
n.1: Ends in the mud contaminate the bore.
n.2: Trench water in the bore adds contamination.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: A push-fit joint is about to be made. The inside of both parts should be:
o: clean and free of soil or debris
packed with grease for a tight seal
left with a little grit for extra grip
wetted with trench water before joining
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clean inner faces keep contamination out of the bore when the joint is made.

n.1: Grease inside the joint contaminates the bore.
n.2: Grit is contamination, not a jointing aid.
n.3: Trench water in the joint contaminates the main.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Standing water inside a pipe left overnight is a concern because it:
o: makes the pipe heavier to lift out
washes the markings off the bore
may hold germs that contaminate the supply
cools the pipe below the design level
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Water sitting in the bore can carry germs into the drinking-water supply.

n.0: Weight is not the hygiene concern.
n.1: Losing markings is not the real risk.
n.3: Pipe temperature is not the hygiene issue.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The safest way to keep the bore clean between deliveries and laying is to:
o: remove the caps to check the bore daily
leave the manufacturer's caps in place
store the pipe open on the wet ground
point both ends into the spoil heap
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Keeping the supplied caps on protects the bore right up until the pipe is jointed.

n.0: Removing caps to check lets dirt in each time.
n.2: Open pipe on wet ground soils the bore.
n.3: Ends in the spoil heap contaminate the bore.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Short scenario: the bore has a smear of mud near the end. Before jointing you should:
o: joint it and let water clear the mud
wipe over only the outside of that end
smear it around evenly so it is less obvious
clean the bore until it is free of mud
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Mud in the bore is contamination, so it is cleaned out fully before the joint is made.

n.0: Relying on water to clear mud leaves contamination in.
n.1: The bore, not just the outside, must be clean.
n.2: Spreading the mud does not remove it.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Blowing or wiping out a pipe before jointing is done to:
o: make the whole pipe warmer before use
test just how strong the pipe wall really is
remove any dirt or debris from the bore
polish up the outside of the pipe
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Clearing the bore of dirt and debris protects the water the pipe will carry.

n.0: Warming the pipe is not the purpose.
n.1: It does not test the pipe's strength.
n.3: Polishing the outside is not the aim.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: If insects or leaves get into an open pipe end, the operative should:
o: leave them as they will decay away
joint the pipe and forget about them
flush them along to the next length
clean them out before the pipe is used
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Anything that gets into the bore is removed before use so it cannot contaminate the water.

n.0: Leaving them to decay contaminates the main.
n.1: Jointing over them traps contamination inside.
n.2: Flushing them along still leaves them in the system.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: Keeping the bore dry as well as clean is helpful because:
o: a wet bore joints more strongly
a damp bore keeps the pipe cooler
moisture makes the pipe easier to cut
dry, clean pipe gives germs nowhere to sit
Hygienic Site Practices.w: A clean, dry bore denies germs the moisture and dirt they need, protecting the supply.

n.0: Wetness does not make a joint stronger.
n.1: Cooling is not the hygiene reason.
n.2: Ease of cutting is not the point.

Hygienic Site Practices.q: The main purpose of all the measures that keep the bore clean is to:
o: make the finished pipe cheaper to install on site
help the new pipe to pass its pressure test
keep the outside of the pipe looking new
deliver safe, clean drinking water to the public
Hygienic Site Practices.w: Every bore-protection measure exists to keep the drinking water safe for the people who use it.

n.0: Cost saving is not the purpose of bore hygiene.
n.1: The pressure test is separate from bore cleanliness.
n.2: The outside appearance is not the hygiene aim.

Materials & Approved Products.q: On a clean water main, which fittings are you permitted to install?
o: Any fitting that is physically strong enough for it
Only fittings approved for contact with drinking water
Whatever fittings the local merchant has in stock
Any fitting that will physically connect to the existing pipe
Materials & Approved Products.w: You may fit only products approved as suitable for contact with potable water.

n.0: Mechanical strength does not make a fitting safe for drinking water.
n.2: What a merchant stocks is not proof that a fitting is approved.
n.3: Simply fitting the pipe does not mean it is approved for water contact.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which regulation forbids using a fitting that is unsuitable or likely to contaminate water?
o: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
Regulation 4 of the Water Fittings Regulations
The Confined Spaces Regulations of 1997
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health rules
Materials & Approved Products.w: Regulation 4 forbids using any fitting that could contaminate water or is unsuitable.

n.0: That Act covers general workplace safety, not fitting suitability for water.
n.2: Those regulations cover confined space entry, not water fittings.
n.3: COSHH covers hazardous substances at work, not water fitting approval.

Materials & Approved Products.q: A scheme that tests and lists products as suitable for drinking water is:
o: A CE mark stamped on the box
The manufacturer's own money-back guarantee
Approval under the WRAS scheme
The merchant's internal stock reference code
Materials & Approved Products.w: WRAS approval shows a product has been tested as suitable for drinking water.

n.0: CE marking covers other safety matters, not drinking-water suitability.
n.1: A guarantee covers faults, not whether the product is safe for water.
n.3: A stock code simply identifies a product on the shelf.

Materials & Approved Products.q: You run out of approved pipe and a colleague offers spare pipe of unknown type. You should:
o: Use it straight away because it is the same diameter
Use it as the job needs finishing today
Use it if it looks clean and undamaged
Not use it until you confirm it is approved
Materials & Approved Products.w: If you are unsure whether a product is approved, check before using it.

n.0: Matching diameter does not prove the pipe is approved for water.
n.1: A deadline does not make an unapproved pipe acceptable.
n.2: Looking clean does not prove the pipe is approved for water.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Approved materials for drinking water are chosen mainly because they:
o: are always the cheapest option available
come in a much wider choice of colours
do not contaminate or spoil the water
are quicker and easier to install on site
Materials & Approved Products.w: Approved materials are those that will not contaminate or affect the quality of the water.

n.0: Cost is not why a material is approved for drinking water.
n.1: Colour choice is not why a material is approved.
n.3: Ease of fitting is not why a material is approved.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which statement about installing water fittings is correct?
o: Any food-grade plastic fitting is acceptable
Only approved fittings may touch drinking water
Garden-hose fittings are fine on mains pipe
Second-hand fittings are always acceptable here
Materials & Approved Products.w: Only fittings approved for contact with drinking water may be used on the supply.

n.0: Food-grade does not automatically mean approved for mains water.
n.2: Garden-hose fittings are not approved for potable mains use.
n.3: Second-hand fittings are not automatically approved or clean.

Materials & Approved Products.q: A householder offers their own tap to fit on the rising main. First you must be sure it is:
o: the same colour as the existing tap
cheaper than one from the merchant
approved for use with drinking water
made somewhere within the United Kingdom
Materials & Approved Products.w: Any fitting on the supply must be approved as suitable for drinking water.

n.0: The colour of the tap has nothing to do with approval.
n.1: A lower price does not make a tap approved for water.
n.3: Where a tap is made does not make it approved.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Why must an operative avoid 'making do' with unapproved fittings?
o: They may not match the existing pipework
They can put the water quality at risk
They usually cost a bit more to buy in
They can be harder to store on the van
Materials & Approved Products.w: Unapproved fittings can contaminate the water and are not permitted on the supply.

n.0: Matching pipework is not the safety reason they are avoided.
n.2: Cost is not the safety reason unapproved fittings are avoided.
n.3: Storage is not the safety reason unapproved fittings are avoided.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which is the best evidence that a fitting may be used on drinking water?
o: It has been used on this site before
It appears on an approved products list
It was a fairly expensive fitting to buy in
It carries a well-known brand name
Materials & Approved Products.w: A fitting listed as approved has been tested as suitable for drinking water.

n.0: Previous use on site does not prove a fitting is approved.
n.2: A high price does not prove a fitting is approved.
n.3: A well-known brand does not prove a fitting is approved.

Materials & Approved Products.q: New fittings for a potable supply should always be:
o: painted over before they are installed
the largest size that will physically fit
bought from an online marketplace seller
approved and kept clean before fitting
Materials & Approved Products.w: Fittings must be approved for drinking water and kept clean and protected before use.

n.0: Painting a fitting does not make it approved or clean.
n.1: The largest size is not the requirement for a fitting.
n.2: The place of purchase does not make a fitting approved.

Materials & Approved Products.q: The main purpose of the Water Fittings Regulations is to:
o: prevent contamination and waste of water
make water fittings cheaper to buy
speed up the installation of pipework
increase the pressure in the water mains
Materials & Approved Products.w: The Regulations exist to prevent contamination, waste, misuse and undue consumption of water.

n.1: Lowering the cost of fittings is not the purpose of the Regulations.
n.2: Speeding up installation is not the purpose of the Regulations.
n.3: Raising mains pressure is not the purpose of the Regulations.

Materials & Approved Products.q: On site you are unsure if a valve is approved for potable water. You should:
o: fit it and note it for later checking
fit it because valves rarely cause harm
leave the decision to the householder
check its approval before installing it
Materials & Approved Products.w: If unsure, check the product is approved before using it, not afterwards.

n.0: Fitting first and checking later can leave contaminated water in use.
n.1: Assuming valves are harmless is not a safe basis to fit one.
n.2: The approval decision is yours, not the householder's.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which document would confirm a product is suitable for drinking water?
o: A current WRAS approval certificate
A delivery note from the supplier
A general product warranty card
A general health and safety data sheet
Materials & Approved Products.w: A WRAS approval certificate confirms the product is approved for drinking water.

n.1: A delivery note only records what was delivered, not approval.
n.2: A warranty card covers faults, not water suitability.
n.3: A safety data sheet covers handling, not water approval.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Fittings carrying a WRAS approval have been checked to make sure they:
o: will not spoil or contaminate the water
will last for at least fifty years in use
are the cheapest ones on the market
can withstand very high temperatures
Materials & Approved Products.w: WRAS approval confirms a fitting will not contaminate or affect water quality.

n.1: Approval is not a guarantee of a fixed lifespan.
n.2: Approval is not about being the cheapest option.
n.3: Approval is not a test of high-temperature resistance.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Non-approved plastics can be dangerous on a drinking water system because they may:
o: freeze far more slowly in winter
expand and block the pipe bore
leach chemicals into the water
make the water flow much faster
Materials & Approved Products.w: Non-approved plastics can leach chemicals into the water, affecting its quality.

n.0: Slower freezing is not the contamination concern with plastics.
n.1: Blocking the bore is not why the plastics are banned.
n.3: Flow speed is not the contamination concern here.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Using the wrong materials on a main can taint the water, which means it:
o: gets an off taste or smell
increases in pressure very suddenly
turns a permanent shade of blue
flows only during the daytime
Materials & Approved Products.w: Tainting means the water picks up an unpleasant taste or odour from the material.

n.1: A sudden pressure rise is not what tainting means.
n.2: A permanent colour change is not what tainting means.
n.3: Timing of the flow is not what tainting means.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Why can some unapproved materials encourage bacteria to grow in the water?
o: They make the water colder than normal
They raise the water pressure in the pipe
They reduce the rate of flow through the main
They can release nutrients bacteria feed on
Materials & Approved Products.w: Some materials release substances that act as nutrients, supporting bacterial growth.

n.0: Cooler water is not why bacteria would grow.
n.1: Higher pressure is not why bacteria would grow.
n.2: Reduced flow is not why bacteria would grow.

Materials & Approved Products.q: A material is banned from drinking water systems mainly because it could:
o: harm the quality or safety of the water
be tricky to cut to the right length
take a good deal longer than usual to install
come in only one available colour
Materials & Approved Products.w: Materials are banned when they could contaminate the water or affect its safety.

n.1: Being hard to cut is not why a material is banned.
n.2: A longer install time is not why a material is banned.
n.3: Limited colour is not why a material is banned.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which is a genuine risk of using non-approved jointing paste?
o: It may taint the taste of the water
It may make the joint far too tight
It may set much too quickly to use
It may leave a stain on your clothes
Materials & Approved Products.w: The wrong jointing paste can taint the water's taste and smell.

n.1: An over-tight joint is not the contamination risk.
n.2: A fast set time is not the contamination risk.
n.3: Staining clothes is not the contamination risk.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Non-approved materials are kept off drinking water systems to protect:
o: the appearance of the pipework
public health and water quality
the speed of the installation
the profit margin that is made on the job
Materials & Approved Products.w: The aim is to protect public health by keeping water free of contamination.

n.0: Appearance is not the interest being protected.
n.2: Installation speed is not the interest being protected.
n.3: Profit is not the interest being protected.

Materials & Approved Products.q: A pipe made from an unapproved plastic could give the water:
o: a much higher flow rate
a much lower freezing point
a far steadier pressure
a chemical taste or odour
Materials & Approved Products.w: Chemicals leaching from unapproved plastic can give the water a taste or smell.

n.0: A higher flow rate is not the effect of unapproved plastic.
n.1: A lower freezing point is not the effect of unapproved plastic.
n.2: A steadier pressure is not the effect of unapproved plastic.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Customers complain the water tastes odd after a repair. A likely cause is:
o: the water being turned off for far too long
an unapproved material used in the repair
the pipe being flushed too thoroughly
the stop tap being opened too slowly
Materials & Approved Products.w: Unapproved materials can taint water and cause taste and odour complaints.

n.0: A shut-off does not taint the water this way.
n.2: Thorough flushing does not taint the water.
n.3: Opening a tap slowly does not taint the water.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Why is 'it looks food-safe' not a good enough reason to use a material?
o: It may well be the wrong shade of blue here
It may be slightly heavier to carry
It may cost a little more per metre
It may still leach or taint the water
Materials & Approved Products.w: Only tested, approved materials are safe; appearance does not prove that.

n.0: Shade is not the safety concern with a material.
n.1: Weight is not the safety concern with a material.
n.2: Cost is not the safety concern with a material.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Bacterial growth supported by the wrong material is a concern because it can:
o: slow the flow at the tap
discolour the outside of pipes
make the water unsafe to drink
increase the water bill sharply
Materials & Approved Products.w: Bacteria supported by unsuitable materials can make the water unsafe to drink.

n.0: Slower flow is not the health concern here.
n.1: External discolouring is not the health concern here.
n.3: A higher bill is not the health concern here.

Materials & Approved Products.q: Which best explains why leaching is a problem in drinking water pipes?
o: The pipe becomes weaker and splits open
Chemicals pass from the material into the water
The water pressure inside gradually builds up higher
The pipe changes colour on the outside
Materials & Approved Products.w: Leaching means chemicals move from the material into the water people drink.

n.0: Splitting is not what leaching means.
n.2: A pressure build-up is not what leaching means.
n.3: External colour change is not what leaching means.

Materials & Approved Products.q: An operative must never fit an unapproved material even for a quick repair because it can:
o: contaminate the drinking water supply
void the manufacturer's tool warranty
make the repair take a little longer
use up more of the approved stock
Materials & Approved Products.w: Even a temporary unapproved fitting can contaminate the supply and is not allowed.

n.1: A tool warranty is not the safety reason it is banned.

o: To warm the pipe wall up so the chlorine dose will react much faster inside it
To fill every air pocket with grease so the joints will not leak once in use
To colour the water so any leaks from the new joints can be spotted at once while the job is being carried out
To physically push out loose soil, jointing debris and other material left inside the pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Swabbing sends a foam pig through the main to shift debris so the later chlorination works on a clean pipe.

n.0: Chlorination does not depend on warming the pipe; swabbing is about removing solids, not heat.
n.1: Swabbing removes debris; it is not a jointing or lubrication step.
n.2: Swabbing does not dye the water; leak testing is a separate pressure-test activity.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: What is a swab (pig) used on a water main most likely made of?
o: A steel brush head that is dragged through on a long rigid rod
A bag of chlorine granules that dissolves slowly as it passes before the main is put back into use
A dense foam plug shaped to fit the bore and travel along inside the pipe
A rubber balloon that is inflated to block the pipe permanently
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Foam swabs are sized to the pipe bore so they scour the wall and carry debris ahead of them.

n.0: Swabs are foam plugs driven by water flow, not rod-mounted steel brushes.
n.1: The swab removes debris mechanically; it is not the chlorine dosing method.
n.3: A swab travels through and is recovered; it is not left in to block the main.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Debris left inside a new main before disinfection is a problem mainly because it can:
o: Shield bacteria from the chlorine so parts of the pipe are not properly disinfected
Make the water taste sweeter than the customer would normally expect
Increase the pressure rating of the pipe once it is put into use according to the operative on site
Cause the chlorine to turn the inside of the pipe permanently blue
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Solids give organisms somewhere to hide and use up chlorine, so cleaning first makes disinfection effective.

n.1: Debris does not sweeten water; the concern is hygiene and effective disinfection.
n.2: Debris has no bearing on the pressure rating of the pipe.
n.3: Chlorine does not dye the pipe; the issue is shielded contamination.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A repaired main has been swabbed and the swab has come out. What does the operative check about it?
o: That the swab has been recovered and accounted for so none is left inside the main
That the swab is the same colour it was before being sent through the pipe
That the swab still smells strongly of chlorine after it is retrieved
That the swab has grown noticeably larger from soaking up the water at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A swab left in the pipe would obstruct flow and harbour contamination, so it must be counted out.

n.1: Swabs pick up dirt and change appearance; recovery is what matters, not colour match.
n.2: The swab clears debris; a chlorine smell on it is not the point of the check.
n.3: Swabbing is about recovering the swab and debris, not its swelling.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Swabbing is carried out on a new main so that the later disinfection:
o: Acts on a clean pipe wall rather than being wasted on loose dirt and debris
Can be skipped entirely because the pipe is already known to be clean
Will set the joints hard so the main can be pressurised straight away
Produces a bright colour change that proves the water is now safe once the pipe has been rejoined
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Clean pipework lets the chlorine reach the surfaces that matter instead of being used up by debris.

n.1: Swabbing supports disinfection; it does not remove the need to chlorinate.
n.2: Swabbing does not cure joints; that is unrelated to disinfection.
n.3: Swabbing removes solids; it does not produce a safety colour indicator.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which sequence is correct for bringing a new main into use?
o: Disinfect first, then swab out the debris, then put it straight into supply
Sample the water first, then swab, then leave the main open to the air for the customer supplied by that main
Flush the main first, then swab it, then supply without any disinfection
Swab out debris, then disinfect by chlorination, then flush and sample before supply
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The order is clean first, disinfect, then flush and confirm by sample before the main is used.

n.0: Swabbing comes before disinfection so chlorine acts on a clean pipe.
n.1: Sampling to confirm safety comes last, not first, and the main is not left open.
n.2: Disinfection is required and cannot be left out of the sequence.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If a main is not swabbed and debris is left in before chlorination, the likely result is:
o: The water company can charge the customer a lower price for the work
The pipe will corrode from the inside within a matter of hours as the work is being signed off
The chlorine will evaporate before it is even added to the pipe
Chlorine is used up by the debris so disinfection may be incomplete in places
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Debris exerts a chlorine demand and shelters organisms, so the dose may not disinfect everywhere.

n.0: Swabbing is a hygiene step; it has nothing to do with customer pricing.
n.1: Missing a swab is a disinfection risk, not an immediate corrosion cause.
n.2: Chlorine is dosed into the water; debris does not make it evaporate beforehand.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: On a new plastic main, swabbing before disinfection is done to:
o: Roughen the smooth bore so that chlorine can grip the pipe wall
Test whether the plastic pipe can survive being frozen solid
Add a protective wax lining to the inside of the new pipe throughout the length of the new main
Remove jointing swarf, soil and any material that entered during installation
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Installation can leave shavings and soil inside, and swabbing clears these before chlorination.

n.0: Swabbing removes debris; it is not meant to roughen the pipe.
n.1: Swabbing has no connection to freeze testing the pipe.
n.2: Swabbing removes material; it does not apply a lining.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A colleague asks why the main was swabbed when it 'looked clean' from the outside. The best answer is:
o: The inside can hold soil and swarf you cannot see, so swabbing clears it before disinfection
A clean outside always proves the inside is clean, so swabbing was not needed
Swabbing is only ever done to make the pipe look tidier for inspection
The swab replaces the need to disinfect the main at all while the job is being carried out at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A clean-looking exterior says nothing about hidden internal debris that swabbing removes.

n.1: The inside can be contaminated even when the outside looks clean, so swabbing is justified.
n.2: Swabbing is a hygiene measure, not a cosmetic one.
n.3: Swabbing prepares the pipe; disinfection still has to be carried out.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Swabbing a main mainly deals with which kind of contamination?
o: Dissolved chlorine that has been left in the pipe from earlier work
Loose solid material such as soil, grit and jointing debris inside the pipe
Air that has become trapped at the highest point of the main before the main is put back into use
Scale that has built up over many years of the pipe being in use
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Swabs shift physical debris; chemical disinfection then deals with micro-organisms.

n.0: Swabbing removes solids, not dissolved chlorine, which flushing handles.
n.2: Trapped air is vented separately; a swab targets solid debris.
n.3: New/repaired-main swabbing targets installation debris, not long-term scale removal here.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: on a new main the swab is fired through but no debris comes out. The operative should:
o: Assume the pipe is unsafe and immediately abandon the whole main
Record the result and continue with the disinfection procedure as planned
Skip disinfection because a clean swab proves the water is safe according to the operative on site
Send the swab through many more times until debris finally appears
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A clean swab run is a good sign; the process still moves on to chlorination.

n.0: A clean swab run does not condemn the main; the work continues.
n.2: Swabbing does not confirm safety; disinfection and sampling still follow.
n.3: Repeating pointlessly is not required; a clean run is recorded and work continues.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why is swabbing done before chlorination rather than after it?
o: So the debris carries the chlorine further along the main for you
So the chlorine works on a clean pipe instead of being spent on removing debris
So the swab is disinfected on its way through the pipe as well at that stage of the disinfection work
Because chlorine makes the debris far too heavy to move afterwards
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Cleaning first means the disinfectant is not wasted and can reach the pipe surfaces.

n.0: Debris consumes chlorine; it does not usefully carry it along.
n.2: The point is a clean pipe for disinfection, not disinfecting the swab.
n.3: Chlorine does not weigh debris down; the order is about effective disinfection.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which best describes a foam swab travelling through a main?
o: It floats on the surface of the water without touching the pipe wall
It dissolves completely into the water to release its cleaning agent
It is pushed along by water pressure, scouring the bore and gathering debris
It is pulled backwards against the flow by a winch on the surface once the pipe has been rejoined
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Water behind the swab drives it through so it wipes the wall and collects loose material.

n.0: A swab fits the bore and contacts the wall; it does not merely float.
n.1: Swabs are recovered whole; they do not dissolve into the water.
n.3: Swabs are driven forward by flow, not winched back against it.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A new main has been jointed and is ready for hygiene work. The first hygiene task is normally to:
o: Swab the main to clear out any debris before it is chlorinated
Take the final water quality sample before anything else is done
Add the neutralising chemical ready for the water to be discharged
Set the main into supply and swab it while customers are using it
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The recognised order starts by cleaning the pipe, then disinfecting it.

n.1: The passing sample comes at the end, after disinfection and flushing.
n.2: Neutralising relates to disposing of chlorinated water later, not the first step.
n.3: The main is not supplied before it is cleaned, disinfected and passed.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The purpose of removing debris from a main before disinfection is best summarised as:
o: Reducing the amount of water the main can hold once in service
Making sure the main will always run at a higher pressure as the work is being signed off
Guaranteeing the water will taste of chlorine for the customer
Giving the disinfectant a clean surface to act on so no contamination is sheltered
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Debris shelters organisms and consumes chlorine, so removing it makes disinfection reliable.

n.0: Debris removal is about hygiene, not the volume the main holds.
n.1: Swabbing does not raise the operating pressure of the main.
n.2: The aim is effective disinfection, not a lasting chlorine taste.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Swarf and soil that get into a main during installation are dealt with by:
o: Leaving them in place because chlorine will dissolve them completely
Swabbing the pipe so the loose material is carried out before chlorination
Raising the water temperature until the debris breaks down on its own
Adding extra jointing paste to trap the debris against the wall throughout the length of the new main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Physical debris is removed mechanically by swabbing, ahead of chemical disinfection.

n.0: Chlorine does not dissolve soil and swarf; they must be swabbed out.
n.2: Heat is not used to break down installation debris in a main.
n.3: Trapping debris does not remove it; swabbing carries it out.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: How is a new or repaired main normally disinfected before it goes into supply?
o: By heating the pipe until any organisms inside are killed by the temperature
By leaving the empty pipe open to fresh air for several dry days
By coating the inside of the pipe with a thick layer of grease while the job is being carried out
By dosing the water with chlorine to a set concentration and holding it for a contact time
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorination to a specified strength, held for the required time, is the standard disinfection method.

n.0: Mains are disinfected chemically by chlorination, not by heating the pipe.
n.1: Air-drying does not disinfect a main; chlorinated water is used.
n.2: Grease does not disinfect; chlorination of the water is the method.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: When chlorinating a main, the target chlorine concentration to use is set by:
o: Whatever strength the operative personally feels is about right on the day
The colour that the customer would most like the tap water to be
The outside air temperature measured at the start of the shift
The water company's own disinfection procedure for that type of work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The dose and contact time come from the undertaker's written procedure, not guesswork.

n.0: Doses are specified by the company's procedure, not chosen on a hunch.
n.1: Customer colour preference has no part in setting a disinfection dose.
n.2: Air temperature does not set the specified chlorine concentration.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: During disinfection, the 'contact time' means the period for which:
o: The swab is left sitting inside the pipe before it is fired through
The chlorinated water is held in the main so the disinfectant can act
The main is left completely empty before any water is added according to the operative on site
The customer is asked to stop using their taps in the street
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Contact time is the hold that lets the chlorine work on the pipe and any organisms.

n.0: Contact time refers to the chlorine hold, not to the swab.
n.2: Contact time needs chlorinated water present, not an empty main.
n.3: Contact time is a chemistry hold in the main, not a customer stoppage.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A main is being filled with chlorinated water. It should be filled so that:
o: Large air gaps are deliberately kept at the top to save on water at that stage of the disinfection work
Only the bottom half of the pipe ever comes into contact with the water
The disinfectant reaches all parts of the main with no air pockets left behind
The water is kept moving fast so it never rests against the wall
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Full wetting with no trapped air ensures every surface is exposed to the chlorine.

n.0: Trapped air leaves surfaces undisinfected, so gaps are not wanted.
n.1: Partial filling leaves the crown undisinfected; the whole bore must be wetted.
n.3: Contact time needs the water to dwell, not to rush past the wall.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: you have dosed a main to the specified chlorine strength. The next step is to:
o: Hold that chlorinated water in the main for the required contact time
Immediately flush the main out before the chlorine has time to act
Put the main straight into supply while the chlorine is still strong
Take the final bacteriological sample from the chlorinated water at once
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: After dosing, the chlorine must dwell for the set time before checks and flushing.

n.1: Flushing before the contact time defeats the disinfection.
n.2: Highly chlorinated water is never sent to customers; it must be flushed first.
n.3: The pass sample is taken later from flushed water, not from the strong chlorine.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why must the correct contact time be observed when chlorinating a main?
o: Because a longer wait always makes the water taste much better
The disinfectant needs time in contact with the pipe to work effectively
Because the pipe must cool down before it can be used again
Because the swab needs time to dissolve inside the main for the customer supplied by that main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorine acts over time, so cutting the hold short can leave the main not properly disinfected.

n.0: Contact time is about disinfection, not improving taste.
n.2: There is no cooling step; the hold is for the chlorine to act.
n.3: The swab is recovered earlier; contact time concerns the chlorine hold.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Disinfecting a main by chlorination is intended to:
o: Increase the flow rate the main can deliver to customers
Give the water a permanent blue tint for identification
Make the joints on the main set hard more quickly as the work is being signed off
Kill or inactivate micro-organisms so the water will be safe to drink
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorination deals with the microbiological risk so the main can be brought into supply safely.

n.0: Chlorination is a hygiene measure, not a way to raise flow.
n.1: Chlorination does not colour the water blue.
n.2: Chlorination does not cure or harden pipe joints.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Who decides the exact dose and hold time for disinfecting a particular main?
o: The customer whose property is nearest to the length of new main
The water company, through its written disinfection procedure for that work
The delivery driver who dropped off the chlorine chemicals throughout the length of the new main
Whichever operative happens to have the largest measuring jug
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The undertaker's procedure specifies the concentration and contact time to be used.

n.0: Customers do not set disinfection doses; the company's procedure does.
n.2: Suppliers deliver chemicals; they do not set the disinfection regime.
n.3: Equipment on hand does not set the dose; the written procedure does.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A disinfection procedure specifies a concentration and a contact time so that operatives:
o: Can add as much chlorine as they like provided they wait a while
Never have to check the residual chlorine level afterwards at all
Can skip flushing the main once the contact time has finished while the job is being carried out
Apply a consistent, proven method rather than guessing the strength each time
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Written figures give a repeatable, effective process that does not rely on individual judgement.

n.0: The procedure fixes the strength; you do not add as much as you like.
n.1: A residual check is still required to confirm the dose held.
n.2: Flushing after disinfection is still required before supply.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: the water company procedure sets a concentration and a hold time you have not memorised. You should:
o: Use figures you remember from a completely different water company
Pick a round number that seems easy to measure out quickly before the main is put back into use
Leave out the chlorine and rely on flushing to clean the main
Follow the figures given in the company's procedure for the job in hand
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The correct dose and hold come from the written procedure, which is the authority to follow.

n.0: Another company's figures may not apply; follow the procedure for this job.
n.1: Convenience is not a basis for the dose; the procedure governs it.
n.2: Flushing does not disinfect; the specified chlorination must be done.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Chlorinated water used to disinfect a main is introduced so that it:
o: Comes into contact with the whole inner surface of the pipework being treated
Only touches the newly made joints and none of the pipe barrel
Runs through so quickly that it barely wets the pipe wall according to the operative on site
Sits only in the lowest fitting on the length of new main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Every internal surface must meet the disinfectant, which means fully charging the main.

n.1: The whole bore, not just the joints, must be disinfected.
n.2: Contact time requires the water to dwell, not rush through.
n.3: The full length and height of the main must be reached, not one low point.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The disinfection stage of bringing a main into supply comes:
o: Before the main has been swabbed to remove any loose debris at that stage of the disinfection work
After the main has been swabbed clean and before it is flushed and sampled
After the passing water quality sample has already been taken
Only once the main is already delivering water to customers
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Order is swab, disinfect, then flush and take the passing sample.

n.0: Swabbing comes first so chlorine acts on a clean pipe.
n.2: The pass sample follows disinfection and flushing, not before.
n.3: Disinfection is completed before the main is put into supply.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If chlorinated water is not held for the full contact time, the risk is that:
o: The main may not be fully disinfected even though chlorine was added
The pipe will burst because the chlorine raises the pressure
The customers will be charged twice for the same water main
The swab will be trapped and cannot be recovered later on once the pipe has been rejoined
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Adding chlorine is not enough on its own; without the hold the disinfection may be incomplete.

n.1: Chlorine dosing does not raise pressure enough to burst the pipe.
n.2: Contact time is a hygiene control, not a billing matter.
n.3: The swab is recovered before dosing; contact time is separate.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which statement about chlorinating a main is correct?
o: A splash of chlorine at one end is enough with no set contact time
The chlorine only needs to touch the outside of the pipe wall for the customer supplied by that main
The dose is chosen to match the colour of the surrounding soil
The main is dosed to a set strength and the chlorine is held for a contact time
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The method combines a specified concentration with a required hold, both from procedure.

n.0: A specified dose and a full contact time are both needed, not a splash.
n.1: Disinfection treats the inside of the main, which carries the water.
n.2: Soil colour has nothing to do with the disinfection dose.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A repaired section is being disinfected. The chlorinated water should stay in the pipe:
o: For only a few seconds, just long enough to fill the pipe as the work is being signed off
For the contact time the water company's procedure requires for that work
Until the customer telephones to say the taps are running again
For as long as it takes the swab to travel back out again
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The hold period is set by the procedure and must be observed for effective disinfection.

n.0: Filling is not the hold; the specified contact time must be observed.
n.2: Customer calls do not govern the contact time; the procedure does.
n.3: The swab run is separate; contact time is the chlorine hold.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: After the contact time, the operative checks the 'residual chlorine'. This means checking:
o: How warm the water in the main has become during the hold throughout the length of the new main
How much chlorine is still present in the water after the hold period
How much debris the swab collected on its way through the pipe
How far the water has travelled along the length of the main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The residual test confirms enough chlorine remained through the contact time to disinfect.

n.0: Residual chlorine is a chemical measurement, not a temperature check.
n.2: Residual chlorine concerns the chlorine level, not swab debris.
n.3: Residual chlorine is about chlorine remaining, not distance travelled.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why is the residual chlorine checked after the contact time?
o: To decide what colour the customer's water will finally be
To measure how much the main has expanded under pressure
To confirm enough chlorine remained throughout the hold for disinfection to work
To find out how heavy the recovered swab has become while the job is being carried out
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: If the residual has held, it shows the dose was maintained and the main should be disinfected.

n.0: Residual testing checks disinfection, not the customer's water colour.
n.1: The residual test is chemical, not a measure of pipe expansion.
n.3: Residual chlorine is unrelated to the weight of the swab.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If the residual chlorine after the contact time is much lower than expected, this may mean:
o: The chlorine has been used up, so disinfection may be incomplete and needs review
The water is now definitely safe and can be supplied straight away
The pipe has grown too cold for the customers to use it before the main is put back into use
The swab has been left behind somewhere in the length of main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A big drop suggests demand from debris or contamination, so the process may have to be repeated.

n.1: A low residual is a warning sign, not proof the water is safe.
n.2: A low residual is a chemistry result, not a temperature issue.
n.3: A low residual points to chlorine demand, not a lost swab.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The residual chlorine reading is taken using:
o: A test that shows the amount of chlorine left in a water sample
A tape measure run along the outside of the new main
A stopwatch timing how long the swab took to pass through
A thermometer pushed into the soil beside the pipe according to the operative on site
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A simple chlorine test on the water gives the residual figure the operative records.

n.1: Residual chlorine is measured chemically on the water, not with a tape.
n.2: A stopwatch times events; it does not measure chlorine residual.
n.3: Soil temperature does not give the chlorine residual reading.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: after the hold, the residual chlorine is at the level the procedure expects. This suggests:
o: The main can be supplied now without any flushing or sampling
Enough chlorine was maintained during the contact time for disinfection to work
The swab must be sent through the main a second time at that stage of the disinfection work
The water is now too weak in chlorine to be discharged safely
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A held residual indicates the dose survived the hold, supporting effective disinfection.

n.0: Flushing and a passing sample are still required before supply.
n.2: A good residual does not call for another swab run.
n.3: A held residual is a good result, not a sign the water is too weak.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Checking the residual chlorine is important because adding chlorine alone does not prove:
o: That the required strength was actually held right through the contact time
That the pipe was the correct diameter for the job once the pipe has been rejoined
That the customer's stop tap has been fully closed
That the trench has been backfilled to the right depth
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Only the residual check confirms the dose was maintained, not just added at the start.

n.1: Residual checking is about chlorine, not verifying pipe diameter.
n.2: The residual test relates to disinfection, not stop-tap position.
n.3: Backfill depth is unrelated to the residual chlorine check.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A low or zero residual chlorine after the contact time usually calls for:
o: Putting the main straight into supply to save time on the job
Adding more debris to the pipe to use up the spare chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Reducing the contact time on the next main to match this one
Reviewing and, if needed, repeating the disinfection before the main is used
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: If the chlorine did not hold, the main may not be disinfected and the process is repeated.

n.0: A failed residual is not a reason to supply; it is a reason to redo the work.
n.1: Adding debris is never done; a failed residual means repeating disinfection.
n.2: A short residual does not justify cutting contact time elsewhere.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The residual chlorine check fits into the process:
o: Before any chlorine has been added to the water in the main
After the passing bacteriological sample has been taken as the work is being signed off
After the contact time has elapsed and before the main is flushed out
Only once the main is already delivering water to homes
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: You hold for contact time, confirm the residual, then flush and take the sample.

n.0: There is no chlorine to measure before it has been dosed.
n.1: The residual check comes before flushing and the final sample.
n.3: The residual is checked before supply, not after the main is live.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A held residual chlorine reading gives the operative confidence that:
o: The main will never need disinfecting again in the future
The swab travelled the full length of the main correctly
The disinfectant stayed strong enough throughout the required contact time
The customers can be billed for the extra chlorine used throughout the length of the new main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It shows the dose was not exhausted by demand, so the main is likely disinfected.

n.0: A good residual now does not exempt future work from disinfection.
n.1: The residual reading says nothing about the swab's journey.
n.3: The residual check is a hygiene control, not a billing input.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Residual chlorine is best described as the chlorine that:
o: Has completely left the water and gone into the air above it
Remains available in the water after some has been used up disinfecting
Has soaked permanently into the wall of the plastic pipe while the job is being carried out
Was spilled on the ground beside the trench during dosing
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It is the leftover disinfectant, showing enough was present to deal with demand.

n.0: Residual is what remains in the water, not what has left it.
n.2: Residual chlorine is measured in the water, not absorbed into the wall.
n.3: Residual refers to chlorine in the main's water, not spillage.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Once disinfection is complete and checked, why is the main flushed?
o: To wash the strong chlorinated water out before the main is used or sampled
To add more chlorine so the water is even stronger for supply
To warm the main up ready for the winter months ahead before the main is put back into use
To push the swab back into the pipe for a second cleaning run
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Flushing removes the high-chlorine water so customers do not receive it and a fair sample can be taken.

n.1: Flushing removes chlorinated water; it does not add more chlorine.
n.2: Flushing is about clearing chlorinated water, not warming the pipe.
n.3: The swab is already recovered; flushing clears the chlorinated water.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Flushing a main after disinfection removes the heavily chlorinated water so that:
o: The chlorine can be sold back to the supplier for a refund
Customers are not supplied with water that is too strong in chlorine to drink
The main can be left empty and out of use permanently according to the operative on site
The swab has more room to move around inside the pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Super-chlorinated water is unsuitable for supply, so it is flushed out first.

n.0: Flushing disposes of chlorinated water; it is not resold for money.
n.2: Flushing prepares the main for supply, not for permanent disuse.
n.3: The swab is recovered earlier; flushing clears chlorinated water.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: the residual chlorine has held for the full contact time. The next step is usually to:
o: Send the main into supply immediately with the strong chlorine still in it
Add a fresh dose of chlorine and start the contact time again
Flush the main through to clear the strong chlorinated water out of it
Take the passing sample straight from the strongly chlorinated water
