Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: After a satisfactory residual, the strong water is flushed away before sampling and supply.

n.0: Highly chlorinated water is flushed out first, never supplied.
n.1: A held residual means move on to flushing, not re-dosing.
n.3: The sample is taken from flushed water, not the strong chlorine.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Flushing after disinfection continues until the water leaving the main:
o: Turns a deep blue colour to show the chlorine is present once the pipe has been rejoined
No longer carries the high chlorine level used for the disinfection
Stops flowing altogether from the end of the length of main
Becomes noticeably warmer than when the flush first started
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Flushing runs until the chlorine has been cleared to a normal supply level.

n.0: Chlorine does not turn the water blue; flushing lowers the chlorine.
n.2: Flushing needs flow to clear the chlorine; it does not run to a stop.
n.3: Flushing is judged by chlorine clearance, not by temperature.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which best explains the order 'disinfect, then flush'?
o: The flush disinfects the main and the chlorine simply flavours it for the customer supplied by that main
Flushing first, then chlorine, keeps the water cleaner for longer
The chlorine is held to disinfect, then the strong water is washed away before use
Both happen at once so the chlorine and flush cancel each other out
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: You first let the chlorine act, then remove it so the main can be sampled and supplied.

n.0: Chlorine disinfects; flushing removes it. The roles are not swapped.
n.1: The order is disinfect then flush, not the reverse.
n.3: They are separate steps in sequence, not done simultaneously.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If a main were put into supply without flushing after disinfection, customers might get:
o: Water with an unacceptably strong taste and smell of chlorine
Water that is completely free of any chlorine at all
Water that has been warmed to a comfortable drinking temperature
Water carrying the recovered swab along to their taps
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Un-flushed super-chlorinated water would be far too strong for customers to receive.

n.1: Un-flushed water would be very high in chlorine, not free of it.
n.2: Flushing concerns chlorine strength, not warming the water.
n.3: The swab is recovered before this stage; flushing clears chlorine.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Flushing is carried out after disinfection and before:
o: The main has been swabbed to clear out any loose debris throughout the length of the new main
The chlorine has been added and the contact time started
The bacteriological sample is taken and the main is put into supply
The residual chlorine has first been dosed into the pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Flushing clears the strong chlorine so a representative sample can be taken before supply.

n.0: Swabbing happens at the very start, well before flushing.
n.1: Flushing follows the contact time; it does not precede dosing.
n.3: Dosing comes before the contact time; flushing comes after it.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Water being flushed from a main after disinfection is:
o: Perfectly ordinary tap water that can be poured into any river
Completely clean rainwater that never needs any handling care while the job is being carried out
Strong chlorinated water that must be dealt with responsibly, not just tipped anywhere
Drinking water that should be given straight to nearby customers
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The flush water is heavily chlorinated and needs careful, environmentally safe disposal.

n.0: Flush water is heavily chlorinated and cannot simply go into a river.
n.1: Flush water is chlorinated waste, not clean rainwater.
n.3: Strong chlorinated flush water is not given to customers.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The main reason flushing follows the residual check is to:
o: Refill the main with the same strong chlorine a second time
Cool the pipe down before the swab is sent through it before the main is put back into use
Raise the chlorine level higher than the procedure allows
Clear the disinfecting chlorine out once it has done its job in the main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: After confirming the chlorine held, it is flushed away so the water is fit to sample and supply.

n.0: Flushing removes the chlorine; it does not refill with more.
n.1: The swab and cooling are not part of the post-disinfection flush.
n.2: Flushing lowers the chlorine, it does not push it higher.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: you are flushing a disinfected main. You keep flushing until:
o: The very first drop of water appears at the flushing point
The water starts to foam heavily as it leaves the pipe according to the operative on site
The chlorine in the water leaving the main has dropped to a normal supply level
Exactly ten minutes have passed, whatever the chlorine reads
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Flushing continues until the chlorine reads at a level acceptable for supply.

n.0: The first flow is still strong; flushing continues past that point.
n.1: Foaming is not the endpoint; chlorine clearing to normal is.
n.3: The endpoint is the chlorine level, not a fixed clock time.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Before a disinfected main can be put into supply, a water quality sample must:
o: Be poured back into the main so none of the water is wasted
Be taken and pass the required bacteriological standard for drinking water
Show that the water is still strongly chlorinated at the tap
Prove that the swab was recovered from the pipe undamaged at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A passing microbiological sample is the final confirmation before the main carries supply.

n.0: Samples are analysed, not returned to the main.
n.2: The sample is taken from flushed water, not strongly chlorinated water.
n.3: The sample checks water quality, not the condition of the swab.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: What is checked in the bacteriological sample taken from a new main?
o: Whether harmful micro-organisms are present in the water at unacceptable levels
How strongly the water is coloured by the chlorine dose
How far the swab travelled along the main during cleaning
How much pressure the main can hold before it leaks once the pipe has been rejoined
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The microbiological test confirms the water is free of contamination before supply.

n.1: The sample is a microbiological check, not a colour measurement.
n.2: Sample analysis tests the water, not the swab's journey.
n.3: Pressure is a separate test; the sample checks water quality.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If the bacteriological sample from a new main fails, the main should:
o: Not be put into supply until the problem is corrected and a sample passes
Still be put into supply because the chlorine was added earlier
Be flushed once more and then supplied without any re-testing
Be handed straight to the customer with a warning to boil it for the customer supplied by that main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A failed sample means the water is not confirmed safe, so the main is held back and re-tested.

n.1: Adding chlorine earlier does not override a failed sample.
n.2: A fresh passing sample is required, not just another flush.
n.3: A failed main is not supplied on a boil notice; it is corrected first.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The bacteriological sample is taken:
o: After the main has been disinfected and flushed, from water fit to represent supply
Before the main has been chlorinated at all, straight from the ground
From the strong chlorinated water during the contact time
From the swab as it is pulled out of the end of the main as the work is being signed off
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The sample follows disinfection and flushing so it reflects the water customers would receive.

n.1: The sample comes after disinfection and flushing, not before dosing.
n.2: The sample is from flushed water, not the strong disinfection charge.
n.3: The sample is water for analysis, not taken off the swab.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why must a sample pass before a new main is put into supply?
o: To prove the operative used the most expensive chlorine available
To show the main can be filled and emptied very quickly throughout the length of the new main
To record how long the whole job took from start to finish
To confirm the water is safe to drink before customers receive it
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The passing sample is the final proof of safety that protects public health.

n.0: The sample confirms safety, not the cost of chemicals used.
n.1: A pass confirms water quality, not the speed of filling.
n.2: The sample is a safety check, not a timekeeping record.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: disinfection and flushing are done and the sample has passed. The main can now:
o: Only be used once the strong chlorine is added back into it
Be left open to the air for several more days before use while the job is being carried out
Never be used because a sample can only ever be a warning
Be put into supply because the water has been confirmed fit to drink
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A passing sample after correct disinfection and flushing clears the main for supply.

n.0: Strong chlorine is not re-added; a passed main is ready for supply.
n.1: A passed main is ready for supply, not left open to the air.
n.2: A passing sample clears the main; it is not merely a warning.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A bacteriological sample that passes tells you that:
o: The chlorine in the water is still at its full disinfection strength
The main has the correct diameter for the flow required before the main is put back into use
The swab collected the maximum possible amount of debris
No harmful organisms were found at unacceptable levels in that water
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A pass shows the microbiological quality met the standard for drinking water.

n.0: A pass follows flushing, when the chlorine has been reduced, not at full strength.
n.1: Sampling checks water quality, not the pipe's diameter.
n.2: The sample tests water, not how much the swab picked up.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The passing water quality sample is best described as:
o: The first task carried out before any swabbing takes place
The final confirmation that the disinfected main is safe to bring into use
A test of how strong the chlorine dose was during the hold
A measure of how much water the main can hold in total according to the operative on site
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It is the closing check that lets the main be put into supply with confidence.

n.0: Sampling is the last confirming step, not the first task.
n.2: The residual check tests chlorine strength; the sample tests water quality.
n.3: The sample confirms safety, not the volume the main holds.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: If a main is opened for a repair, put back and sampled, the sample is used to:
o: Decide how much to charge the customer for the repair work at that stage of the disinfection work
Prove the repair clamp was tightened to the correct torque
Show which direction the water flows along the repaired main
Confirm the repaired main is not contaminated before it goes back into supply
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Even after a repair, the sample proves the water is safe before customers are served again.

n.0: The sample is a safety check, not part of customer billing.
n.1: Sampling checks water quality, not the tightness of the clamp.
n.2: The sample confirms safety, not the direction of flow.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Taking a bacteriological sample correctly matters because:
o: A messy sample makes the water taste better for the customer once the pipe has been rejoined
The sample bottle can be reused straight away without cleaning
A poor sampling technique could give a misleading result about the water's safety
The chlorine in the main is refreshed each time a sample is taken
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The result is only trustworthy if the sample is taken properly, so technique is important.

n.0: Sampling technique affects the result's reliability, not the taste.
n.1: Correct technique includes clean handling; bottles are not casually reused.
n.3: Sampling removes a small quantity; it does not refresh the chlorine.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The correct place of the passing sample in the overall process is:
o: The last check, after disinfection and flushing, before the main is supplied
The very first step, before the main has even been swabbed
Immediately after dosing, while the chlorine is at full strength
At the same moment the swab is first fired into the main for the customer supplied by that main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Swab, disinfect, flush, then take the passing sample; supply follows a pass.

n.1: The passing sample is the final step, not the first one.
n.2: The sample is taken after flushing, not at full chlorine strength.
n.3: Sampling is a later confirming step, not simultaneous with swabbing.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A repaired main has been disinfected and flushed but the sample has not yet been taken. The main should:
o: Remain out of supply until a sample has been taken and has passed
Be brought into supply now to reduce disruption to customers
Be dosed with chlorine once more before anyone samples it as the work is being signed off
Be assumed safe because disinfection and flushing were done
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Without a passing sample the water is not confirmed safe, so the main stays off supply.

n.1: Supply waits for a passing sample; disruption does not override that.
n.2: Re-dosing is not required simply because the sample is outstanding.
n.3: Disinfection and flushing are not enough; the sample must confirm it.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Before heavily chlorinated water from disinfecting a main is discharged to a stream, it must be:
o: De-chlorinated or neutralised so the chlorine does not harm the watercourse
Warmed up so it matches the temperature of the stream water
Dyed a bright colour so people can see where it goes throughout the length of the new main
Left standing in the sun for several weeks before release
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Super-chlorinated water is toxic to aquatic life, so the chlorine is neutralised before discharge.

n.1: Temperature is not the issue; the chlorine must be neutralised first.
n.2: Dyeing does not make the water safe to discharge; neutralising does.
n.3: Ad-hoc standing is not the controlled method; neutralising is required.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why must super-chlorinated water be neutralised before it enters a watercourse?
o: Because the chlorine would make the river flow too quickly
Because the strong chlorine can kill fish and other aquatic life
Because the water would otherwise freeze the surface of the river
Because the chlorine would turn the river permanently blue
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorine is very toxic to fish and stream life, so it is removed before any discharge.

n.0: Chlorine does not change how fast a river flows; the concern is toxicity.
n.2: Neutralising is about toxicity to wildlife, not freezing the river.
n.3: The risk is harm to aquatic life, not colouring the river.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: De-chlorinating flush water before discharge is done to protect:
o: The colour of the water so it matches the local river
The pressure inside the main once it is put into supply
The taste of the water for customers at their taps before the main is put back into use
Fish, wildlife and the wider environment from the strong chlorine
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Neutralising the chlorine safeguards aquatic life and the surrounding environment.

n.0: De-chlorination protects wildlife, not the water's appearance.
n.1: Neutralising discharge water has nothing to do with main pressure.
n.2: De-chlorination concerns safe disposal, not customer taste.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: you have a tanker of strong chlorinated water from disinfecting a main. Before discharge you should:
o: Neutralise the chlorine so it is safe to release without harming the environment
Tip it straight into the nearest surface drain to save time according to the operative on site
Pour it back into the disinfected main ready for the customer
Add extra chlorine to make sure it is fully sterilised first
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The chlorine is chemically neutralised first so the discharge does no environmental harm.

n.1: Strong chlorinated water is neutralised first; it is never simply tipped away.
n.2: Chlorinated waste is not returned to a main destined for supply.
n.3: Adding more chlorine makes disposal worse, not safer.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Discharging strong chlorinated water to a drain or stream without neutralising it could:
o: Improve the quality of the river water for the fish living there
Have no effect at all because rivers dilute everything instantly
Poison fish and damage the environment downstream of the discharge
Make the river run clearer and more attractive to look at at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Untreated chlorine harms aquatic life, so releasing it directly is not acceptable.

n.0: Strong chlorine harms, rather than improves, life in the river.
n.1: Rivers do not make strong chlorine harmless instantly; it must be neutralised.
n.3: The real effect is harm to aquatic life, not a clearer river.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: De-chlorination of super-chlorinated water means:
o: Adding a second, stronger dose of chlorine to the water once the pipe has been rejoined
Removing or neutralising the chlorine so the water is safe to discharge
Heating the water until all of the chlorine has boiled off
Colouring the water so the chlorine can be seen more clearly
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It is the step that reduces the chlorine to a level safe for the environment.

n.0: De-chlorination lowers the chlorine; it does not add more.
n.2: De-chlorination is a controlled neutralising step, not boiling.
n.3: De-chlorination removes chlorine; it does not colour the water.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Who is responsible for making sure disinfection flush water is safely disposed of?
o: The fish and wildlife living in the nearest stream or river for the customer supplied by that main
Whichever customer happens to live closest to the discharge point
The operatives and company carrying out the work, following the correct procedure
Nobody, because chlorinated water is always harmless to release
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The people doing the work must neutralise and dispose of the chlorinated water properly.

n.0: Wildlife cannot manage disposal; the operatives are responsible.
n.1: Customers are not responsible for disposing of the flush water.
n.3: Chlorinated water is not harmless; responsible disposal is required.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The environmental risk that de-chlorination guards against is mainly to:
o: The pressure rating of the newly installed water main
The colour of the paint used on nearby road markings as the work is being signed off
The speed at which customers receive their water supply
Aquatic life such as fish in streams, drains and watercourses
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorine is especially toxic to fish, so neutralising protects watercourses.

n.0: De-chlorination protects wildlife, not the main's pressure rating.
n.1: De-chlorination has nothing to do with road paint.
n.2: Neutralising discharge water does not affect supply speed.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Strong chlorinated water from disinfection should never be:
o: Discharged directly into a stream or drain without being neutralised first
Neutralised before it is released into the surrounding ground
Handled carefully by the operatives carrying out the work throughout the length of the new main
Disposed of in line with the water company's own procedure
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Direct discharge of chlorinated water harms the environment, so it is neutralised beforehand.

n.1: Neutralising is exactly what should be done, not avoided.
n.2: Careful handling is correct; it is not something to avoid.
n.3: Following procedure for disposal is correct, not prohibited.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: a stream runs beside the excavation where a main was disinfected. When getting rid of the flush water you must:
o: Make sure the chlorine is neutralised so the stream and its life are protected
Direct the strong chlorinated water into the stream as quickly as you can
Add more chlorine so the stream is disinfected at the same time
Ignore the stream because chlorine cannot travel through soil while the job is being carried out
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: With a watercourse nearby, the chlorine must be removed before any water is released.

n.1: Strong chlorinated water is neutralised, never rushed into the stream.
n.2: The stream is not to be dosed; the flush water is neutralised first.
n.3: The chlorine can reach and harm the stream, so it must be neutralised.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Neutralising chlorinated water before discharge is an example of an operative:
o: Saving chlorine so it can be used again on the next main before the main is put back into use
Speeding the job up by skipping the disposal stage altogether
Protecting the environment as part of doing the disinfection job properly
Making the water stronger so it lasts longer in the main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Safe disposal of the flush water is part of the responsible completion of the work.

n.0: Neutralising destroys the chlorine's activity; it is not saved for reuse.
n.1: Neutralising is a required step, not something skipped to save time.
n.3: Neutralising weakens the chlorine and concerns disposal, not the main.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The best description of what happens to super-chlorinated water after disinfection is:
o: It is bottled up and given to customers as a free supply
It is pumped straight back into the drinking water network
It is neutralised to remove the chlorine, then discharged safely away from wildlife
It is left in the open trench to soak away on its own according to the operative on site
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The chlorine is taken out first so the discharge does not damage the environment.

n.0: Chlorinated waste is not supplied to customers as free water.
n.1: Strong chlorinated waste is not returned to the supply network.
n.3: Uncontrolled soaking away of strong chlorine is not acceptable disposal.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why must a water main be disinfected whenever it has been opened for repair?
o: Because opening the main always makes the water flow the wrong way at that stage of the disinfection work
Because the customer will otherwise be charged too little for water
Because opening the main could have let in dirt or bacteria that must be removed
Because the pipe will not fit back together without chlorine added
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Any opening risks contamination entering, so disinfection restores the water to a safe standard.

n.0: Disinfection deals with possible contamination, not the direction of flow.
n.1: Disinfection is a hygiene requirement, not a matter of billing.
n.3: Chlorine does not help the pipe fit; it deals with contamination.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A main is disinfected after being opened mainly to protect:
o: The colour of the customer's water at the kitchen tap
The value of the pipe material used in the repair once the pipe has been rejoined
The health of customers who will drink the water it supplies
The speed at which the trench can be backfilled again
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Disinfection removes any contamination introduced so the water stays safe to drink.

n.0: Disinfection protects health, not the colour of the water.
n.1: Disinfection is about public health, not the pipe's value.
n.3: Backfill speed has nothing to do with why disinfection is done.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which situations require a main to be disinfected before it goes back into supply?
o: Only when the main is brand new and has never held water before
Only when the customer specifically asks for it to be done for the customer supplied by that main
Whenever it has been opened, repaired or could have been contaminated
Only when the weather is warm enough for bacteria to grow fast
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Any opening, repair or possible contamination triggers the need to disinfect before supply.

n.0: Repaired and possibly contaminated mains also need disinfection, not only new ones.
n.1: Disinfection is required by procedure, not only on customer request.
n.3: Disinfection is required regardless of the weather conditions.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: a burst main has been repaired with a new section of pipe. Before it goes back into supply it should be:
o: Put back into supply at once because only a short section was replaced
Left to stand empty for a week so any germs die off by themselves
Disinfected, flushed and sampled because it was opened and could have been contaminated
Charged with extra pressure to force out any germs that got in as the work is being signed off
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Opening the main for the repair means it must be disinfected and confirmed clean before use.

n.0: Even a short repair means the main was opened and must be disinfected.
n.1: Leaving it empty does not disinfect it; the proper procedure is required.
n.3: Pressure does not disinfect; chlorination and sampling are required.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The reason opening a main creates a risk is that it can:
o: Make the water inside the pipe suddenly become much colder
Cause the pipe to shrink so it no longer fits the fittings
Turn the water a bright colour that customers will notice throughout the length of the new main
Allow soil, water or bacteria from outside to get into the pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: An open main can admit contamination from the surroundings, which disinfection then removes.

n.0: The risk from opening is contamination getting in, not a temperature drop.
n.1: Opening a main is a contamination risk, not a shrinkage problem.
n.2: The concern is contamination entering, not a colour change.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Even if a repaired main 'looks fine', it is still disinfected because:
o: Harmful bacteria and dirt cannot be seen but may have entered while it was open
Disinfection is only ever done to give the water a nicer taste
A repaired main must always be painted before it is reused while the job is being carried out
The chlorine is needed to glue the repair section into place
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Contamination is invisible, so disinfection is done regardless of how the pipe looks.

n.1: Disinfection guards against invisible contamination, not to flavour water.
n.2: Painting is not part of returning a repaired main to supply.
n.3: Chlorine does not act as a glue; it deals with contamination.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Disinfecting a main after it has been opened is required in order to:
o: Lower the pressure so the repair joint is not over-stressed
Increase the amount of water the main can carry in future
Restore the water quality to the safe standard expected for drinking water
Make the repair invisible from the surface of the road before the main is put back into use
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The step brings the water back to a fit-to-drink standard after possible contamination.

n.0: Disinfection is about hygiene, not managing pressure on the joint.
n.1: Disinfection does not change the carrying capacity of the main.
n.3: Disinfection has nothing to do with hiding the repair at the surface.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A short section of main was cut into and rejoined. Disinfection is:
o: Not required because only a very small section was ever opened according to the operative on site
Only required if dirty water was actually seen entering the pipe
Still required because the main was opened and could have been contaminated
Replaced entirely by simply flushing the main through with water
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Any opening, however small, means disinfection before the main returns to supply.

n.0: Even a small opening requires disinfection before supply.
n.1: Possible contamination is enough; you do not wait to see dirt enter.
n.3: Flushing alone does not disinfect; chlorination is still needed.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The underlying principle is that a main is disinfected whenever there is a chance that:
o: Contamination could have entered the pipe while it was open or being worked on
The customer might want a stronger taste of chlorine in the water
The pipe might need to be a slightly different colour when reused
The main could be made to carry a much higher pressure at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Any realistic chance of contamination triggers disinfection before the main is used.

n.1: Disinfection responds to contamination risk, not customer taste preferences.
n.2: Pipe colour has nothing to do with the need to disinfect.
n.3: The trigger is contamination risk, not raising the main's pressure.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: an operative wants to save time by not disinfecting a repaired main. This is wrong because:
o: The opened main could be contaminated and customers could be put at risk
Disinfection is optional and only affects how quickly water flows
The chlorine is only there to make the pipe easier to backfill once the pipe has been rejoined
Skipping it simply means the main will be a slightly wrong colour
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Skipping disinfection risks supplying contaminated water, which endangers public health.

n.1: Disinfection is required for safety; it is not about flow speed.
n.2: Chlorine disinfects the water; it plays no part in backfilling.
n.3: Skipping disinfection is a health risk, not a colour issue.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Disinfection whenever a main is opened is part of the wider aim of:
o: Keeping the public clean water supply safe and free from contamination
Reducing the amount the water company spends on chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Making sure the pipe is always exactly the same temperature
Ensuring every customer receives brightly coloured water
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It protects the integrity of the drinking water network against contamination.

n.1: The aim is public health protection, not saving on chlorine.
n.2: Disinfection is a hygiene measure, unrelated to pipe temperature.
n.3: The aim is safe, uncontaminated water, not coloured water.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A contractor asks whether disinfection can be skipped on a planned main renewal. The correct position is:
o: It cannot be skipped, because the new main has been open and must be disinfected first
It can be skipped because planned work is always cleaner than repairs
It can be skipped as long as the pipe was delivered in a wrapper
It can be skipped provided the contractor signs a short form as the work is being signed off
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A renewed main has been open to the surroundings, so it is disinfected before supply.

n.1: Planned or not, an opened main is disinfected before it is supplied.
n.2: Delivery wrapping does not remove the need to disinfect after installation.
n.3: No form removes the requirement to disinfect an opened main.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: during disinfection you notice the main was not fully filled and part of the crown is dry. You should:
o: Correct the filling so the whole bore is in contact with the chlorinated water
Carry on regardless, since the bottom of the pipe is wet enough
Take the passing sample now to save going back to the job later
Discharge the water to the stream while you decide what to do throughout the length of the new main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A dry crown is not disinfected, so the main must be properly charged before the hold counts.

n.1: A dry crown stays undisinfected; the whole bore must be wetted.
n.2: A sample cannot pass reliably from a partly undisinfected main.
n.3: Chlorinated water is neutralised before discharge, not released mid-job.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The overall aim of swabbing, chlorinating, checking, flushing and sampling a main is to:
o: Colour the water so the customer can tell it is from a new pipe
Bring it into supply as a clean, disinfected main delivering safe drinking water
Raise the pressure of the main above its normal working level
Warm the pipe so it is comfortable to work near in winter while the job is being carried out
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Each step builds toward a main that is clean, disinfected and confirmed safe for customers.

n.0: The aim is safe water, not a colour to mark a new pipe.
n.2: The steps are hygiene steps, not a way to raise pressure.
n.3: The purpose is a safe, disinfected main, not warming the pipe.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which of these is the correct final gate before a disinfected main is put into supply?
o: A bacteriological sample that meets the required drinking water standard
A residual chlorine reading at full disinfection strength at the tap
A swab run that brings out the largest possible amount of debris
A tanker of neutralised water ready to discharge to the stream before the main is put back into use
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The passing microbiological sample is the last check before the main carries supply.

n.1: Supply follows flushing, when chlorine is reduced, not at full strength.
n.2: Swabbing is an early step, not the final gate before supply.
n.3: Neutralised discharge is about disposal, not the gate for supply.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: a colleague suggests discharging strong chlorinated water down a road gully that runs to a stream. You should:
o: Neutralise the chlorine first so nothing harmful reaches the stream
Agree, because road gullies are designed to take any waste water
Agree, but only after adding more chlorine to be on the safe side
Agree, because chlorine has no effect on fish in flowing water according to the operative on site
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The gully leads to a watercourse, so the chlorine must be neutralised before any discharge.

n.1: Gullies can lead to streams; strong chlorine must be neutralised first.
n.2: Adding chlorine worsens the discharge; it must be neutralised, not increased.
n.3: Chlorine is toxic to fish, so it must be neutralised before discharge.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: An operative records the residual chlorine at the far end of a chlorinated main to make sure:
o: The far end of the main is colder than the point of dosing
The swab managed to travel the full length of the pipe at that stage of the disinfection work
The customer at the far end is happy with the water pressure
The disinfectant reached the whole length, not just the point where it was dosed
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Checking at the far end confirms the chlorine carried right through the main during the hold.

n.0: The far-end check is about chlorine reaching there, not temperature.
n.1: The residual reading confirms chlorine reach, not the swab's journey.
n.2: A residual reading is a chlorine check, not a pressure or customer check.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The residual chlorine result is normally written down so that:
o: The customer can be sent a bill for the chlorine that was used
The swab can be matched to the correct length of new main once the pipe has been rejoined
There is a record showing the disinfection was carried out and held correctly
The trench can be signed off as backfilled to the right depth
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Recording the residual gives evidence that the main was properly disinfected before supply.

n.0: The record is evidence of disinfection, not a basis for billing chlorine.
n.1: The residual record concerns chlorine, not tracking the swab.
n.3: The residual record relates to disinfection, not backfill depth.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: your residual chlorine reading is taken but comes back far higher than the procedure figure. This mainly matters because:
o: It proves the main has already been fully flushed and sampled
It shows the swab collected too much debris on its run for the customer supplied by that main
It means the contact time can be safely reduced next time
The water is too strongly chlorinated and must be flushed before it can be supplied
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A very high residual confirms the water is not yet fit for supply and needs flushing out.

n.0: A high residual shows the strong water is still present, not flushed away.
n.1: A high residual is about chlorine strength, not swab debris.
n.2: A high residual does not justify shortening the contact time.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Measuring residual chlorine both when dosing and after the hold lets the operative see:
o: How far the water level has dropped inside the main as the work is being signed off
How much of the chlorine has been used up during the contact time
How many customers were using their taps during the hold
How much the pipe has expanded since it was first filled
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Comparing the two readings shows the demand and whether enough chlorine remained.

n.0: Residual readings measure chlorine, not the water level in the main.
n.2: The residual comparison is a chlorine check, not a count of customers.
n.3: Residual readings track chlorine, not any expansion of the pipe.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: A satisfactory residual chlorine reading after the hold is a sign to the operative that they can:
o: Take the main into supply immediately with the strong chlorine in it
Move on to flushing the main out ready for sampling and supply
Send the swab through the main one final time for luck
Discharge the water into the nearest stream without any treatment
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Once the residual has held, the next stage is flushing before the passing sample is taken.

n.0: Supply follows flushing and a passing sample, not a residual reading alone.
n.2: A good residual does not require another swab run.
n.3: Strong chlorinated water must be neutralised before any discharge.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The flow used to flush a disinfected main needs to be enough to:
o: Lift the swab back up to the top of the main again while the job is being carried out
Warm the pipe wall up along the whole length of the main
Colour the water so the flushing progress can be watched
Move the strong chlorinated water right out of the whole length of pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Adequate flow carries the heavily chlorinated water out so none is left behind.

n.0: The swab is already recovered; flushing moves out the chlorinated water.
n.1: Flushing clears chlorine; it is not intended to warm the pipe.
n.2: Flushing is judged by chlorine clearing, not by any colour change.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: after disinfection you begin flushing but the water still smells strongly of chlorine. You should:
o: Stop flushing at once and put the main straight into supply
Keep flushing until the chlorine has dropped to a normal supply level
Take the passing sample now while the chlorine is still strong
Add more chlorine to mask the smell before you carry on before the main is put back into use
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: A strong chlorine smell means the strong water is still present, so flushing continues.

n.0: Strongly chlorinated water is not supplied; flushing must continue.
n.2: The sample is taken from flushed water, not the strong chlorine.
n.3: Adding chlorine makes it worse; flushing lowers the level.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Flushing a main after disinfection is best thought of as:
o: Adding a fresh charge of disinfectant for extra safety
Sending the swab back through to pick up more debris according to the operative on site
Filling the main with air to dry the inside of the pipe
Washing out the disinfectant once it has finished doing its job in the pipe
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: It removes the spent strong chlorine so the main can be sampled and supplied.

n.0: Flushing removes chlorine; it does not add a fresh charge.
n.1: The swab work is finished before flushing the chlorine out.
n.2: Flushing uses water to clear chlorine, not air to dry the pipe.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The point of flushing before the sample is taken is to make sure the sample:
o: Contains as much chlorine as possible when it reaches the lab
Represents the water customers will actually receive, not the strong chlorine
Carries some of the debris the swab left behind in the pipe
Is taken from the coldest part of the length of new main at that stage of the disinfection work
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Flushing first means the sample reflects normal supply water rather than disinfection strength.

n.0: The sample should reflect supply water, not maximum chlorine.
n.2: A good sample is clean, not carrying swab debris.
n.3: The sample reflects supply quality; the coldest point is not the aim.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Which best completes the sequence: disinfect, check residual, ___, sample?
o: Swab the main to remove the leftover debris once the pipe has been rejoined
Charge the main with a second dose of chlorine
Flush the strong chlorinated water out of the main
Bring the main straight into customer supply
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: After the residual check, the main is flushed before the passing sample is taken.

n.0: Swabbing happens first, not between the residual check and sampling.
n.1: A second dose is not part of the standard sequence here.
n.3: Supply comes after the passing sample, not before flushing.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The dose and contact time in a disinfection procedure are described as 'specified' because they are:
o: Chosen by the operative to match how the day is going
Worked out from the colour of the water in the main for the customer supplied by that main
Copied from whatever the last customer happened to request
Set in advance by the water company rather than decided on site each time
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: They are pre-set figures from the procedure, giving a consistent and proven method.

n.0: The figures are set by the procedure, not chosen freely on site.
n.1: Water colour does not set the specified dose and contact time.
n.2: Customers do not set the specified disinfection figures.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: a main has been disinfected and flushed, the residual is normal and the sample has passed. The correct action is to:
o: Re-dose the main with chlorine before letting anyone use it
Leave the main empty for a further week as a precaution as the work is being signed off
Bring the main into supply, as every hygiene stage has now been completed
Take several more samples over the next month before supply
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: With swab, disinfection, residual, flushing and a passing sample all done, the main is ready.

n.0: No re-dosing is needed once all stages, including the pass, are complete.
n.1: A passed main is ready for supply, not to be left standing empty.
n.3: A passing sample clears the main; repeated delay is not required.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Bacteria and dirt entering an opened main are a concern because the main carries:
o: Clean drinking water that people will use straight from the tap
Only water used for watering gardens and washing cars
Water that is always boiled by customers before any use
Waste water on its way to the sewage treatment works throughout the length of the new main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Because the water is for drinking, any contamination must be removed before supply.

n.1: The main carries drinking water, so contamination is a health concern.
n.2: Customers drink mains water without boiling, so it must be safe.
n.3: A clean water main carries drinking water, not sewage.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The reason strong chlorine is used to disinfect a main and then removed is that it:
o: Makes the pipe joints set harder the longer it is left in while the job is being carried out
Improves the colour of the water for the customer's benefit
Kills organisms during the hold but is too strong to leave in the supply
Increases the pressure the main can safely carry in service
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Chlorine at disinfection strength deals with organisms but must be flushed before customers drink it.

n.0: Chlorine does not cure joints; it disinfects and is then flushed out.
n.1: Chlorine is used to disinfect, not to improve the water's colour.
n.3: Chlorine has no bearing on the main's pressure rating.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: you finish disinfecting a main near a fishpond. When disposing of the flush water you are most concerned to:
o: Keep the water as strongly chlorinated as possible for disposal
Discharge it quickly so the job can be signed off sooner
Neutralise the chlorine so it cannot reach and harm the fish
Pour it into the pond so the pond is disinfected too
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: With a pond nearby, the chlorine must be removed before the water is discharged.

n.0: Strong chlorine harms fish, so it must be neutralised, not kept strong.
n.1: Speed does not override the need to neutralise near a fishpond.
n.3: The pond is not to be dosed; the flush water is neutralised first.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Why is a passing sample needed as well as a good residual chlorine reading?
o: The two readings always give exactly the same information according to the operative on site
The residual shows chlorine held, but the sample confirms the water is actually clean
The sample measures the pressure the main can carry safely
The residual reading tells you nothing useful about the main
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The two checks are different: one confirms the dose held, the other confirms microbiological safety.

n.0: They test different things, so one cannot replace the other.
n.2: The sample is a microbiological check, not a pressure test.
n.3: The residual is useful; it confirms the disinfection dose held.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: An operative should treat every main that has been opened as:
o: Potentially contaminated until it has been disinfected and passed a sample
Automatically clean because the water inside looked clear
Ready for supply as soon as the pipe is rejoined at that stage of the disinfection work
Free of any risk because chlorine is already in the network
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Assuming possible contamination until confirmed clean is the safe working approach.

n.1: Clear-looking water can still be contaminated; disinfection is required.
n.2: Rejoining the pipe does not make the water safe; disinfection is needed.
n.3: Network chlorine does not remove the need to disinfect an opened main.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: The overall reason for the swab, chlorinate, check, flush and sample routine is to protect:
o: The colour of the water so new mains can be spotted easily
Public health by making sure only safe drinking water enters the network
The pressure of the network so mains never leak again once the pipe has been rejoined
The speed of the job so contractors can move on quickly
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: The whole routine exists to keep contamination out of the water customers drink.

n.0: The routine protects health, not the appearance of the water.
n.2: The routine is about hygiene and safety, not preventing leaks.
n.3: The purpose is safe water, not the speed of completing work.

Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.q: Scenario: a trainee asks what 'super-chlorinated' water is. The best answer is water that has been:
o: Left in the sun until the chlorine naturally became stronger
Dosed with chlorine well above normal supply strength to disinfect the main
Passed through the swab several times to pick up chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Cooled below freezing so the chlorine concentrates at the top
Disinfection & Chlorination of Mains.w: Super-chlorinated means a high chlorine strength used for disinfection, far above drinking levels.

n.0: Super-chlorination is a deliberate high dose, not a result of sunlight.
n.2: The swab does not chlorinate the water; a high dose does.
n.3: Super-chlorination is about a high dose, not freezing or concentrating.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Who is allowed to take water directly from a fire hydrant on the public clean water network?
o: Only people authorised to do so, using approved equipment for the purpose
Any operative on site who needs water for the day's work if time is short
Anyone holding a current driving licence for the works vehicle on the day
Members of the public provided they replace the water later for the shift
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Hydrants feed the public main, so only authorised persons using approved equipment may draw from them.

n.1: Being on site is not the same as being authorised; unauthorised drawing is not permitted.
n.2: A driving licence has nothing to do with authority to use a hydrant.
n.3: Members of the public may not open hydrants, and water cannot simply be replaced.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An operative wants to fill a bowser from a hydrant. What must they have before doing so?
o: A signed timesheet showing the hours booked for the task so the work is not held up
A high-visibility vest and a set of traffic cones alone as long as the job gets done
The proper authorisation and an approved standpipe fitted with backflow protection
A verbal agreement between two operatives on the crew to get the task done quickly
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Drawing from a hydrant needs both authorisation and an approved standpipe with backflow protection.

n.0: A timesheet records work done, not permission to use a hydrant.
n.1: Site safety kit does not grant any authority to open a hydrant.
n.3: Two operatives cannot authorise themselves to draw from the main.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: What is a standpipe used for on the clean water network?
o: To connect safely to a hydrant so water can be drawn from the main
To measure the chlorine level in the water at the tap that morning
To store several hours of drinking water on the vehicle on the day
To seal off a burst section of pipe during a repair during the job
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A standpipe is the fitting that lets an authorised user connect to a hydrant and draw water.

n.1: A standpipe is a connector, not a water-quality measuring device.
n.2: Storage is done in a bowser or tank, not in the standpipe itself.
n.3: A burst is isolated with valves, not with a standpipe.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Using a hydrant without authorisation is best described as:
o: Not permitted, because it risks the safety of the public supply
Acceptable during an emergency if nobody objects at the time on the day
Fine as long as the standpipe is returned to the store after that morning
Allowed for small quantities but banned for large ones to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Unauthorised use is prohibited because it can put the whole public supply at risk.

n.1: Even in emergencies, hydrant use must follow the proper authority.
n.2: Returning kit does not make unauthorised use acceptable.
n.3: The quantity does not change the need for authorisation.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which piece of equipment is designed to be attached to a hydrant to draw water?
o: A length of ordinary garden hose pushed onto the outlet on the day
An approved standpipe with the correct backflow protection fitted
A domestic bucket lowered into the open hydrant chamber that morning
A pressure gauge screwed straight onto the hydrant thread to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: An approved standpipe fitted with backflow protection is the correct connection to a hydrant.

n.0: A plain hose gives no proper connection and no backflow protection.
n.2: Dipping a bucket into the chamber is not a safe connection.
n.3: A gauge only reads pressure; it does not draw water safely.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Before an operative opens a hydrant, what should they be sure of?
o: That they are authorised and are using the correct approved equipment
That the weather is dry enough to keep the area tidy if time is short
That at least two colleagues are watching them work while the work is on
That the vehicle is parked within ten metres of the point that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The key requirement is proper authorisation together with the correct approved equipment.

n.1: Dry weather is helpful but is not what authorises hydrant use.
n.2: Having witnesses does not create authority to use the hydrant.
n.3: Parking distance has nothing to do with the right to draw water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: A contractor offers to lend you their hydrant key so you can grab water quickly. What is the correct response?
o: Accept it because borrowing a key counts as being authorised
Decline unless you are properly authorised to use the hydrant
Use it once but promise not to make a habit of it that morning
Use it only if the contractor watches you the whole time on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Authority does not transfer with a key; only a properly authorised person may use the hydrant.

n.0: Borrowing a key does not make a person authorised.
n.2: A single unauthorised use still puts the supply at risk.
n.3: Being watched does not grant the authority you still lack.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why are hydrants controlled so that only authorised people use them?
o: Because the keys are expensive and easily lost on site on the day
Because opening them wastes a small amount of electricity that morning
Because each hydrant can only be opened a set number of times to save time
Because misuse can contaminate or disrupt the public water supply
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Control exists to protect the public supply from contamination and disruption.

n.0: Cost of keys is not the reason hydrant use is controlled.
n.1: Hydrants are not electrically powered, so this is untrue.
n.2: Hydrants are not limited to a fixed number of openings.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An authorised standpipe user finds the nearest hydrant is not on their permit area. They should:
o: Only use a hydrant they are actually authorised to use
Use it anyway since all hydrants carry the same water
Use it and note the location for the paperwork later
Use it briefly as long as no one from the area sees on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Authorisation is specific, so the user must keep to hydrants they are permitted to use.

n.1: Authorisation is specific and does not cover every hydrant.
n.2: Recording it afterwards does not make the use authorised.
n.3: Whether or not they are seen has no bearing on authority.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: What does authorised use of a hydrant primarily protect?
o: Only the operative's own drinking water for the shift on the day
The paintwork and fittings of the works vehicle if time is short
The battery life of the site's monitoring equipment that morning
The quality and reliability of water for everyone on the supply
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Authorised use protects the clean, reliable water that the whole supply delivers.

n.0: Authorised use protects everyone downstream, not just one person.
n.1: Vehicle condition is unrelated to why hydrant use is controlled.
n.2: Monitoring equipment is not the reason for controlling hydrants.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: What device must be fitted to a standpipe to stop water flowing back into the main?
o: A double check valve that only lets water flow one way
A pressure reducing valve set to a low outlet reading
A simple isolation tap fitted at the hose connection
A flexible rubber washer inside the hydrant outlet on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A double check valve allows flow one way only, preventing backflow into the main.

n.1: A pressure valve controls pressure, not the direction of flow.
n.2: An isolation tap stops flow but does not prevent backflow.
n.3: A washer only seals a joint; it cannot stop backflow.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: What is the purpose of the double check valve on a standpipe?
o: To boost the pressure so the hose fills the tank faster that morning
To filter dirt and grit out of the water as it passes for the shift
To prevent contaminated water being drawn back into the public main
To reduce the noise the water makes as it flows out if time is short
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The double check valve blocks reverse flow, keeping contamination out of the main.

n.0: The valve does not raise pressure; it controls flow direction.
n.1: A check valve does not filter particles from the water.
n.3: Noise reduction is not a function of a check valve.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Backflow from a standpipe into the main could happen if:
o: The hose is coiled too tightly on the reel before use on the day
The standpipe is painted a bright colour for visibility that morning
Pressure in the main drops and pulls water back through the hose
The operative fills the tank slightly above halfway to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A pressure drop in the main can suck water back, which the check valve is there to stop.

n.0: How the hose is coiled does not cause water to reverse.
n.1: The colour of the standpipe has no effect on flow direction.
n.3: Filling past halfway does not create a backflow event.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An operative notices the double check valve on their standpipe is damaged. They should:
o: Carry on and keep the hose end high to compensate on the day
Tape over the valve and continue the task for now that morning
Swap it end-for-end so the flow runs the other way to save time
Stop using it and report the fault before drawing any water
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Without a working check valve there is no backflow protection, so it must not be used until fixed.

n.0: Holding the hose high does not replace a working check valve.
n.1: Taping a damaged valve does not restore backflow protection.
n.2: Reversing the fitting does not repair the protection.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which statement about backflow protection is correct?
o: Every standpipe drawing from a hydrant needs backflow protection
Only standpipes used near rivers need any protection that morning
Protection is optional if the job takes under an hour on the day
It is only needed when the water is for drinking if time is short
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: All standpipes taking water from a hydrant must have backflow protection fitted.

n.1: Backflow risk exists at any hydrant, not only near rivers.
n.2: Time on the job does not remove the need for protection.
n.3: Protection is needed regardless of what the water is for.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: A double check valve protects the public main by:
o: Letting water pass freely in both directions at once on the day
Closing completely and stopping all flow through it that morning
Allowing water out but blocking any flow back the other way
Adding chlorine automatically as the water leaves to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: It permits forward flow to the hose but blocks reverse flow into the main.

n.0: Free flow both ways is exactly what the valve prevents.
n.1: A closed valve would stop the job, not protect the main.
n.3: The valve does not dose chemicals into the water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: Your standpipe has no check valve fitted and none is available. What should you do?
o: Draw the water quickly before pressure has time to drop on the day
Fit any spare valve you can find, whatever its type that morning
Do not draw water until proper backflow protection is fitted
Keep a second operative ready to shut the hydrant fast to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Without correct backflow protection the main is at risk, so no water should be drawn.

n.0: A quick draw does not remove the backflow risk.
n.1: Only correct, approved protection should be used.
n.3: A quick shut-off does not replace a check valve.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why is backflow into the main considered dangerous?
o: It slowly wears out the hydrant's internal thread on the day
It can push contaminated water into everyone's supply
It makes the standpipe harder to unscrew afterwards
It causes the hose to fill more slowly than usual that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Backflow can carry contamination from the hose or tank straight into the public supply.

n.0: Thread wear is not the health concern with backflow.
n.2: Difficulty unscrewing is not why backflow matters.
n.3: Fill speed is unrelated to the danger of backflow.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Where on the equipment is the double check valve normally part of the set-up?
o: Buried in the ground beneath the hydrant chamber on the day
Inside the bowser at the far end of the delivery hose that morning
Fitted to the standpipe between the hydrant and the hose
Clipped to the operative's belt as a spare part to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The check valve is fitted on the standpipe, in the line between hydrant and hose.

n.0: The valve is part of the standpipe, not buried underground.
n.1: It sits at the standpipe, not inside the storage bowser.
n.3: It must be fitted in line, not carried loose on a belt.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An approved standpipe differs from an unapproved one mainly because it:
o: Includes the correct backflow protection to guard the main
Is always made from a brighter coloured metal that morning
Is a few centimetres longer than the older type on the day
Comes supplied with its own dedicated carry bag to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Approval centres on having the correct backflow protection fitted.

n.1: Colour is not what makes a standpipe approved.
n.2: Length is not the defining feature of an approved standpipe.
n.3: A carry bag has nothing to do with approval.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Where should the free end of the hose be kept while drawing water?
o: Resting in a puddle to keep the coupling cool on the day
Held up off the ground and clear of puddles and tanks
Dropped into the open bowser to save holding it that morning
Laid flat in the gutter so it does not roll away to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Keeping the end up and away from standing water stops contamination being drawn in.

n.0: A puddle is dirty water that can contaminate the supply.
n.2: Letting the end sit in the tank risks drawing water back.
n.3: The gutter is dirty and can contaminate the hose end.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why must the hose end be kept out of puddles, tanks and ponds?
o: So the hose does not become tangled during the job on the day
So the coupling threads do not rust over time that morning
So dirty water cannot be drawn back into the clean supply
So the operative keeps their boots dry on site to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: An immersed end can let contaminated water be drawn back into the clean supply.

n.0: Tangling is a nuisance but not the hygiene reason here.
n.1: Rust is a maintenance issue, not the contamination risk.
n.3: Dry boots are unrelated to protecting the water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Before connecting the hose to the standpipe, the operative should:
o: Rinse them briefly in the nearest available puddle
Check both are clean and free of dirt or debris
Rub the ends in soil to remove any old grease
Leave any dirt in place to save time on the job
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Clean, debris-free fittings prevent dirt entering the clean water.

n.0: Puddle water is dirty and would contaminate the fittings.
n.2: Soil adds contamination rather than cleaning the fitting.
n.3: Leaving dirt on the fittings risks contaminating the water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: How should a standpipe and hose be stored between jobs to stay hygienic?
o: Thrown loose in the van footwell with other tools
Left outside on the ground overnight to air off
Coiled around a dirty wheel to keep them tidy on the day
Kept clean with the open ends protected from dirt
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Clean storage with protected ends keeps contamination away from the fittings.

n.0: Loose storage lets the ends pick up dirt and grease.
n.1: Leaving them on the ground exposes the ends to contamination.
n.2: A dirty wheel would transfer contamination to the fittings.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: You put the hose down for a moment and the end lands in a muddy puddle. What should you do?
o: Clean the end before using it again to avoid contamination
Carry on, as a little mud will not affect the water on the day
Shake it once and connect it straight away if time is short
Dip it in the tank to rinse the mud off it while the work is on
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A contaminated end must be cleaned before reuse so dirt is not drawn into the supply.

n.1: Even a little mud can carry contamination into the supply.
n.2: A quick shake does not remove the contamination.
n.3: Dipping it in the tank spreads contamination further.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Keeping the hose end elevated during filling mainly helps to:
o: Make the water come out at a higher pressure on the day
Cool the water down before it reaches the tank that morning
Let the operative see the far coupling more easily
Stop dirty surface water being pulled into the flow
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: An elevated end keeps it clear of dirty surface water that could be drawn in.

n.0: Height of the end does not change the supply pressure.
n.1: Elevation does not cool the water in the hose.
n.2: Visibility is minor next to the contamination concern.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which practice keeps standpipe use hygienic?
o: Setting the couplings down on the bare road surface
Handling the couplings so the inside faces stay clean
Wiping the couplings with an oily workshop rag on the day
Blowing into the hose to clear it before use that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Keeping the coupling faces clean prevents contamination entering the water path.

n.0: The road surface would contaminate the coupling faces.
n.2: An oily rag leaves contamination on the fittings.
n.3: Blowing into the hose introduces contamination by mouth.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: A hose end that has been lying in a tank of stored water should be treated as:
o: Perfectly clean because the tank holds water too on the day
Ready to use once it has simply dried off if time is short
Possibly contaminated and cleaned before it is used again
Safe as long as the tank looked clear inside that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Contact with stored tank water may contaminate the end, so it must be cleaned first.

n.0: Stored tank water is not necessarily clean or fresh.
n.1: Drying does not remove contamination from the end.
n.3: A clear look does not prove the water is uncontaminated.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why is a dirty hose a problem when drawing from a hydrant?
o: A dirty hose is heavier and tires the operative on the day
Dirt on it can be carried into the clean water supply
Dirt makes the hose stiffer and harder to coil that morning
A dirty hose looks unprofessional to the public to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Dirt on the hose can enter the water and contaminate the clean supply.

n.0: Weight is a comfort issue, not the hygiene concern.
n.2: Stiffness does not affect the safety of the water.
n.3: Appearance is not the real reason a dirty hose matters.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: The best way to keep the connection point clean while working is to:
o: Leave them open so any water can drain out freely
Keep couplings capped or covered when not connected
Rest them against the kerb to keep them off the van
Push a rag from your pocket into each open end on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Capping or covering open ends keeps dirt out of the connection point.

n.0: Open ends collect dirt and debris while uncovered.
n.2: The kerb is dirty and would contaminate the ends.
n.3: A pocket rag can introduce its own contamination.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: What is the main risk of using a dirty standpipe on the network?
o: Contamination can be introduced into the public water supply
The standpipe may become slightly harder to fit that morning
The hydrant chamber may fill up with rainwater for the shift
The water may come out at a lower flow rate if time is short
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A dirty standpipe can carry contamination straight into the public supply.

n.1: A tight fit is a nuisance, not the real hazard here.
n.2: A wet chamber is not the contamination concern raised.
n.3: Flow rate is not the danger posed by a dirty standpipe.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Unauthorised standpipe use is a concern because it can:
o: Slightly increase the water bill for the site that morning
Introduce contamination that reaches many other properties
Make the hydrant key wear out more quickly if time is short
Cause the standpipe to be a little harder to store on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Unauthorised use bypasses controls and can spread contamination widely.

n.0: Billing is not the reason unauthorised use is a concern.
n.2: Key wear is trivial next to the contamination risk.
n.3: Storage difficulty is not why unauthorised use matters.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Contaminated water drawn back through a standpipe is dangerous because it:
o: Can slow down the meter reading at the property on the day
Can make people ill who drink from the same supply
Can change the colour of the standpipe fitting that morning
Can shorten the working life of the hose reel to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Contamination in the supply can cause illness for anyone drinking the water.

n.0: A slower meter is not a health hazard to anyone.
n.2: A colour change to the fitting harms no one.
n.3: Wear on the reel is not a public health issue.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: An operative drops the standpipe in a farmyard and simply picks it up and fits it. The main danger is:
o: The standpipe getting a few scratches on the outside
The operative getting mud on their gloves on the day
Dirt from the yard being carried into the clean main
The task taking a couple of minutes longer that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Farmyard dirt on the fitting can be carried into the clean main.

n.0: Scratches are cosmetic and do not endanger the water.
n.1: Muddy gloves are a comfort issue, not the hazard.
n.3: A short delay is not the real danger here.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which of these most increases the risk of contaminating the supply?
o: Filling the tank slowly rather than quickly if time is short
Using a brand new hydrant key from the store during the job
Parking the vehicle a little further from the point on the day
Using an unauthorised standpipe with no backflow protection
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: An unauthorised standpipe with no backflow protection leaves the main unprotected.

n.0: Fill speed does not create a contamination risk.
n.1: A new key does not increase contamination risk.
n.2: Parking distance has no bearing on contamination.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why does contamination from one standpipe matter to the wider public?
o: Because each home has its own separate pipe network on the day
Because the standpipe belongs to a single property that morning
Because contamination stays inside the hose only to save time
The main is shared, so pollution can spread to many homes
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Because the main is shared, contamination introduced at one point can reach many homes.

n.0: Homes share the same main, so this reasoning is wrong.
n.1: A standpipe on the main is not tied to one property.
n.2: Contamination can pass beyond the hose into the main.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An operative sees another worker drawing water with a filthy hose end trailing in mud. This is a risk because:
o: The worker may slip on the muddy ground nearby on the day
The hose will need washing at the end of the day that morning
The mud will stain the worker's uniform badly to save time
Muddy water may be drawn back into the clean supply
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A muddy end can allow contaminated water to be drawn into the clean supply.

n.0: Slipping is a personal safety point, not the water risk.
n.1: End-of-day washing is not the immediate hazard.
n.2: A stained uniform does not endanger the water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which outcome is possible if a contaminated standpipe is used on the public main?
o: An outbreak of illness affecting people on that supply
A short drop in pressure that quickly recovers on the day
A small rise in the water temperature for a day that morning
A minor delay in completing the day's paperwork to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Contamination entering the supply can lead to illness among those it reaches.

n.1: A brief pressure dip is not the contamination outcome.
n.2: A temperature change is not the health hazard here.
n.3: Paperwork delays are unrelated to contamination.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Dirty equipment is a hygiene hazard mainly because contamination:
o: Makes the couplings look unpleasant to the eye on the day
Adds a little extra weight for the operative that morning
Can pass from the equipment into the water people drink
Slows the operative down while cleaning up later to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The hazard is that contamination on the kit can transfer into drinking water.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason dirty equipment is hazardous.
n.1: Extra weight is a comfort issue, not a hygiene hazard.
n.3: Cleaning time is not the core hygiene concern.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: The safest way to avoid contaminating the supply through a standpipe is to:
o: Work as fast as possible to limit exposure time on the day
Use clean, approved equipment exactly as authorised
Only draw water during the early morning hours that morning
Keep the tank lid off so you can watch the level to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Clean, approved equipment used as authorised is the reliable way to protect the supply.

n.0: Speed does not make dirty or unauthorised use safe.
n.2: Time of day does not reduce contamination risk.
n.3: An open lid can let contamination in, not keep it out.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: When opening a hydrant, an operative should turn the valve:
o: As fast as possible to clear any air out quickly
Halfway then fully closed several times over on the day
Slowly and steadily to avoid a surge in the main
Only a fraction so barely any water comes out that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Opening slowly and steadily prevents a pressure surge that could disturb the main.

n.0: A fast opening can cause a damaging surge in the main.
n.1: Repeated slamming stresses the main and is not correct.
n.3: Barely opening it does not achieve a proper draw.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Before drawing water for use, it is good practice to:
o: Seal the outlet and leave it under pressure on the day
Run the hydrant briefly to flush the first water away
Pour a cleaning chemical into the open outlet that morning
Warm the outlet with a blowtorch before opening to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A short flush clears the first, possibly stale water before the water is used.

n.0: Sealing it under pressure does nothing to make it hygienic.
n.2: Adding chemicals into the hydrant is not correct practice.
n.3: Heating the outlet is unnecessary and not good practice.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which of the following is part of hygienic hydrant operation?
o: Leaving the chamber lid open to speed up the work on the day
Using the same rag for the outlet and the tyres that morning
Keeping the outlet and connection clean throughout the job
Standing the standpipe in the chamber water during the job
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Keeping the outlet and connection clean throughout protects the water quality.

n.0: An open chamber lets dirt and debris reach the outlet.
n.1: One rag for both would transfer dirt to the outlet.
n.3: Chamber water is dirty and would contaminate the fitting.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why should a hydrant be closed slowly at the end of the task?
o: To let the operative time the job more accurately on the day
To make the valve last twice as long in service that morning
To keep the closing as quiet as possible for neighbours to save time
To avoid a sudden pressure surge that can disturb the main
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Closing slowly prevents a surge that could stir up sediment or damage the main.

n.0: Timing the job is not the reason to close slowly.
n.1: Slow closing is about surge, not valve lifespan.
n.2: Noise is a minor point next to protecting the main.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: On opening the hydrant the first water runs cloudy. The hygienic response is to:
o: Collect the cloudy water and use it anyway on the day
Let it run until it flushes clear before using it
Close it at once and move to another hydrant that morning
Stir the water in the tank to clear the cloud to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Flushing until the water runs clear removes the stale or disturbed first water.

n.0: Cloudy water may be unsafe and should not be used.
n.2: Cloudy first water usually just needs flushing clear.
n.3: Stirring the tank does not make the water safe.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Keeping the hydrant chamber tidy during operation helps because:
o: It makes the standpipe easier to photograph on the day
It stops the vehicle blocking the footpath that morning
It lets more daylight into the chamber below to save time
It keeps grit and dirt away from the open connection
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A tidy chamber keeps grit and dirt clear of the open connection.

n.0: Photographs have nothing to do with hygiene here.
n.1: Parking is a separate matter from a tidy chamber.
n.2: Daylight in the chamber does not protect the water.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: When operating a hydrant, the operative's hands and gloves should be:
o: Coated in grease for a better grip on the key on the day
Clean, so they do not transfer dirt to the fittings
Wet from the nearest puddle for a firmer hold that morning
Left as they are, since gloves never carry dirt to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Clean hands and gloves avoid transferring dirt onto the connection.

n.0: Grease on the hands would contaminate the fittings.
n.2: Puddle water on the hands spreads contamination.
n.3: Gloves can carry plenty of dirt and must be kept clean.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: A key part of operating a hydrant hygienically is making sure the standpipe:
o: Is left slightly loose so it can be removed fast on the day
Is stored in the chamber water until it is needed that morning
Has its check valve removed for a stronger flow to save time
