Is clean and correctly fitted before the water is turned on
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A clean, correctly fitted standpipe is essential before the water flows.

n.0: A loose fitting risks leaks and is not correct.
n.1: Chamber water would contaminate the standpipe.
n.2: Removing the check valve loses backflow protection.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: After finishing, before removing the standpipe the operative should:
o: Leave it part open to drain the standpipe out on the day
Unscrew the standpipe while water still flows that morning
Kick the standpipe loose to save unscrewing it to save time
Close the hydrant fully so it stops flowing safely
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The hydrant should be closed fully first so it is no longer under flow.

n.0: Leaving it part open wastes water and risks a hazard.
n.1: Removing it under flow is unsafe and messy.
n.2: Kicking the fitting can damage it and is not correct.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Good hydrant operation means opening the valve:
o: Sharply, so the job is finished more quickly on the day
Without looking, to save time on the task for the shift
Gently, watching that everything is working as expected
Only after dark to avoid drawing attention that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Gentle opening while watching the flow keeps operation safe and controlled.

n.0: A sharp opening risks a surge and is not correct.
n.1: Not watching the hydrant is careless and unsafe.
n.3: Time of day is irrelevant to correct operation.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: If a hydrant is found to be damaged or leaking, the operative should:
o: Ignore it, as someone else will notice it later
Attempt a permanent repair using their own tools
Report it to the right person as soon as possible
Cover it over and carry on with the day's work on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Faults must be reported promptly so they can be dealt with properly.

n.0: Assuming others will report it can leave a fault unfixed.
n.1: Operatives should report faults, not carry out repairs.
n.3: Hiding a fault leaves the supply and public at risk.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: After finishing with a standpipe, what should the operative do with it?
o: Clean it and return it to its proper storage
Leave it beside the hydrant for the next crew
Throw it in the back of the van still muddy
Give it to a passer-by who asks about it on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Cleaning and returning it to proper storage keeps it hygienic and controlled.

n.1: Leaving it out exposes it to dirt and possible misuse.
n.2: Storing it muddy lets contamination build up on it.
n.3: Handing kit to the public risks unauthorised use.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: You notice the double check valve on a returned standpipe is faulty. You should:
o: Report the fault so the standpipe is not reused unsafely
Put it back on the shelf and say nothing if time is short
Leave a loose note only you would understand that morning
Use it once more yourself before mentioning it on the day
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Reporting the fault stops the unsafe standpipe being used again.

n.1: Silently returning it lets it be reused without protection.
n.2: An unclear note may never reach the right person.
n.3: Using a faulty valve first still risks the supply.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why is it important to report problems with hydrants and standpipes?
o: So faults are fixed before they can affect the supply
So the operative can claim extra pay for the day on the day
So the paperwork looks fuller at the week's end that morning
So the same hydrant is never opened again to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Prompt reporting means faults can be corrected before they harm the supply.

n.1: Reporting is about safety, not about extra pay.
n.2: Reporting is not done to pad out the paperwork.
n.3: Reporting does not mean a hydrant is closed forever.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An operative spots that a hydrant marker plate is missing. The correct action is to:
o: Do nothing, since the hydrant still works fine
Paint a new marker themselves on the kerb on the day
Remove the hydrant cover to compensate for it
Report the missing marker so it can be replaced
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A missing marker should be reported so a proper replacement can be arranged.

n.0: A missing marker still needs reporting even if it works.
n.1: Operatives should report it, not improvise a marker.
n.2: Removing the cover does not solve a missing marker.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: When returning equipment at the end of a job, it should be:
o: Left dirty so the next user can wash it instead
Split up so parts end up in different vehicles
Returned only if the next job is nearby on the day
Clean, complete and ready for safe use next time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Returning it clean, complete and ready keeps it safe for the next user.

n.0: Passing on dirty kit spreads contamination to others.
n.1: Splitting the kit up risks it being incomplete or lost.
n.2: Equipment should be returned regardless of the next job.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: If an operative accidentally contaminates a hydrant or standpipe, they should:
o: Report it straight away so action can be taken
Keep quiet and hope nothing comes of it on the day
Rinse it in a puddle and carry on working that morning
Wait until the end of the week to mention it
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Immediate reporting allows the risk to be assessed and dealt with quickly.

n.1: Staying quiet leaves a contamination risk unaddressed.
n.2: A puddle rinse adds contamination rather than fixing it.
n.3: A delay allows any contamination to spread first.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Reporting a hydrant fault promptly mainly protects:
o: The operative's own set of personal tools on the day
The appearance of the street where it sits
The fuel used by the works vehicle that day
The public who rely on that water being safe
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Prompt reporting protects the public who depend on a safe supply.

n.0: Reporting is about the supply, not the operative's tools.
n.1: Street appearance is not why faults are reported.
n.2: Fuel use is unrelated to reporting a hydrant fault.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: A standpipe returned to store should be:
o: Left wet and open so it can drain out slowly on the day
Stored next to fuel cans and oily rags for the shift
Wrapped in the same cloth used on the wheels that morning
Left clean and dry with its ends protected from dirt
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Clean, dry storage with protected ends keeps the standpipe hygienic.

n.0: Wet, open ends invite contamination during storage.
n.1: Storing it by fuel and oil risks contaminating it.
n.2: A wheel cloth would transfer road dirt to the fitting.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: You cannot fully close a hydrant and it keeps weeping water. You should:
o: Leave it weeping, as it is only a small amount on the day
Force the valve hard until something gives way that morning
Pack the outlet with rag to stop the drip to save time
Report it promptly so it can be attended to properly
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A hydrant that will not close should be reported so it can be repaired.

n.0: A small leak still needs reporting so it is fixed.
n.1: Forcing the valve could cause serious damage.
n.2: Packing it with rag is a bodge, not a proper fix.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why can misusing a single standpipe put the whole public supply at risk?
o: Because it connects directly to the shared water main
Because standpipes store water for the whole street
Because each standpipe has its own private main on the day
Because the water only flows one way, away from it that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: A standpipe links to the shared main, so misuse there can affect everyone on it.

n.1: A standpipe does not store the street's water supply.
n.2: Standpipes draw from the shared main, not a private one.
n.3: Backflow can occur, which is exactly the concern.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: The public supply is described as at risk from misuse because water:
o: Is completely sealed inside each separate hose on the day
Can be drawn back and spread contamination to others
Cannot move once it has left the hydrant outlet that morning
Only reaches one house from any given hydrant to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Under the wrong conditions water can flow back, carrying contamination to many users.

n.0: Water is not sealed off; it links back to the main.
n.2: Water can flow back if pressure conditions allow.
n.3: A hydrant feeds far more than a single house.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Scenario: A colleague says 'it's just one bucket, it can't hurt the whole town'. The best reply is:
o: Even one contaminated draw can affect the shared main
They are right, small amounts are always harmless on the day
It only matters if the bucket itself is rusty that morning
It is fine as long as nobody is watching them to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Contamination from even a small draw can enter and spread through the shared main.

n.1: Small amounts of contamination can still be harmful.
n.2: The risk is contamination, not whether the bucket rusts.
n.3: Being unobserved does not make the practice safe.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Misuse of a standpipe threatens the supply mainly through:
o: Backflow carrying pollution into the pipes everyone uses
The extra weight of water on the pipe network on the day
The noise of the water disturbing local residents that morning
The colour of the standpipe confusing the public to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: The threat is backflow drawing contamination into the pipes serving everyone.

n.1: Water weight is not how misuse threatens the supply.
n.2: Noise does not endanger the safety of the water.
n.3: A standpipe's colour poses no threat to the supply.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Why is protecting the main the responsibility of every authorised user?
o: Because only the newest operatives handle standpipes on the day
Because one careless action can affect many people's water
Because the main belongs to whoever opens it first that morning
Because water is tested at every single property to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Because the main is shared, one careless act can affect a great many people.

n.0: Experience level does not remove anyone's responsibility.
n.2: No individual owns the shared public main.
n.3: Testing every property is not what makes users responsible.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: The reason a shared main makes contamination serious is that:
o: Each home filters its own water before use that morning
Contamination is trapped at the point it enters on the day
The main empties itself out every single night to save time
Polluted water can travel to homes far from the source
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: On a shared main, contamination can travel well beyond where it entered.

n.0: Homes do not individually filter the mains supply.
n.1: Contamination is not trapped; it can move through pipes.
n.2: The main does not empty each night to clear itself.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: An operative who follows all the standpipe rules is helping to:
o: Keep clean, safe water flowing to the public
Reduce the amount of paperwork for the office
Make the standpipe worth more if it is sold
Ensure the vehicle passes its next inspection
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Following the rules keeps clean, safe water flowing to everyone on the supply.

n.1: Following the rules is about safe water, not paperwork.
n.2: Resale value is irrelevant to why the rules matter.
n.3: Vehicle inspections are unrelated to standpipe rules.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: Which best explains why 'restricted operations' controls apply to standpipe use?
o: Because the equipment is heavy and awkward to move
Because the work directly affects water people drink
Because standpipes are expensive to buy new on the day
Because the tasks take a long time to finish that morning
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Controls apply because the work bears directly on the safety of drinking water.

n.0: Weight is not why these controls exist.
n.2: Cost is not the basis for restricted operations.
n.3: Task length is not why the controls apply.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: If contamination enters the main through a misused standpipe, the likely result is:
o: People downstream may receive unsafe drinking water
Only the operative's own tap is briefly affected on the day
The hydrant simply stops working for a while that morning
The water pressure rises for the rest of the day to save time
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Contamination in the main can reach and endanger everyone downstream.

n.1: Contamination is not limited to a single tap.
n.2: The main concern is unsafe water, not a stopped hydrant.
n.3: A pressure rise is not the outcome of contamination.

Standpipes & Hydrants.q: The overall message about standpipes and the public supply is that:
o: Any use is fine as long as the job gets done on the day
Only the water company can ever cause a problem
The risk ends once the standpipe is removed that morning
Correct, authorised use protects everyone's water
Standpipes & Hydrants.w: Correct, authorised use is what keeps the shared supply safe for everyone.

n.0: Careless use can put the whole supply at risk.
n.1: Operatives' actions can also affect the supply.
n.2: Contamination introduced can persist after removal.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: When a water main bursts, why is there a risk of contamination getting into the pipe?
o: The break lets dirty water, soil and other material get inside the pipe
The high pressure inside a burst main sterilises everything around the break
Chlorine in the water always keeps the inside of a burst pipe perfectly clean
Burst mains only ever leak outwards so nothing can enter the pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A burst opens the pipe to the surrounding ground, so soil, dirty water and debris can be drawn or wash into the main.

n.1: A burst does not sterilise anything; it exposes the pipe interior to contamination.
n.2: Chlorine helps but cannot guarantee a burst pipe stays clean once it is open to the ground.
n.3: Pressure can drop and drain, allowing dirty water to be drawn back into the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which of the following is the main way germs and dirt can enter a main during a repair?
o: Through the open ends of the pipe once it has been cut into
Only through the water meter fitted at the customer's boundary
Solely through the air valve located far away on the network
Exclusively through a correctly closed and locked washout
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Cutting into a main leaves open ends exposed to the trench, which is the main route for dirt and germs to get in.

n.1: A meter is not the route by which contamination enters an open repair.
n.2: A distant air valve is not how dirt enters the pipe you have cut open.
n.3: A properly closed washout is not an entry point for contamination.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A colleague says 'the water was flowing out so nothing could have got in'. Why is this belief risky?
o: Because outward flow proves the main is already fully disinfected
Because flowing water means a sample is never needed at all
Because outward flow always removes the need to cap or protect the open pipe ends
Because pressure can fall and dirty water can then be pulled back in
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Once pressure drops or the main is drained, contaminated water and soil can be drawn back into the open pipe.

n.0: Outward flow does not disinfect the main or remove the need for treatment.
n.1: A sample may still be required regardless of how the water was flowing.
n.2: Open ends must still be capped to stop material entering the pipe.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: During a burst, which materials are most likely to enter the exposed main?
o: Soil, surface water, bacteria and debris from the trench
Only clean, treated drinking water from the same network
Nothing at all, because pipes seal themselves once broken
Purely harmless air with no soil, bacteria or surface water
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The trench around a burst holds soil, surface water, bacteria and debris that can all get into the open pipe.

n.1: Clean treated water is not the contamination risk; the surrounding ground is.
n.2: Broken pipes do not seal themselves; the opening stays exposed.
n.3: Trench conditions include far more than harmless air.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why does contamination during a burst matter for public health?
o: Because contaminated drinking water can make the public ill
Because dirty water improves the taste of the supply
Because bacteria in the main help to clean the pipe walls
Because contamination only affects the colour and nothing else
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Clean water mains supply drinking water, so any contamination that enters can reach the public and cause illness.

n.1: Dirty water does not improve taste and is a health risk.
n.2: Bacteria in a main are a hazard, not a cleaning aid.
n.3: Contamination can affect health, not merely appearance.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repair team leaves a cut main open overnight in an uncovered trench. What is the concern?
o: The pipe will automatically re-pressurise and clean itself by morning
Nothing, because contamination cannot happen while nobody is working
The main becomes stronger the longer its ends are left exposed
Vermin, insects and dirty water may enter the open pipe overnight
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Leaving open ends exposed lets vermin, insects, soil and dirty water get into the main, contaminating the supply.

n.0: An open, drained main does not re-pressurise or self-clean overnight.
n.1: Contamination can occur at any time an open main is left exposed.
n.2: Exposure weakens hygiene control; it does not strengthen the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which statement best describes how a hand or dirty tool can contaminate a repair?
o: Touching the pipe interior with soiled hands or tools transfers germs
Tools and hands are always sterile so they never pose any risk
Contamination can only ever happen through water and never through direct contact
Only brand-new pipe can carry germs, never the operative's tools
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Germs are transferred when soiled hands or unclean tools touch the inside of the pipe or fittings.

n.1: Hands and tools are not sterile and can carry contamination.
n.2: Direct contact is a recognised route of contamination, not only water.
n.3: Any surface, including tools, can carry germs into the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Standing water in a flooded trench around a broken main is a hazard mainly because it:
o: Is always cleaner than the drinking water inside the pipe
Helps flush the main so no disinfection is later needed
Contains chlorine that instantly treats the whole main
Can carry soil and bacteria straight into the open pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Trench water is contaminated with soil and bacteria and can flow directly into any open end of the main.

n.0: Trench water is dirtier than the treated supply, not cleaner.
n.1: Trench water contaminates rather than flushes the main.
n.2: Trench water is not chlorinated and does not treat the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why is a sudden loss of pressure during a burst a contamination concern?
o: Low pressure guarantees the main is now completely sterile
Low pressure has no real effect at all on what can get into an open pipe
Low or negative pressure can draw dirty water back into the main
Low pressure only affects the customer's taps and nothing else
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: When pressure falls or goes negative, external dirty water can be sucked back into the pipe through the break.

n.0: Low pressure does not sterilise the main.
n.1: Low pressure directly affects the risk of back-drawn contamination.
n.3: The effect reaches the main itself, not just customer taps.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A scenario: mud splashes onto the cut face of a pipe just before jointing. The correct view is that:
o: The mud must be cleaned off before the joint is made
The mud will be harmlessly sealed inside and can be ignored
The mud improves the seal so it should be left in place
The mud only matters if the customer happens to notice it
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Mud on the jointing face carries contamination into the main, so it must be cleaned off before jointing.

n.1: Sealing mud inside traps contamination in the supply.
n.2: Mud does not improve a joint; it compromises hygiene.
n.3: The hazard exists whether or not anyone notices it.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Contamination entering a repaired clean-water main is serious because the main carries:
o: Waste water that is naturally expected to be dirty and unfit anyway
Drinking water that people use without further treatment
Only industrial cooling water that no one ever drinks
Rainwater that is filtered again before reaching taps
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A National Water Hygiene main carries potable drinking water used directly by the public, so contamination reaches consumers.

n.0: These are clean-water mains, not waste-water sewers.
n.2: The mains supply public drinking water, not just industrial use.
n.3: The water is already treated potable water, not re-filtered rainwater.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which of these would NOT normally be a route for contamination into a broken main?
o: A sealed, watertight joint on an intact section
Dirty water flooding straight down into the open trench
Soil falling into an uncapped pipe end
Soiled tools touching the inside of the pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A sealed, watertight joint on an intact length of pipe keeps contamination out, so it is not an entry route.

n.1: Flood water in the trench is a common entry route.
n.2: Soil entering an open end is a clear contamination route.
n.3: Soiled tools touching the interior transfer contamination.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A burst on a busy road has debris and traffic dirt around it. Why treat this as a contamination risk?
o: Traffic dirt sterilises the pipe and needs no attention
Road debris cannot physically reach an open pipe end
Only rural bursts, never urban ones, risk contamination
Road debris and dirt can be washed into the open main
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Debris and dirt from a road surface can be washed or knocked into the exposed main just like any other soil.

n.0: Traffic dirt contaminates rather than sterilises the pipe.
n.1: Debris can readily reach an open end in the trench.
n.2: Urban and rural bursts both carry a contamination risk.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Before cutting into a main, why should the water be isolated and controlled?
o: To make the repair take much longer for no clear benefit
To stop the trench filling with water and to work in clean conditions
To increase the pressure so more water sprays into the trench
To ensure the pipe stays full of flowing water during the cut
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Isolating and controlling the water keeps the trench from flooding and lets the repair be done in clean, controlled conditions.

n.0: Proper control makes the job safer and cleaner, not needlessly slow.
n.2: The aim is to stop water entering the trench, not raise pressure.
n.3: You isolate so the pipe is not flowing while you work on it.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: If a trench floods with water during a repair, what should be done?
o: Carry on jointing while the open pipe ends still sit beneath the water
Leave the water in place as it keeps the pipe cool
De-water the trench so the pipe ends stay out of the water
Add more water to dilute any dirt that has collected
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A flooded trench must be de-watered (pumped or bailed out) so the open pipe ends are not sitting in contaminated water.

n.0: Jointing under water lets contamination into the main.
n.1: Leaving flood water risks it entering the open pipe.
n.3: Adding water increases the flooding and the contamination risk.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Controlling the water at a repair helps mainly by:
o: Guaranteeing a passing sample without any flushing
Keeping the excavation and open pipe ends free of dirty water
Removing any need to disinfect or clean the new fittings at all
Making sure the main stays pressurised while it is cut
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Water control keeps the trench and the open ends clear of contaminated water so the repair stays hygienic.

n.0: Control does not replace flushing or a required sample.
n.2: Fittings must still be cleaned and disinfected.
n.3: You isolate to depressurise the section, not keep it live.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which action best prevents an excavation filling with contaminated water during a repair?
o: Opening every nearby valve to raise the flow
Removing the caps from both open ends of the pipe
Isolating the section and pumping out any water that collects
Ignoring any ground water seeping into the trench
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Isolating the section stops mains water flooding in, and pumping keeps any collected water out of the excavation.

n.0: Opening valves would add water and worsen flooding.
n.1: Removing caps lets contamination into the open ends.
n.3: Ignoring ground water lets the trench fill and risks ingress.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A trench keeps filling with ground water faster than expected. The best response is to:
o: Stop pumping so the water can settle around the pipe
Break the joint open to let the trench water flow through
Leave the pipe ends open so the water can drain inside them
Keep a pump running to hold the water level below the pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Continuous pumping keeps the water level below the working area so the open pipe stays out of contaminated water.

n.0: Letting water settle around the pipe risks contamination.
n.1: Opening a joint to trench water contaminates the main.
n.2: Open ends must be capped, not used to drain trench water.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why is it important to keep the water level in the trench below the open pipe ends?
o: So contaminated trench water cannot run into the open main
So the pipe stays permanently under high pressure while it is cut
So the trench water can be used to flush the new joint
So no pump is ever required for any repair job
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Keeping the water level low stops contaminated trench water reaching and entering the open ends of the pipe.

n.1: The section is isolated and not under pressure while worked on.
n.2: Trench water must never be used to flush the main.
n.3: Pumping is often exactly what keeps the level low.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Isolating a section of main before repair usually involves:
o: Opening all upstream valves to keep it flowing
Removing the customer's stop tap from their property
Draining the reservoir that feeds the whole district
Closing the correct valves to stop water reaching the break
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Isolation means closing the appropriate valves so water stops reaching the section being worked on.

n.0: Opening valves keeps water flowing, the opposite of isolating.
n.1: You control network valves, not a customer's private stop tap.
n.2: You isolate a local section, not drain an entire reservoir.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repair is being done in a deep, wet trench. Why is water control especially important here?
o: Deep trenches never collect water so control is pointless
Wet ground automatically disinfects the pipe interior
Standing water can easily reach and enter the open ends
Deep water raises pressure inside the isolated main
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: In a deep, wet trench standing water readily reaches the open pipe, so keeping it de-watered is vital to hygiene.

n.0: Deep trenches often collect the most water, not the least.
n.1: Wet ground contaminates rather than disinfects the pipe.
n.3: An isolated section is not pressurised by trench water.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The purpose of de-watering a flooded excavation before jointing is to:
o: Cool the fittings down so that they are far easier to push together
Keep the open pipe ends and fittings out of dirty water
Add extra water into the main to speed up flushing
Raise the trench floor so the pipe sits higher up
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: De-watering removes the contaminated water so the open ends and fittings can be handled without being immersed.

n.0: De-watering is about hygiene, not cooling fittings.
n.2: It removes water rather than adding any to the main.
n.3: It clears the water; it does not raise the trench floor.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which is a sign that water is NOT being properly controlled at a repair?
o: The trench is dry and the pipe ends are capped
The section has been isolated at the correct valves
A pump is running to keep the excavation clear
The open pipe ends are sitting under muddy water
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Open pipe ends under muddy water show the excavation is flooded and water control has failed.

n.0: A dry trench with capped ends shows good control.
n.1: Correct isolation is part of proper water control.
n.2: A running pump is helping to control the water.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: You arrive to find the isolation valves have not fully closed and water is still trickling in. You should:
o: Start jointing anyway since the flow is only small
Open the pipe ends to let the trickle wash them clean
Leave the trench to flood so the flow slows naturally
Establish a proper isolation before opening the pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A reliable isolation must be in place before the main is opened, or water and contamination will enter the work area.

n.0: Even a small flow undermines hygiene and control.
n.1: Trickling water washes contamination in, not out.
n.2: Letting the trench flood increases the contamination risk.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Good water control at a repair supports hygiene by ensuring that:
o: The main stays live and pressurised throughout the cut
Trench water is deliberately fed through the new joint
No pump or bailing is ever needed on any job
The excavation stays dry and the pipe ends stay clean
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Controlling the water keeps the excavation dry and the open pipe ends clean, which protects the supply.

n.0: The section is isolated and depressurised while worked on.
n.1: Trench water must never be fed through the joint.
n.2: Pumping or bailing is often required to keep the trench dry.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should the open ends of a pipe be capped or plugged when work stops?
o: To make the exposed pipe look tidy for a passing site inspector
To trap air pressure inside the isolated section
To stop soil, vermin and dirty water entering the pipe
To stop the pipe from drying out on the inside
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Capping open ends keeps out soil, vermin and dirty water, protecting the inside of the main from contamination.

n.0: Capping is for hygiene, not appearance.
n.1: An isolated section is not being held under air pressure.
n.3: The purpose is to keep contamination out, not to keep it damp.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: How should new pipe and fittings be stored on site before use?
o: Kept clean, capped and off the ground away from dirt
Laid directly in the muddy trench to keep them handy
Left uncapped so any water inside can drain out freely
Dragged through the spoil heap to check they are strong
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Pipes and fittings should be kept clean, capped and clear of the ground so they are not contaminated before fitting.

n.1: Laying them in mud contaminates them before use.
n.2: Leaving them uncapped lets dirt and vermin get inside.
n.3: Dragging them through spoil contaminates the surfaces.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A length of new pipe has soil inside it. Before fitting it you should:
o: Fit it as it is, since flushing it later will sort the soil out
Tip the soil towards the far end and joint over it
Leave the soil in to help bed the joint firmly
Clean out the inside so no soil is built into the main
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Any soil inside a pipe must be cleaned out before fitting, or it becomes a permanent contamination source in the main.

n.0: Flushing may not clear built-in soil and is no excuse to fit dirty pipe.
n.1: Moving soil along the pipe still leaves contamination inside.
n.2: Soil does not bed a joint; it contaminates the supply.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Keeping the excavation clean during a repair mainly means:
o: Filling the trench with spoil while you work
Keeping mud, spoil and standing water away from the pipe
Letting surface water run freely into the trench
Storing fittings loose in the bottom of the hole
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A clean excavation keeps mud, spoil and standing water clear of the open pipe and fittings, protecting the main.

n.0: Filling the trench with spoil brings contamination to the pipe.
n.2: Surface water running in floods the trench and risks ingress.
n.3: Loose fittings on the trench floor pick up contamination.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why keep tools used inside the pipe clean and, where possible, disinfected?
o: Because clean tools make the joint look neater to customers
Because dirty tools transfer contamination into the main
Because dirty tools speed up the repair considerably
Because tool hygiene only matters on brand-new mains
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Tools that go inside the pipe can carry germs into the supply, so they should be clean and disinfected where practical.

n.0: Tool hygiene is about contamination, not appearance.
n.2: Dirty tools do not make a repair quicker; they risk the supply.
n.3: Tool hygiene matters on repairs as well as new mains.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: An operative wants to rest the open pipe end on the spoil heap for a moment. This is:
o: Wrong, because spoil will contaminate the inside of the pipe
Fine, because spoil is always clean, dry material
Advised, because the spoil supports the pipe safely
Acceptable, provided it is only for a short time
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Resting an open end on the spoil heap lets soil and germs into the pipe, so it should never be done.

n.1: Spoil is dirty ground material, not clean.
n.2: Supporting the pipe must not involve contaminating its interior.
n.3: Even brief contact with spoil can contaminate the pipe.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The best way to keep the inside of a repaired main clean during the work is to:
o: Keep ends capped and handle fittings with clean hands
Leave both ends open so fresh air can circulate through
Wipe the inside with any rag found in the works van
Rinse the fittings in the water lying in the trench
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Capping ends and handling clean fittings with clean hands keeps contamination out of the pipe interior.

n.1: Open ends let in dirt, vermin and dirty water.
n.2: A dirty rag can add contamination rather than remove it.
n.3: Trench water is contaminated and must not touch the fittings.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which practice would MOST compromise the cleanliness of a repair?
o: Capping the pipe ends whenever work pauses
Keeping the new fittings on a clean sheet off the ground
Dropping the new coupling into the muddy trench floor
Wiping tools clean before they enter the pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Dropping a coupling into muddy trench water contaminates it, so it must not be fitted without cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: Capping ends helps keep the pipe clean.
n.1: Keeping fittings off the ground protects them.
n.3: Wiping tools clean supports good hygiene.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Spoil is falling from the trench side towards the open pipe end. The correct action is to:
o: Continue working and clean the pipe only after backfilling
Push the spoil into the pipe to weigh it down
Support the trench side and keep spoil out of the pipe
Ignore it, as spoil cannot enter a horizontal pipe
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The trench must be kept from shedding spoil into the pipe; the sides should be supported and the ends protected.

n.0: Contamination built in cannot simply be cleaned after backfill.
n.1: Pushing spoil in deliberately contaminates the main.
n.3: Spoil can readily fall into a horizontal open end.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Handling new fittings, an operative should avoid:
o: Touching the sealing faces with muddy, unwashed hands
Keeping the fittings capped until the moment of use
Placing the fittings on a clean surface off the ground
Checking the fittings are clean before jointing them
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Muddy hands on the sealing faces transfer contamination into the main, so hands and faces must be kept clean.

n.1: Keeping fittings capped until use is good practice.
n.2: A clean, raised surface protects the fittings.
n.3: Checking fittings are clean is exactly what should be done.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should the number of people reaching into the open main be kept to a minimum?
o: Because fewer people make the finished repair look more professional
Because only supervisors are legally allowed near the pipe
Because every extra hand is another chance to add contamination
Because more hands always make the joint physically weaker
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Each person reaching into the main is another opportunity to introduce germs, so contact should be limited.

n.0: The reason is hygiene, not appearances.
n.1: It is a hygiene control, not a legal restriction on who may help.
n.3: Extra hands do not weaken the joint; they raise contamination risk.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Keeping the pipe interior clean during a repair is important chiefly because:
o: It makes the pipe cheaper to install
It lets you skip flushing before returning to supply
It keeps the outside of the pipe looking clean
Anything left inside becomes part of the drinking water supply
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Whatever is left inside a repaired main ends up in the drinking water, so the interior must be kept clean.

n.0: Interior cleanliness is a hygiene matter, not a cost saving.
n.1: Cleanliness does not remove the need for flushing.
n.2: The concern is the interior and the supply, not the outside look.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Before a repaired main is returned to supply, fittings that were exposed should be:
o: Left exactly as they are since the water will clean them
Painted over to seal any dirt permanently inside
Cleaned and disinfected to remove any contamination
Rinsed only in the water found in the trench
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Exposed fittings are cleaned and disinfected before the main returns to supply so contamination is not left inside.

n.0: Water flowing past does not reliably clean contaminated fittings.
n.1: Painting over dirt traps contamination in the supply.
n.3: Trench water is contaminated and must never be used to rinse fittings.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: What is 'swabbing' a repaired section of main intended to do?
o: Add extra chlorine taste to the finished water
Physically push out dirt and debris left inside the pipe
Test the pressure the new joint can withstand
Colour the water so leaks are easier to see
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Swabbing pushes a swab through the pipe to physically remove loose dirt and debris before the main returns to supply.

n.0: Swabbing removes debris; it is not about adding taste.
n.2: Pressure is checked separately, not by swabbing.
n.3: Swabbing is not a leak-detection dye method.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Flushing a repaired main before returning it to supply is done to:
o: Fill the main slowly to avoid any air being trapped only
Raise the water pressure permanently across the district
Wash out any remaining dirt, debris and disinfectant
Warm the water so samples are easier to collect
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Flushing runs water through at a good rate to wash out remaining dirt, debris and any disinfectant used.

n.0: Careful filling matters, but flushing is chiefly about washing the main out.
n.1: Flushing does not permanently raise district pressure.
n.3: Flushing is not about warming the water for sampling.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why is a bacteriological sample taken after certain repairs?
o: To measure how quickly the water is flowing along the repaired main
To check the colour of the water for the customer
To confirm the pressure meets the design figure
To confirm the water is safe before returning to supply
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A bacteriological sample confirms the water is free of harmful bacteria before the main is returned to public supply.

n.0: A sample checks water quality, not flow rate.
n.1: It is a microbiological check, not a colour check.
n.2: Pressure is verified separately, not by a bacteriological sample.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: In what order are these steps generally carried out on a repaired main?
o: Sample first, then flush, then swab, then disinfect fittings
Flush first, then take a sample, then clean the fittings
Clean and disinfect fittings, then swab and flush, then sample
Return it to supply first, then swab, flush and sample it much later
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Fittings are cleaned and disinfected, the section is swabbed and flushed, then a sample is taken before returning to supply.

n.0: Sampling comes after cleaning, swabbing and flushing, not first.
n.1: Fittings are cleaned before flushing, and sampling comes last.
n.3: You must not return to supply before swabbing, flushing and sampling.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Disinfecting a fitting before it goes into a clean-water main means:
o: Simply wiping off the visible mud with a dry cloth
Leaving it in the sun for a while to dry out
Rinsing it once in the nearest available puddle
Treating it so harmful germs on it are killed
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Disinfection kills harmful germs on the fitting so they are not introduced into the drinking water supply.

n.0: Wiping off visible mud does not kill germs.
n.1: Drying in the sun does not disinfect a fitting.
n.2: A puddle is contaminated and cannot disinfect anything.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repaired main has been swabbed but the swab came out heavily soiled. You should:
o: Return the main to supply as the swab has done its job
Take the bacteriological sample straight away regardless
Continue swabbing and flushing until the main runs clean
Cap the ends and simply leave the loose dirt to settle out on its own
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A heavily soiled swab shows debris remains, so swabbing and flushing continue until the main runs clean.

n.0: A dirty swab means the main is not yet clean enough to return.
n.1: Sampling should follow effective cleaning, not precede it.
n.3: Letting dirt settle does not remove it from the supply.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which of these should be flushed to waste rather than sent into supply?
o: Clean, sampled water that has already passed
The first dirty water and disinfectant after a repair
Water from a main that was never opened at all
Treated water drawn from a completely untouched reservoir
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The first flush of dirty water and any disinfectant from a repair is run to waste, not sent into the public supply.

n.0: Clean, passed water is fit to enter supply.
n.2: Water from an unopened main needs no flushing to waste.
n.3: Untouched treated water is already fit for supply.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should flushing be done at a good flow rate rather than a slow trickle?
o: A trickle uses more chlorine than a fast flow does
A good flow rate scours out loose dirt more effectively
A slow trickle of water raises the pressure right across the network
Fast flushing is only ever needed on brand-new mains
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A good flow rate creates enough velocity to scour and carry away loose dirt and debris from the repaired main.

n.0: Flow rate is about scouring, not chlorine use.
n.2: Flushing does not raise network pressure.
n.3: Effective flushing applies to repairs, not just new mains.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A bacteriological sample from a repaired main fails. The correct action is to:
o: Keep the main off supply and re-clean, flush and re-sample
Put the main straight into supply since one fail is normal
Ignore the result because the water looked perfectly clear
Take no further action until a customer complains of illness
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A failed sample means the main is not safe, so it stays off supply and is re-treated and re-sampled until it passes.

n.1: A failed sample must not be overridden and put into supply.
n.2: Clear-looking water can still fail bacteriologically.
n.3: Action is needed at once, not only after illness is reported.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Swabbing and flushing together are used on a repaired main to:
o: Increase the chlorine taste for the paying customer
Remove loose debris and wash the section clean
Test how much pressure the joint can hold
Warm the pipe so it seals more tightly
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Swabbing dislodges and pushes out debris and flushing washes the loosened material away, cleaning the section.

n.0: They clean the main; they do not add taste.
n.2: Pressure testing is a separate activity.
n.3: They do not warm the pipe or affect the seal.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: When is a bacteriological sample most clearly required after a repair?
o: Only when the customer specifically asks for one
Only on repairs carried out during the summer
Never, because visual inspection is always enough
Where the procedure specifies one before returning to supply
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A sample is taken where the procedure for that job specifies one, to confirm the water is safe before returning to supply.

n.0: Sampling follows the procedure, not customer requests.
n.1: The requirement is not limited to summer repairs.
n.2: Visual inspection cannot confirm bacteriological safety.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: When recommissioning a repaired main, why is it filled slowly and carefully?
o: To avoid disturbing sediment and trapping air in the main
To make the job take as long as reasonably possible
To force trapped air deeper into the customer's pipes
To raise the pressure in the main well above the normal working level
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Slow, careful filling avoids stirring up sediment and helps air escape rather than being trapped in the main.

n.1: Careful filling is about quality, not simply taking longer.
n.2: Slow filling helps air escape, not push it into customer pipes.
n.3: Recommissioning restores normal pressure, not an excessive one.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which is a correct step when bringing a repaired main back into service?
o: Open all valves fully at once to fill it as fast as possible
Leave the main empty and let customers draw it full
Skip venting because trapped air improves the flow
Open valves slowly and vent trapped air as the main fills
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Valves are opened slowly and air is vented as the main fills, avoiding surges and trapped air.

n.0: Opening everything at once causes surges and disturbs sediment.
n.1: The main should be filled and checked, not left for customers to fill.
n.2: Trapped air causes problems and should be vented out.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Recommissioning a main after a repair should not be completed until:
o: The next scheduled maintenance visit takes place
The customer confirms the water tastes acceptable
The required flushing and any specified sample are done
The trench has been completely backfilled, reinstated and made good
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The main is only recommissioned once the required flushing and any specified sample have been completed satisfactorily.

n.0: Recommissioning is completed with the job, not at a later visit.
n.1: Customer taste feedback does not replace flushing and sampling.
n.3: Backfilling is separate from the hygiene steps that clear the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: During recommissioning, why check that the water runs clear at a downstream point?
o: To measure the exact pressure at the customer's tap
To confirm the trench has been backfilled correctly
To confirm dirty water has been flushed through and cleared
To prove the chlorine has been completely removed
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Running water clear at a downstream point confirms the dirty water and debris have been flushed out of the section.

n.0: Clarity indicates cleanliness, not a precise pressure reading.
n.1: It relates to water quality, not backfilling.
n.3: Clear water does not by itself prove all chlorine is gone.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repaired main has been filled and flushed. The next recommissioning step is typically to:
o: Backfill the trench before checking the water at all
Check the water and take any sample the procedure requires
Return it to supply immediately without any checks
Leave the valves half open and go on to the next job
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: After filling and flushing, the water is checked and any specified sample taken before the main is returned to supply.

n.0: Backfilling should not come before the water quality checks.
n.2: Returning to supply without checks skips a vital step.
n.3: Valves are not left half open; the job is completed properly.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should surges and rapid pressure changes be avoided when recommissioning a main?
o: Because they can disturb deposits and discolour the water
Because they make the new joint permanently stronger
Because they are needed to force air out quickly
Because they help the sample pass more reliably
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Surges stir up deposits in the pipe and can discolour the water, so pressure is changed gradually.

n.1: Surges do not strengthen the joint; they cause quality problems.
n.2: Air is vented gently, not forced out with surges.
n.3: Surges make discolouration more likely, not less.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Recommissioning is the stage where a repaired main is:
o: Cut open and exposed to the dirty trench for the first time
Left isolated and out of use for several weeks
Deliberately drained down and abandoned in place
Brought carefully back into normal service and supply
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Recommissioning is the controlled process of bringing the repaired main back into normal service and supply.

n.0: Cutting open is part of the repair, not recommissioning.
n.1: Recommissioning brings the main back, it does not leave it idle.
n.2: The main is returned to service, not abandoned.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Before finally returning a repaired main to full supply, an operative should confirm that:
o: Flushing, any sample and quality checks have been completed
The tools have been loaded back onto the works van
The nearest hydrant has been repainted a bright colour
The road markings around the site have been refreshed
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Full return to supply follows confirmation that flushing, any required sample and quality checks are complete.

n.1: Loading tools is housekeeping, not a hygiene confirmation.
n.2: Hydrant painting is unrelated to water quality clearance.
n.3: Road markings do not confirm the water is safe.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Venting air during recommissioning is important because trapped air can:
o: Improve the taste of the water at the tap
Guarantee a passing bacteriological sample
Cause discoloured water and disrupt the flow
Permanently increase the pressure in the main
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Trapped air can disrupt flow and stir up deposits, causing discolouration, so it is vented as the main fills.

n.0: Trapped air does not improve taste; it causes problems.
n.1: Air has nothing to do with guaranteeing a sample passes.
n.3: Air does not permanently raise the main's pressure.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: You notice dirty water has entered the open main during a repair. You should:
o: Cap it up quickly and return it to supply straight away
Clean and disinfect the section and re-flush before use
Ignore it because the flush at the end will remove everything
Add the dirty water into the customer's tank to dilute it
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Ingress of dirty water means the section must be cleaned, disinfected and re-flushed before it can be returned to supply.

n.0: Returning it to supply spreads the contamination to consumers.
n.2: Ingress is a serious event that cannot simply be ignored.
n.3: Dirty water must never be routed into a customer's supply.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The best first response to water ingress during a repair is to:
o: Carry on jointing so the pipe is sealed sooner
Stop, control the water and prevent further ingress
Open the far valve to let the dirty water flow onward
Backfill immediately to hide the affected section
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The priority is to stop and control the water so no more dirty water enters, before cleaning up the section.

n.0: Jointing over ingress seals contamination inside the main.
n.2: Sending dirty water onward spreads the contamination.
n.3: Backfilling over ingress hides but does not fix the problem.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Ingress of contaminated water into a clean-water main is serious because it can:
o: Only affect the colour of the water for a short while
Introduce harmful bacteria into the public supply
Improve the disinfection of the whole network
Reduce the pressure but never affect water quality
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Contaminated ingress can carry harmful bacteria into the drinking water supply, putting the public at risk.

n.0: It is a health risk, not just a brief colour change.
n.2: Ingress contaminates the supply rather than disinfecting it.
n.3: It affects water quality directly, not merely pressure.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: After dealing with ingress and re-treating a section, what confirms it is safe to return to supply?
o: A satisfactory bacteriological sample where one is required
The water no longer smells of the trench
The trench has been fully backfilled and reinstated
Enough time has simply passed since the ingress
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Where a sample is required, a satisfactory bacteriological result confirms the re-treated section is safe to return to supply.

n.1: Smell alone does not confirm bacteriological safety.
n.2: Backfilling does not prove the water is safe.
n.3: Time passing does not make a contaminated section safe.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A pipe end briefly dipped into muddy trench water before being capped. You should treat the section as:
o: Perfectly clean, because the contact was only very brief
Improved, because the mud will seal small gaps in the joint
Contaminated, needing cleaning and disinfection before use
Unaffected, as trench water is the same as tap water
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Even brief contact with muddy water contaminates the interior, so the section is cleaned and disinfected before use.

n.0: Brief contact is still enough to contaminate the pipe.
n.1: Mud does not seal joints; it contaminates the supply.
n.3: Trench water is dirty and is not equivalent to tap water.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: If dirty water is being drawn into the main because of low pressure, the priority is to:
o: Let the ingress continue so the pipe fills up quicker
Open more valves to lower the pressure further
Cap the ends and leave the dirty water inside
Restore control and stop the dirty water entering
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Restoring control to stop the ingress is the priority, before cleaning and treating the affected section.

n.0: Allowing continued ingress worsens the contamination.
n.1: Lowering pressure further increases the ingress.
n.2: Capping in the dirty water traps contamination in the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which is a clear sign that dirty water may have got into a repaired section?
o: The flushed water runs clear from the first moment
Muddy or discoloured water appears when flushing
A passing sample is returned by the laboratory
The trench around the pipe has stayed completely dry
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Muddy or discoloured water on flushing indicates dirt has entered the section and it needs further cleaning.

n.0: Water clear from the start suggests no ingress.
n.2: A passing sample indicates the water is satisfactory.
n.3: A dry trench suggests ingress was avoided.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The safest attitude to any suspected ingress of dirty water is to:
o: Assume it caused no harm unless proven otherwise
Deal with it only if a customer later complains
Treat the section as contaminated until confirmed clean
Return the main to supply and monitor it for problems after
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Suspected ingress is treated as contamination until cleaning, flushing and any sample confirm the section is clean.

n.0: Assuming no harm risks putting contaminated water into supply.
n.1: Waiting for a complaint means the public is exposed first.
n.3: Returning first and monitoring later exposes consumers to risk.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repair is finished but the specified sample has not yet been taken. What should happen?
o: Return it straight to supply and take the required sample next week
Skip the sample as the water already looks clear
Let the customer decide whether a sample is needed
Keep the section off supply until the sample is taken
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The section stays off supply until the required sample has been taken (and passed), protecting the public.

n.0: Returning first and sampling later exposes consumers to any risk.
n.1: Clear-looking water does not remove the sampling requirement.
n.2: Sampling is a procedural requirement, not a customer choice.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: It is raining hard and the trench keeps filling. The correct practical decision is to:
o: Keep pumping and protect the open ends from the water
Ignore the rain and joint the pipe under the water
Speed up and skip disinfection to beat the weather
Leave the job wide open and return only when the weather has cleared
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: You keep the excavation de-watered and the open ends protected so the wet conditions do not contaminate the main.

n.1: Jointing under water lets contamination into the pipe.
n.2: Skipping disinfection to save time compromises the supply.
n.3: Leaving an open main exposed invites further contamination.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: You realise a new fitting was dropped in the mud but a colleague has already jointed it in. You should:
o: Say nothing, since the fitting is now sealed in place
Raise it so the section can be cleaned, disinfected and flushed
Wait to see whether the final sample happens to pass
Note it for the records but take no action on site
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A muddy fitting jointed into the main is a contamination risk, so it must be flagged and the section cleaned, disinfected and flushed.

n.0: Sealing in a dirty fitting leaves contamination in the supply.
n.2: Hoping the sample passes ignores a known contamination event.
n.3: Recording it is not enough; the contamination must be dealt with.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which decision on a repair job best protects public health?
o: Returning to supply before flushing to save time
Rinsing fittings in trench water to speed things up
Leaving open pipe ends uncapped between shifts
Refusing to return the main until it has passed its checks
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Holding the main off supply until it passes its flushing, disinfection and any sample is the decision that protects the public.

n.0: Returning before flushing can send contaminated water to consumers.
n.1: Trench water contaminates fittings rather than cleaning them.
n.2: Uncapped ends let contamination into the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A supervisor pressures the team to reconnect a main quickly before it has been sampled. The right response is to:
o: Explain the sample must be taken before returning to supply
Reconnect at once and take the sample the following day
Reconnect but warn the customer to boil their water
Reconnect and hope the water quality turns out fine
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The required sample must be taken before the main returns to supply, and the operative should say so rather than cut the step.

n.1: Reconnecting before sampling exposes consumers to any contamination.
n.2: A boil notice does not replace the required hygiene steps.
n.3: Hoping for the best is not an acceptable hygiene decision.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: You have only trench water to hand and the fittings need rinsing. You should:
o: Use the dirty trench water rather than delay the repair
Rinse the fittings once and joint them quickly
Skip rinsing entirely and fit them as they are
Use clean water and disinfection, not trench water
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Fittings must be cleaned with clean water and disinfected; trench water is contaminated and must never be used.

n.0: Trench water would contaminate the fittings, not clean them.
n.1: A single rinse in dirty water still leaves contamination.
n.2: Fitting dirty items builds contamination into the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: On a repair, keeping fittings capped, hands clean and the trench de-watered are all examples of:
o: Steps that can be skipped if the job is running late
Optional extras only needed on brand-new mains
Everyday hygiene precautions that protect the water supply
Measures required only when a sample is being taken
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: These are routine hygiene precautions that together protect the drinking water supply during any repair.

n.0: Hygiene steps are not skipped for time pressure.
n.1: They apply to repairs as well as new mains.
n.3: They are needed throughout, not only at sampling.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The most reliable way to decide whether a repaired main is fit to return to supply is to:
o: Follow the flushing, disinfection and sampling procedure
Judge it by how clear the water looks in a bucket
Rely on how quickly the joint went together
Ask whether the customer is happy for it to return
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Fitness to return is decided by following the flushing, disinfection and sampling procedure, not by appearance or convenience.

n.1: Clear-looking water can still be unsafe.
n.2: How fast the joint was made says nothing about hygiene.
n.3: The decision follows procedure, not customer preference.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A short scenario: mid-repair you drop a coupling into the muddy trench. The best decision is to:
o: Wipe it on your sleeve and fit it straight away
Clean and disinfect it, or use a fresh clean one
Fit it now and rely on the final flush to clean it
Leave it in the mud and joint over the gap instead
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A coupling dropped in mud must be cleaned and disinfected before use, or replaced with a clean one.

n.0: Wiping on a sleeve does not remove or kill contamination.
n.2: Flushing may not clear a fitting that went in contaminated.
n.3: Jointing over a gap is not a proper or hygienic repair.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which of these is the correct sequence of decisions when a main bursts?
o: Return to supply, then isolate, then clean up later
Isolate and control the water, repair, then clean and return
Backfill first, then flush, then isolate the section
Sample it first, then repair it, then decide whether to isolate at all
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: You isolate and control the water, carry out the repair, then clean, flush, sample and return the main to supply.

n.0: You cannot return to supply before isolating and repairing.
n.2: Backfilling and flushing do not come before isolation.
n.3: Sampling is a final check, not the first step of a burst repair.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repaired main passes its sample but the trench is still flooded. Before backfilling you should:
o: De-water the trench and make sure it stays clean
Backfill straight away as the sample has passed
Add the flood water into the main to save flushing
Leave the flood water in to settle the ground
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The trench should still be de-watered and kept clean; a passing sample does not mean a flooded trench can be ignored.

n.1: A passing sample does not make backfilling a flooded trench acceptable.
n.2: Flood water must never be added into the main.
n.3: Leaving flood water risks re-contaminating the work.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: An operative is unsure whether a repaired section needs a sample before return. The best action is to:
o: Assume no sample is needed and return it to supply
Take no sample but keep an eye on customer complaints
Check the procedure and follow the sampling requirement
Return the main and arrange a sample only if problems arise
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: When unsure, the operative checks the procedure for that job and follows its sampling requirement before returning to supply.

n.0: Assuming no sample is needed risks returning unsafe water.
n.1: Waiting for complaints exposes the public first.
n.3: Sampling after problems arise is too late to protect consumers.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should an operative never return a repaired main to supply 'to save time' before it is cleared?
o: Because the associated paperwork always takes rather longer that way
Because untreated contamination could reach the public
Because the joint needs several days to set first
Because the water pressure will be far too high
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Returning a main before it is cleared risks sending contaminated water to the public, which is why the steps are never skipped.

n.0: The reason is public safety, not paperwork timing.
n.2: Joints do not need days to set before supply.
n.3: The concern is contamination, not excessive pressure.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repair on a small-diameter service pipe still needs hygiene precautions because:
o: It still supplies drinking water that people consume
Small pipes never carry drinking water to anyone
Small-bore pipes are far too narrow for any germ to be able to enter
Only large trunk mains can ever be contaminated
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Even a small service pipe carries drinking water to consumers, so the same hygiene care is needed.

n.1: Service pipes do carry drinking water to customers.
n.2: Germs are microscopic and easily enter small pipes.
n.3: Contamination is not limited to large trunk mains.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Keeping a swab clean and in good condition before use matters because:
o: A dirty swab makes the pipe joint set more firmly
A clean swab raises the pressure inside the pipe
Swab condition only affects how the water looks
A dirty swab could itself add contamination to the main
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A dirty swab would introduce contamination as it passes through, so swabs are kept clean before use.

n.0: A swab's condition does not affect how a joint sets.
n.1: A swab does not change the pressure in the main.
n.2: A dirty swab is a contamination risk, not just an appearance issue.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: During a live-main repair, protective covering over the open ends helps by:
o: Stopping dirt, insects and water getting inside
Increasing the water pressure at the break
Making the pipe easier to see from the road
Warming the pipe so the new joints seal more quickly
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Covering the open ends keeps dirt, insects and water out of the pipe interior while work is paused.

n.1: Covering ends does not raise pressure.
n.2: Visibility is not the purpose of covering the ends.
n.3: Covering does not warm the pipe or affect the seal.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which best explains why disinfectant is flushed out before a main returns to supply?
o: Disinfectant makes the water permanently safer to drink
Strong disinfectant should not reach customers' taps
Disinfectant increases the pressure across the network
Disinfectant helps a bacteriological sample fail
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The disinfectant used to treat the main is flushed out so that strong chemical does not reach consumers.

n.0: Residual strong disinfectant is not left in for customers to drink.
n.2: Disinfectant does not raise network pressure.
n.3: Flushing disinfectant supports a valid sample, it does not fail it.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A colleague suggests using the customer's own tap water in a bucket to rinse a clean fitting. This is:
o: Wrong, because tap water is never clean enough for this
Wrong, because only trench water may be used on site
Advised only if the fitting is going into a sewer
Acceptable, as it is treated drinking water kept clean
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Clean, treated drinking water kept free of contamination is suitable, unlike dirty trench water.

n.0: Treated tap water is clean and suitable when kept clean.
n.1: Trench water is contaminated and must not be used.
n.2: These are potable mains, not sewers.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The reason open pipe ends are capped as soon as a main is cut is to:
o: Make the isolated section hold high pressure
Stop the pipe interior from ever drying out
Allow trench water to drain harmlessly inside
Prevent contamination entering during the whole job
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Capping the ends immediately keeps contamination out from the moment the pipe is opened until it is jointed.

n.0: Capping is not about holding pressure in an isolated section.
n.1: The aim is to keep contamination out, not keep it damp.
n.2: Trench water must be kept out, not drained into the pipe.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A burst main has soaked the surrounding ground with sewage from a nearby damaged sewer. This means:
o: Extra care and thorough disinfection are especially vital
The repair can proceed exactly as any normal job
No flushing is needed here because sewage is mostly just water
The main can return to supply without a sample
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Sewage contamination makes thorough water control, disinfection, flushing and sampling especially important.

n.1: Sewage contamination raises the risk and demands extra care.
n.2: Sewage makes flushing and disinfection more important, not less.
n.3: A sample is more clearly needed, not less, in these conditions.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: What is the main reason to limit how long a repaired main is left open before jointing?
o: Open pipe looks untidy to members of the public
The longer it is open, the greater the contamination risk
Long jobs always cost the water company more money
The pipe material weakens the longer it is exposed
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: The longer a main stays open, the more chance dirt, vermin and water have to get inside, so exposure is minimised.

n.0: Tidiness is not the hygiene reason for limiting exposure.
n.2: Cost is not the reason exposure is minimised.
n.3: Pipe material does not weaken simply from being exposed.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repaired main is being flushed but there is nowhere obvious to discharge the dirty water. You should:
o: Discharge it back into the same main downstream
Arrange a suitable discharge point before flushing
Send it into the customer's property drainage
Skip flushing since there is nowhere for the water to go
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A suitable, safe discharge point must be arranged so the dirty flush water is run to waste properly, not skipped.

n.0: Discharging dirty water back into the main defeats the flush.
n.2: Flush water is not put into a customer's drainage.
n.3: Flushing is essential and must not be skipped for convenience.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why is it important that only trained, hygiene-aware operatives handle open clean-water mains?
o: They understand how to avoid contaminating the supply
They can complete the repair without any tools
They are specially allowed to skip flushing and sampling
They can return mains to supply without any checks
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Trained operatives understand the hygiene precautions needed to avoid contaminating the drinking water supply.

n.1: Training does not mean working without tools.
n.2: Training reinforces the steps; it does not license skipping them.
n.3: Trained operatives still carry out the required checks.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A repaired section will not run clear no matter how long it is flushed. The likely reason is that:
o: The chlorine has made the water permanently cloudy
The sample has already been taken and passed
Debris or dirt remains and swabbing may be needed
The pressure in the main is simply too low to flush
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Water that will not clear usually means debris remains, so further swabbing and flushing are needed before sampling.

n.0: Chlorine at treatment levels does not make water permanently cloudy.
n.1: A passed sample would not leave the water failing to clear.
n.3: Low pressure alone does not explain persistent dirt in the water.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Which statement about returning a repaired main to supply is correct?
o: It can return once the visible mud has been wiped off
It can return as soon as the joint stops leaking
It returns only after required flushing, disinfection and sampling
It can return whenever the operative feels confident
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: A repaired main returns to supply only after the required flushing, disinfection and any specified sample are completed.

n.0: Wiping off mud does not clear the main for supply.
n.1: A watertight joint alone does not confirm the water is safe.
n.3: Confidence is not the standard; the procedure is.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A quick scenario: you finish a joint and see the flush water is brown. You should:
o: Return the main to supply as brown is only rust
Take the sample now before the water clears
Cap the ends and let the brown water settle
Keep flushing until the water runs clear
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Brown flush water shows dirt is still present, so flushing continues until the water runs clear.

n.0: Brown water is not fit to return to supply.
n.1: A sample should follow effective flushing, not brown water.
n.2: Letting it settle does not remove the dirt from the main.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: Why should backfilling not begin until the hygiene checks on a repair are complete?
o: It could hide problems and hamper any further flushing
Backfilling the trench makes the water sample pass much more easily
Backfilling is what disinfects the repaired section
The trench must stay open to raise the water pressure
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Backfilling too early can hide issues and make it harder to re-flush or re-treat if a check is not satisfactory.

n.1: Backfilling does not affect whether a sample passes.
n.2: Backfilling does not disinfect anything.
n.3: An open trench does not raise water pressure.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: The overall aim of the hygiene steps taken on a live or repaired main is to:
o: Getting the repair done as fast and as cheaply as possible
Keep the water pressure as high as it can be
Ensure the joint looks neat for inspection
Protect consumers from contaminated drinking water
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Every hygiene step on a repair exists to protect consumers by keeping their drinking water free of contamination.

n.0: Speed and cost are not the purpose of the hygiene steps.
n.1: The steps are about safety, not maximising pressure.
n.2: A neat joint is not the aim; safe water is.

Working on Live & Repaired Mains.q: A short scenario: the isolation is holding but ground water is seeping into one end of the trench. You should:
o: Joint the pipe with the end sitting in the seepage
Open the isolated valve to flush the seepage through
Pump the seepage away and keep the pipe end clear
Leave the seepage as it is too small to matter
Working on Live & Repaired Mains.w: Even minor seepage is pumped away so the open pipe end stays clear of contaminated ground water.

n.0: Jointing in seepage lets contamination into the main.
n.1: Opening the valve floods the work with more water.
n.3: Even small seepage can reach an open end and must be controlled.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why is foul water or sewage found in or near a trench a serious concern when laying a clean-water main?
o: It is both a contamination risk to the drinking water and a health risk to the workers
It slows the excavation work down and makes the trench sides harder to shore up safely
It only matters if the pipe being laid is made of an older material such as iron
It is a problem for the road surface above but not for the pipe or the operatives
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Sewage or foul water threatens both the potable supply it could pollute and the health of the crew.

n.1: The main danger is contamination and disease, not simply slower digging.
n.2: Pipe material does not change the fact that foul water carries disease and can contaminate.
n.3: It directly endangers the drinking water and the workers, not only the road surface.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A disease operatives can catch from contact with foul or sewage-contaminated water is:
o: Weil's disease (leptospirosis), caught from contact with contaminated foul water
Hay fever, which is brought on by breathing in ordinary summer pollen
Sunburn, which is caused by long spells working outdoors in strong sunlight
A muscle sprain, which is caused by lifting heavy pipe lengths without help
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Weil's disease (leptospirosis) is a recognised illness caught from contact with foul, contaminated water.

n.1: Hay fever comes from pollen, not from foul water in a trench.
n.2: Sunburn is caused by the sun, not by contact with sewage.
n.3: A sprain is a lifting injury, not an infection from foul water.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Stomach infections such as gastroenteritis can be caught on a water job by:
o: Swallowing germs after handling sewage-contaminated foul material
Standing near the running excavator for too long during the day
Wearing gloves that are slightly too large for the operative's hands
Looking directly at a freshly welded joint on the new water main
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Germs from foul material get into the mouth if hands are not washed, causing stomach infections.

n.1: Standing near plant does not spread gastroenteritis.
n.2: Ill-fitting gloves are a nuisance but do not cause a stomach infection.
n.3: Looking at a joint cannot give you gastroenteritis.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which statement about sewage in an excavation is correct?
o: It is harmless once it has been sitting in the trench for a few hours
It is only a risk in hot weather and can be safely ignored in winter
