It carries germs that can both contaminate the main and make people ill
It becomes safe to touch as soon as it is diluted with some rainwater
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Sewage carries harmful germs that are both a contamination risk to the main and a health risk to people.

n.0: Standing for a few hours does not make sewage safe.
n.1: Foul water is a hazard in all weathers, not just in the heat.
n.3: Dilution with rainwater does not remove the germs in sewage.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Foul water is described as a 'double' hazard on a clean-water job mainly because it:
o: Costs money to pump away and delays the backfilling of the trench
Stains the new pipework and makes the printed fittings harder to read
Smells unpleasant for the crew and for the members of the public nearby
Can pollute the drinking-water supply and can also cause disease
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: It is a double hazard because it can contaminate the drinking water and can also make people ill.

n.0: Cost and delay are minor next to contamination and disease.
n.1: Staining is cosmetic and is not the reason foul water is dangerous.
n.2: The smell is unpleasant but is not the real hazard.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: You notice a foul smell and grey water seeping into your trench. This most likely means:
o: The new water main has already been charged and is leaking cleanly
The weather is about to change and heavy rain is on the way shortly
The surrounding soil is simply damp and needs no further action taken
Sewage or foul water is entering the excavation and is a hazard
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A foul smell and grey seepage are classic signs of sewage or foul water entering the dig, which is a hazard.

n.0: Clean main water would not smell foul or look grey.
n.1: A smell in the trench is not a weather forecast.
n.2: Foul-smelling grey water is contamination, not harmless damp soil.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The health risk from foul water in a trench is greatest when an operative has:
o: Clean, dry overalls on that have just been issued that same morning
A cut, graze or broken skin that the contaminated water can reach
Eaten a full meal shortly before starting the day's digging work
A colleague standing a safe distance away from the open trench
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Broken skin lets germs from foul water into the body, so cuts and grazes greatly raise the risk.

n.0: Clean overalls reduce risk rather than increase it.
n.2: Having eaten earlier does not make foul water more dangerous.
n.3: A colleague standing clear does not affect the operative's own risk.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why does foul water in an excavation put the public at risk, not just the crew?
o: Because the noise of pumping it out can disturb nearby residents at night
Because it can contaminate the drinking water that reaches people's taps
Because it makes the road closure last longer than was first planned
Because it attracts insects into the gardens of the neighbouring houses
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: If foul water gets into the main, contaminated drinking water can reach the public at their taps.

n.0: Pumping noise is a nuisance, not a contamination risk to the public.
n.2: A longer road closure is an inconvenience, not a health hazard.
n.3: Insects near gardens are not why foul water endangers the public.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease) is a particular worry on water jobs because it is:
o: Only ever caught from drinking water straight from the new main
A mild rash that clears up on its own without any real concern
Spread only between operatives and never from the ground itself
A serious illness linked to contact with contaminated foul water
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Weil's disease is a serious illness linked to contact with foul, contaminated water on site.

n.0: It is caught from contact with foul water, not only from drinking.
n.1: It is a serious infection, not a mild self-clearing rash.
n.2: It comes from contaminated water and ground, not just from workmates.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which is the best reason to treat any unidentified water in a trench as foul?
o: It saves the cost of testing the water before the job can continue
Assuming it is contaminated protects both the crew and the main
It gives the crew an excuse to finish the shift a little earlier
The water company always prefers extra paperwork to be completed
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Treating unknown water as contaminated is the safe approach that protects the workers and the main.

n.0: Saving on testing is not the reason to assume the worst.
n.2: Finishing early is not a valid safety reason.
n.3: Paperwork preference has nothing to do with the real hazard.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Sewage-contaminated water is a contamination risk to a new main chiefly because it:
o: Is usually a different colour from the clean water the main carries
Contains harmful germs that must never be allowed inside the pipe
Is normally slightly warmer than the surrounding groundwater is
Flows a little more slowly than clean water does through the ground
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The germs in sewage-contaminated water are the real danger and must never get inside the pipe.

n.0: Colour is not why the water is a contamination risk.
n.2: Temperature has nothing to do with the contamination hazard.
n.3: Flow rate is irrelevant to the danger the germs present.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Breathing problems and stomach upsets on a foul-contaminated site are best avoided by:
o: Working faster so that less time is spent close to the open trench
Opening more of the trench so that fresh air can circulate freely
Keeping foul water out and following good hygiene and protection
Swapping tasks with a colleague every half an hour through the shift
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping foul water out and following good hygiene and protective measures is what prevents illness.

n.0: Working faster still exposes the crew to the same hazard.
n.1: A wider trench does not remove the contamination.
n.3: Rotating tasks does not stop germs from causing illness.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which of these is a genuine health hazard from foul water on a water-main job?
o: Temporary deafness caused by the constant noise of the trench pump
Eye strain from reading the pipe markings in fairly poor daylight
Backache from bending over the edge of a deep open excavation
Gastroenteritis and Weil's disease from contact with the sewage
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Gastroenteritis and Weil's disease are real illnesses caught from contact with sewage.

n.0: Deafness relates to noise, not to foul water.
n.1: Eye strain is a lighting issue, not a foul-water hazard.
n.2: Backache is a manual-handling issue, not an infection.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping an excavation 'de-watered' on a clean-water job means:
o: Adding clean water to settle the dust at the bottom of the trench
Leaving rainwater in place to keep the pipe bedding nicely damp
Filling the trench with fresh water before the new pipe is laid
Removing standing and incoming water so the trench stays dry
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: De-watering means removing standing and incoming water so the excavation is kept dry.

n.0: Adding water is the opposite of de-watering.
n.1: Leaving rainwater in the trench is not de-watering.
n.2: Filling the trench with water is the reverse of keeping it dry.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why should a trench be kept as clean and dry as possible before laying the main?
o: So the excavator can reach a greater depth before the shift ends
So the trench looks tidy for any passing members of the public
So dirt and foul water cannot get into the pipe as it is laid
So less imported bedding material is needed at the end of the job
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A clean, dry trench stops dirt and foul water getting into the pipe while it is being laid.

n.0: Cleanliness is about contamination, not digging depth.
n.1: Appearance is not the reason for keeping the trench clean.
n.3: Saving bedding is not why the trench is kept clean and dry.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Water collecting in the bottom of your trench should be:
o: Left alone provided the pipe ends are lifted just clear of it
Stirred so that the silt settles evenly across the trench floor
Topped up with mains water so that the level stays constant
Pumped or bailed out to keep the excavation clean and dry
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Collected water should be pumped or bailed out to keep the excavation clean and de-watered.

n.0: Lifting the ends clear still leaves a wet, contaminated trench.
n.1: Stirring the silt does not remove the water or the hazard.
n.2: Topping the water up keeps the trench wet, which is wrong.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The main reason for de-watering the excavation before pipe-laying is to:
o: Make the trench sides easier to batter back to a safe angle
Reduce the weight the crew has to lift when backfilling later
Stop dirty or foul water getting into the new main during work
Allow the concrete surround to be poured a little more quickly
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: De-watering is done so that dirty or foul water cannot get into the new main during the work.

n.0: Battering the sides is a separate stability matter.
n.1: Backfill weight is not the reason for de-watering.
n.3: Speeding the concrete is not the purpose of keeping the trench dry.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: When water is being pumped out of a trench, the discharge should be:
o: Aimed at the pipe ends to give them a final rinse before jointing
Left to soak into the trench floor a short distance from the pump
Directed well away so that it cannot run straight back into the dig
Sent into the open end of the new main to test it for any leaks
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Discharge must be sent well clear so the same water cannot flow straight back into the excavation.

n.0: Trench discharge water must never be used to rinse pipe ends.
n.1: Letting it soak nearby lets it drain back into the trench.
n.3: Discharge water must never be put into the drinking main.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A clean trench matters on a potable job above all because:
o: Anything left in the trench could end up inside the drinking main
A tidy site is quicker to hand back to the highway authority
Clean spoil is much easier to load into the wagon for removal
Dry ground is more comfortable for the crew to kneel on all day
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Whatever is left in a trench can get into the pipe, so cleanliness protects the drinking main.

n.1: Hand-back speed is not the main reason for a clean trench.
n.2: Ease of loading spoil is a side benefit, not the point.
n.3: Crew comfort is minor next to protecting the water.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which practice helps keep an excavation clean while the main is being laid?
o: Storing the spoil heap right on the very edge of the open trench
Keeping mud, rubbish and foul water out of the open excavation
Leaving off-cuts and packaging in the trench to be buried later
Allowing surface run-off from the road to drain into the trench
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping mud, rubbish and foul water out of the excavation keeps it clean for pipe-laying.

n.0: Spoil on the edge tends to fall back in and dirty the trench.
n.2: Burying rubbish leaves contamination beside the pipe.
n.3: Letting road run-off in brings dirt and possible foul water.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: If groundwater keeps flowing into the excavation, the correct response is to:
o: Carry on and lay the pipe quickly while the water is still shallow
Push the water to one end and lay the pipe at the drier end first
Wait for the water to find its own level and then start the jointing
Keep pumping so that the trench stays de-watered throughout the work
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You keep pumping so the trench stays de-watered for the whole of the pipe-laying.

n.0: Laying quickly in water still risks contaminating the pipe.
n.1: Working at one wet end still leaves the trench flooded.
n.2: Waiting for a level leaves the trench full of water.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping the excavation dry also protects the operatives because it:
o: Makes the trench warmer and more pleasant to work in each day
Means fewer barriers are needed around the top of the excavation
Reduces slips, and limits their contact with any foul water present
Allows heavier plant to be parked closer to the trench edge safely
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A dry trench means fewer slips and less contact with foul water, which protects the crew.

n.0: A dry trench is not really about warmth or comfort.
n.1: Edge barriers are needed regardless of how wet the trench is.
n.3: Parking plant near the edge is a separate safety issue.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Silt and debris at the bottom of a trench should be dealt with by:
o: Laying the pipe on top of it to save time bringing in bedding
Cleaning it out so the pipe sits on clean, sound bedding material
Mixing it with the bedding material so that nothing is wasted
Leaving it in place as it will be pressed down during backfilling
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Silt and debris are cleaned out so the pipe rests on clean, sound bedding.

n.0: Laying on silt gives poor support and leaves dirt by the pipe.
n.2: Mixing debris into bedding weakens and dirties the support.
n.3: Leaving silt in place still leaves contamination in the trench.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Rainwater that has run across the road and into your trench should be treated as:
o: Clean, since rain itself is naturally pure whenever it falls
A useful way of washing loose soil off the bottom of the trench
Possibly dirty, so it is pumped out before laying the new main
Harmless once it has mixed with the groundwater already there
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Run-off picks up dirt and possibly foul matter, so it is treated as dirty and pumped out.

n.0: Once it has crossed the road, rain is no longer clean.
n.1: Run-off adds dirt to the trench rather than cleaning it.
n.3: Mixing with groundwater does not make it harmless.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The best time to make sure the trench is clean and de-watered is:
o: After the pipe has been jointed and the trench is being backfilled
Before and during pipe-laying, so nothing dirty gets into the main
Only if an inspector is expected to visit the site during the day
At the very end of the job when the surface is being reinstated
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The trench must be clean and dry before and during pipe-laying so nothing dirty enters the main.

n.0: After jointing is too late to protect the pipe interior.
n.2: Cleanliness is needed whether or not an inspector attends.
n.3: At reinstatement the pipe is already laid and cannot be protected.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which of these keeps an excavation in the right condition for laying a potable main?
o: Allowing a little foul water in to help keep the dust down while digging
Pumping out water and clearing debris so the trench stays clean and dry
Letting the spoil wash back in so the bedding beds down naturally
Leaving the pump switched off overnight to save on the running costs
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Pumping out water and clearing debris keeps the trench clean and dry, ready for the main.

n.0: Foul water must be kept out, never let in.
n.2: Spoil washing back in dirties the trench and the bedding.
n.3: Switching off the pump lets the trench flood again.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: When work stops for a break, the open end of a new water main should be:
o: Left open so that any water inside it can drain away overnight
Capped or plugged to stop dirt and foul water getting inside
Rested on the trench floor so that it does not roll during the break
Rinsed out with trench water to remove any loose material first
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Open ends are capped or plugged so dirt and foul water cannot get into the pipe during the break.

n.0: Leaving it open lets contamination straight in.
n.2: Stopping it rolling does nothing to keep the inside clean.
n.3: Trench water must never be used to rinse the pipe.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: New pipes and fittings waiting to be laid should be stored so that they are:
o: Lying in the bottom of the trench ready to be jointed quickly
Close to the spoil heap so that they are easy to reach when needed
Kept off foul ground and away from any contamination on the site
Left uncapped so the crew can check inside them at any moment
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Pipes and fittings are kept off foul ground and clear of contamination until they are laid.

n.0: The trench floor is often wet and dirty, not a safe store.
n.1: The spoil heap is dirty ground, not a clean storage place.
n.3: Uncapped ends let dirt and foul water into the fittings.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why must the open ends of a new main be capped whenever work pauses?
o: To stop the pipe from drying out and cracking in the sunshine
To make the pipe easier to spot for the next crew on the job
To keep dirt, foul water, animals and rubbish out of the pipe
To hold the correct water pressure inside the pipe overnight
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Capping keeps dirt, foul water, animals and rubbish out of the pipe while work is paused.

n.0: Water pipe does not crack from drying out in the sun.
n.1: Capping is about cleanliness, not being easy to spot.
n.3: An empty pipe is not holding any pressure to protect.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A length of new main has been left lying in foul, sewage-stained ground. You should:
o: Lay it as planned since the outside of the pipe does not matter
Clean it and keep it clear of foul ground before it is used
Rinse the outside only and then joint it into the main straight away
Turn it over so the clean side faces upward and carry on laying
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The pipe is cleaned and kept clear of foul ground before use so no contamination is carried into the main.

n.0: A pipe fouled on the outside can still carry germs into the main.
n.2: A quick rinse alone is not enough to make it safe.
n.3: Turning it over still leaves the fouled surface being handled.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping the new main away from foul water and foul ground helps to:
o: Speed up the jointing because the pipe becomes easier to handle
Prevent contamination reaching the drinking water it will carry
Reduce the amount of bedding material the job will need overall
Make the finished pipe run look neater once it is backfilled
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping the main clear of foul water and ground prevents contamination reaching the drinking water.

n.0: Ease of jointing is not the reason to avoid foul ground.
n.2: It has nothing to do with the quantity of bedding.
n.3: Appearance after backfill is not the point.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: If a pipe cap or plug is lost on site, the best action is to:
o: Leave the pipe open and simply lay it more quickly than planned
Stuff the end with a rag from the van to keep the worst out
Fit a proper replacement cap before leaving the pipe end open
Tip the pipe downward so that nothing can settle inside the end
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A proper replacement cap is fitted so the end is never left open to contamination.

n.0: Laying quickly still leaves the end open to dirt.
n.1: A rag is not a clean, reliable seal for the pipe.
n.3: Tipping the pipe still leaves the end open to foul water.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Storing fittings on clean boards or sheeting rather than bare ground helps because it:
o: Keeps them away from foul ground so that they stay clean inside
Makes them much easier to count at the end of the working day
Stops them rolling into the open trench and getting damaged
Keeps them warmer so that the jointing seals more reliably
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Boards or sheeting keep fittings off foul ground so they stay clean inside for jointing.

n.1: Counting is not why fittings are kept off the ground.
n.2: Preventing rolling is a minor benefit, not the reason.
n.3: Warmth has nothing to do with keeping fittings clean.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The reason a new main is kept clear of foul ground is that:
o: Foul ground is usually softer and gives the pipe rather poor support
Contamination from foul ground could get into the drinking supply
Pipes laid in foul ground are harder to trace with a locator later
Foul ground stains the outside of the pipe and spoils its look
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Foul ground carries contamination that could reach the drinking supply, so the main is kept clear of it.

n.0: Support quality is not the main worry with foul ground.
n.2: Tracing difficulty is not why foul ground is avoided.
n.3: Staining is cosmetic, not the real hazard.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Before a capped pipe end is opened up for jointing, the operative should:
o: Shake the pipe hard to loosen anything that is stuck inside the end
Check that the inside is clean and free of dirt or foul water
Fill the pipe with trench water to flush the inside out quickly
Leave the cap off for an hour so that the inside can fully dry out
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The operative checks the inside is clean and free of dirt or foul water before jointing.

n.0: Shaking does not confirm the inside is clean.
n.2: Trench water must never be put inside the pipe.
n.3: Leaving it open just invites more contamination in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which is the correct way to protect a stack of new pipes overnight on site?
o: Roll them into the open trench where they are out of the way
Leave every end open so that rainwater can run straight through
Cap the ends and keep them off foul or contaminated ground
Cover them with the spoil dug out of the trench for protection
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Capping the ends and keeping the pipes off foul ground protects them overnight.

n.0: The trench is wet and dirty, not a safe overnight store.
n.1: Open ends let rain and dirt straight into the pipes.
n.3: Spoil is dirty ground and would contaminate the pipes.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Capping open pipe ends is important even for a short tea break because:
o: Contamination can enter a pipe in only a few unguarded minutes
The pipe could roll out of the trench while the crew are away
An uncapped pipe loses its shape if it is left out in the sun
The next shift will not know which pipe was being worked on
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Contamination can enter an open pipe in just a few minutes, so ends are capped even for short breaks.

n.1: Rolling is a separate issue and not the reason to cap.
n.2: Pipe does not lose its shape over a tea break.
n.3: Identifying the pipe is not why ends are capped.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Foul water must be kept away from the outside of new fittings as well because:
o: It makes the fittings slippery and awkward to grip when jointing
It leaves marks that make the fittings harder to identify later on
Handling contaminated fittings can carry germs into the main
It cools the fittings down and slows the jointing process a little
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Foul water on the outside can be carried on the hands into the main, so fittings are kept clean.

n.0: Being slippery is a handling nuisance, not the real risk.
n.1: Marks on fittings are cosmetic, not the hazard.
n.3: Cooling is irrelevant to the contamination risk.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A good habit when laying a potable main is to keep pipe ends:
o: Open and facing upward so the crew can see straight inside them
Resting in any water in the trench to keep the jointing seals damp
Wiped with trench spoil to remove grease before they are jointed
Capped until the very moment each length is jointed into the run
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping ends capped until the moment of jointing keeps dirt and foul water out of the pipe.

n.0: Open upward ends still let dirt and rain fall in.
n.1: Resting ends in trench water contaminates the pipe.
n.2: Wiping with spoil puts dirt onto the jointing surface.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Where a new water main has to run close to an existing sewer, you should:
o: Take extra care and keep the water main protected from the sewer
Lay the water main below the sewer so that gravity keeps them apart
Join the two pipes together at one point so they can be traced as a pair
Treat both pipes the same, as neither one carries drinking water yet
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Extra care is taken so the water main is kept protected and separated from the sewer.

n.1: The water main is normally kept above, not below, a sewer.
n.2: Joining a water main to a sewer would be dangerous and wrong.
n.3: The water main carries drinking water and must be protected.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why is extra care needed where a water main and a sewer are close together?
o: The two pipes are usually made from exactly the same material
The sewer will always be laid at a greater depth than the water main
The water main is heavier and could crush the sewer beneath it
Any leak from the sewer could contaminate the drinking-water main
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A sewer leak so close by could contaminate the drinking-water main, which is why extra care is needed.

n.0: The pipe material is not the reason for extra care.
n.1: Sewers are not always deeper than the water main.
n.2: The concern is contamination, not the main crushing the sewer.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: When a water main and a sewer run near each other, the water main should be:
o: Painted a bright colour so that it is not confused with the sewer
Left uncapped so that any contamination can drain away from it
Kept protected and separated so that foul water cannot reach it
Laid touching the sewer so that both can share the same trench
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The water main is kept protected and separated so foul water from the sewer cannot reach it.

n.0: Colour does not stop contamination from a nearby sewer.
n.1: Leaving it uncapped lets contamination in, not out.
n.3: Laying it touching the sewer removes vital separation.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A new potable main crosses close to an old sewer of unknown condition. The safe assumption is:
o: The sewer is fine because old sewers rarely give any real trouble
The two can safely share support as they are at a similar depth
No special precautions are needed as the main will be pressurised
The sewer may leak, so the water main must be protected from it
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You assume the old sewer may leak, so the water main is protected and kept separated from it.

n.0: Assuming an old sewer is sound is not a safe assumption.
n.1: Sharing support removes the separation that is needed.
n.2: Pressure does not make it safe to skip precautions.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping the water main above the sewer where they cross is preferred because it:
o: Makes the water main much easier to reach for any future repairs
Allows both of the pipes to be backfilled at the very same time
Reduces the chance of foul water reaching the clean-water main
Keeps the sewer warmer and so less likely to freeze in the winter
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: With the main above the sewer, any leaking foul water is less likely to reach the clean main.

n.0: Ease of future repair is not the reason for the arrangement.
n.1: Backfilling timing is not why the main is kept above.
n.3: Keeping the sewer warm is not the purpose.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: 'Protecting the water main from the sewer' on a shared route mainly means:
o: Wrapping the sewer so that it cannot be seen from the water main
Fixing the two pipes together to stop either one from moving about
Keeping separation and barriers so that foul water cannot reach it
Laying the water main first so that the sewer can be added on top
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Protection means keeping separation and using barriers so foul water cannot reach the main.

n.0: Hiding the sewer from view does nothing to protect the main.
n.1: Fixing the pipes together removes the separation needed.
n.3: Putting the sewer on top of the main is the wrong way round.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: If you are unsure how close a sewer is to your new main, you should:
o: Carry on and lay the main quickly before the sewer is exposed
Find out and take extra care to keep the main clear of the sewer
Assume there is plenty of room and keep the pipes side by side
Dig faster so that the two pipes spend less time open together
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You find out the sewer's position and take extra care to keep the water main clear of it.

n.0: Rushing before you know the layout is unsafe.
n.2: Assuming there is room without checking is a gamble.
n.3: Digging faster does nothing to protect the main.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which situation calls for the greatest care in protecting a potable main?
o: A dry, disused cable duct passing some way above the new main
A clean surface-water drain running parallel a good distance off
An empty gas service pipe crossing high over the open excavation
A leaking sewer running only a short distance from the new main
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: A leaking sewer close to the main is the biggest contamination risk and needs the greatest care.

n.0: A dry cable duct carries no foul water to contaminate the main.
n.1: A clean surface-water drain well off is a low risk.
n.2: An empty gas pipe is not a foul-water contamination risk.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A sewer is found crossing the line of your new water main. Best practice is to:
o: Break into the sewer to reroute it away from the water main
Keep the main separated and protected as it crosses the sewer
Lay the water main resting directly on top of the sewer pipe
Leave both ends of the water main open near the sewer crossing
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The main is kept separated and protected where it crosses the sewer so foul water cannot reach it.

n.0: Operatives do not break into and reroute live sewers.
n.2: Resting the main on the sewer removes the separation.
n.3: Open ends near a sewer invite contamination in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Extra separation between a water main and a sewer is required so that:
o: The two pipes do not rub together and wear each other away in time
Each pipe can be located separately with a signal tracer later on
The sewer can be dug up without disturbing the water main above it
A future sewer leak cannot contaminate the drinking-water main
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Separation is required so that a future sewer leak cannot contaminate the drinking main.

n.0: Preventing wear is not the main reason for separation.
n.1: Tracing pipes separately is not why the gap is needed.
n.2: Ease of future digging is not the purpose of separation.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Where a water main and sewer must be laid in the same area, the operative should:
o: Give the sewer priority and lay it directly above the water main
Assume the sewer is watertight and needs no special attention
Maintain separation and shield the main from any foul leakage
Reduce the gap between them to save some space in the trench
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The operative maintains separation and shields the water main from any foul leakage.

n.0: The sewer should not sit above the drinking main.
n.1: Assuming the sewer is watertight is not safe.
n.3: Reducing the gap removes needed protection.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The main danger where a sewer passes close to a clean-water pipe is:
o: Foul contents leaking across into the drinking-water main
The sewer making the water main harder to trace with equipment
The two pipes settling at slightly different rates over the years
The sewer taking up the room needed for the water main's bedding
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The main danger is foul contents leaking from the sewer into the drinking-water main.

n.1: Tracing difficulty is not the real danger here.
n.2: Different settlement is a minor engineering point.
n.3: Bedding room is not the chief hazard from a close sewer.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Good practice when a water main and sewer share a crossing point is to:
o: Bind the two pipes tightly together so that neither one can move
Lay them touching to keep the excavation as narrow as possible
Separate and protect the water main so that foul water cannot reach it
Leave the water main uncapped so that any leak can drain freely away
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You separate and protect the water main so foul water from the sewer cannot reach it.

n.0: Binding them together removes the separation.
n.1: Laying them touching gives no protection to the main.
n.3: Leaving the main uncapped lets contamination in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: After handling anything foul on site, an operative should always:
o: Wipe their hands on their overalls and carry straight on working
Rinse their hands quickly in whatever water is in the trench
Wait until the end of the shift to wash back at the site depot
Wash their hands thoroughly before eating, drinking or smoking
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Hands must be washed thoroughly after foul contact and before eating, drinking or smoking.

n.0: Wiping on overalls leaves germs on the hands.
n.1: Trench water is contaminated and does not clean the hands.
n.2: Waiting until the shift ends lets germs reach the mouth first.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why is washing before eating, drinking or smoking so important on a foul-contaminated site?
o: It keeps the mess off the sandwiches and stops them tasting odd
It stops harmful germs being carried from the hands to the mouth
It is only really needed so the crew look presentable at break time
It keeps the gloves clean so that they last a bit longer on the job
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Washing stops germs on the hands being carried to the mouth when eating, drinking or smoking.

n.0: Taste is not the reason for washing hands.
n.2: It is about health, not appearance at break time.
n.3: Glove life has nothing to do with hand hygiene.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The best facilities for cleaning up after contact with foul material are:
o: A quick shake of the hands followed by a wipe on a dry cloth
Clean water and soap, with the hands dried properly afterwards
The standing water found at the bottom of the open trench
A small splash of bottled drinking water kept in the site van
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Clean water and soap, with proper drying, are what is needed to clean up after foul contact.

n.0: Shaking and a dry wipe do not remove germs.
n.2: Trench water is contaminated, not for washing.
n.3: A splash of bottled water is not proper washing.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: An operative gets foul water on a cut on their hand. They should:
o: Ignore it as small cuts tend to heal quickly enough on their own
Cover it with tape and keep working without washing it first
Rinse it in the trench water and just carry on with the task
Wash it well, cover it, and report it if it is at all serious
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The cut is washed well, covered, and reported if serious, because foul water on broken skin is a real risk.

n.0: Ignoring foul water on a cut risks a serious infection.
n.1: Covering without washing traps contamination in the wound.
n.2: Trench water is contaminated and would make it worse.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Good personal hygiene on a water job includes:
o: Sharing gloves with a workmate to save on protective equipment
Eating lunch at the trench edge to save walking to the welfare unit
Washing hands and forearms after any contact with foul material
Keeping the same dirty gloves on right through the whole working day
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Washing the hands and forearms after any foul contact is basic good hygiene on a water job.

n.0: Sharing gloves spreads contamination between workers.
n.1: Eating at the trench edge risks swallowing contamination.
n.3: Dirty gloves worn all day keep spreading germs.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Smoking with unwashed hands after touching foul material is risky because:
o: The cigarette will pick up an unpleasant taste from all the dirt
It wastes time that could be spent finishing the excavation
Germs on the hands can pass to the mouth with the cigarette
The smell of the smoke will linger on the dirty work gloves
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Germs on unwashed hands transfer to the mouth via the cigarette, so hands are washed first.

n.0: Taste is not the health concern here.
n.1: Time-wasting is not why unwashed smoking is risky.
n.3: Lingering smell is irrelevant to the germ risk.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why should hands be washed before drinking a cup of tea on a foul-contaminated site?
o: So that the mug is not left with dirty marks around its rim
So that the tea does not go cold while the hands are washed
So that the crew set a tidy example to the watching public
So that harmful germs are not swallowed along with the drink
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Washing first stops germs on the hands being swallowed with the drink.

n.0: Marks on the mug are not the health issue.
n.1: The tea's temperature is not the reason to wash.
n.2: Setting an example is not the real purpose.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The purpose of good personal hygiene after handling sewage is mainly to:
o: Keep the operative's overalls looking clean for the following day
Meet the site rules on general appearance during the rest breaks
Protect the operative from illnesses such as gastroenteritis
Avoid leaving marks on the tools and equipment around the site
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Good hygiene after handling sewage protects the operative from illnesses such as gastroenteritis.

n.0: Clean overalls are not the aim of hand hygiene.
n.1: It is about health, not appearance rules.
n.3: Keeping tools mark-free is not the purpose.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which is the correct order after finishing work in a foul-contaminated trench?
o: Have your break first, then wash your hands at the end of it
Wipe your hands on a rag, then eat straight away to save some time
Remove gloves, wash your hands thoroughly, then have your break
Keep your gloves on while eating so that your hands stay covered
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You remove gloves and wash your hands thoroughly, then take your break.

n.0: Breaking first means germs reach your food before washing.
n.1: A rag wipe does not clean the hands before eating.
n.3: Eating with dirty gloves on still spreads contamination.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Welfare facilities with washing water are provided on site so that operatives can:
o: Cool down and take slightly longer breaks in hot summer weather
Wash down their tools before returning them to the site store
Clean themselves properly after any contact with foul material
Rinse the mud off their boots before getting into the site van
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Welfare washing facilities are there so operatives can clean themselves after foul contact.

n.0: Cooling down is not the main reason for welfare facilities.
n.1: Tool washing is not the purpose of welfare units.
n.3: Boot rinsing is not why washing water is provided.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A workmate is about to eat a sandwich straight after clearing foul debris. You should:
o: Say nothing at all as it is entirely their own personal choice
Remind them just to wipe their hands on their overalls first
Tell them to wash their hands thoroughly before they eat
Suggest they eat quickly before the foul smell gets any worse
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: You tell them to wash their hands thoroughly first, so they do not swallow germs.

n.0: Staying silent leaves them at real risk of illness.
n.1: Wiping on overalls does not remove the germs.
n.3: Eating quickly does nothing to remove contamination.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping cuts and grazes covered on a foul-contaminated site matters because:
o: A plaster keeps the wound clean enough to carry on working hard
Covered cuts are less likely to be noticed by the site inspector
It stops contaminated foul water reaching the broken skin
It stops the wound rubbing against the inside of the work gloves
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Covering cuts stops foul water reaching the broken skin, where germs could get into the body.

n.0: The point is protection from foul water, not just staying at work.
n.1: Hiding cuts from an inspector is not the reason.
n.3: Rubbing on gloves is a minor issue, not the hazard.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The single most important personal-hygiene rule after touching foul material is to:
o: Change your gloves for a fresh pair before the next task begins
Rinse your face with any water that happens to be close to hand
Wash your hands well before you eat, drink or smoke anything
Finish the job first and leave all of the washing until you get home
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Washing hands before eating, drinking or smoking is the key rule after foul contact.

n.0: Fresh gloves help but do not replace washing your hands.
n.1: Rinsing with any nearby water may add more contamination.
n.3: Leaving washing until home lets germs reach your mouth first.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The golden rule when foul water is present near an open main is that:
o: A small amount of foul water inside the main will do very little harm
Sewage-contaminated water must never be allowed into the main
Foul water can enter the main as long as it is flushed out later
Foul water is only a real problem once the main has been charged
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The rule is absolute: sewage-contaminated water must never be allowed to get into the main.

n.0: Even a small amount of foul water in the main is unacceptable.
n.2: You cannot let it in and rely on flushing it out later.
n.3: Foul water is a problem before charging, not only after.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: If foul water is rising in the trench near an open pipe end, the first priority is to:
o: Carry on jointing quickly before the water rises any higher
Let the water run through the pipe to flush it out on its own
Tip the pipe up and pour the foul water back into the trench
Keep the pipe end capped and stop the foul water reaching it
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping the end capped and stopping foul water reaching it protects the main from contamination.

n.0: Rushing the joint still risks foul water getting into the pipe.
n.1: Letting foul water through the pipe contaminates it.
n.2: The pipe should not have foul water in it to pour out.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Sewage-contaminated water reaching a drinking main could result in:
o: A slightly slower flow of water when the main is finally charged up
The main needing to be repainted before it can be brought into use
The pipe joints loosening because of the extra water pressure
People becoming ill from drinking the contaminated water
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: If sewage reaches the main, people can become ill from drinking the contaminated water.

n.0: Contamination is a health issue, not a matter of flow speed.
n.1: Repainting has nothing to do with the contamination.
n.2: Joints do not loosen because foul water gets in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which action risks letting sewage-contaminated water into the new main?
o: Capping the pipe ends firmly whenever the crew stop for a break
Laying an uncapped pipe end down into foul water in the trench
Pumping the trench out and directing the discharge well away
Storing spare fittings on clean boarding clear of the wet ground
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Laying an uncapped end into foul water lets the sewage-contaminated water straight into the main.

n.0: Capping the ends keeps foul water out, not in.
n.2: Pumping the discharge away keeps the trench clear.
n.3: Clean, dry storage keeps fittings uncontaminated.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Why must the crew be certain no foul water has entered the main before it is used?
o: Because foul water inside the pipe makes it a good deal heavier to handle
Because contaminated water could make members of the public ill
Because the water company charges extra for a wet delivery of pipe
Because it changes the colour of the pipe from the inside surface
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Foul water in the main could make the public ill, so the crew must be sure none has got in.

n.0: Weight is not the concern with foul water in the pipe.
n.2: There is no such charge for a wet pipe delivery.
n.3: Internal colour change is not the reason it matters.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The best way to stop foul water entering a new main during a break is to:
o: Keep every open end securely capped until the work starts again
Lay the pipe ends flat in the bottom of the wet, dirty trench
Leave the ends open so that any water inside can drain out freely
Point the open ends toward the incoming flow of the foul water
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Keeping every open end securely capped during the break stops foul water getting into the main.

n.1: Ends laid in the wet trench take in foul water.
n.2: Open ends let foul water in rather than keeping it out.
n.3: Pointing ends at the flow invites foul water straight in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: A pipe end that has been sitting in foul water in the trench should be:
o: Cleaned and checked to be sure that no contamination is inside it
Jointed straight away before any more foul water can build up in it
Left as it is, since a quick charge will flush it all out anyway
Turned over and jointed from the drier upper side of the pipe
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The end is cleaned and checked so no contamination from the foul water is left inside before jointing.

n.1: Jointing it dirty seals contamination into the main.
n.2: Charging does not reliably remove sewage contamination.
n.3: Turning it over does not clean the contaminated inside.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Discharge water from de-watering the trench should never be:
o: Directed to a proper outfall well clear of the open excavation
Checked to make sure that it is not causing a nuisance nearby
Allowed to run back and get into the open drinking-water main
Pumped steadily so that the trench is kept dry during the work
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Discharge water must never be allowed back into the open drinking main.

n.0: Directing it to a proper outfall is correct practice.
n.1: Checking it causes no nuisance is sensible, not forbidden.
n.3: Steady pumping to keep the trench dry is correct.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Keeping sewage out of the main is important throughout the job because:
o: Once foul water is in the main it is hard to make the water safe again
It only really matters during the final pressure test of the main
The main can safely be cleaned of any sewage after it is buried
A little contamination early on is diluted once the main is charged
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Once foul water gets into a main it is difficult to make the water safe, so sewage is kept out throughout.

n.1: Contamination matters at every stage, not just the test.
n.2: Cleaning a buried, contaminated main is not simple.
n.3: Dilution does not make contaminated water safe.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: You must break off jointing with the pipe end open. The safest action is to:
o: Leave it open but tell a workmate to keep an eye on it for you
Lay a length of timber across the top of the open pipe end
Lower the open end into the trench water to keep the seal wet
Fit a cap so that no foul water can enter the main while you are away
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Fitting a cap keeps foul water out of the main while jointing is paused.

n.0: A watching workmate does not physically keep foul water out.
n.1: Timber across the end does not seal it against foul water.
n.2: Lowering it into trench water lets contamination straight in.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: Which of these keeps sewage-contaminated water out of a new potable main?
o: Laying the pipe with the ends open so the crew can inspect inside
Resting the open pipe ends in the standing water in the trench
Capping ends and keeping foul water pumped clear of the pipe
Directing the de-watering discharge back toward the pipe run
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: Capping ends and keeping foul water pumped clear of the pipe keeps sewage out of the main.

n.0: Open ends let contamination straight into the pipe.
n.1: Resting ends in standing water contaminates the pipe.
n.3: Aiming discharge at the pipe risks foul water reaching it.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: If sewage does get into a section of new main, the crew must:
o: Charge the main quickly so that the flow washes the sewage out
Carry on and let the water company deal with it much later on
Ignore it provided that only a small amount of sewage got in
Report it and make sure the section is cleaned before it is used
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: The crew report it and make sure the affected section is cleaned before it goes into use.

n.0: Charging it does not reliably clear the contamination.
n.1: Leaving it for later risks contaminated water reaching people.
n.2: No amount of sewage in a drinking main is acceptable.

Excavations & Working Near Sewers.q: The overriding aim of all these precautions around foul water is to:
o: Finish the excavation and the reinstatement as quickly as possible
Make sure the public receives clean, safe drinking water
Keep the paperwork in order for the site supervisor's own records
Reduce the amount of clean water used in flushing out the main
Excavations & Working Near Sewers.w: All the precautions exist to make sure the public receives clean, safe drinking water.

n.0: Speed of work is not the overriding aim.
n.2: Paperwork is a means, not the ultimate aim.
n.3: Saving flushing water is not the purpose of the precautions.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under which Act is it a criminal offence to contaminate water that is likely to be used for human consumption?
o: The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 duties
The Water Industry Act 1991 and its offences
The Environmental Protection Act 1990 rules
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Section 70 of the Water Industry Act 1991 makes it a criminal offence to contaminate or pollute water likely to be used for drinking.

n.0: These cover fittings and preventing waste, but the contamination offence sits in the Water Industry Act.
n.1: This Act covers general health and safety duties, not the specific water-contamination offence.
n.3: This deals with wider environmental matters, not the drinking-water contamination offence you are taught.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which section of the Water Industry Act 1991 sets out the offence of contaminating drinking water?
o: Regulation 4 of the fittings regulations
Section 14 of the Water Industry Act 1991
Section 74 of the Water Industry Act 1991
Section 70 of the Water Industry Act 1991
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Section 70 of the Water Industry Act 1991 creates the offence of contaminating water likely to be used for human consumption.

n.0: Regulation 4 covers approved materials in the fittings regulations, not the contamination offence.
n.1: This is not the section that deals with contaminating drinking water on the network.
n.2: This is not the section covering the drinking-water contamination offence you are taught.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under Section 70 of the Water Industry Act 1991, who can be prosecuted if drinking water is deliberately contaminated?
o: An individual worker as well as the company
Only the water company that holds the contract
Only the site manager who is on duty
Only the client who ordered the work done
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The offence applies to individuals, so a worker can be personally prosecuted, not just their employer.

n.1: Personal responsibility means an individual can be prosecuted, not only the company.
n.2: Liability is not limited to a manager; the operative doing the work can also be prosecuted.
n.3: The person who actually contaminates the water can be held personally responsible.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The offence of contaminating drinking water under the Water Industry Act 1991 applies to water that is:
o: Only found inside a customer's own home
Only held within a covered service reservoir
Only present inside a water treatment works
Likely to be used for human consumption
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act protects water likely to be used for human consumption, wherever it is on the supply.

n.0: The protection is not limited to household plumbing; it covers water across the supply.
n.1: Reservoir storage is covered, but the offence is not limited only to reservoirs.
n.2: The offence covers water across the network, not only inside the treatment works.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Besides contamination, the Water Industry Act 1991 also creates offences relating to which of the following?
o: Charging customers an incorrect water tariff
Wasting or misusing public water supplies
Building new homes without planning consent
Failing to insure the company's work vehicles
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act covers waste and misuse of water as well as contamination of drinking supplies.

n.0: Billing tariffs are not the water-protection offences you are taught under this Act.
n.2: Planning permission is a separate matter and not part of these water offences.
n.3: Vehicle insurance has nothing to do with the water offences in this Act.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A contractor knowingly allows dirty water to enter a drinking main. Under the Water Industry Act 1991 this is best described as:
o: A criminal offence for which they may be prosecuted
A minor issue that is dealt with by a warning
A civil matter to be settled privately between the firms
An acceptable everyday risk on live networks
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Contaminating water likely to be used for human consumption is a criminal offence under Section 70.

n.1: Contaminating drinking water is treated as a criminal offence, not simply a warning.
n.2: It is a criminal matter, not merely a private dispute between companies.
n.3: Allowing contamination is never an acceptable risk on a live drinking-water network.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Why does the Water Industry Act 1991 make contaminating drinking water a criminal offence?
o: To raise extra money through the court fines
To cut down on paperwork for water companies
To protect public health from unsafe water
To speed up the installation of new pipework
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The offence exists to protect people who drink the water from harm.

n.0: The purpose is protecting health, not generating income from fines.
n.1: Reducing paperwork is not why the contamination offence exists.
n.3: The offence is about safety, not the speed of installing pipes.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative deliberately opens a hydrant to waste large volumes of treated water. This is most likely an offence under:
o: The Working Time Regulations 1998 on hours
The Water Industry Act 1991 and its provisions
The Consumer Rights Act 2015 on services
The Data Protection Act 2018 on personal data
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Water Industry Act 1991 creates offences for wasting and misusing public water supplies.

n.0: These govern working hours, not the wasting of treated water.
n.2: This covers goods and services to consumers, not wasting the water supply.
n.3: This concerns personal data, not the misuse of public water.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which statement about prosecution under the Water Industry Act 1991 is correct?
o: Only foreign contractors can ever be prosecuted
Prosecution can never involve individual workers
Both individuals and companies can face prosecution
Only the Government itself can be prosecuted
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The law allows both an individual and their employer to be prosecuted for a contamination offence.

n.0: Nationality is irrelevant; anyone can be prosecuted for the offence.
n.1: Individuals absolutely can be prosecuted, which is why personal responsibility matters.
n.3: The Government is not the target; workers and companies can be prosecuted.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The main purpose of Section 70 of the Water Industry Act 1991 is to:
o: Keep water safe for human consumption
Set the yearly price of customer water bills
Decide who owns the underground pipe network
Arrange the training of new water operatives
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Section 70 protects drinking water by making its contamination a criminal offence.

n.1: Pricing is not the aim of this contamination offence.
n.2: Ownership of pipes is not what Section 70 addresses.
n.3: Training is not the function of this legal offence.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 exist mainly to prevent which three things?
o: Contamination, waste and misuse of water
Noise, dust and heavy traffic on the site
Overtime, project delays and extra costs
Flooding, ground subsidence and erosion
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The regulations are designed to prevent contamination, waste and misuse of the public water supply.

n.1: These are general site nuisances, not what the water fittings rules target.
n.2: Costs and delays are commercial issues, not the aim of these regulations.
n.3: Ground conditions are not what these water fittings regulations control.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: In Scotland, the equivalent of the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 is known as the:
o: Scottish Plumbing Rules made back in 1999
Water Byelaws 2014 that apply in Scotland
Highland Water Order introduced in 2010
Clyde Supply Regulations dating from 2005
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Scotland applies the Water Byelaws 2014 to achieve the same protection of water fittings.

n.0: This is not the correct name for Scotland's water fittings rules.
n.2: No such order governs water fittings in Scotland.
n.3: This is an invented title and not the Scottish equivalent.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Regulation 4 of the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 requires that fittings used are:
o: The cheapest option that can be found
Of an approved and suitable standard
Painted in a bright, easily seen colour
Manufactured only from copper materials
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Regulation 4 requires that materials and fittings meet an approved, suitable standard to protect water quality.

n.0: Cost is not the test; the fittings must be of an approved standard.
n.2: Colour is irrelevant; the requirement is about approved suitability.
n.3: There is no rule that fittings must be copper; they must simply be approved.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Why must only approved materials and fittings be used on a public water supply?
o: To make sure the job is finished much faster
To match the outside colour of the pipe
To avoid contaminating the drinking water supply
To reduce the overall weight of the fittings
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Approved materials help ensure the fittings do not contaminate or taint the drinking water.

n.0: Speed is not the reason approved materials are required.
n.1: Appearance is not why approved fittings must be used.
n.3: Weight is not the purpose of the approval requirement.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative wants to fit a component that is not on any approved list. Under the fittings regulations they should:
o: Use it as long as it looks strong enough
Use it and simply note it down on the timesheet later
Not use it and select an approved fitting instead
Use it because it works out slightly cheaper
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Only approved fittings should be used, so an unapproved component must be replaced with an approved one.

n.0: Appearance of strength does not make a fitting approved for potable water.
n.1: Recording it does not make an unapproved fitting acceptable.
n.3: Lower cost never justifies using an unapproved fitting on drinking water.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 apply to work on:
o: Private rainwater butts standing in gardens
Ornamental garden ponds and water features
Pipes and fittings connected to the public supply
Sealed central heating systems inside people's homes
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The regulations govern fittings and pipework connected to the public water supply.

n.0: Rainwater butts alone are not the focus of these supply regulations.
n.1: Garden features are not what these water fittings regulations control.
n.3: The regulations are wider than sealed heating systems alone.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Using a non-approved fitting that later taints the drinking water could breach:
o: The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999
The Highway Code guidance for road users
The building's own detailed fire safety action plan
The company's staff annual holiday policy
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Fitting requirements sit in the Water Fittings Regulations, which require approved materials.

n.1: Road rules are unrelated to approved water fittings.
n.2: Fire plans do not govern approved water fittings.
n.3: An internal holiday policy has nothing to do with water fittings law.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which best describes the aim of Regulation 4 in the water fittings regulations?
o: Ensuring that fittings are always the newest model
Ensuring that fittings arrive in flat packs
Ensuring fittings do not spoil the water quality
Ensuring that fittings are made overseas
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Regulation 4 is about using suitable, approved materials so water quality is protected.

n.0: Being newest is not the requirement; being approved and suitable is.
n.1: Packaging has nothing to do with the fittings requirement.
n.3: Where a fitting is made is irrelevant to its approval.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A colleague in Scotland asks which rules cover preventing waste and contamination of water fittings. You answer:
o: The 1999 Regulations simply do not exist there
There are no rules covering fittings in Scotland
The Water Byelaws 2014 are what apply in Scotland
Only English law is ever applied in Scotland
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Scotland uses the Water Byelaws 2014 to prevent waste, misuse and contamination through fittings.

n.0: Scotland just uses its own equivalent, the Water Byelaws 2014.
n.1: There are rules; the Water Byelaws 2014 apply in Scotland.
n.3: Scotland has its own water byelaws rather than using English regulations.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The requirement to prevent 'misuse' of water under the fittings regulations means water should not be:
o: Tested for its quality by the company
Kept stored inside a covered tank
Delivered along approved metal pipes
Used in a wasteful or an improper way
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Preventing misuse means water must not be used wastefully or improperly.

n.0: Testing water quality is a good practice, not misuse.
n.1: Covered storage is proper practice, not misuse.
n.2: Delivery through approved pipes is normal, not misuse.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 places general duties on:
o: Both employers and their employees
Only on employers, never on workers
Only on the members of the public
Only on the water quality regulator
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act sets duties for employers and also requires employees to act safely.

n.1: Employees also carry duties under the Act, not employers alone.
n.2: The Act's duties fall mainly on those at work, not just the public.
n.3: The regulator does not carry the Act's workplace duties in place of employers.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, an employee's duty includes:
o: Setting the whole company's yearly spending budget
Choosing which insurance policy the firm buys
Deciding what water charges customers will pay
Taking reasonable care of their own and others' safety
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Employees must take reasonable care for their own safety and that of others affected by their work.

n.0: Budgeting is a management task, not a health and safety duty of the worker.
n.1: Insurance choices are not the employee's safety duty under the Act.
n.2: Setting charges is unrelated to the Act's safety duties.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which Act would apply if an operative was injured because safety equipment was not provided?
o: The Water Byelaws 2014 used in Scotland
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 duties
The Water Industry Act 1991 and its offences
The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Providing safe equipment is a duty under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

n.0: These cover water fittings in Scotland, not general workplace safety.
n.2: This deals with water contamination and waste, not safety equipment duties.
n.3: These govern approved fittings, not the provision of safety equipment.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, an employer's general duty is to:
o: Guarantee every worker a promotion each year
Provide free daily transport to the workplace
Pay overtime rates for every single task
Provide a safe place and system of work
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Employers must, so far as is reasonably practicable, provide a safe workplace and safe systems of work.

n.0: Promotions are not a health and safety duty under the Act.
n.1: Transport is not a duty imposed by the Act.
n.2: Overtime pay is a contractual matter, not a safety duty.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative notices a colleague not wearing required protective equipment. Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 the best response is to:
o: Ignore it because it is their own free choice
Encourage safe working and report the concern
Remove their own protective equipment as well
Wait for an injury to happen before acting
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act expects everyone to support safe working and raise concerns rather than ignore them.

n.0: Safety is a shared duty, so ignoring an unsafe practice is not acceptable.
n.2: Copying unsafe behaviour increases risk rather than reducing it.
n.3: Acting only after an injury defeats the purpose of preventing harm.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a duty employees owe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974?
o: Recruiting brand new members of staff
Cooperating with their employer on safety
Approving the site's whole water design
Auditing the company's yearly accounts
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Employees must cooperate with their employer so that safety duties can be met.

n.0: Hiring is not part of an employee's safety duty.
n.2: Design approval is not the employee's health and safety duty.
n.3: Accounts auditing is unrelated to the Act's safety duties.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 is mainly concerned with:
o: Setting the retail price of drinking water
Approving the design of new pipe fittings
Regulating the profits of water companies
Protecting people at and around the workplace
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act's focus is protecting the health and safety of workers and others affected by work.

n.0: Pricing is not covered by this safety Act.
n.1: Approving fittings is covered by the water fittings regulations instead.
n.2: Company profits are not the subject of this Act.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: What is the main role of the Drinking Water Inspectorate (DWI)?
o: Checking water companies supply safe, wholesome water
Setting the hourly wages paid to operatives
Selling pipes and fittings to working sites
Delivering the water directly to each customer's own tap
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI is the regulator that checks water companies provide safe, wholesome drinking water.

n.1: Wages are not set by the drinking water regulator.
n.2: The DWI is a regulator, not a supplier of materials.
n.3: Delivery is the water company's job, not the inspectorate's.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The initials DWI stand for:
o: The Domestic Water Installers group
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
The District Waste Investigators unit
The Drainage Works Inspectorate body
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: DWI stands for the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the drinking water regulator.

n.0: This is not what DWI stands for in the water industry.
n.2: This is not the correct meaning of the initials DWI.
n.3: DWI refers to drinking water, not drainage works.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which body would investigate if a water company supplied unsafe drinking water?
o: The local parish or town council
The fire and rescue service
The vehicle licensing agency
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Drinking Water Inspectorate regulates and investigates the safety of public drinking water.

n.0: A parish council does not regulate drinking-water quality.
n.1: Fire services do not investigate drinking-water safety.
n.2: This agency deals with vehicles, not water quality.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Drinking Water Inspectorate helps to ensure that tap water is:
o: Safe and wholesome for people to drink
Provided free of charge to households
Sold at exactly the same price everywhere
Supplied to homes in sealed bottles
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI's purpose is to ensure drinking water is safe and wholesome for the public.

n.1: The DWI does not make water free; it checks its safety.
n.2: Pricing is not the DWI's role.
n.3: The DWI oversees mains water quality, not bottled delivery.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A water company must be able to show the Drinking Water Inspectorate that its water is:
o: Cheaper than a rival supplier's water
Being sold in the very largest volumes
Meeting the required safety standards
Coloured to reveal where it came from
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Companies must demonstrate to the DWI that their water meets the required safety standards.

n.0: Price comparisons are not what the DWI requires.
n.1: Volume sold is not the DWI's standard.
n.3: Drinking water is not coloured, and colour is not a DWI standard.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Drinking Water Inspectorate is best described as:
o: The regulator of drinking water quality
A supplier of site tools and plant
A trade union that represents plumbers
A training college for new operatives
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI is the regulator responsible for overseeing drinking water quality.

n.1: The DWI regulates water; it does not supply tools.
n.2: It is a regulator, not a union.
n.3: The DWI is not a training provider.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Everyone working on the water network has a personal responsibility to:
o: Finish the job in the fastest time possible
Keep any problems they find to themselves
Protect water quality and report any concerns
Ignore any small leaks found on the main
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Each worker must protect water quality and report contamination or concerns without delay.

n.0: Speed must never come before protecting water quality.
n.1: Problems must be reported, not hidden.
n.3: Even small issues should be acted on, not ignored.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: If an operative suspects that drinking water has been contaminated, they should:
o: Wait right until the very end of their shift
Report it straight away to the right person
Say nothing so as to avoid any blame
Carry on and hope that it soon clears
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Suspected contamination must be reported immediately so it can be dealt with.

n.0: Delaying a report could allow unsafe water to reach the public.
n.2: Hiding a problem is a breach of personal responsibility.
n.3: Ignoring suspected contamination risks public health.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Whose responsibility is it to protect water quality on a live network?
o: Only the most senior company director
Only the person who signs the job off
Everyone who is working on the network
Only the newest apprentice on the team
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Protecting water quality is a shared personal responsibility for everyone on the network.

n.0: Responsibility is not limited to directors; it applies to all.
n.1: Everyone shares the duty, not just the person signing off.
n.3: The duty is shared, not placed on one apprentice.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative sees a possible contamination risk but is unsure. The best action is to:
o: Report the concern so that it can be checked
Assume that it is fine and simply move on
Only mention it if somebody asks them later
Deal with it themselves and say nothing
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: When unsure, a concern should still be reported so it can be properly assessed.

n.1: Assuming it is fine could allow a real risk to continue.
n.2: Concerns should be raised proactively, not only if asked.
n.3: Concerns should be reported, not hidden and handled alone.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Reporting a contamination concern promptly is important because it:
o: Reduces the operative's take-home wages
Helps to protect public health quickly
Slows down the whole of the project
Avoids having to do any paperwork
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Prompt reporting lets action be taken quickly to protect people from unsafe water.

n.0: Reporting does not reduce wages.
n.2: Protecting health matters more than project speed, and reporting need not stall work.
n.3: Reporting usually involves recording, not avoiding, paperwork.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of these best shows good personal responsibility on the water network?
o: Skipping the hygiene steps whenever busy
Following hygiene rules and reporting problems
Hiding your own mistakes from the team
Blaming other people whenever any fault is found
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Good responsibility means following hygiene rules and reporting problems honestly.

n.0: Skipping hygiene puts water quality at risk.
n.2: Hiding mistakes prevents problems being fixed.
n.3: Shifting blame does not protect water quality.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative accidentally drops a dirty tool into an open main. They should:
o: Fish the tool back out and then say nothing
Cover over the open pipe and simply walk away
Stop, report it and follow the correct procedure
Leave the tool where it is and finish the shift
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Any potential contamination must be reported and the correct procedure followed.

n.0: Removing it quietly ignores the reporting duty and possible contamination.
n.1: Hiding the problem does not protect the water.
n.3: Ignoring it risks contaminated water reaching the public.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Personal responsibility on the network means that an operative should never:
o: Put on the correct clean protective clothing
Ignore a possible risk to the water quality
Wash their hands thoroughly before working
Follow the agreed site hygiene action plan
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: A responsible worker must never ignore a risk to water quality.

n.0: Wearing clean clothing is good practice, not something to avoid.
n.2: Hand washing is required good practice.
n.3: Following the hygiene plan is exactly what should be done.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: What is a possible consequence for an individual who contaminates drinking water?
o: They can be prosecuted for a criminal offence
They are given a small rebate on their tax
They are awarded some extra holiday time
They are simply moved to a different depot
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Contaminating drinking water can lead to prosecution of the individual responsible.

n.1: Contamination brings penalties, not a rebate.
n.2: There is no reward; prosecution is the risk.
n.3: The consequence is legal action, not a simple transfer.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which statement about the consequences of contaminating water is correct?
o: Both the worker and the company may face action
Only a verbal warning is ever going to be given
No action at all is taken while on live sites
Only the regulator can be blamed for it
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Legal action can be taken against the individual worker and their employer.

n.1: Contamination can lead to prosecution, not just a warning.
n.2: Action can and does follow contamination on live networks.
n.3: The regulator is not blamed for a worker's contamination.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A worker who deliberately contaminates a drinking main risks:
o: Being criminally prosecuted as an individual
Receiving a guaranteed rise in their pay
Getting an automatic promotion at work
Being allowed a much longer lunch break
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Deliberate contamination can result in the individual facing criminal prosecution.

n.1: There is no reward; the risk is prosecution.
n.2: Contamination leads to penalties, not promotion.
n.3: This trivialises what is a serious criminal matter.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The threat of prosecution for contaminating water is intended to:
o: Encourage careful and hygienic working
Make every job take a great deal longer
Reduce the total number of operatives
Increase the overall cost of the fittings
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The legal threat encourages everyone to work carefully and protect water quality.

n.1: The aim is safe working, not slower work for its own sake.
n.2: It is not about reducing staff numbers.
n.3: Prosecution is about safety, not the price of fittings.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A drinking water main and a contaminated source are close together. The law expects the operative to:
o: Connect the two of them together to save buying new pipe
Leave both of them open to the surrounding air
Mix the two so that the pressure is balanced
Keep the drinking water protected from contamination
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The operative must keep drinking water protected, as required by law and good practice.

n.0: Connecting a clean main to a contaminated source risks a criminal offence.
n.1: Leaving mains open invites contamination.
n.2: Mixing clean and contaminated water is never acceptable.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which legislation requires the use of approved materials to protect drinking water quality?
o: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 duties
The Water Industry Act 1991 offences on their own
The Drinking Water Inspectorate's own charter
The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999
