Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Regulation 4 of the 1999 fittings regulations requires approved, suitable materials.

n.0: This covers safety duties, not approved water fittings.
n.1: The Act covers offences, but the approved-materials rule is in the fittings regulations.
n.2: The DWI is a regulator; the materials rule sits in the fittings regulations.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative is told to protect water quality 'so far as is reasonably practicable'. This wording comes from:
o: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
The Water Byelaws 2014 for Scotland
The Water Fittings Regulations 1999
The Water Industry Act 1991 offences
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The phrase 'so far as is reasonably practicable' is a hallmark of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

n.1: These are Scotland's fittings rules, not the source of that duty wording.
n.2: These require approved fittings but are not where that duty phrase comes from.
n.3: This creates offences but is not the source of that safety wording.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would the Drinking Water Inspectorate be most interested in?
o: A delay in a company's monthly payroll
A report of unsafe or discoloured tap water
A dispute over the office parking spaces
A change to a firm's company logo
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI focuses on drinking water safety, so unsafe or discoloured water would concern it.

n.0: Payroll is not a drinking-water quality matter.
n.2: Parking disputes are nothing to do with the DWI.
n.3: Branding is not the DWI's concern.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative is unsure whether a job is 'notifiable' under the fittings regulations. The safest step is to:
o: Assume that it never needs to be checked
Check with a competent person before proceeding
Skip the fittings rules for that job entirely
Guess the answer and carry on regardless
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: When unsure, checking with a competent person keeps the work within the regulations.

n.0: Assuming removes the safeguard the regulations provide.
n.2: The fittings rules must be followed, not skipped.
n.3: Guessing risks breaching the regulations and harming water quality.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under the Water Industry Act 1991, which action is an offence?
o: Reporting a suspected leak on the main
Allowing the water to become contaminated
Fitting only approved parts and fittings
Washing your hands before starting work
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Allowing drinking water to be contaminated is an offence under the Act.

n.0: Reporting a leak is responsible, not an offence.
n.2: Using approved fittings is exactly what the law wants.
n.3: Hand washing is good hygiene, not an offence.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Good hygiene and following the law both aim to ensure that water reaching the public is:
o: The very cheapest possible to supply
Delivered as quickly as it possibly can be
Coloured so it is easy to trace
Safe and fit for human consumption
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The shared aim of hygiene rules and the law is water that is safe to drink.

n.0: Cost is not the aim; safety is.
n.1: Speed does not override safety.
n.2: Drinking water is not coloured for tracing.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: If an operative breaks the fittings regulations by using unapproved parts, the likely concern is that they may:
o: Finish the whole job far too quickly
Save the company far too much money
Cause contamination of the water supply
Use up too much of the clean water
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Unapproved parts risk contaminating the supply, which the regulations aim to prevent.

n.0: Speed is not the concern with unapproved parts.
n.1: Saving money is not the risk; contamination is.
n.3: The main risk is contamination, not water use.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Reporting problems on the network is part of an operative's:
o: Optional extra duties done for pay
Personal and legal responsibility
Weekly vehicle cleaning schedule
Yearly annual holiday planning
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Reporting problems is part of each worker's personal and legal responsibility.

n.0: Reporting is a duty, not an optional paid extra.
n.2: Reporting is not part of a cleaning rota.
n.3: Reporting has nothing to do with holiday planning.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which body checks that water companies comply with drinking water quality standards?
o: The company's own internal sales team
The site's appointed traffic marshal
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
The local community library service
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Drinking Water Inspectorate checks companies meet drinking water quality standards.

n.0: A sales team is not an independent regulator.
n.1: Traffic marshals manage vehicles, not water standards.
n.3: Libraries have no role in water regulation.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A subcontractor argues that water hygiene law 'only applies to the water company'. The correct view is that:
o: It applies to no one working on the site
It applies only to the office-based staff
It also applies to individual operatives
It applies only to the managers on site
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The law applies to individual operatives too, who carry personal responsibility.

n.0: The law clearly applies to those working on the network.
n.1: Office staff are not the focus; operatives on site are covered.
n.3: Responsibility is not limited to managers alone.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Water Byelaws 2014 in Scotland and the 1999 Regulations elsewhere both aim to:
o: Prevent waste, misuse and contamination
Standardise the paint colours on pipes
Set the national wage for all plumbers
Speed up the building of new houses
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Both sets of rules aim to prevent waste, misuse and contamination of water.

n.1: Paint colours are not the aim of these rules.
n.2: Wages are not covered by these water rules.
n.3: Construction speed is not the aim of these rules.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative finds an unapproved connection someone else fitted to a drinking main. They should:
o: Leave it alone since it is not their own work
Report it so that it can be corrected properly
Add another one to match the first fitting
Paint over the connection and then move on
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: An unapproved connection should be reported and corrected to protect water quality.

n.0: Personal responsibility means acting even on others' errors.
n.2: Repeating a fault makes the problem worse.
n.3: Hiding a fault does not protect the water.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which statement about the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 is correct?
o: It sets duties on both employers and workers
It sets the legal limits for water quality
It approves the pipe fittings that are used
It fixes the size of household water bills
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act places general health and safety duties on both employers and workers.

n.1: Water quality limits are not set by this safety Act.
n.2: Fittings approval sits in the water fittings regulations.
n.3: The Act does not set customers' bills.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The purpose of water hygiene legislation for operatives is ultimately to:
o: Increase the total cost of doing jobs
Keep the public's drinking water safe
Reduce the amount of training needed
Limit exactly who is allowed to drink
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: All the legislation shares the aim of keeping public drinking water safe.

n.0: Higher costs are not the aim of the legislation.
n.2: The legislation supports, rather than reduces, proper training.
n.3: The aim is safe water for the public, not limiting access.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of these is an offence under the Water Industry Act 1991?
o: Filling out a required hygiene record
Attending a routine safety toolbox talk
Wearing clean overalls to do the work
Wasting treated public water without cause
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Wasting public water without justification is an offence under the Act.

n.0: Recording hygiene is good practice, not an offence.
n.1: Attending safety talks is expected, not an offence.
n.2: Clean overalls support hygiene and are not an offence.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A trainee asks who they must report suspected contamination to. The best answer is:
o: No one at all, so as not to cause alarm
Only to a colleague over their lunch break
The appropriate person set out in site procedures
The nearest passing adult member of the general public
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Contamination should be reported to the appropriate person named in site procedures.

n.0: Not reporting risks public health and breaches responsibility.
n.1: An informal chat is not proper reporting.
n.3: The public is not the correct body to receive such reports.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An employer who fails to provide safe systems of work may breach:
o: The Water Byelaws 2014 for Scotland
The Water Fittings Regulations 1999
The Water Industry Act 1991 offences
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Failing to provide safe systems of work breaches the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

n.0: These cover Scottish water fittings, not safe systems of work.
n.1: These cover approved fittings, not safe working systems.
n.2: This covers water offences, not safe systems of work.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Drinking Water Inspectorate would be concerned if a company:
o: Painted all of its work vans in a brand new colour
Held a social event for its own staff
Bought some new chairs for the office
Supplied water that failed the safety standards
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI is concerned with water that fails safety standards.

n.0: Van colour is not a DWI concern.
n.1: Social events are not the DWI's concern.
n.2: Office furniture is nothing to do with the DWI.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Choosing an approved fitting rather than a random spare part mainly helps to:
o: Make the work van lighter to drive
Reduce the number of tools that are needed
Shorten the length of the working day
Avoid tainting the drinking water supply
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Approved fittings are chosen to avoid tainting or contaminating the drinking water.

n.0: Vehicle weight is not why approved fittings matter.
n.1: Tool count is not the reason for approved fittings.
n.2: Approved fittings are about safety, not a shorter day.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative is offered a shortcut that risks contaminating water but saves time. The correct choice is to:
o: Take the shortcut so as to please the client
Take it as long as nobody is watching them
Take it in order to finish the job early
Refuse it and work in the safe, legal way
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The safe and legal method must be followed even if a shortcut would save time.

n.0: Pleasing a client never justifies risking contamination.
n.1: Being unobserved does not make an unsafe shortcut acceptable.
n.2: Finishing early is not worth risking public health.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under the fittings regulations, 'waste' of water refers to water that is:
o: Tested by the water company for quality
Stored inside a covered service reservoir
Lost needlessly rather than used properly
Delivered to homes through the mains
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Waste means water lost needlessly, which the regulations aim to prevent.

n.0: Testing water is a proper activity, not waste.
n.1: Proper storage is not waste.
n.3: Normal delivery is not waste.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: If a member of the public reports brown water from their tap, the ultimate regulator of that quality issue is:
o: The operative's own line manager
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
The manufacturer of the pipe
The local passenger bus company
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Drinking Water Inspectorate is the regulator overseeing drinking water quality.

n.0: A line manager is not the national water quality regulator.
n.2: Manufacturers make products but do not regulate quality.
n.3: A bus company has no water regulatory role.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which best describes an operative's legal position when working on drinking water?
o: They can never be held responsible at all
They are covered only by the company that employs them
They can be personally prosecuted for contamination
They are outside the scope of all water law
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: An operative can be personally prosecuted for contaminating drinking water.

n.0: Personal responsibility means they can be held to account.
n.1: Individuals, not just companies, carry legal responsibility.
n.3: Operatives are firmly within the scope of water law.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A colleague says hygiene rules are 'just company policy, not law'. The accurate reply is that:
o: They are only optional guidelines to follow
They are backed by legislation as well
They apply abroad but not here in the UK
They were quietly withdrawn some years ago
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Water hygiene requirements are backed by legislation, not merely internal policy.

n.0: They are legal requirements, not optional.
n.2: They apply on the UK network where the work is done.
n.3: These requirements remain in force.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The best reason to report a near miss that could have contaminated water is that it:
o: Guarantees the operative a cash bonus
Ends the need for any hygiene rules
Removes the need to record the work
Helps prevent a real contamination later
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Reporting near misses helps prevent a genuine contamination event in the future.

n.0: Reporting is a duty, not a route to a bonus.
n.1: Hygiene rules remain necessary regardless.
n.2: Recording work is still required.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999?
o: Preventing the contamination of the water
Preventing the wasteful loss of the water
Preventing the misuse of the water supply
Setting the country's national minimum wage
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The regulations prevent contamination, waste and misuse; they do not set the minimum wage.

n.0: This is a genuine purpose of the regulations.
n.1: Preventing waste is a genuine purpose of the regulations.
n.2: Preventing misuse is a genuine purpose of the regulations.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative must stop work because continuing could contaminate a main. The law supports this because it:
o: Always favours finishing the job quickly
Puts protecting the water quality first
Ignores any small contamination risks
Leaves such choices entirely to chance
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The law prioritises protecting water quality, supporting the decision to stop.

n.0: Finishing quickly does not override water protection.
n.2: Even small risks are taken seriously.
n.3: The law expects deliberate protection, not chance.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Who is responsible for reporting a burst that is discharging into a drinking main?
o: Any operative who becomes aware of it
Only a director based at head office
Only the person who first laid the pipe
Only next year's routine inspection team
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Any operative aware of the problem has a responsibility to report it.

n.1: Responsibility is not limited to directors.
n.2: It is not restricted to whoever first laid the pipe.
n.3: It must be reported now, not at a future inspection.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Water Industry Act 1991 helps ensure that operatives treat drinking water as:
o: A product that they can freely waste
Something that must be protected by law
A resource that has no legal rules
A private company matter and nothing more
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act makes clear drinking water must be legally protected from contamination and waste.

n.0: Wasting water is an offence, not a free choice.
n.2: There are clear legal rules protecting water.
n.3: It is a public safety matter, not purely private.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A worker deliberately damages a valve, causing dirty water to enter the supply. This could lead to:
o: A cash reward for having reported a fault properly
Prosecution under the Water Industry Act 1991
A day off in return for extra effort
A written note of thanks sent from the DWI
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Deliberately causing contamination can lead to prosecution under the Act.

n.0: Damaging a valve is not reporting a fault; it is an offence.
n.2: There is no reward for causing contamination.
n.3: The DWI would be concerned, not thankful.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 expects employees to:
o: Redesign the company's own set of tools and plant
Set their own personal limits on the risk
Ignore the rules that apply on the site
Not interfere with anything provided for safety
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Employees must not misuse or interfere with items provided in the interests of safety.

n.0: Redesigning tools is not an employee's safety duty.
n.1: Risk controls are set through proper procedures, not personal choice.
n.2: Ignoring site rules breaches the Act's duties.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which action best protects water quality and meets the law at the same time?
o: Using approved fittings and reporting concerns
Using any handy spare part that will fit
Keeping quiet about a spillage that occurs
Reusing a tool that was dropped and dirtied
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Using approved fittings and reporting concerns meets both hygiene and legal duties.

n.1: Unapproved parts can breach the fittings regulations.
n.2: Not reporting a spillage breaches personal responsibility.
n.3: A contaminated tool risks the water supply.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Drinking Water Inspectorate mainly protects the interests of:
o: Only the very largest of the local water firms
Only the customers who live overseas
The members of the public who drink the water
Only the makers of the pipe fittings
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The DWI protects the public by ensuring their drinking water is safe.

n.0: The DWI serves the public, not just big firms.
n.1: It protects the public supplied in this country.
n.3: Manufacturers' interests are not the DWI's focus.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative signs a hygiene declaration before working on the network. This mainly shows they accept:
o: A promise of extra overtime being paid
Their personal responsibility for water quality
A right to skip all of the required safety checks
An exemption from the water hygiene law
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Signing shows the operative accepts personal responsibility for protecting water quality.

n.0: The declaration is about responsibility, not overtime.
n.2: It does not allow skipping checks.
n.3: It does not exempt anyone from the law.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of these best fits the definition of 'misuse' of the water supply?
o: Testing the water for genuine safety reasons
Storing the water inside a sealed clean tank
Using clean mains water for an improper purpose
Supplying the water on to people's homes
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Misuse means using clean mains water for an improper purpose the supply is not meant for.

n.0: Testing is legitimate, not misuse.
n.1: Proper storage is not misuse.
n.3: Supplying homes is the intended use, not misuse.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative could be prosecuted as an individual for:
o: Attending a required annual water hygiene course
Wearing the correct PPE while working
Contaminating water meant for human consumption
Following the agreed site hygiene plan
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: An individual can be prosecuted for contaminating water meant for human consumption.

n.0: Training is expected, not an offence.
n.1: Wearing PPE is good practice, not an offence.
n.3: Following the plan is exactly what is required.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: If in doubt about whether a material is approved for drinking water, the operative should:
o: Use it now and then check on it afterwards
Not use it until its approval is confirmed
Use it as long as it fits together neatly
Use it in order to avoid any job delay
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Unapproved or unconfirmed materials should not be used until their approval is confirmed.

n.0: Checking after use risks contamination that has already occurred.
n.2: A neat fit does not mean a material is approved.
n.3: Avoiding delay never justifies risking contamination.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The general duties in the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 apply:
o: Only to staff who are based in the office
Only to the most senior of the directors
Only to inspectors who visit the site
To everyone at work, including operatives
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Act's general duties apply to everyone at work, operatives included.

n.0: Field operatives are covered too, not just office staff.
n.1: Duties extend beyond directors to all workers.
n.2: Inspectors are not the sole focus; all workers are covered.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: What should an operative do first if they see raw sewage near an open drinking main?
o: Finish making the connection as quickly as they can
Stop work and report the risk immediately
Take a short break and come back to it later
Carry on with the work and say nothing at all
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The immediate step is to stop and report the serious contamination risk.

n.0: Rushing the connection could draw contamination into the main.
n.2: Delaying leaves a serious risk unaddressed.
n.3: Ignoring the risk endangers public health.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which is the correct combination of what water fittings law aims to prevent?
o: Noise, dust and vibration from the works
Overtime, delays and rising project costs
Contamination, waste and misuse of water
Traffic, parking and access to the site
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The fittings regulations aim to prevent contamination, waste and misuse of water.

n.0: These are site nuisances, not what the fittings law targets.
n.1: These are commercial issues, not the law's aim.
n.3: These are site logistics, not the law's aim.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The main legal reason to keep tools and hands clean when working on a main is to:
o: Keep the tools looking brand new
Speed up the whole of the day's work
Prevent contaminating the drinking water
Reduce the ongoing cost of gloves
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Cleanliness is required to prevent contaminating drinking water, in line with the law.

n.0: Appearance is not the legal reason for cleanliness.
n.1: Speed is not why cleanliness is required.
n.3: Cost saving is not the reason for clean working.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A water company failing to meet drinking water standards would answer to the:
o: The company's own internal marketing department
Drinking Water Inspectorate as regulator
Site's appointed first aid officer
The local amateur sports and social club
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The Drinking Water Inspectorate holds companies to account on drinking water standards.

n.0: Marketing does not regulate water standards.
n.2: First aiders treat injuries, not water quality compliance.
n.3: A sports club has no regulatory role.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Under the law, protecting drinking water quality is:
o: A job that belongs only to the regulator
A duty shared by everyone on the network
A task that belongs only to a manager
An optional extra task to be done
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Protecting water quality is a shared legal and personal duty for everyone on the network.

n.0: The regulator oversees, but everyone shares the duty.
n.2: The duty is not limited to managers.
n.3: It is a duty, not optional.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following most clearly breaks the Water Industry Act 1991?
o: Reporting a fault promptly to the boss
Carefully fitting an approved valve to the main
Letting a contaminant enter a drinking main
Following the rules on wholesome water
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Letting a contaminant enter a drinking main is an offence under the Act.

n.0: Prompt reporting is responsible, not an offence.
n.1: Using approved fittings complies with the law.
n.3: Following the rules is compliance, not a breach.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative who ignores a known contamination risk is failing in their:
o: Right to take a mid-shift tea break
Personal and legal responsibility
Free choice over their own work boots
Preference for a certain lunch time
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Ignoring a known risk is a failure of personal and legal responsibility.

n.0: A tea break is unrelated to this responsibility.
n.2: Footwear choice is not the point here.
n.3: Lunch timing has nothing to do with the duty.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The word 'wholesome' used by the Drinking Water Inspectorate means water that is:
o: Safe and clean enough to drink
The cheapest of all to produce
The very fastest to be delivered
The most heavily coloured to trace
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Wholesome water is safe and clean enough for people to drink, which the DWI checks.

n.1: Cost is not what 'wholesome' means.
n.2: Speed is not what 'wholesome' means.
n.3: Wholesome water is not coloured; it is clean and safe.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: If an approved fitting is not available, the correct action under the regulations is to:
o: Improvise using whatever part is to hand
Use a garden hose fitting for the job
Wait and obtain an approved fitting
Leave the main open in the meantime
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Work should wait until an approved fitting is available rather than using an unapproved part.

n.0: Improvising with unapproved parts breaches the regulations.
n.1: A garden hose fitting is not approved for the drinking main.
n.3: Leaving the main open invites contamination.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A key message of the National Water Hygiene scheme is that the law makes water protection:
o: A duty only for the largest of firms
A duty only during formal inspections
A personal duty for every operative
A duty that nobody can enforce
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The scheme stresses that protecting water is a personal duty for every operative.

n.0: It applies to all who work on the network, not just large firms.
n.1: The duty applies all the time, not only at inspections.
n.3: The duty is enforceable, including by prosecution.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: An operative sees a colleague about to connect an unapproved pipe to a drinking main. They should:
o: Help them to finish it off much faster
Look away and just continue their task
Wait to see whether it starts to leak
Speak up and stop the unsafe connection
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The right action is to speak up and prevent the unsafe, non-compliant connection.

n.0: Helping complete an unsafe connection makes matters worse.
n.1: Ignoring it breaches personal responsibility.
n.2: Waiting risks contamination that could already occur.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Which statement correctly links the offence and who can be charged?
o: Contaminating water can see an individual charged
Only the local councils can ever be charged
Contamination is never treated as a chargeable offence
Only the DWI itself can ever be charged
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Contaminating drinking water is an offence for which an individual can be charged.

n.1: Councils are not the only ones; individuals can be charged.
n.2: It is a criminal offence and is chargeable.
n.3: The DWI is the regulator, not the offender.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Following approved procedures on the network is important because it:
o: Keeps the work legal and the water safe
Guarantees an operative the highest wages
Removes the need for any further training
Avoids the need for all record keeping
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Approved procedures keep the work within the law and keep the water safe.

n.1: Procedures are about safety and legality, not wages.
n.2: Training is still needed alongside procedures.
n.3: Records are usually still required.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: A supervisor tells an operative to skip a hygiene step to save time. The operative should:
o: Obey the instruction without any question
Raise the concern and keep to the safe method
Skip two steps in order to catch up
Say nothing and just skip it quietly
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The operative should raise the concern and continue working the safe, legal way.

n.0: Following an unsafe instruction can breach the law and risk water quality.
n.2: Skipping more steps increases the contamination risk.
n.3: Silently skipping hygiene breaches personal responsibility.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: The Water Fittings Regulations require that materials in contact with drinking water are:
o: The oldest stock kept in the van
Chosen by the lowest price alone
Approved as suitable and not harmful
Any spare metal that is to hand
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: Regulation 4 requires materials to be approved as suitable and not harmful to the water.

n.0: Age of stock is irrelevant to approval.
n.1: Price alone does not make a material approved.
n.3: Random spare metal is not necessarily approved or safe.

Legislation & Responsibilities.q: Overall, the legislation covered by the Blue Card scheme exists to make sure that:
o: Every water job is always the cheapest one
Only experts are ever allowed to drink tap water
The water is always delivered to homes by hand
Public drinking water stays safe and protected
Legislation & Responsibilities.w: The legislation exists so that public drinking water remains safe and protected.

n.0: Cost is not the purpose of the legislation.
n.1: The aim is safe water for the public, not restricting who drinks it.
n.2: Delivery method is not the point of the legislation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: What is the common name for the card issued under the National Water Hygiene scheme?
o: The Green Card, used for general construction skills
The Gold Card, held by qualified site managers
The Blue Card, which shows water hygiene competence
The Red Card, issued to trainees while on site
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The scheme issues the Blue Card, confirming the holder has passed the water hygiene assessment.

n.0: The Green Card relates to construction skills, not the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.1: A Gold Card is not the card issued by the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.3: The scheme does not issue a red trainee card for water hygiene.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Holding a valid Blue Card mainly shows that the operative:
o: understands how to protect public water quality
is qualified to design new water treatment works
may carry out gas work on domestic properties
has completed a full plumbing apprenticeship scheme
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The Blue Card shows the holder understands how to work without harming water quality.

n.1: The card shows hygiene awareness, not competence to design treatment works.
n.2: The card covers water hygiene, not gas work of any kind.
n.3: The card is not a plumbing apprenticeship qualification.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The Blue Card is best described as proof of:
o: awareness of how to keep public water supplies safe
membership of a recognised trade union body
insurance cover for accidental damage on site
permission to drive water company vehicles legally
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card is proof the holder is aware of how to protect public water quality.

n.1: The card is not proof of trade union membership.
n.2: The card is not an insurance document.
n.3: The card does not grant permission to drive vehicles.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A contractor asks a new starter what the Blue Card certifies. The best answer is that the holder:
o: has passed an assessment on protecting water quality
has been vaccinated against all waterborne diseases
owns the correct tools for water main repair
is a fully time-served water network engineer
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The Blue Card certifies the holder has passed the water hygiene assessment.

n.1: The card is not proof of vaccination against disease.
n.2: The card is not about tool ownership.
n.3: The card is not an engineering time-served qualification.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The National Water Hygiene assessment is aimed at people who work on:
o: building hot and cold water services only
swimming pool and spa circulation systems
industrial cooling towers and chiller systems
the public clean (potable) water supply
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The scheme covers work on the public clean (potable) water supply.

n.0: The scheme is about the public supply, not building hot and cold systems.
n.1: Pool and spa systems are outside the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.2: Cooling towers are not covered by the National Water Hygiene scheme.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which statement about the Blue Card is correct?
o: It replaces the need for any site induction
It allows the holder to sign off water samples
It shows the holder protects drinking water
It certifies the holder as a laboratory analyst
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card shows the holder can work in a way that protects drinking water.

n.0: A site induction is still required; the card does not replace it.
n.1: The card does not authorise signing off water samples.
n.3: The card does not certify laboratory analysis work.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The card gives water companies confidence that the holder:
o: can manage a full water treatment shift alone
is trained to repair any type of pump motor
will follow good hygiene practice on site
holds a recognised health and safety diploma too
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card assures companies the holder follows good hygiene practice.

n.0: The card is not proof of treatment-shift management.
n.1: The card is not proof of pump repair skills.
n.3: The card is not a health and safety diploma.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: During a toolbox talk an operative calls the Blue Card 'just a safety card'. The best correction is that it is:
o: a card about protecting water quality
a card that covers only manual handling training
a licence to operate excavation plant on site
a general first aid at work certificate only
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The Blue Card is specifically about protecting water quality.

n.1: The card is not limited to manual handling training.
n.2: The card is not a plant operator licence.
n.3: The card is not a first aid certificate.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The scheme exists so that everyone working on the public supply:
o: is paid at the same nationally agreed rate
understands how work affects water quality
carries identical tools and equipment on site
reports directly to the local water regulator
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The scheme ensures workers understand how their work affects water quality.

n.0: The scheme is about water quality, not pay rates.
n.2: The scheme does not standardise tools and equipment.
n.3: Workers do not report to the regulator through the scheme.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A valid Blue Card is evidence that the holder has:
o: worked in the water industry for many years
met the water hygiene knowledge and health rules
attended a one-day confined space refresher
been approved to authorise other people's cards
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card evidences the holder has met the knowledge and health requirements.

n.0: The card is not evidence of years of experience.
n.2: The card is not a confined space qualification.
n.3: The card does not authorise issuing cards to others.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The National Water Hygiene scheme is administered through which organisation?
o: HSE, the Health and Safety Executive
EUSR, the Energy & Utility Skills Register
CITB, the Construction Industry Training Board
DWI, the Drinking Water Inspectorate for England
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The scheme is administered through EUSR, the Energy & Utility Skills Register.

n.0: The HSE regulates safety generally; it does not run the scheme.
n.2: CITB covers construction training, not this water scheme.
n.3: The DWI regulates water quality but does not run the card scheme.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: When an operative passes the assessment, their record is held on the register run by:
o: CSCS (Construction Skills Certification Scheme)
EUSR (the Energy & Utility Skills Register)
Ofwat (the economic regulator of water)
Gas Safe (the register of gas installers)
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Passing records are held on the EUSR register.

n.0: CSCS is a construction card scheme, not this register.
n.2: Ofwat regulates water economics, not card records.
n.3: Gas Safe is the gas installer register, not this scheme.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: What does the abbreviation EUSR stand for?
o: Energy & Utility Skills Register
European Utility Standards Regulator body
Energy Users Safety Requirements scheme
Essential Utility Site Register system
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: EUSR stands for the Energy & Utility Skills Register.

n.1: EUSR is not a European standards regulator.
n.2: EUSR does not stand for energy users safety requirements.
n.3: EUSR is not an essential utility site register.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A supervisor wants to check whether a worker's Blue Card is genuine. The scheme record is held by:
o: the local council building control team office
EUSR, which holds the card holder register
the operative's own employer records only
the card printing company that made the card
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: EUSR maintains the register where card details can be checked.

n.0: Building control does not hold water hygiene card records.
n.2: The employer's own records are not the scheme register.
n.3: The printer does not hold the official scheme register.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: EUSR is best described as:
o: the skills register for the energy sector
a government department that sets water policy
a trade union representing water industry staff
a private company that supplies public water
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: EUSR is the skills register for the energy and utilities sector.

n.1: EUSR is a skills register, not a government department.
n.2: EUSR is not a trade union.
n.3: EUSR does not supply water to the public.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The body administering National Water Hygiene registration is part of the wider:
o: energy and utility skills registration system
construction site card certification scheme
national health screening and testing service
environmental permitting and licensing regime
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The scheme sits within the energy and utility skills registration system.

n.1: The scheme is not part of a construction card scheme.
n.2: It is not part of a national health service scheme.
n.3: It is not an environmental permitting regime.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which of these holds National Water Hygiene card records?
o: The Environment Agency regional office
The British Standards Institution offices
The Water Regulations Advisory Scheme
EUSR (the Energy & Utility Skills Register)
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: EUSR holds the National Water Hygiene card records.

n.0: The Environment Agency does not hold these card records.
n.1: The BSI does not hold water hygiene card records.
n.2: WRAS advises on fittings, not card records.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Registration under the scheme is recorded so that:
o: the operative can claim their training tax back
the card will then never need renewing again
the worker is added to a company pension scheme
employers can confirm a card is valid on EUSR
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Recording on EUSR lets employers confirm a card is valid.

n.0: Registration is not for reclaiming training tax.
n.1: Registration does not remove the need to renew.
n.2: Registration is unrelated to pension enrolment.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A hiring agency phones to verify a candidate's water hygiene status. They should be directed to:
o: the candidate's previous training college
the card manufacturer's customer sales line
the site's own visitor sign-in book records
the EUSR register with the card details
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The EUSR register holds card details for verification.

n.0: A former college does not verify current card status.
n.1: The card maker does not verify registration.
n.2: A visitor book does not verify water hygiene status.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The National Water Hygiene scheme sits under which sector's skills register?
o: the energy and utilities sector register (EUSR)
the construction and civil engineering register
the transport and logistics skills register
the healthcare and clinical professionals register
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: It sits under the energy and utilities sector register, EUSR.

n.1: It is not under a construction sector register.
n.2: It is not under a transport sector register.
n.3: It is not under a healthcare register.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A valid Blue Card is required before an operative may carry out:
o: any work on a domestic central heating system
Restricted Operations on the public supply
general groundworks well away from water mains
electrical testing inside a plant control room
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A valid card is required for Restricted Operations on the public supply.

n.0: Domestic heating work is not a Restricted Operation under this scheme.
n.2: Groundworks away from mains are not restricted operations.
n.3: Electrical testing in a control room is not a restricted operation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: 'Restricted Operations' are tasks that could:
o: affect the pressure recorded at a customer's tap
affect the cost of running the treatment works
affect the working hours of the on-site team
affect the quality of water in the public supply
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Restricted Operations are tasks that could affect public water quality.

n.0: The definition is about water quality, not pressure alone.
n.1: The definition is about quality, not running costs.
n.2: The definition is about quality, not working hours.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Why is a card required for Restricted Operations?
o: so that the work can be billed to the customer
so that fewer workers are needed on the job
so the work does not risk water quality
so that the job can be finished more quickly
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card requirement protects water quality during restricted work.

n.0: The card is not about billing the customer.
n.1: The card is not about reducing worker numbers.
n.3: The card is not about speeding up the job.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An operative without a valid card is asked to help inside a service reservoir. They:
o: may work if a supervisor watches them closely
may work as long as they are wearing gloves
may work because it is only a short task
must not do the work until they are carded
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Restricted work requires a valid card first.

n.0: Supervision does not remove the need for a valid card.
n.1: Gloves do not remove the need for a valid card.
n.2: A short task still requires a valid card.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Who needs to hold National Water Hygiene registration?
o: only managers who plan the network jobs
anyone whose work can affect water quality
only staff based inside the treatment works
only workers who take official water samples
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Anyone whose work can affect public water quality needs the card.

n.0: It is not limited to managers who plan jobs.
n.2: It is not limited to treatment works staff.
n.3: It is not limited to sampling staff.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The card requirement applies to work on:
o: private garden irrigation and sprinkler systems
the public clean water distribution network
sealed building fire sprinkler storage tanks
sewage and foul drainage networks only
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The requirement applies to work on the public clean water network.

n.0: Private garden systems are outside the scheme.
n.2: Sealed sprinkler tanks are not the public supply.
n.3: The scheme covers clean water, not foul drainage.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Restricted Operations are controlled because water quality problems can:
o: only ever affect the operative doing the work
always be seen straight away by the naked eye
reach many customers on the network
be fixed simply by boiling water at the tap
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Contamination can spread to many customers through the network.

n.0: Problems affect customers, not just the operative.
n.1: Contamination is often not visible to the eye.
n.3: Boiling does not remove all contamination risk.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Before starting a job that could contaminate the mains, an operative must:
o: hold a valid National Water Hygiene card
obtain written permission from the local police
pass a separate confined space medical first
register the job with the local fire service
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A valid card is required before such restricted work.

n.1: Police permission is not required for this work.
n.2: A confined space medical is a separate matter.
n.3: The fire service does not authorise this work.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A team is fitting a new section of water main. This work:
o: is exempt because the pipe is brand new
needs no card because it is done outdoors
hold a valid National Water Hygiene card
only needs a card for the site supervisor
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Fitting a new main can affect water quality, so it is restricted.

n.0: New pipe is not exempt from being a restricted operation.
n.1: Being outdoors does not remove the card requirement.
n.3: All those doing the restricted work need a card.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The main reason certain water tasks are 'restricted' is to:
o: reduce the amount of paperwork done on site
limit how many firms can bid for the work
make the jobs take a bit longer to finish
keep the public drinking water safe to use
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Tasks are restricted to keep drinking water safe.

n.0: Restriction is about safety, not paperwork.
n.1: Restriction is not about limiting bidders.
n.2: Restriction is not intended to slow jobs down.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: How long does National Water Hygiene registration normally last?
o: one year from the date it is issued
five years from the date it is issued
ten years from the date it is issued
three years from the date it is issued
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Registration lasts three years from issue.

n.0: The registration lasts three years, not one.
n.1: The registration lasts three years, not five.
n.2: The registration lasts three years, not ten.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: When a Blue Card expires, the holder must:
o: simply pay a fee to have the card extended
send a new photograph to update the card
attend a short online refresher session only
take the assessment again to stay registered
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The assessment must be re-taken to keep registration.

n.0: Renewal needs the assessment, not just a fee.
n.1: A new photo does not renew registration.
n.2: An online refresher alone does not renew it.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: After the registration period ends, continued restricted work requires the operative to:
o: complete a first aid course as a replacement
gain two more years of network experience
pass the water hygiene assessment once more
simply be signed off by their line manager
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Continued work needs the assessment to be passed again.

n.0: A first aid course does not renew registration.
n.1: Extra experience does not renew registration.
n.3: A manager sign-off does not renew registration.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An operative's card shows an issue date three years and one month ago. They should be treated as:
o: still valid for at least another twelve months
valid provided they still carry the old card
no longer validly registered until re-assessed
permanently registered after their first pass
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: After three years the card has expired and needs re-assessment.

n.0: The card is not valid past three years.
n.1: Carrying an expired card does not make it valid.
n.3: Registration is not permanent after one pass.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The three-year period is set so that operatives:
o: refresh their hygiene knowledge regularly
can change their employer far more easily
must pay for a brand new card every year
can avoid any further training for life
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The three-year cycle keeps knowledge refreshed.

n.1: The cycle is not about changing employers.
n.2: The cycle is three years, not annual payment.
n.3: The cycle ensures ongoing, not lifelong-free, training.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which statement about card renewal is correct?
o: the assessment is re-taken every three years
the card stays valid for the holder's lifetime
renewal happens automatically each single year
renewal only needs a line manager's signature
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The assessment must be re-taken every three years.

n.1: The card is not valid for life.
n.2: Renewal is not automatic each year.
n.3: Renewal needs the assessment, not a signature.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A card issued in June 2024 would normally expire in:
o: June 2025, one year after it was issued
June 2029, five years after it was issued
June 2034, ten years after it was issued
June 2027, three years after it was issued
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Three-year validity means a June 2024 card expires June 2027.

n.0: Validity is three years, so not June 2025.
n.1: Validity is three years, so not June 2029.
n.2: Validity is three years, so not June 2034.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: If registration has lapsed, an operative may return to restricted work only after they:
o: wait six months and then simply reapply
complete an unrelated general safety course
successfully sit the assessment again
ask the register to reissue the old card
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A lapsed holder must pass the assessment again to return.

n.0: A waiting period alone does not restore it.
n.1: An unrelated course does not restore registration.
n.3: The register will not simply reissue a lapsed card.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A worker says their card 'never runs out once you pass'. The correct response is that:
o: it lasts three years and must then be renewed
it lasts ten years before any renewal is due
it only ever expires if the job role changes
it stays valid while they remain employed
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card lasts three years and must be renewed.

n.1: The card lasts three years, not ten.
n.2: Expiry is by time, not by change of role.
n.3: Validity is not tied to remaining employed.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The reassessment requirement every three years mainly helps to:
o: increase the number of cards that are in issue
raise extra money for the water regulator
keep the workforce's knowledge current
reduce the need for any site inductions
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Regular reassessment keeps hygiene knowledge current.

n.0: Reassessment is about knowledge, not card counts.
n.1: Reassessment is not a fundraising exercise.
n.3: Reassessment does not remove site inductions.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Card holders must meet the scheme's health requirements, which include:
o: an annual eyesight and hearing test only
health screening and declaring illness
a fitness test for confined space entry
a criminal record background check first
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The health rules include screening and declaring relevant illness.

n.0: The rules are broader than eyesight and hearing.
n.2: The health rules are about hygiene, not a fitness test.
n.3: A criminal record check is not part of the health rules.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which illness is an example of something that must be declared under the scheme?
o: a common seasonal head cold or sniffle
a fully healed old sports knee injury
mild hay fever during the summer months
diarrhoea, or being a carrier of typhoid
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Illnesses such as diarrhoea or being a typhoid carrier must be declared.

n.0: A common cold is not the key declarable illness here.
n.1: A healed injury is not a declarable water risk.
n.2: Hay fever is not a declarable water-contamination risk.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An operative has had diarrhoea in the last day or two. Under the scheme they should:
o: ignore it if they still feel able to work
only mention it if a manager directly asks
wait until the card is next up for renewal
declare it before doing any restricted work
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Such illness must be declared before restricted work.

n.0: Feeling able to work does not remove the duty to declare.
n.1: The duty to declare does not depend on being asked.
n.2: It must be declared now, not at renewal.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The health rules exist because an operative's illness could:
o: slow down the rest of the work team badly
contaminate the public water they are working on
invalidate the site's public liability insurance
affect only the operative's own take-home pay
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Illness can spread contamination into the water supply.

n.0: The rules are about contamination, not work pace.
n.2: The rules are about water safety, not insurance.
n.3: The concern is public health, not the worker's pay.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Health screening under the scheme is used to check that operatives:
o: medically fit to work near drinking water
can lift heavy loads without any help
have no history of any allergies at all
are able to work long night shifts safely
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Screening checks fitness to work near drinking water.

n.1: Screening is about hygiene fitness, not lifting.
n.2: Screening is not an allergy history check.
n.3: Screening is not about night-shift capacity.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A typhoid carrier applying for restricted work must:
o: keep it private as personal information
only tell their own doctor, not the scheme
declare this as a relevant health matter
wait until symptoms actually appear to report
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Being a typhoid carrier is a relevant illness that must be declared.

n.0: This health matter must be declared, not kept private.
n.1: It must be declared to meet the scheme's rules.
n.3: A carrier must declare it whether or not symptoms show.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A worker returns from holiday abroad with a stomach bug causing diarrhoea. Before restricted work they should:
o: say nothing since it happened while on holiday
carry on because they are now back at work
report the illness in line with the health rules
assume it is fine after just one day off
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The illness must be reported under the health rules before restricted work.

n.0: Where it started does not remove the duty to report.
n.1: Being back at work does not remove the duty to report.
n.3: Assuming it is fine does not meet the health rules.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which of these is part of the National Water Hygiene health requirements?
o: passing a treadmill cardiovascular fitness test
declaring illnesses affecting water safety
providing a full personal dental health record
having a routine chest x-ray every single year
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Declaring illnesses affecting water safety is a health requirement.

n.0: A treadmill test is not part of these health rules.
n.2: A dental record is not part of these health rules.
n.3: An annual chest x-ray is not part of these rules.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: The reason operatives must declare certain illnesses is to:
o: help the employer plan their holiday cover
record sickness absence for sick-pay purposes
decide who is given the easier daily tasks
stop harmful organisms reaching the supply
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Declaration helps stop harmful organisms entering the supply.

n.0: Declaration is about water safety, not holiday cover.
n.1: Declaration is about safety, not sick pay.
n.2: Declaration is not about allocating easier tasks.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Health screening for the scheme is best described as a check that someone is:
o: medically suitable to work on clean water
physically strong enough for heavy manual work
completely free of any minor cold or cough
willing to work outdoors in all weathers
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Screening checks medical suitability to work on clean water.

n.1: Screening is about hygiene, not physical strength.
n.2: Screening does not bar every minor cold.
n.3: Screening is not about willingness to work outdoors.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: When carrying out restricted work, an operative should:
o: leave the card safely back at the depot
carry their valid National Water Hygiene card
carry only a photocopy of their old card
rely on the supervisor's card being present
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: You should carry your valid card when doing restricted work.

n.0: The card should be carried, not left at the depot.
n.2: A photocopy is not the required valid card.
n.3: You need your own valid card, not the supervisor's.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Why should you carry your valid card on site?
o: so it can be shown as proof when asked
so that it does not get lost while at home
so that it can be updated at any time needed
so that it counts towards your weekly wages
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Carrying it lets you show proof of registration when asked.

n.1: The reason is to show proof, not to avoid losing it.
n.2: Carrying it is not about updating the card.
n.3: The card does not count towards wages.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An inspector asks an operative to show evidence of water hygiene registration. The operative should:
o: promise to email a copy over to them later
point to a nearby colleague who holds one
explain that the card is back at the office
produce their valid card there and then
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: You should be able to produce your valid card on request.

n.0: A promise to email later is not producing the card.
n.1: Another person's card does not cover you.
n.2: An explanation is not the same as showing the card.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An expired card carried on site is:
o: not acceptable proof of current registration
still valid provided it looks undamaged
acceptable for another three months after expiry
fine as long as the work is being supervised
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: An expired card does not prove current registration.

n.1: Appearance does not make an expired card valid.
n.2: There is no extra grace period making it valid.
n.3: Supervision does not make an expired card acceptable.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which statement about carrying the card is correct?
o: any old version of the card will be fine
the card should be valid and with you at work
the card can simply stay in the site office
a verbal claim of holding one is enough
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: You should carry a valid, in-date card at work.

n.0: An old or expired version is not acceptable.
n.2: The card should be with you, not left in the office.
n.3: A verbal claim is not proof; the card is needed.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An operative has left their valid card in another jacket at home. Best practice is that they:
o: bring a valid card before restricted work
carry on since they know they have passed
borrow a workmate's card just for the day
use last year's expired card for the shift
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The valid card should be brought before restricted work.

n.1: Knowing you passed is not the same as carrying the card.
n.2: You cannot use someone else's card.
n.3: An expired card cannot be used for the work.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Carrying a valid card matters because it allows others to:
o: see exactly how long you have been employed
check which depot you are normally based at
confirm you are registered to do the work
record the amount of overtime for the week
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: The card lets others confirm you are registered.

n.0: The card does not show length of employment.
n.1: The card is not a record of your base depot.
n.3: The card is not used to record overtime.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: If asked, a carded operative should be able to:
o: recite the card number from memory only
show a receipt for the assessment fee paid
give the name of the trainer who taught them
show a current, in-date water hygiene card
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: You should be able to show a current, valid card.

n.0: Reciting a number is not showing the card.
n.1: A payment receipt is not the card itself.
n.2: A trainer's name is not proof of registration.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A card that is still within its three-year period is described as:
o: provisional until a manager finally signs it
valid and acceptable to carry on site
temporary until the very next renewal date
informal proof that always needs backing up
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A card within its three years is valid to carry.

n.0: A manager's signature is not needed for validity.
n.2: It is valid, not merely temporary, within the period.
n.3: It is formal, valid proof within the period.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: During an audit, several operatives cannot produce a valid card. The correct action is that they:
o: keep working and sort the cards out later on
swap cards around so each person shows one
stop restricted work until a valid card is shown
carry on if the job is very nearly finished
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Restricted work should stop until a valid card is produced.

n.0: Restricted work should not continue without a valid card.
n.1: Swapping cards is not acceptable or honest.
n.3: Being nearly finished does not allow uncarded work.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which of the following is a Restricted Operation?
o: painting the railings at a depot car park
filing paperwork in the main site office
washing a company van out on the yard
working inside a service reservoir
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Working inside a service reservoir can affect water quality, so it is restricted.

n.0: Painting depot railings does not affect water quality.
n.1: Office paperwork is not a restricted operation.
n.2: Washing a van is not a restricted operation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A task counts as a Restricted Operation when it could:
o: affect the general appearance of the work site
affect the delivery time of site materials
affect the quality of the public water supply
affect the noise levels near nearby homes
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A task is restricted when it could affect public water quality.

n.0: Restriction is about water quality, not appearance.
n.1: Restriction is about water quality, not deliveries.
n.3: Restriction is about water quality, not noise.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which activity would normally be a Restricted Operation?
o: digging a trench well away from any main
connecting a new pipe into a live water main
unloading fittings from a delivery lorry
setting out traffic cones around the works
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Connecting into a live main can affect water quality, so it is restricted.

n.0: A trench away from mains is not a restricted operation.
n.2: Unloading fittings is not itself a restricted operation.
n.3: Setting out cones is not a restricted operation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: An operative will be handling components that touch drinking water. This work is:
o: unrestricted because it is only small parts
exempt because the components are all new
a Restricted Operation needing a valid card
restricted only if the main is a large one
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Handling parts that touch drinking water is restricted.

n.0: Small parts touching water are still restricted.
n.1: New components are not exempt from restriction.
n.3: Restriction does not depend on the main's size.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which of these is least likely to be a Restricted Operation?
o: swabbing the inside of a clean water main
fitting a new valve on the supply network
entering a clean water storage tank to work
mowing grass at a depot well away from mains
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Mowing grass away from mains does not affect water quality.

n.0: Swabbing a main can affect water quality, so it is restricted.
n.1: Fitting a valve on the network is a restricted operation.
n.2: Entering a clean water tank is a restricted operation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Work on the clean water network is restricted mainly because it can:
o: increase the energy that is used at the pumps
let contamination into water that people drink
change the colour of the pipe's outer coating
add to the amount of traffic around the site
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Such work can let contamination into drinking water.

n.0: Restriction is about contamination, not pump energy.
n.2: Restriction is about water quality, not pipe coating.
n.3: Restriction is about water quality, not traffic.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which of these best describes a Restricted Operation?
o: any task carried out near a water company site
any task that uses water company owned tools
any task that could contaminate the public supply
any task done during normal daytime working hours
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: A Restricted Operation is any task that could contaminate the supply.

n.0: Being near a site does not by itself make work restricted.
n.1: Using company tools does not define a restricted operation.
n.3: The time of day does not define a restricted operation.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: A worker is asked to disinfect and swab a new length of main before use. This is:
o: general labouring that needs no card at all
restricted work that needs a valid card
office work outside the scope of the scheme
restricted only if it is carried out after dark
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Disinfecting and swabbing a main is restricted work.

n.0: This directly affects water quality, so a card is needed.
n.2: It is hands-on work on the main, within the scheme.
n.3: Restriction does not depend on the time of day.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Handling pipes, fittings or tools that will touch potable water is:
o: treated as a Restricted Operation
treated as ordinary construction site work
considered outside the scope of the scheme
only restricted for brand new employees
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Handling items that touch potable water is a Restricted Operation.

n.1: It is not ordinary construction work under this scheme.
n.2: It is within the scope of the scheme.
n.3: Restriction applies to everyone, not just new staff.

The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.q: Which statement about Restricted Operations is correct?
o: jobs that can affect drinking water quality
they are jobs done only at the treatment works
they are jobs that always need two operatives
they are jobs that are limited to daytime hours
The Water Hygiene Card & Scheme.w: Restricted Operations are jobs that can affect drinking water quality.

n.1: They are not limited to the treatment works.
n.2: They are not defined by needing two people.
n.3: They are not defined by being daytime only.
